# Piwi Dashboard

> Free, self-hosted, zero telemetry. CI throws away every report it makes. Piwi keeps them, then groups the failures by root cause, scores the flaky tests, and finds the locator you should have used.

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/guide/getting-started -->

# Getting started

Piwi is a **server plus a Playwright reporter**. The reporter runs inside `npx playwright test` and sends the results
to the server, which keeps every run with its traces and renders the dashboard. Three steps set up both.
[What Piwi does](./what-piwi-does) says what the server does with those runs: its five jobs, and the pieces around it.
New to the vocabulary (*run*, *test case*, *execution*, *cluster*)? [Core concepts](./core-concepts) defines each term the
dashboard uses.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/moving-parts.svg" alt="The reporter, inside a Playwright run on your machine or in CI, streams results and uploads traces to the Piwi server, which keeps them in its database and artifact storage and serves the dashboard to your browser">
  <figcaption>The same reporter runs locally and in CI; one server keeps every run.</figcaption>
</figure>

## 1. Run the dashboard

The dashboard is one Node process. Pick the way to run it that fits:

| Path | Best for | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| [Desktop app](/features/desktop) | One developer running Playwright locally, with no server at all | An installer; the runtime is bundled, so no Docker and no Node. Windows x64, Apple-silicon macOS and Linux x86-64; the installers are not code-signed, so the first launch needs a click-through |
| Docker *(below)* | A shared instance for a team, or anything long-lived | Docker; about 300 MB RAM, 1 vCPU, `linux/amd64` or `linux/arm64`, and disk for the traces ([sizing](/operate/deployment#resource-requirements)) |
| [`npx @piwitests/server`](/operate/deployment#npm-npx-quick-local-run) | A quick local run without Docker | Node.js 22 or later; `.data/` in the current directory |
| [One-click deploy](/operate/one-click-deploy) | A shared instance with no server of your own | An account on the host, and what it charges |

With Docker:

::: code-group

```sh [Linux / macOS]
docker pull phenx/piwitests-server:latest
mkdir -p .data && sudo chown -R 1001:1001 .data # the container runs as non-root UID 1001
# Reachable from this machine only: with authentication off, anyone who reaches the port is an administrator.
# Publish it on every interface (-p 3000:3000) only once authentication is on.
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 -v $(pwd)/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

```ps1 [Windows (PowerShell)]
docker pull phenx/piwitests-server:latest
# Reachable from this machine only: with authentication off, anyone who reaches the port is an administrator.
# Publish it on every interface (-p 3000:3000) only once authentication is on.
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 -v ${PWD}/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

:::

The dashboard answers at `http://localhost:3000`. On Linux hosts the container runs as the non-root UID 1001, which is
why the snippet creates `.data` with the right owner; see
[Permission issues with volumes](/operate/deployment#permission-issues-with-volumes) if the container cannot write to
it. [Deployment](/operate/deployment) covers Docker Compose, PostgreSQL and Kubernetes.

The desktop app installs from the latest release. [Piwi Runner](/features/piwi-runner), below it, is not a dashboard:
it runs the tests a team instance asks for, on a machine without the desktop app, which takes the same requests.

- Piwi Desktop: The dashboard on your computer, with your local runs. On the [latest release](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/releases/latest): Windows x64, per user (.exe): `Piwi-Desktop_x64-setup.exe`; Windows x64, per machine (.msi): `Piwi-Desktop_x64.msi`; macOS, Apple silicon (.dmg): `Piwi-Desktop_aarch64.dmg`; Linux x86-64, any distribution (.AppImage): `Piwi-Desktop_amd64.AppImage`; Debian, Ubuntu, x86-64 (.deb): `Piwi-Desktop_amd64.deb`; Fedora, RHEL, x86-64 (.rpm): `Piwi-Desktop_x86_64.rpm`.
- Piwi Runner: Runs the tests a team instance asks for, without the dashboard. Not needed beside the desktop app, which takes the same requests. On the [latest release](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/releases/latest): Windows x64, per user (.exe): `Piwi-Runner_x64-setup.exe`; Windows x64, per machine (.msi): `Piwi-Runner_x64.msi`; macOS, Apple silicon (.dmg): `Piwi-Runner_aarch64.dmg`; Linux x86-64, any distribution (.AppImage): `Piwi-Runner_amd64.AppImage`; Debian, Ubuntu, x86-64 (.deb): `Piwi-Runner_amd64.deb`; Fedora, RHEL, x86-64 (.rpm): `Piwi-Runner_x86_64.rpm`.

With the desktop app, keep it running: a reporter with no server configured finds it by itself. Its URL and access
token, for when you need them, are in its **Settings → Desktop app** under **Send results to this app**.

Your test project needs Node.js 22 or later for the reporter ([Reporter](./reporter#installation)), however you run the
dashboard. Want to look around first? The [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) runs in your browser on seeded data.

## 2. Connect your suite

The dashboard's connect wizard, on **Home** while it has no project and on **Settings → Connect a suite** after, builds every snippet below
from your project name and its own URL, and offers three ways to the same setup: one command, a prompt for a coding
agent, or the steps by hand.
Each ends in [`wrapConfig`](./reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig) around your config and the
[capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures) in your specs: the reporter entry alone keeps your runs, and those two add the
failure screenshots and traces, the network and console capture, and locator healing.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/home-empty-connect-waiting.png" alt="The connect wizard on an instance with no project: the project name, the three ways to connect (one command, coding agent, by hand) with the init command, the fixtures import and the test command, and a status line waiting for the first run">
  <figcaption>The connect wizard, waiting for the first run.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Fast path: one command

From your Playwright project, one command installs the reporter, wraps your `playwright.config`, creates the
[capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures) file and records the connection in `.env.example`:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter init --server-url http://localhost:3000 --project my-project
```

It prints one line per step, `+` for a file it created, `~` for one it changed, `=` for one already set, `!` for a
step left to you:

```txt
Piwi setup for "my-project":

  ~ [updated] dependency — Installed @piwitests/reporter
  ~ [updated] config playwright.config.ts — Wrapped defineConfig(...) with wrapConfig(...) and added the import
  + [created] fixtures tests/fixtures.ts — Created capture fixtures — import `test` from here in your specs
  ~ [updated] env .env.example — Recorded PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL, PIWI_API_KEY
  + [created] skill:investigate-failure .claude/skills/investigate-failure/SKILL.md — installed skill
  + [created] skill:apply-locator-healing .claude/skills/apply-locator-healing/SKILL.md — installed skill
  + [created] skill:stabilize-flaky-tests .claude/skills/stabilize-flaky-tests/SKILL.md — installed skill
  + [created] skill:run-the-right-tests .claude/skills/run-the-right-tests/SKILL.md — installed skill
  + [created] skill:write-the-missing-test .claude/skills/write-the-missing-test/SKILL.md — installed skill
  + [created] skill:fix-a-reported-bug .claude/skills/fix-a-reported-bug/SKILL.md — installed skill

Next:
  • If your dashboard has authentication on, create an API key (Settings → Account → API keys) and put it in .env as PIWI_API_KEY: the reporter reads it from the .env next to your Playwright config. Keep .env out of git; in CI, set PIWI_API_KEY as a secret.
  • In your specs, import `test` (and `expect`) from your fixtures file instead of `@playwright/test`.
  • Run `npx playwright test` — the run should appear at http://localhost:3000.
  • For a machine-readable check, set PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE=piwi-run.json and read runUrl from that file after the run.
```

Every step is idempotent, so it is safe to re-run. When `init` finds a config shape it will not rewrite, or a fixtures
file that already exists, it reports that step as `manual` with the exact change to make instead of touching the file.
Pass `--dry-run` to preview, or `--json` for a machine-readable plan that a coding agent can follow to finish the manual
steps. `init` also adds the [Piwi agent skills](/features/agent-skills) to the project. See
`npx @piwitests/reporter init --help` for all options.

> The package is `@piwitests/reporter` and its command is `piwi`. Invoke it through the package name,
> `npx @piwitests/reporter <command>`, so npx resolves this package: `npx piwi` would fetch an unrelated `piwi`
> package from npm. Once the reporter is a dependency of your project, `npx piwi <command>` works too.

Then import `test` from the fixtures file in your specs, the one change `init` leaves to you:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from './fixtures'
```

A coding agent can do both: the **Coding agent** path on **Connect a suite** gives it a prompt that runs `init --json`, finishes
the steps it reports as `manual` and moves the specs onto the fixtures.

If authentication is on, pass an [API key](/operate/api-keys#using-the-api-key-in-the-reporter) as `PIWI_API_KEY`; **Connect a suite** creates one in place. When
developers run the [desktop app](/features/desktop) and CI reports to a shared dashboard, add `--desktop-app prefer`:
[local runs then land in the app](./reporter#local-runs-to-the-desktop-app-ci-to-a-team-server). To wire the reporter
in by hand, or to send one run without editing your config, see [Reporter](./reporter).

## 3. Run your tests

```bash
npx playwright test
```

The run streams into the dashboard while it executes, and the reporter prints a `View run:` link at the end. Open it.

While it runs, the wizard's status line changes from *Waiting for the first run* to the run reporting, with a link to watch it:

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/home-empty-connect-reporting.png" alt="The wizard's status line: a run of checkout is reporting now, with a Watch it link">
  <figcaption>The checkpoint: your first run is reporting.</figcaption>
</figure>

If nothing shows up, read the first lines the reporter prints. This one means it found no server to report to:

```txt
[Piwi Dashboard] Not enabled — set PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL or serverUrl to enable.
```

Set `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, in the environment or the `.env` next to your Playwright config, or rerun `init` with
`--server-url`. From WSL, a dev container or another machine, the URL is the dashboard's address as that machine
reaches it, not `localhost`.

The home page and a project's page leave out partial runs (a run of a few files) until you change their **Filters**,
and a project's page leaves out branches other than the default one too. The **Filters** block counts the runs it
hides, with **Include partial runs** and **Show all branches** to bring them back. Your own runs from outside CI (with
sign-in off, every run that did not come from CI) stay listed whatever these two filters say, marked with what they
would have hidden ("Yours · partial run", "Yours · feature/x"), and not counted among the hidden runs; the charts and
pass rates still follow the filters.

In CI nothing Piwi-specific is needed: the same reporter runs inside `npx playwright test`, pointed at your instance
with `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and `PIWI_API_KEY`. [CI & sharding](./ci) has the pipeline examples.

## Your first failure

When a test fails, its execution page opens on what happened, the most likely cause and the next step, with the
trace, screenshots and logs underneath. [Your first failure, explained](./first-failure) walks through one failing
test from its headline to its evidence.

## Where you write the tests

The dashboard is where you read results. Other tools work where you write the tests, in your editor and in your browser:

- **[Editor extensions](/features/editors)**: the Piwi extension for VS Code and the Piwi plugin for the JetBrains IDEs
  with the LSP API (WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate, Rider). They record a test at the cursor in a browser your
  project's own Playwright opens, run it and stop it at the editor's breakpoints, and show the latest CI failures at
  the lines that failed, with the replacement locator as a quick fix.
- **[Piwi Picker](/features/extension)**: a Chrome, Edge and Firefox extension that picks ranked Playwright locators
  from the page you are looking at and records a flow as a runnable spec. It works with no instance; paired with the
  editor, it sends a recording to the cursor and follows the editor's runs in its Runs window.

[Write, run and fix a test](/features/write-run-fix) takes a test from an empty spec to a passing run, and names the
tool for each step.

# Your first failure, explained

You've landed your first run ([Getting started](./getting-started)) and one test is red. This page walks through reading it. Piwi lays a failing execution out **diagnosis-first**, in one column read top to bottom: *what* broke, *why*, *what to do next*, then the evidence.

Open the failing test from the run page (click its row) to reach its **execution page**.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/failure-headline.png" alt="A failing execution's situation block: the identity line, the headline, the line saying since when it fails, Most likely with its strength, the Next step with the patch to apply, and the Cluster line">
  <figcaption>The situation block: what broke, since when, why, what to do next, and the cluster it belongs to.</figcaption>
</figure>

The top of the page is one **situation block**. Above its heading, a small **identity** line carries the status, the test (`tests/checkout/checkout.spec.ts:9 › Checkout › should complete checkout with credit card`), marks such as `@fixme` or `@slow`, and whether it is [quarantined](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out). The lines below it are the rest of this page, in order.

## 1. The headline: what broke

The heading is a plain-English sentence built from the Playwright error, before you read a word of the raw error itself:

> `Test timed out after 30 s while clicking getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })`

It is read from the action or matcher, the locator, the expected and received values and the timeout; an unknown error shape falls back to the error's first line. A failure in a hook or fixture says where it happened (`In beforeEach: …`), and an `expect` you gave a message leads with it (`"cart shows the item" failed: …`). The verbatim error is one click away under **Raw error**: Piwi never rewrites it, it only leads with a readable summary. The same headline names the test on the run page, in [alerts](/features/notifications), in the [pull-request comment](/features/pr-feedback), in the MCP tools and in your terminal.

A smaller line under the headline says since when it fails, on which commit and by whom, and whether it **still fails**:

> *New regression since a1b2c3d by Alice Chen, 1 day ago · Not the latest Chromium execution: failed again in run #1 and run #2, 51 minutes ago · Open the latest*

*Latest execution of this test* means nothing ran it since; otherwise the line says what the newer runs did (failed again, with another error, or passed) and **Open the latest** goes to the newest execution. Only the same Playwright project counts, and the line names it when another project ran later: a Firefox pass does not clear a Chromium failure. An exceptional case (a new regression, a newly flaky test, an infrastructure failure) leads the line. A test that passed on retry reads *Passed on retry* in its status and leads with its failed attempt's error, and the line says which attempt failed (*Failed on attempt 1, passed on attempt 2*), with a link to it.

## 2. Most likely: why

Under the headline, the **Most likely** line gives one explanation. It is built from **[clues](/features/evidence#clues)**: deterministic, rule-based findings correlated from the evidence, with *no model involved*. When the clues match a known pattern (some patterns need only one clue), the line is a [story](./concepts#story), one sentence that chains them:

> *The button "Pay" stayed disabled because POST /api/checkout/quote was still in flight (28.4 s); the console said so 7.8 s before the click gave up.*

A strong or medium story leads; otherwise the cluster's [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) may, by one rule on
this page and the cluster page ([which one leads](/reference/clues#most-likely)). The line carries a strength
(*Strong*, *Medium* or *Weak*, or the diagnosis's confidence) and how many clues **agree**; **All clues** lists every
clue, each with a **citation**: click it and the page jumps to the proof. With no clue and no diagnosis, the line is
absent.

A test that did not run gets its reason here instead: the test that blocked it, or where the run stopped (*The run reached its maximum number of failures (3 failed) and stopped before this test started*), with a meta line when Playwright reported it.

## 3. Next: what to do

The **Next** line names the one thing to do, chosen for you rather than offered as a menu: apply the diagnosed patch,
replace the [broken locator](/features/locator-healing), reproduce it, re-run in CI, mark the cluster resolved, or,
for a test that did not run, open what blocked it. A code change shows on the line itself, with where it comes from
and a button that copies it (**Copy apply command** or **Copy locator**); the **···** menu copies the command that
re-runs this test. How the step is chosen and every action it offers: [The next step](/features/fix-plans#the-next-step).

## 4. The cluster: who else, and the ticket

The **Cluster** line names the [failure cluster](/features/failure-clusters) the failure joins and how many other tests of the run share it, with its triage status, whether an earlier fix did not hold, and who owns the test. It ends with the cluster's [issue](/features/issue-tracking) and its status, or offers to create or link one.

With [coverage](/features/server-coverage), a **What changed** line counts the changed lines the test ran and names the first of its [suspect lines](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines).

The **History** line shows this test's recent executions as one strip in the outcome colors, this one ringed, with how long it has been failing and the run it last passed in. Each square opens its execution; the **Test history** link at the top of the page opens the test's own page, its [history across runs](/features/evidence#the-test-case-page).

The block closes on a **facts** line, one size smaller: the failing file and line (open it in your IDE), browser and viewport, duration against its average, the attempts, the branch, and the CI build. A **Details** popover holds the rest, and **Raw error** shows the verbatim error with a **Copy failure** action.

## 5. The evidence: see it

One **evidence card** with tabs holds everything captured, opening on the tab that best shows the failure
([which one](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first)); a click on any citation switches tabs for you. The one
to know first is **Timeline**: it places the test's steps, console entries, network requests and backend logs on a single clock and marks the **moment of failure**, so "console (1) / network (3)" becomes *what the app was doing when the test gave up*. **Screen** holds the failure screenshot, the visual diff against the [last green run](/features/run-changes#one-execution-s-baseline), and the failure-time page state; **Source** shows the test source as a real call stack, so a failure inside a helper shows the helper. Each tab is described on [Failure evidence](/features/evidence).

::: tip Most of this needs one file
The error, trace, headline and clustering work with the reporter alone, and an uploaded trace recovers the console, network and failure-time snapshot. Web Vitals, page state and locator healing come from the [capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures), one file in your test setup. A tab that needs them and never received any data is left out, and until you decide on the fixtures one footer line names what they would add.
:::

## 6. More ways to fix

Right above the evidence, **[More ways to fix](/features/fix-plans#more-ways-to-fix)** is one line with a button for
every *other* way to fix, verify or reproduce: a [replacement locator](/features/locator-healing), the
[AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) and its validated patch, verify, reproduce and bisect, fixed before, the tests it
blocked. A button opens its section in a side panel beside the page, and a **Next** action that works in a section,
such as **Full patch**, opens it.

## You're not reading it alone

This execution is one member of a **[failure cluster](/features/failure-clusters)**: Piwi groups every test that failed for the same reason, so forty red tests become three problems you triage once. Once a later run passes every test it covers, the cluster records [whether the fix held](/features/failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work).

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › should complete checkout with credit card](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-run-cases/37): The Pay click times out: the situation block says since when, ties it to the quote request still in flight, and offers the diagnosed patch.

# Core concepts

Piwi reuses Playwright's vocabulary where it can, but a dashboard that keeps history needs a few distinctions
Playwright doesn't have to make, most importantly between *a test* and *one run of that test*. This page names the
dozen words a first run meets; the [Glossary](./concepts) defines every word the docs and the dashboard use, each
under the anchor other pages link.

## The object model

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/data-model-grid.svg" alt="A project as a grid: test runs are columns, test cases are rows, and each cell holds that test case's executions in that run; one failure cluster spans failed executions of two test cases across two runs">
  <figcaption>A project holds one suite's results. A failure cluster groups executions, not test cases: it can span several of each.</figcaption>
</figure>

Read it in two directions:

- **Down**: "what happened in this run?" A run holds executions; each execution points at the test it is an attempt
  of.
- **Across**: "how has this test behaved?" A test case holds every execution of itself, in every run, over time.
  That's the axis flakiness, pass rate and duration trends are computed on.

## The words a first run meets

- **[Project](./concepts#project)**: one suite's results, created the first time results arrive under a new
  `projectName`.
- **[Test run](./concepts#test-run)**: everything one `npx playwright test` invocation produced; one CI pipeline's
  shards make one run.
- **[Test case](./concepts#test-case)**: a test's identity across time (file, `describe` path and title), the same on
  every browser. "This test is flaky" is about a test case.
- **[Execution](./concepts#execution)**: one attempt of one test case, in one run, on one browser. A retry is an
  execution of its own.
- **[Pass rate](./concepts#pass-rate)** and **[flaky rate](./concepts#flaky-rate)**: the share of a test's results
  that passed, and that passed only on a retry.
- **[Baseline](./concepts#baseline-last-green-run)**: the earlier run a run is compared with to answer "what
  changed?", by default the last passing one.
- **[New regression, newly flaky](./concepts#new-regression-newly-flaky)**: what a test did differently from the
  baseline.
- **[Environment](./concepts#environment)**: a free-text label on a run (`staging`, `production`) that analysis can be
  narrowed to.
- **[Failure cluster](./concepts#error-fingerprint-failure-cluster)**: the failed executions that share an error
  fingerprint, triaged once.
- **[Cluster state](./concepts#cluster-state)**: where a cluster stands, in one sentence (*still failing*, *stopped
  failing*, *regressed*).
- **[Flakiness score](./concepts#flakiness-score)**: how flaky a test is over its history, which ranks the flaky
  tests.
- **[Tags & ownership](./concepts#tags-ownership)**: the tags and the owner a test declares, which filter the views
  and route its failures.

## Where each concept lives in the UI

| Concept | URL | Docs |
|---|---|---|
| Project | `/projects/:id` | [UI overview](/features/ui-overview#project-detail) |
| Test run | `/test-runs/:id` | [UI overview](/features/ui-overview#test-run-detail) |
| Test case | `/test-cases/:id` | [Failure evidence](/features/evidence#the-test-case-page) |
| Execution | `/test-run-cases/:id` | [Failure evidence](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) |
| Failure cluster | `/failure-clusters/:id` | [Failure clusters](/features/failure-clusters) |
| Cross-project view | `/analytics` | [Analytics](/features/analytics) |
| Quality report | *Quality report* on `/analytics` and `/projects/:id` | [Quality reports](/features/quality-reports) |
| Report schedule, report snapshot | `/reports`, `/reports/:id` | [Quality reports](/features/quality-reports#report-schedules) |

# Reporter

The `@piwitests/reporter` package is a Playwright reporter that uploads test results, traces, attachments and reports
to the dashboard while your tests run. [Getting started](./getting-started#fast-path-one-command) sets it up with one
command, `npx @piwitests/reporter init`; this page covers manual setup.

## Installation

```bash
npm install --save-dev @piwitests/reporter
```

It needs `@playwright/test` 1.59 or later and Node.js 22 or later, or [Bun](./bun). A feature needing a later
Playwright names the version on its page.

### Try it without editing your config

Playwright's `--add-reporter` (1.63 or later) appends this reporter to your config's reporters, where `--reporter` replaces them, so one run can go to a dashboard without a config edit. Most reporter options have a `PIWI_*` [environment variable](/reference/reporter-options):

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL=http://localhost:3000 PIWI_API_KEY=your-api-key PIWI_PROJECT_NAME=my-project npx playwright test --add-reporter @piwitests/reporter
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL='http://localhost:3000'; $env:PIWI_API_KEY='your-api-key'; $env:PIWI_PROJECT_NAME='my-project'; npx playwright test --add-reporter @piwitests/reporter
```

:::

This is a trial path: you get results and your configured traces and screenshots, not the [capture fixtures](#capture-fixtures) or [`wrapConfig`](#installing-via-wrapconfig)'s capture defaults. [`piwi run`](/reference/cli#select-run) appends it the same way when the config has no Piwi reporter.

## Installing via wrapConfig

`wrapConfig` wraps your whole config in one call: it injects the reporter, chains Piwi's [global setup](#global-setup-phase), and defaults the failure-evidence capture options. It is the recommended setup, written by `npx @piwitests/reporter init` and the dashboard's **Connect a suite** page.

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test'
import { wrapConfig } from '@piwitests/reporter'

export default wrapConfig(
  defineConfig({
    testDir: './tests',
    // no `screenshot` / `trace` needed: wrapConfig fills them in
  }),
  {
    serverUrl: process.env.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL || 'http://localhost:3000',
    projectName: 'my-project',
  },
)
```

The first argument is your Playwright config; the second is the [Piwi options](#configuration-options). An option in
the config wins over its `PIWI_*` variable, so the server URL reads `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` first, as `init` writes it: a
CI job that sets the variable reports there. `wrapConfig` also:

- Sets `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` and `trace: 'retain-on-failure'` on the **top-level** `use` block when unset (a value you set, `'off'` included, and per-project `use` blocks are kept). They unlock the DOM snapshot, full call stack, full network with bodies and the visual diff **without** the capture fixtures. The trace records no ARIA snapshots, which slow each action on a large page: [`defaultCapture`](/reference/reporter-options#defaultcapture) gives their cost and how to record them. Opt out with `defaultCapture: false` (or `PIWI_DEFAULT_CAPTURE=false`); the reporter logs one line at the start of the run naming what it defaulted.
- Forwards `failOnFlakyTests` into Playwright's native config so a flaky-only run exits non-zero locally.
- Forwards the `PIWI_*` variables into the global setup process, so registering the run uses the reporter's server and credentials.

## Basic configuration

When a config cannot be wrapped, add the bare reporter entry and the capture options `wrapConfig` would set. It
gives up the rest of `wrapConfig`: the run appears only when the first test starts unless you add the
[global setup](#global-setup-phase) yourself, and `failOnFlakyTests` does not reach Playwright.

```typescript
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test'

export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['list'],
    ['@piwitests/reporter', {
      serverUrl: process.env.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL || 'http://localhost:3000',
      projectName: 'my-project',
    }],
  ],
  use: {
    trace: 'retain-on-failure',
    screenshot: 'only-on-failure',
    video: 'retain-on-failure', // optional: wrapConfig does not set it
  },
})
```

The `use` block is Playwright's: the reporter uploads what Playwright records and what a test attaches with `testInfo.attach()`. Videos can be large: pair `retain-on-failure` with [storage cleanup](/operate/storage#storage-management).

::: tip You don't also need Playwright's `html` reporter
The dashboard is complete without it: running it alongside only repeats end-of-run work (and opens a browser on a local failure). Keep it for the standalone report, which Piwi uploads (`uploadReport`).
:::

<a id="performance-metrics-web-vitals"></a>

## Capture fixtures

The reporter works without test-code changes. The **capture fixtures** add network timing, Web Vitals, console
capture, failure-time ARIA snapshots and the locator snapshots behind [locator healing](/features/locator-healing):
[Capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures) covers setup, what each records and its cost.

## Configuration options

Options go in the reporter's entry in `playwright.config.ts` or `wrapConfig`'s second argument. Most can also be
set with a `PIWI_*` environment variable, which an option in the config overrides, except `PIWI_DESKTOP_APP` and,
outside `wrapConfig`, `PIWI_VERBOSE`, which override the option. `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`,
`PIWI_API_KEY` and `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME` also come from the config folder's
[`.env`](/reference/reporter-options#values-from-env), below the environment. [Reporter options](/reference/reporter-options)
lists every option with its default and variable, and [Test metadata](/reference/test-metadata) what the reporter
records on its own, [errors outside the tests](/reference/test-metadata#errors-outside-the-tests),
[what each test printed](/reference/test-metadata#test-output) and [hooks](/reference/test-metadata#hooks) included.

### Finding the desktop app automatically

If nothing sets a server (no URL or API key in the config, the environment or that `.env`), the reporter
uploads to the [desktop app](/features/desktop) on the same machine, which publishes its loopback URL and access token
to `~/.piwi/desktop.json` (`%USERPROFILE%\.piwi\desktop.json` on Windows) while it runs. `PIWI_DESKTOP_CONFIG`
overrides the path. A CI job or a project pointed elsewhere is never redirected unless it opts in below.

The token goes only to a server that proves it holds it: before each request that carries it, the reporter
sends a one-time challenge to `/api/health` and checks the answer's proof. With no proof, or the wrong one, no
token is sent, nothing is uploaded and the reporter says so; an app before 0.56 gives none: update it.
A run the app starts itself (a reproduction or flake lab) exports `PIWI_DESKTOP_KEY=1` beside `PIWI_API_KEY`, marking
the key as the app's, as does a `PIWI_API_KEY` equal to the token in `desktop.json`, while that file exists, also after a crash (the app
deletes it on a clean quit). Any other key is sent as before.

### Local runs to the desktop app, CI to a team server

With `desktopApp: 'prefer'`, a run not on CI lands in the desktop app whenever it is running, even with `serverUrl`
set, so local runs stay out of a shared dashboard; CI runs, and local runs with the app closed, go to `serverUrl` with
its credentials. URL and token always move together. A run is on CI when a CI provider's variable is set, or `CI` is
anything but `false` or `0`. `'off'` never uses the app. `PIWI_DESKTOP_APP`
overrides the option: `off` sends one local run to `serverUrl`. `init --desktop-app prefer` writes it.

[Run on my machine](/features/run-on-my-machine#what-leaves-your-machine) runs report to the instance that asked.

## Sharding

Playwright's `--shard` jobs merge into one dashboard run when every shard uses the same
`projectName`. `runLabel` is the manual override when your CI isn't detected. See
[CI & sharding](./ci#sharding).

## Live streaming

The reporter streams results as tests complete: the run appears when the suite starts, each test's trace and
attachments upload when it finishes (`liveFileUploads`), and the run's page shows each running test's step. A
test's final failed attempt prints its headline and a link right away; at the end the reporter prints `View run: <url>`
(see [CI → Getting the run URL back out](./ci#getting-the-run-url-back-out-of-ci)). A server without streaming support
gets the batch upload instead. `streamingBatchSize` and `streamingBatchDelay` set how often results are sent.

### Disabling streaming

`streaming: false` sends all results at the end of the run, then each test's files and each report in their own request.

## Global setup phase

A run appears on the dashboard when the first test starts. If your config has a `globalSetup` step
(seeding, authenticating, building), register the run before it so the dashboard shows an **initializing** state during
setup. `wrapConfig` does this for you; otherwise export `createGlobalSetup` from the `globalSetup` file
(`globalSetup: './global-setup.ts'`); it reads its options from the reporter entry:

```typescript
// global-setup.ts
import { createGlobalSetup } from '@piwitests/reporter'

export default createGlobalSetup({}, async (config) => {
  // your own setup, run after registration
})
```

Registration is best-effort: with the server unreachable, the run is created when tests begin. Playwright's UI mode
(`--ui`) skips registration, since it swaps the reporter out, as does `streaming: false`, whose run the dashboard
receives in one batch at its end; your own setup still runs.

## Multiple reports

Each report attached to a run gets its own dashboard button.

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['list'],
    ['html', { outputFolder: 'playwright-report', open: 'never' }],
    ['monocart-reporter', { name: 'My Tests', outputFile: 'monocart-report/index.html' }],
    ['blob'],
    ['@piwitests/reporter', {
      serverUrl: process.env.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL || 'http://localhost:3000',
      projectName: 'my-project',
      reports: [
        { type: 'html' },
        { type: 'monocart' },
        { type: 'blob', dir: 'blob-report', label: 'Blob archive' },
      ],
    }],
  ],
})
```

`html` (the html reporter's folder, `playwright-report/` by default) and `monocart` (`monocart-report/`) open in a new
tab; `blob` (`blob-report/`) downloads as an archive. Any other type is accepted, read from `dir` or else
`<type>-report/`. Reports upload compressed; one over the dashboard's upload limit
([`PIWI_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`](/reference/configuration#ingest-limits), 500 MB by default) is left out alone.

## With authentication enabled

With authentication on, the reporter needs a credential: an API key in `PIWI_API_KEY` or the `apiKey` option, or a
username and password. [API keys → Using the API key in the reporter](/operate/api-keys#using-the-api-key-in-the-reporter)
covers both, and where to keep them.

## Troubleshooting

**No traces or screenshots.** Playwright records neither by default. Set `trace` and `screenshot` in `use`, or install
through [`wrapConfig`](#installing-via-wrapconfig).

**No network, Web Vitals, console or locator data.** Every spec must import `test` from your fixtures file, not
`@playwright/test`, and `collectPerformanceMetrics` must not be `false`; see
[Capture fixtures → Troubleshooting](./capture-fixtures#troubleshooting).

**Connection errors.** Check that `serverUrl` answers from where the tests run; `PIWI_VERBOSE=true` logs every
request. A run the reporter could not deliver (dashboard down, no credential, a sign-in page answering in its place)
is saved locally, owner-only, and sent to the same `serverUrl` on the project's next run without traces or
attachments; it never fails the Playwright run. A stream that cannot start while the dashboard is down or busy retries
for the run's life, its events kept within
[`maxStreamBufferBytes`](/reference/reporter-options#maxstreambufferbytes); one starting late says how late. Live events the
dashboard refuses, or has not taken two and a half minutes after they first failed, leave the live stream so the later
ones flow; if test results are among them, the run is sent again as a batch at its end.
[`submitTimeout`](/reference/reporter-options#submittimeout) (15 minutes by default) bounds that end-of-run work, so an
unresponsive dashboard cannot hold the CI job.

# Bun

Playwright 1.65 and later run under [Bun](https://bun.sh) with `bunx --bun playwright test`, and so do the Piwi
reporter and the [capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures): set up as under Node, they send the same results and
attachments, with the limits below.

## Run the suite under Bun

```bash
bunx --bun playwright test
```

`--bun` runs Playwright's command line on Bun, and the workers it starts run on the same Bun. Without it, `bunx`
follows the script's `node` line and the suite runs on Node. Any `playwright test` option goes after it, as with
`npx`.

The setup is the [reporter](./reporter)'s: `wrapConfig` in `playwright.config.ts` and the fixtures in your tests. In a
project Bun installs (a `bun.lock`), `npx @piwitests/reporter init` adds the reporter with `bun add -d`. The Piwi
server is not part of this: it runs on Node, wherever you [deploy](/operate/deployment) it.

## What Piwi records

The reporter sends the run as it does under Node: each test's results, retries, errors and attachments, the traces
and screenshots Playwright records, and the capture fixtures' evidence, streamed as the tests finish.

The [machine panel](/features/cpu-memory-disk#the-panel) measures the runner, its workers and their browsers by role,
as under Node: Piwi tells a worker by the script Playwright runs in it, whichever runtime runs that script.

## Limits

- **The trace has no console.** The trace Playwright records under Bun holds no console messages. The capture
  fixtures still record them; in a project without the fixtures, the console card cannot be recovered from the trace.
- **Call stacks lose their async frames.** Bun's stacks leave out most of the `async` frames Node keeps. Where Piwi
  places something by its stack, such as an error Playwright gives no location or the line that opened a page left
  open, a call made after an `await` in a helper or a package can name no line of your tests.
- **A test's column can be off by one.** Under Bun 1.4.4 and later, Playwright can report a test's column one off
  ([microsoft/playwright#43934](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/43934)), and Piwi keeps the location
  it reports. The file and the line are right, and a test's history does not depend on the column.
- **The worker's event loop busy time is not measured.** Bun's `performance.eventLoopUtilization()` reads no idle
  and no active time, so the panel's **Workers** line leaves it out and its **Not measured** line names it, and each
  execution's Performance tab shows no busy share. The loop's delay and the context switches are measured.
- **No heap after garbage collection.** Bun reports no garbage collections to the performance observer Piwi reads, so
  a worker's heap is never judged [piling up](/features/resource-leaks#what-it-reports), and the panel's **Not
  measured** line names it. Its open file descriptors are still judged.

## Related

- [Reporter](./reporter): the setup, the same under Bun
- [Capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures): what they record
- [CPU, memory & disk](/features/cpu-memory-disk): the machine panel

# Capture fixtures

The [reporter](./reporter) uploads complete test results (statuses, errors, traces, HTML reports) without any change to your test code. The **capture fixtures** are an optional, one-file addition that observes your tests from the inside for slow-endpoint analysis, Web Vitals, console capture, failure-time ARIA snapshots, and [locator healing](/features/locator-healing).

## Setup

**Option A — extend your existing fixtures:**

```ts
// tests/fixtures.ts
import { test as base, expect } from '@playwright/test'
import { piwiFixtures } from '@piwitests/reporter'

export const test = base.extend(piwiFixtures)
export { expect }
```

**Option B — one-line extend with `extendPiwiFixtures`:**

```typescript
// tests/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test'
import { extendPiwiFixtures } from '@piwitests/reporter'

export const test = extendPiwiFixtures(base)
export { expect } from '@playwright/test'
```

Then import `test` from your fixtures file **in every spec**. A spec importing `test` from `@playwright/test` still runs and reports, uncaptured:

```typescript
import { test, expect } from './fixtures'

test('homepage loads', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/')
  // network, console, Web Vitals, and locator data are captured automatically
})
```

That's the entire setup: nothing to start, wrap, or await inside your tests.

## What gets captured

| Data | Captured | Powers |
|------|----------|--------|
| **Network requests**: method, URL, status, duration, start time, content type, for fetch, XHR, document and `other` traffic only (static assets are skipped), and API calls; one that failed without a response keeps its error (`net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`) | per request | [Slow endpoints](/features/slow-tests); [backend log correlation](./backend-logs) via the `X-Piwi-Logs` response header; the [failure timeline](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) |
| **Console entries**: `warning`, `error` and `assert` messages, and each exception the page threw and nothing caught (`pageerror`), with source location and a timestamp (not `console.log`) | as they happen | The console card and the failure timeline on the [execution page](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first); [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) evidence |
| **Web Vitals**: TTFB, DOM Interactive, DOMContentLoaded, Load Complete, First Paint, First Contentful Paint, plus LCP, CLS and INP (Chromium-only) | at test teardown | Web vitals card with color-coded thresholds; [performance trends](/features/slow-tests) |
| **ARIA snapshot** of the final page state: the YAML dump, plus the JSON aria tree on Playwright 1.63 or later; its **screenshot** when Playwright keeps failure screenshots | on failure | Failure evidence on the [execution](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) and cluster pages; [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) context; the JSON tree feeds [locator healing](/features/locator-healing)'s rename matching and the page diff |
| **Browser dialogs**: an `alert`/`confirm`/`prompt`/`beforeunload` dialog's type, message and close time, through Playwright 1.63's `dialogclosed` event | as each dialog closes | A *dialogs* lane on the [failure timeline](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) and a *a dialog was open when the action failed* [clue](/features/evidence#clues) |
| **Locator snapshots**: element attributes, stable-ancestor anchors, same-role position and ranked alternative locators for each element a test proves resolvable, stamped with the call site | for each successful action and each passing web-first assertion (`toBeVisible()`, `toHaveText()`, …) | [Locator healing](/features/locator-healing); when a failing name-based locator (`getByRole`, `getByText`, `getByLabel`, …) matches nothing, a fresh suggestion is attached to the test as a Playwright annotation |
| **Locator pages**: the [page key](/guide/concepts#page-key) each locator call ran on, never a query or raw id | at each locator action and assertion | [Locator pages](/features/locator-usage#pages); **This page** in [Tested elements](/features/tested-elements) |
| **Code reach** (opt-in): executed files | teardown | [Code reach](/features/code-reach) |

::: tip Test source is captured without any fixture
On a failure the reporter also reads the **call stack's in-project source**: the line that threw plus the helpers and page objects above it, as line-numbered snippets. It needs no fixture, and renders as the **Test source** call stack on the [execution](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) and cluster pages.
:::

## With and without the fixtures

Nothing breaks without the fixtures. This is what you give up:

| Dashboard feature | Reporter only | Reporter + fixtures |
|-------------------|:-:|:-:|
| Run history, errors, traces, HTML reports, streaming, sharding, CI/SCM metadata | ✅ | ✅ |
| Failure clustering & flaky-test analytics | ✅ | ✅ |
| AI failure diagnosis | ✅ error + code-diff grounding | ✅ richer evidence: ARIA snapshot, console, network |
| Slow API endpoints table | — | ✅ |
| Web Vitals & performance trends | — | ✅ |
| Console warnings/errors card | — | ✅ |
| Failure-time ARIA snapshot + locator suggestion | — | ✅ |
| Dialogs lane on the failure timeline (Playwright 1.63+) | — | ✅ |
| Locator healing (ranked alternatives panel) | — | ✅ |
| The page each locator was used on | — | ✅ |
| Backend log correlation | — | ✅ with a [backend integration](./backend-logs) |

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/evidence-fixtures-footer-wide.png" alt="The evidence card of a project without the fixtures: the Source tab open and empty, the other tabs dimmed, and the footer says network, console, state and performance are not captured, with Add fixtures and two ways to decline">
  <figcaption>Without the fixtures, the evidence card names what is missing; the line goes once a run brings them.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Where capture works

Capture works however your tests create pages or call an API:

- the standard `page` fixture,
- `browser.newPage()` and `browser.newContext().newPage()`, in your own fixtures too,
- popups (`window.open`) and pages a context opens on its own,
- the `request` fixture, `page.request` and `playwright.request.newContext()`, each call with its
  [backend logs](./backend-logs) and [server coverage](/features/server-coverage).

Semantics worth knowing:

- **`beforeAll` / `afterAll` activity is not captured**: only a test's own activity is attributed to it.
- **Multi-page tests** attribute Web Vitals, the failure ARIA snapshot and screenshot to the most recently active page.
- **[Watch](/features/live-view) shows one page**: the `page` fixture's once it opens, for a test that takes it; else
  the page of the test's latest call, whichever context it is in, and before its first call, or once that page closed,
  the page opened last, a `beforeAll`'s too (reporter 0.73.0 or later,
  [`captureResources`](/reference/reporter-options#what-gets-captured) on). A page of a browser the test launches
  itself never shows.
- **Repeated call sites** (actions in a loop, a page-object method called several times) probe the element once per test; a failed probe is retried on the line's next run.
- **Assertion capture is positive-presence only** — negated (`.not.…`), absence (`toBeHidden`), multi-element (`toHaveCount`) and page-level (`toHaveURL`) assertions never probe.

## Composing with your own fixtures

`piwiFixtures` is a plain Playwright fixtures object, so it composes with your own fixtures in any order:

```typescript
import { test as base, mergeTests } from '@playwright/test'
import { piwiFixtures, extendPiwiFixtures } from '@piwitests/reporter'

// Your fixtures first, capture second
export const test = base.extend<MyFixtures>({ /* ... */ }).extend(piwiFixtures)

// Capture first, your fixtures second
export const test = extendPiwiFixtures(base).extend<MyFixtures>({ /* ... */ })

// Or merge two independent test objects
export const test = mergeTests(myTest, extendPiwiFixtures(base))
```

Two rules:

- The fixture names **`piwiCapture`** and **`piwiResources`** (the [resource ledger](/features/resource-leaks)) are reserved: a fixture of your own with either name replaces Piwi's.
- If you **override `browser` or `page` yourself**, extend with `piwiFixtures` *after* your override so the capture wrapping still applies.

## Cost & opt-outs

Capture never fails or noticeably slows a test:

- Per call site: one DOM read, rarely two, and an ARIA snapshot (500 ms deadline) unless the attributes settle its
  accessible name; one more per new document.
- At teardown: draining in-flight captures is capped at 2 seconds.
- A capture that can't complete (mid-navigation, detached element) is dropped silently; it never throws into your test.
- Capture adds no steps to the report or trace, and errors, step locations and stacks name your own call.

`collectPerformanceMetrics: false` discards all fixture data; `captureLocators: false` turns off only the locator
snapshots and pages, and `capturePageState: false` only the test-end app state (URL, storage key names, cookie flags,
focus, hover, never values). Two opt-in aids for headed local runs, `inspectOnFailure` and `pickLocatorOnFailure`, open
[the failing page for inspection](/features/locator-healing#inspect-the-failing-page-live-local-runs) or
[let you pick a replacement locator](/features/locator-healing#pick-a-replacement-locator-on-the-failing-page-local-runs);
a third, `PIWI_PAUSE_AT` (semicolon-separated `file:line`: `tests/login.spec.ts:42;tests/pages/checkout.page.ts:9`),
is set by an editor on a run it starts, to [pause at its breakpoints](/features/editor-breakpoints).
Set all but `collectPerformanceMetrics` through [`wrapConfig`](./reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig) or their `PIWI_*`
variable: the test workers never see a plain reporter entry's options.

## Green page sampling on pass

For the [page diff](/features/evidence#page-diff), the fixtures also sample the ARIA snapshot at the end of a *passing* test, a "last known good" page to diff a later failure against. The server decides when:

- At the start of every run the global setup makes **one extra request** for the tests whose newest green snapshot is older than 24 hours (or missing), and the reporter caches that set for the run's workers.
- A passing test is sampled only when in that set: in steady state, nothing is.
- The server keeps at most one green snapshot per test per day.

If that request fails, the set stays empty and **nothing is sampled**. Turn it off with `sampleAriaOnPass: false` (or `PIWI_SAMPLE_ARIA_ON_PASS=false`).

## Troubleshooting

- **Data missing for some specs only** — those specs import `test` from `@playwright/test` instead of your fixtures file.
- **No fixture data at all**: check that `collectPerformanceMetrics` is not `false`, and that tests leave `about:blank`.
- **ARIA snapshot or locator healing missing**: the same causes, or `captureLocators` is off.
- **An evidence card says "not captured"**: that project has never had the fixtures active; the in-app connect wizard, which each empty card links (**Settings → Connect a suite**), shows the fixtures to add. A card that reads *nothing happened* means the fixtures ran and this execution produced nothing. With an uploaded trace, the console, network and ARIA cards are recovered from it and marked *derived from the trace*.

## Try it

A runnable example project exercising every capture path, a failing test included, lives in [`examples/sample-app`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/examples/sample-app).

# CI & sharding

There is no Piwi-specific step to add to CI: the reporter runs inside `npx playwright test` and pushes results as they
happen. You set two environment variables.

```yaml
env:
  PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
  PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}   # only if authentication is enabled
```

With authentication off, the server's `PIWI_SITE_URL` or `PIWI_ALLOWED_HOSTS` must name the domain or container name
in that URL ([why](/operate/authentication#disabling-authentication)).

Everything else — branch, commit, author, workflow, build URL, shard index — is
[detected automatically](#what-gets-detected).

A `serverUrl` written in the Playwright config wins over `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`. `init` writes it as
`process.env.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL || '<the URL you gave>'`, so the variable takes over in CI; a config that names the URL
alone keeps sending to that URL.

## GitHub Actions

```yaml
name: e2e
on: [push]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps
      - run: npx playwright test
        env:
          PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
          PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

Piwi keeps every result, so the job's output can hold the failures alone: Playwright 1.65's `failures` reporter
prints only them, and `onlyFailures: true` keeps an `html`, `json` or `junit` report to them (`wrapConfig` adds Piwi):

```ts
reporter: process.env.CI ? [['failures'], ['junit', { outputFile: 'junit.xml', onlyFailures: true }]] : 'list',
```

The shallow clone `actions/checkout` makes is enough for the reporter: Piwi reads diffs from your Git host's API
([Source control](./source-control)). [`run impact --base`](/reference/cli#select-run) and
[`preflight --base`](/reference/cli#preflight) diff the checkout itself and need the base commit: set
`fetch-depth: 0` on `actions/checkout`.

## GitLab CI

```yaml
e2e:
  image: mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.65.1-noble   # the version of your @playwright/test
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx playwright test
  variables:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_API_KEY: $PIWI_API_KEY
```

## Other systems

Jenkins, CircleCI, Azure DevOps, Travis, Buildkite, TeamCity, Bitbucket, Semaphore, AppVeyor and Drone
are recognized too; set the same two variables. An unrecognized CI means less auto-filled metadata.

## What gets detected

Unconfigured, the reporter records:

- **Source control**: commit SHA, message, author, branch, pull-request number, the pull request's target branch,
  and the repository URL. On a pull-request build the target branch is recorded as the run's **base branch**, which
  [baselines](/guide/concepts#baseline-last-green-run) fall back to when the branch has no history of its own.
- **CI**: provider, workflow or job name, build number, and a link back to the CI build.
- **Origin**: [what launched it](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin).
- **Environment**: Playwright version, browser and viewport, [run environment](/features/run-environment).
- **Shard index**: from Playwright's own `--shard` config.

[Test metadata](/reference/test-metadata#scm-information-git) lists the variables each field comes from.
`PIWI_BRANCH` and `PIWI_BASE_BRANCH` override the resolved branches; `collectScmInfo: false` or
`collectCiInfo: false` turns a collector off.

## Sharding

Playwright's `--shard=1/3` splits a suite across parallel jobs. Piwi merges them back into **one run**.

```yaml
strategy:
  matrix:
    shard: [1, 2, 3]
steps:
  - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shard }}/3
    env:
      PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
      PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

How the merge works:

1. Each shard derives a **run label**, a stable identifier for the CI pipeline, from the provider's build id
   (`GITHUB_RUN_ID` with `GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT`, `CI_PIPELINE_ID`, `CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_ID` and their equivalents on the
   systems listed above). A re-run of a GitHub Actions workflow is a new attempt, so it starts a new run.
2. Shards sharing a run label, a `projectName` **and** a shard count (the `3` of `--shard=1/3`) resolve to the same
   run, streamed or batched.
3. The run stays `running` until the **last** shard reports. While none of its shards is running, it waits up to an
   hour for the next one, streamed or batched, so a shard may start an hour after the others ended. It also waits up
   to an hour for a shard still in its global setup.
4. Counters accumulate across shards, and the run page shows a shard progress badge (`2/3`) while shards are arriving.
   A shard counts once, even when it reports its end twice (its `/finish` answer lost, then its batch upload).
   The run takes the most severe status its shards reported, as Playwright's `merge-reports` does: `failed`, then
   `timedout`, then `interrupted`. It is `failed` whenever a test failed.
5. The run lasts from the first shard's start to the last shard's end, whether the shards run side by side or one
   after another. Its metadata keeps each shard's start, end, worker count and status under `shards`.

**All shards must use the same `projectName`.**

Playwright counts a sharded run's tests before it splits them, so a shard left with none passes. From Playwright 1.65,
a sharded run fails with `No tests found` when its whole selection is empty, as an unsharded one does, unless it passes
`--pass-with-no-tests`, which `piwi run --plan` adds unless its arguments filter tests.

Jobs sharded with `piwi run --shard`, or [balanced by duration](/features/test-selection#balanced-playwright-shards), merge the same way.

If your CI isn't detected, set the label yourself to anything common to all shards:

```typescript
['@piwitests/reporter', {
  serverUrl: 'https://piwi.example.com',
  projectName: 'my-project',
  runLabel: process.env.BUILD_TAG || 'my-custom-label',
}]
```

### Parallel jobs in one pipeline

A job that is not sharded adds the CI job's id (`GITHUB_JOB`, `CI_JOB_ID`, …) to its run label, so a GitLab
`e2e:chrome` and `e2e:firefox` reporting to one `projectName` stay two runs. The legs of a GitHub Actions matrix
share one job id, and Jenkins, TeamCity and Drone expose none: give each leg its own label, or its own `projectName`.
On GitHub Actions, `strategy.job-index` numbers the jobs of a matrix, whatever its keys:

```yaml
PIWI_RUN_LABEL: ${{ github.run_id }}-${{ github.run_attempt }}-${{ strategy.job-index }}
```

A configured label is used as it is, so each job of the matrix gets a run of its own, a shard too. When the legs are
themselves sharded (`shard: [1, 2, 3]` beside `browser`), put the leg's keys in the label instead (`matrix.browser`):
the shards of a leg share them, and merge into one run. Two matrix jobs of one workflow that report to one
`projectName` also need `github.job` in the label, since each numbers its jobs from 0.

Jobs left sharing a label cancel each other's live runs: the reporter of a cancelled run stops streaming and sends its
results in one batch at the end of its job, so each job still ends in one complete run, without its live progress.

## Watching a run while CI is still going

Streaming is on by default: the run fills in test by test, so a failure's trace is readable before the pipeline
ends ([Live streaming](./reporter#live-streaming)).

## Getting the run URL back out of CI

Later pipeline steps can pick up the run URL. Every channel is best-effort: a failure is logged, never
fatal.

**Always** — one line per failed test, printed the moment its final attempt fails, then a
`View run: <url>` line once the run lands:

```
[Piwi Dashboard] ✗ applies the discount code — getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }) never became enabled — click timed out after 30 s → https://piwi.example.com/test-runs/42/locate?file=tests%2Fcheckout.spec.ts&title=applies%20the%20discount%20code&retry=1&browser=chromium
[Piwi Dashboard] View run: https://piwi.example.com/test-runs/42
```

Between the title and the link is the failure's one-line [headline](./first-failure). The per-test link opens the
failing execution's page, even while the run is still going.

**GitHub Actions (automatic)** — a `::notice::` titled **Piwi live run** as the run starts, so the job's log links the
run while it runs; then step outputs, a job summary listing the failed tests with their links (20 at most, the rest
counted as "+N more"), and a `::notice::` annotation titled **Piwi test run**:

```yaml
- run: npx playwright test
  id: e2e
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
- run: echo "Results: ${{ steps.e2e.outputs.piwi_run_url }}"
  if: always()
```

Available outputs: `piwi_run_url`, `piwi_run_id`, `piwi_run_status`, `piwi_failed_count`, `piwi_project_id`.

**GitLab CI (automatic)** — a dotenv report (`piwi.env` by default, override with `PIWI_DOTENV_FILE`)
carrying `PIWI_RUN_URL`, `PIWI_RUN_ID`, `PIWI_RUN_STATUS`, `PIWI_FAILED_COUNT`, `PIWI_PROJECT_ID` and
`PIWI_CI_BUILD_URL`.
Declare it so later jobs inherit the variables:

```yaml
e2e:
  script:
    - npx playwright test
  artifacts:
    reports:
      dotenv: piwi.env
```

**Any other system** — set `outputFile` (or `PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE`) and read the JSON:

```yaml
- run: npx playwright test
  env:
    PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE: piwi-run.json
- run: cat piwi-run.json   # { runUrl, runId, projectId, projectName, status, ciBuildUrl, failedCount, failures }
```

`failures` lists every test whose final attempt failed as `{ title, file, retry, browser, repeatEachIndex, headline,
url }`, with `url` the per-test link the log prints.

## Pull-request feedback

Piwi can post a summary comment and a commit status on the pull request: see
[Pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback). To re-run a failure cluster's tests in CI, see
[Re-run in CI](/features/ci-rerun).

## Blocking a merge

`npx playwright test` exits non-zero when anything failed. *Did this change break something that was working* needs
the run history, so the dashboard evaluates it: the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) says what fails it, what
only warns and what it leaves out.

```yaml
- run: npx playwright test
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE: piwi-run.json      # records which run to gate on

- run: npx @piwitests/reporter gate --require-tag @critical --max-new-regressions 0
  if: always()
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

The command reads the run id from `PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE` (or `--run-id`, or `./piwi-run.json`) and prints each violation.

A failed gate exits 1 and prints:

```txt
✖ Piwi gate failed — checkout run #412
  248 tests, 3 failed, 1 new, 0 newly flaky, 2 flaky
  1 failing test is quarantined and did not count
  ✖ 1 required @critical test failed: pays by card
  ✖ 1 new regression (limit 0)
  https://piwi.example.com/test-runs/412
```

Every flag and exit code is in the [CLI reference](/reference/cli#gate); `--json` prints the raw result for a
pipeline to parse.

## Notifying people instead

To tell the team when main goes red, use a [notification subscription](/features/notifications), whose rules
live in one place.

## Troubleshooting

**Results don't appear.** Check the CI log for the reporter's own output; run with `PIWI_VERBOSE=true`
for the full request trace. The usual causes are a `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` the runner cannot
reach, or a missing API key while authentication is on.

**Shards create several runs instead of one.** The run label wasn't detected, or the shards disagree on
`projectName` or the shard count. Set `runLabel` explicitly.

**Traces or screenshots are missing.** Playwright records neither by default, so there is nothing to upload. Set
`use: { trace: 'retain-on-failure', screenshot: 'only-on-failure' }` in your Playwright config, or install through
[`wrapConfig`](./reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig), which sets both when they are unset.

**A run is stuck as `interrupted`.** A run silent for two minutes (a cancelled job, a killed runner, a dropped
network) is marked `interrupted` until its next event revives it. A run still in its global setup (`initializing`), or
a sharded run with a shard still in its own, waits an hour for its reporter to begin it. A run still uploading its
files or its reports (`finalizing`) waits ten minutes after the last one arrived, then keeps the status the reporter
sent.
[Analytics](/features/analytics#scope) counts interrupted runs as failing; **full runs only** drops only partial runs.

# Source control

Piwi reads your repository through the Git host's API with an **SCM token** (a personal or project access token for
GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket), saved once as an [SCM credential](/operate/credentials). Nothing needs it
to store runs, but every feature that looks at the code behind a failure, or writes back to a pull request, goes
through it.

## What uses it

| Feature | What it does with the repository | Access |
|---|---|---|
| [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis#scm-grounded-context) | Reads the commits and diffs since the [last green run](/features/run-changes#the-baseline), and the full source of the most suspect files | read |
| The failure cluster's **What changed** panel | Lists commits, shows their diffs, and lets you pin a baseline commit | read |
| [Uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes) | Diffs the run's commit against the pull request's base, or the last passing run, and flags changed files no test reached | read |
| [Did the fix work?](/features/failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work) | Checks whether the commits after a fix touched the failing files | read |
| [Notifications](/features/notifications) | Names the author of the fixing commit on `cluster.fixed` and `cluster.regressed` | read |
| Ownership and the default branch | Reads `CODEOWNERS` for test owners, and the repository's default branch when the project sets none | read |
| [Pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback) | Posts a summary comment and a commit status, and the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#on-the-pull-request)'s status when it is on | write |
| [Re-run in CI](/features/ci-rerun) | Dispatches a workflow or pipeline (a CI server takes its own token) | write |
| [Auto-heal PRs](/features/auto-heal) | Opens a pull request with a locator fix | write |

Every call is best-effort: a missing token, a private repository the token cannot see or an unreachable host is
logged, and the feature shows nothing rather than failing a run.

## Set the credential

Save the token under **Settings → Credentials** (**New credential**, service **Source control**), or with **New
credential** beside any picker below. Its destination is the host's API, which the form offers in one click
(`https://api.github.com/`, `https://gitlab.com/`, `https://api.bitbucket.org/`), or a path under it that keeps the
token to one owner's repositories on GitHub or Bitbucket (`https://api.github.com/repos/acme/`), or to one project on
GitLab (`https://gitlab.com/api/v4/projects/acme%2Fweb/`). Then pick it:

- **Per project**: **Project → Settings → Source control**, field **Credential**. Prefer one per project for write
  access: a token the instance shares can write everywhere it reaches.
- **Instance-wide**: **Settings → Source control**, field **SCM credentials** in its **Repository access** card,
  for every project that picks none. It lists credentials shared with all projects; for each repository, the one
  whose destination holds the repository's API applies, the narrowest first, so one instance can hold a GitHub and a
  GitLab token.
- **Per CI action**: a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket [CI action](/features/ci-actions#repository-host) may name its
  own, so a token scoped to CI dispatches (on GitHub, **Actions: write**, and **Contents: read** for the action's
  **Check**), and the project's keeps reading and writing feedback.

The token is encrypted with [`PIWI_SECRET_KEY`](/reference/configuration#general), never returned by the API, sent
only to its destination, and each use is in the credential's log. A token saved on a project or the instance before
credentials existed is moved to one at startup (below). The page stays open
when the Source control [capability](/operate/capabilities) is declined, so the credentials can still be taken out.

Public repositories work without a token for the read features, within the host's rate limit for anonymous calls.
A private repository needs one, except on the desktop app with a linked folder (below).

### How it is used and logged

Opening a credential for a repository's calls is counted like a **Check** in its log, `ok` once opened (a token the
host refuses shows on the page that read). Each write (a comment, a commit status, an auto-heal branch, commit or pull
request, a dispatch) is a row of its own, checked again before it is sent. A refused credential is logged; the reads
go on without it, and a dispatch, or the **Check** of an action that names its own, is refused.

At startup, a project's token saved before credentials existed moves to a credential bound to the API of its
repository; it waits while the project has no repository, or one on a GitLab host `PIWI_SCM_GITLAB_HOSTS` does not
list. The instance's moves to one credential per API it could reach (GitHub's, Bitbucket's, the GitLab cloud's and
each listed host's), shared with all projects and listed in **Settings → Source control**: delete the ones your
repositories do not use.

### On the desktop app

The [desktop app](/features/desktop) needs no token for the read features. When a project is
[linked to a folder](/features/desktop#projects-from-local-folders) that is a clone of the repository (one of its
remotes points at the run's remote URL), Piwi reads the commits, diffs and files with `git` in that folder, on your
machine. A commit or branch the clone does not have is asked of the host as above, so run `git fetch` in the folder to
see commits pushed since your last fetch. With a credential set, the host is read instead, as on a server, and the
write features always need one. A repository on another host (a self-hosted Bitbucket or Gitea, a GitLab host not listed
below) is read from the clone alone, token or not: what the clone does not have stays unavailable.

### Which repository

Each project reads one repository, shown in the **Repository** field of the **Source control** section. The reporter
records the Git remote URL, the branch and the commit of the checkout it runs in (see
[SCM information](/reference/test-metadata#scm-information-git)), and the first run that names a remote sets the
field. A run whose remote names another repository is left out of every call that uses the token: its commits, diffs
and source are not read, and nothing is written for it. A project admin can change the field, or clear it so that the
next run sets it again. With the instance's credentials, a link to a repository no readable project uses is unfurled
as a public page, without a token.

Supported hosts are `github.com`, `gitlab.com`, `bitbucket.org` and self-hosted GitLab. A remote on a host's SSH
alias (`ssh.github.com`, `ssh.bitbucket.org`, `altssh.bitbucket.org`) names the same repository as on the host. List
each self-hosted GitLab host in [`PIWI_SCM_GITLAB_HOSTS`](/reference/configuration#integrations): Piwi sends a token
only to a host you named. A run without a remote URL has nothing to diff.

### Scopes

| Host | Read features | Write features |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub | read access to repository contents | `repo` (classic), or fine-grained **Contents: write**, **Pull requests: write** and **Commit statuses: write**; **Actions: write** for re-runs |
| GitLab | `read_api` | `api` |
| Bitbucket | repository read | repository write; `pullrequest` for pull-request comments; `pipeline:write` for re-runs |

## Verify

Open a failure cluster from a run that has a commit. The **What changed** panel lists the commits since the last green
run. The diagnosis context preview (**Context sent to AI**) shows the same thing in its data coverage: when the SCM
section is absent, it says why.

## Troubleshooting

- **No commits or diff.** The cluster's **What changed** line keeps the range, shows the host's error when it returned
  one (*GitHub error: Not Found*), and links the host's compare page when there is one; its help hint says what to set
  up: a commit and a repository URL on the run (the reporter reads both from the Git checkout the tests run in, the URL
  from its `origin` remote), a host Piwi reads, an SCM credential, or, with one set, a token that can read the
  repository. A refused credential (disabled, not shared with the project, or bound to another host) is in its log.
  A 404 from GitHub on a private repository means the token cannot see it. On the desktop app, the hint says to fetch
  the commits in the linked folder. The cluster's **More actions › Copy git log** copies the command that lists the
  range in your checkout.
- **No baseline.** The diff starts at the last green run before the failure first appeared; a project with no green
  run falls back to the last run before it where the test passed, and a manual baseline commit overrides both.
- **No pull-request comment.** Pull-request feedback also needs `PIWI_SITE_URL` and a write-scoped token, and posts on
  GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket Cloud only.

## Related

- [AI provider](./ai-provider): the model that reads this context
- [Pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback): what gets posted on a pull request
- [Privacy & data flow](./privacy): what Piwi sends to your Git host
