# Branches

Every run Piwi stores is tagged with the git **branch** it came from, and that branch is a real, queryable dimension — not a string buried in metadata. Filter any view to one branch, compare like with like, and let baselines and flakiness scoring stop mixing your feature branches together.

**Needs:** the reporter only — the branch is collected automatically with the rest of the git metadata (`collectScmInfo`, on by default). Nothing to install or switch on.

## How the branch is recorded

On CI, git alone is unreliable: a pull-request checkout is usually a detached `HEAD`, so `git rev-parse` reports the literal string `HEAD` instead of a branch. The reporter resolves the real branch through a fallback chain instead:

1. **`PIWI_BRANCH`** — an explicit operator override, when you want to name the branch yourself.
2. **The CI provider's branch variables** — `GITHUB_HEAD_REF` / `GITHUB_REF_NAME` on GitHub Actions, the merge-request and commit refs on GitLab, and the equivalents for CircleCI, Travis, Azure, Jenkins and Bitbucket. On a pull-request build the **source** branch wins over the plain ref, so the run records the branch under test.
3. **`git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD`** — the local answer, used only when it is a real branch. A detached `HEAD` is discarded rather than recorded.

When the provider exposes it, the reporter also captures the **pull-request number**, so [pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback) can look the PR up exactly instead of guessing from the branch name, and the pull request's **target branch** (`GITHUB_BASE_REF`, `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME`, `SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_TARGETBRANCH`, `BITBUCKET_PR_DESTINATION_BRANCH`, Jenkins' `CHANGE_TARGET`, Travis' `TRAVIS_BRANCH` on a PR build), which becomes the run's **base branch** — the branch baselines fall back to. Set `PIWI_BASE_BRANCH` to name it yourself. Branch, PR and base-branch detection happen automatically as part of the reporter's git metadata collection (`collectScmInfo`) — see [CI & sharding → What gets detected](/guide/ci#what-gets-detected).

## The default branch

Each project has a **Default branch** setting in the **Source control** section of its **Settings** tab (placeholder `e.g. main`). Leave it blank and Piwi resolves it from your SCM provider; when the provider cannot tell (no token, or no access to the repository), Piwi asks again ten minutes later, and meanwhile falls back to the branch the reporter names, then the branch most of the project's runs are on, then `main`. The default branch is the reference point for the rest of this page: baselines fall back to it, and "already flaky on the default branch" is measured against it.

## Filtering by branch

On a project page, the **Filters** block carries a **branch** multi-select (the git-branch icon) next to the environment filter. It appears once any of the project's runs carries a branch. With no branch picked, the page reads the project's default branch and the runs that report no branch, like [Analytics](./analytics#branch-policy); **All branches** beside it reads every branch, and the branches you pick read exactly those. The header, the runs list, the test catalog, the failure clusters, the flaky leaderboard, the Flake Lab and the performance trends all follow it; a note under the filters counts the runs on other branches they hide. A project's [default environment](./environments#default-environment) works the same way: with no environment picked the page reads it, **All environments** reads every one, and the note counts the runs in other environments.

The branch is an indexed column, so every project tab (the runs list included), Analytics and the MCP `list_runs` tool filter by it in the database. Runs reported before the column existed carry the branch recorded in their metadata, so old history still filters.

## The project status

The badge beside a project in the sidebar shows the outcome of its latest run, and the **Projects** list and the MCP
`list_projects` tool name that run. By default it is the latest run of any environment and branch, so a run on a
work-in-progress branch or in a scratch environment turns a healthy project red. A **status filter** picks the runs
that set the status instead. A project admin turns on **Only runs in a filter** in the **Status** section of the
project's **Settings** tab, and picks environments, branches and **Full runs only** as in the project page's Filters.
With no branch picked it reads the default branch and the runs that report none; **Copy the project page filters** takes
the filters you picked on the project's pages. The badge's tooltip and accessible name carry the filter, and the
Projects list says when no run matches it yet.

The filter is saved on the project, so every user sees the same status. A project is still listed under **Active** in
the sidebar when any of its runs started in the last ten days. Flake Lab and probe runs never set a status.

## Branch-aware baselines

**Baselines are chosen within an environment and a branch.**

- **The run-level baseline**, what the Changes tab, the stored regression signals, the CI gate, pull-request feedback, the bisect window and the AI diagnosis all compare against, follows the [baseline rule](./run-changes#the-baseline), which prefers the run's own branch, then its base branch ([the figure](./run-changes#the-baseline)). Two feature branches reporting interleaved runs never become each other's baseline. When no earlier full run passed, the Changes tab [falls back to the last failed run](./run-changes#when-no-earlier-run-passed).
- **Choosing the base branch** — the Changes tab lets you take the baseline from any branch with an earlier full run, so a long-lived branch can be compared against `release/2` rather than `main`; the choice is in the URL (`?baseBranch=`) and on the API and MCP tool. See [What changed in a run](./run-changes#the-baseline).
- **The environment, visual and page diffs** of one execution prefer the same environment, then the same branch, then
  the most recent pass (the page diff also prefers the same Playwright release, after the environment): there is no
  base-branch rung ([the rule](./run-changes#one-execution-s-baseline)).
- **Pull-request feedback** builds its "new failures vs. pre-existing" split from the same baseline, so a failure the PR did not introduce is reported as pre-existing, and the `max-new-regressions` rule of the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) counts the same new failures. A failure whose test is already flaky on the default branch, in the project's default environment when it has one, is also marked *Also flaky on `main` … — likely not yours*; the mark does not move it out of the new failures or the gate's count.
- **Performance alerts** — the `perf.regression` [notification](./notifications) measures a run against the previous runs on the same branch **in the same environment**.

## From an agent (MCP)

The MCP `list_runs` tool takes a `branch` argument, so an agent can ask "what is failing on `main`" without pulling every run. `list_flaky_tests` takes no branch; it reads the same default-branch view as the dashboard's flaky leaderboard, in the project's default environment unless its `environment` argument names another or `allEnvironments` asks for every one. See the [MCP server](/features/mcp).

## Notifications

Notification subscriptions can filter by branch and alert only on the default branch, so a noisy work-in-progress branch does not page you. See [Notifications & alerts](./notifications).

## Limits

- **Views read the default branch by default.** Analytics counts each project's default branch (plus runs with no branch) until you pick branches or *All branches* (see [Branch policy](./analytics#branch-policy)). The flaky leaderboard does the same unless you scope it, with the [fallbacks](#the-default-branch) while the default branch is unknown. Both read a project's default environment too, when it has one.
- **Branches are a run dimension, not entities.** There is no per-branch merge-readiness verdict, branch-class gate policy, or retention by branch class.
- **A run needs a resolvable branch.** A purely local run with no CI variables, a detached `HEAD`, and no `PIWI_BRANCH` records no branch at all, so it will not appear under any branch filter.

- [CI & sharding](/guide/ci) — how the branch and PR number are detected on each provider
- [Flaky tests](./flaky-tests) — the leaderboard and regression signals the branch filter scopes
- [Analytics](./analytics) — trends you can read one branch at a time
- [Glossary](/guide/concepts) — where branch sits among run, execution and baseline

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/run-changes -->

# What changed in a run

The **Changes** tab on a run compares it against **one baseline** and tells you what moved: which tests newly started failing, which got fixed, and what landed between the two. It's the fastest way to answer "did my push break this, or was it already red?"

## The baseline

Every section reads the **same baseline**, so the "new failures" count is computed once and used throughout. The selector at the top says which run it is, which branch and environment that run is on, and **why it was chosen**.

By default the baseline is the **last passing full run**, chosen by environment first, then branch. The ladder is
walked within the run's environment label first, then again without it. On each pass it takes the most recent passing
run on the **same branch**, else on the **base branch** the run's branch forked from (the pull request's target branch
when the reporter captured one, else the project's [default branch](./branches#the-default-branch)), else on **any
branch**. So a `staging` run on `feature/x` compares with the last passing `staging` run on `feature/x`, then the last
passing `staging` run on `main`, then any passing `staging` run, and only then with a run from another environment. A
run whose branch is unknown has only the any-branch rung; a run with no environment label walks the branch ladder once.
A lab run (a probe or a Flake Lab experiment) is never a baseline. The line under the selector spells out the rung that
applied, for example _"No passing staging run exists on feature/x; the last passing run on the default branch main in
staging."_

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/baseline-ladder.svg" alt="The baseline ladder: same branch, base branch, then any branch, first within the run's environment and then in any environment; with no passing run, the same rungs for the last failed run">
  <figcaption>The baseline rule: six rungs tried in order, the first with an earlier passing run giving the baseline.</figcaption>
</figure>

The same baseline is what the run insights, the stored [regression signals](./flaky-tests#regression-signals), the
[CI merge gate](./merge-gate), [pull-request feedback](./pr-feedback), the bisect window and the git diff behind an
[AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis#scm-grounded-context) compare against. The regression signals compare the last attempt
of each test (of each repetition, with `--repeat-each`) with its outcome in the baseline in the same Playwright
project, and are never set on an earlier attempt of a retried test.

### One execution's baseline

The environment, visual and page diffs of one failing execution compare it with the same test's last passing
execution on the same browser, in a shorter order: the same environment, then the same branch, then the most recent,
with no base-branch rung. The page diff also prefers, right after the environment, a run on the same Playwright
release (major and minor version), since ARIA snapshots can change from one version to the next (Playwright 1.65 leaves out text the browser
does not render). When no passing run from the same environment exists, the card says which environment the
baseline came from (_"compared with a production run; no passing development run of this test exists"_) and leaves
the environment label out of the diff.

### When no earlier run passed

A project that has never had a green run still gets a comparison. When no earlier full run passed, the tab walks the same ladder again for the **last failed run** and says so: _"No earlier full run passed; the last failed run on feature/x in staging."_ The sections read the same way against it: **New failures** are the tests that passed in that run and fail here, **Still failing** the ones that failed in both. Timed-out and interrupted runs stopped before the suite ended, so they are never picked automatically.

Only the Changes tab and the MCP `get_run_insights` tool take a failed run. The stored regression signals, the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) and [pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback) keep comparing with a passing run, so their verdicts never rest on a run that was itself red.

When nothing qualifies (the earlier runs are partial, timed out or interrupted), the tab says so and offers the earlier runs to pick from. On the project's first finished run, it says there is nothing earlier yet.

### Picking another baseline

Two ways to compare against something else:

- **Base branch** — take the baseline from one branch only: its last passing run, else its last failed run, same environment first. The list offers every branch with an earlier full run that passed or failed, so it appears once a branch other than this run's own has one. Deep-linkable as `?baseBranch=<name>`.
- **Run** — compare against one earlier run, whatever its branch, environment or outcome. The list shows the 50 runs before this one, each with its branch, environment, start time and outcome, partial runs marked; type a branch or environment name to filter it. Deep-linkable as `?baseline=<runId>`, so a link to a comparison reopens the same two runs. **Previous run** is the shortcut for the run just before this one.

**Automatic** returns to the default choice. The same options exist on the REST API (see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api)), where `earlierRuns` lists the runs that can be passed as `baseline`, and on the MCP `get_run_insights` tool (`baseBranch`).

## What it shows

- **New failures** — passed in the baseline, failing here.
- **Fixed** — failed in the baseline, passing here.
- **Still failing** — failing in both.
- **Newly flaky / passed on retry** — passed here after an earlier attempt failed. Of these, a test that passed at
  its first attempt in the baseline is also [newly flaky](#what-newly-flaky-says-about-your-change).
- **Slower / faster** — the ten largest duration changes each way.
- **Commits since the baseline** — the commit range, a copyable `git log` command and, when the SCM host is known, a link to the commits.
- **Deployed to Staging**, for a run of a [deployed environment](./deployed-environments) — the application's commit
  each run tested, the application's commits between them, and the environment's deploy markers between the two runs.
- **Environment changes** — the fields that differ (environment, branch, CI provider, browsers, and the [test order](#shuffled-runs) of a shuffled run), in *This run* / *Baseline* columns. The browsers are those of the Playwright projects each run ran: the ones `--project` selects, the projects they depend on, and their teardown projects.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-changes.png" alt="Run Changes tab showing the baseline selector, the tests that newly started failing, the ones that got fixed, and the commits landed since the baseline">
  <figcaption>The Changes tab on a run, read against one baseline — new failures, fixed tests, and the commits landed since.</figcaption>
</figure>

Comparing two runs is also how the [run comparison](./ui-overview#test-run-detail) works: select two runs on the project's Runs tab and the newer one opens on its Changes tab with the older as its baseline.

### What newly flaky says about your change

**Newly flaky** is a change between the two runs, as a new failure is: the test needed a retry here and passed at
its first attempt in the baseline. It does not clear your change. A change can make a test flaky (a new race, a
slower call, a shared state), and so can anything else that differs between the runs. Nor does it convict it: one
first-attempt pass in the baseline is one sample, and a test that has been flaky for weeks passes first time often.

The test's own history settles it. A [flaky rate](/guide/concepts#flaky-rate) near zero until this run points at
the commits since the baseline; one that has been high for weeks points at a flake your run happened to meet, which
[Flaky tests](./flaky-tests) ranks and quarantines. The [CI merge gate](./merge-gate) counts newly flaky tests
apart from new regressions (`--max-new-flaky`), so a pipeline can hold a branch for either.

## Shuffled runs

A test that fails only after another one depends on the order, and a suite run in the same order every time shows the
same neighbor every time, which leaves the flaky test's [**Before** suspect](./flaky-tests#suspects) nothing to
compare. Playwright 1.64's `--shuffle` schedules test files, and the tests of files in parallel mode, in a random
order, and the run keeps its seed: the run's **Details** shows it as **Order**, and clicking the seed copies
`--shuffle <seed>`, which runs the same tests on the same workers in the same order again. Against a baseline that was
not shuffled, or the other way round, the Changes tab lists the **Test order** under Environment changes.

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › a run’s Changes tab](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-runs/2?tab=changes): A run read against its baseline: what failed, what passed only on retry, and the commits landed since.

# Offline export

An investigation is only useful while someone can open it. Piwi can write a failing execution, a
whole failure cluster or a whole run to a file that opens with **no network and no Piwi server** — for a ticket
attachment, a mail to someone without an account, or an archive that outlives your retention window.

The **Export** button sits on a test-case execution (`/test-run-cases/:id`), on a failure cluster
(`/failure-clusters/:id`) and on a run (`/test-runs/:id`). A run and an execution also offer a **Perfetto trace**
(see [below](#perfetto-trace)).

## Formats

| Format | What you get |
|--------|--------------|
| **HTML** | One file. Screenshots and video are embedded as `data:` URIs; error, steps, console, what the test wrote to stdout and stderr, network, ARIA snapshot, test source and the AI diagnosis are all inline. Double-click it. |
| **ZIP** | `report.html` plus the raw artifacts on disk — full-size video, reconstructed `trace.zip` archives, console and network logs, `stdout.txt` and `stderr.txt` — and `data.json` with everything the report shows, machine-readable. |
| **PDF** | A formatted document generated directly — no browser print dialog, so it is identical on the web app, the desktop app and the demo. Screenshots embed; video and trace archives can't live in a PDF, so they're listed as omitted (use ZIP to keep them). |
| **Markdown / JSON** | Text only, for pasting into an issue or feeding an agent. |

A cluster export carries the most recent failing execution of each affected test.

A run export opens on the run: its status, branch, commit and CI build, its tests as a bar split by outcome, its
failures grouped by root cause (each failure cluster, then the failures no cluster holds), its flaky tests, its ten
slowest tests and every test result, by file. Its failing executions follow in detail, the largest group first.

The HTML and PDF reports read the same way. They open on a header colored by the outcome, with the test's full name
(describe blocks, then title), its location and Piwi's one-line reading of the failure, then the execution's figures and
its run: branch, commit, CI build and the run's tests as a bar split by outcome. The error follows with its expected
and received values colored and the call log faded, then the call stack with the failing line marked, and the steps
on the test's timeline, a failed step in red. A cluster export opens on the cluster's state and a bar per recent run.
Dates are in UTC.

## Replay the failure in a browser

A failed execution's **Export** also offers **Bug report (.piwibug)**: the failure as the
[bug report file](/reference/bug-report-file) Piwi Picker writes, to play in your own browser with
[Replay](./replay-a-bug-report#a-report-made-from-a-test-run). It holds the test's steps up to the failure, the failing
assertion with its expected and received values, the failed requests, the console's errors and the failure
screenshot. The line under it counts the steps, those done by hand and the calls of the test the steps leave out; the
button's tooltip names those calls. **Steps (steps.json)**, under **Copy to clipboard**, copies the steps alone, to
paste into Replay.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/execution-replay-export.png" alt="A failed execution's Export menu: downloads as HTML, ZIP, PDF, Markdown or JSON, the bug report to replay in a browser with its 6 steps, a Perfetto trace, and the report or the steps to copy">
  <figcaption>The Export menu of a failed execution: its steps as a bug report to replay.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What an export leaves out, and why it tells you

Exports are bounded so one download cannot exhaust the server:

| Variable | Default | Bounds |
|---|---|---|
| `PIWI_EXPORT_MAX_INLINE_BYTES` | 8 MB | What a single HTML file will embed as a `data:` URI. Larger files stay out of the one-file HTML; the ZIP still carries them at full size. |
| `PIWI_EXPORT_MAX_BYTES` | 500 MB | The whole export. Evidence is added in order — each execution's attachments, then its trace archives — and a file that would pass the budget is left out. The archive is built in memory, so this also bounds what one export costs the server. |
| `PIWI_EXPORT_MAX_CASES` | 25 | Executions carrying full evidence in a cluster export (its affected tests) or a run export (its failing tests). The rest are listed by name. |

Anything left out is listed in an **Omitted from this export** table in the report and in the ZIP's
`README.txt` — an export never drops evidence silently. Defaults and tuning:
[Configuration](/reference/configuration#offline-export).

## Opening a hostile report safely

The exported HTML carries a restrictive `Content-Security-Policy` and escapes every value that came
from a test run, so a report is safe to open even when the failure it describes involved hostile page
content.

## Reading an exported trace

The ZIP carries reconstructed `trace.zip` archives, but reading one still needs a Playwright trace
viewer — `npx playwright show-trace trace.zip`, or the [bundled viewer](./evidence#trace-viewer) on any
Piwi instance. Bundling the viewer's assets into the export itself is on the
[roadmap](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/ROADMAP.md).

## Perfetto trace

A run and an execution also export as a **Perfetto trace** — a [Trace Event Format](https://perfetto.dev/docs/getting-started/other-formats) JSON file that opens the run on a timeline in
[ui.perfetto.dev](https://ui.perfetto.dev) or Chrome's `chrome://tracing`, with no Piwi server needed.

The file lays the run out the way it ran: **one process per shard, one thread per worker**. Each
execution is a slice on its worker's thread, with its hooks, fixtures and steps nested underneath by
start time, and a slice colored by outcome (green passed, red failed). A failing execution adds an
instant marker at the moment it failed. Every slice carries its details in the event arguments —
source location, step params, tags, locks, annotations, status, error message, and links back to the
execution and its attachments on the dashboard.

Open it by dragging the downloaded `.json` onto [ui.perfetto.dev](https://ui.perfetto.dev), or use
**Open trace file** there. Timestamps are relative to the first event, so a run always starts at zero.

The trace **does not embed the attachments themselves** — screenshots, video and trace archives are
referenced by their dashboard URL, so following those links needs the Piwi instance the run came from.
For a self-contained snapshot of one failure, use the HTML or ZIP export above.

## Related
- [Share links](./share-links) — the live counterpart: a revocable read-only URL instead of a file
- [Failure evidence](./evidence) — what the export is a snapshot of
- [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis): cluster exports carry the diagnosis too
- [Storage & retention](/operate/storage#data-retention): retention, and why an export outlives it

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/share-links -->

# Share links

A share link is a read-only URL that anyone can open — no dashboard account, no login. It opens one of four
things:

- an **execution** or a **failure cluster**: the live counterpart of an [offline export](./offline-export), the
  investigation as it stands when the link is opened;
- a **report snapshot**: a stored [quality report](./quality-reports#report-snapshots), as it was generated;
- a saved **analytics dashboard**: a [live dashboard link](#live-dashboard-links), computed at every view.

Share links are **off by default**. Set `PIWI_SHARE_LINKS_ENABLED=true` to allow them — see the
[configuration reference](/reference/configuration#authentication).

The **Share** button, the *Live dashboard links* menu item and the switches that add a link to a scheduled report or
an issue show only while share links are enabled. The [desktop app](./desktop) never shows them, since its server has
no public address, and neither does the [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/), which runs without a server.

## Creating a link

On an execution page, a failure-cluster page or a report snapshot page, open **Share** (next to **Export** or
**Download**); on a saved dashboard, open *Live dashboard links* in the dashboard's menu:

1. Pick an expiry. The dialog offers lifetimes up to `PIWI_SHARE_LINK_MAX_TTL_DAYS` (30 days unless configured;
   setting it to `0` lifts the cap and allows links with no expiry, which work until they are revoked or their
   creator loses access to what they open).
2. **Copy the link immediately — it is shown only once.** The server stores a hash of the token, not the token, so
   there is no way to display the URL again later. Mint a new link instead.

Creating and revoking links requires the **Maintainer** role or above on the project, or an administrator
([roles](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do)); anyone
who can read the project can see which links exist. Each entry in the dialog shows the link's prefix, its expiry state, and how many times it was opened.

## What the viewer sees

The link serves the same self-contained HTML report the [offline export](./offline-export) produces, rebuilt from
the current data on every view — a diagnosis added after the link was minted shows up, a cluster marked fixed reads
as fixed. The same size budgets apply (`PIWI_EXPORT_MAX_*`), so an anonymous view can never cost the server more
than an authenticated export does.

Two consequences of "live" worth knowing:

- **Retention thins a shared cluster over time.** When [data retention](/operate/storage#data-retention) prunes old runs, a
  cluster link keeps resolving but progressively loses member evidence — the same thinning the dashboard shows. A
  link whose entity is pruned entirely answers 404. When the investigation must outlive retention, hand over an
  export file instead.
- **Revocation is immediate.** A revoked link stops resolving on the next request. Turning the feature off entirely
  (`PIWI_SHARE_LINKS_ENABLED` unset) dead-ends every outstanding link at once without deleting anything, so the
  variable doubles as a kill switch. While it is off, the **Share** dialogs and their lists of links are hidden too.

## Report share links

A report snapshot's link renders the stored quality report as one self-contained HTML page. It shows the numbers
the report was generated with, whatever retention deleted since, and answers 404 once the snapshot itself is pruned
(`PIWI_RETENTION_REPORT_DAYS`).

A [report schedule](./quality-reports#report-schedules) can mint one per report: turn on **Share link** in the
schedule form. Each report then gets its own link, which the email, the Slack and Microsoft Teams messages and the webhook's
body carry beside the link to the snapshot, so a stakeholder without an account reads the report in one click. The link expires a week after the
schedule's next report, within `PIWI_SHARE_LINK_MAX_TTL_DAYS`. The token travels encrypted with `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`
from the schedule to the delivery, and is shown to nobody.

## Live dashboard links

A live dashboard link renders a saved dashboard as a quality report computed at every view, and the page reloads
itself every minute: a bookmark for a stakeholder, or a wall screen with nobody signed in. Built-in dashboards have
none; duplicate one first.

- The numbers are computed with the access of the person who minted the link, checked again at every view
  (at most a minute behind). The link dies when that access or the dashboard goes, when it expires, or when it is
  revoked.
- It shows the aggregates and the lists the dashboard carries, never evidence files: no screenshot, no trace, no
  video.

## Status badge

A report link and a live dashboard link each carry two images, shown when the link is minted:

- `/share/<token>/badge.svg`: a badge such as "tests on default branch · 97.8% · 7 d", the test [pass rate](/guide/concepts#pass-rate) on the
  pass-rate color scale, for a README or a wiki page. The dialog copies it as Markdown.
- `/share/<token>/chart.png`: the report's trend. A scheduled report's Slack message draws it as an image, since
  Slack needs a public address to show one.

Both stop resolving with their link. An image proxy (GitHub's for a README, Slack's) may keep showing its copy
for up to five minutes, the time the images may be cached. Images count against their link's request limit, not
the reader's address, since such a proxy fetches for many readers.

## Security properties

- The token is a 256-bit random secret (`psl_` + 64 hex characters) — unguessable at any request rate. The server
  stores its SHA-256 hash and the first 8 hex characters, which the dialog shows as the link's prefix. What Piwi
  records of an issue that carries a link keeps its URL with the token redacted.
- Everything a link serves is data its creator can see: minting requires access to the execution, the cluster,
  every project of the snapshot, or the dashboard, so a link is a narrower delegation of an existing member's read
  access, never an escalation.
- A link works only while its creator can still read what it opens: the project of the execution or the cluster,
  or every project of the snapshot (a live dashboard link follows its creator's access as
  [described above](#live-dashboard-links)). Once they lose that access, the link answers 404 like an unknown link,
  and works again if the access comes back. Deleting their account revokes their links. With authentication off,
  every link works.
- An execution, cluster or report link with no creator is tied to no account, and works until it is revoked or
  expires: one Piwi created itself, in an issue an [automation rule](./issue-automation) filed, one created while
  authentication was off, and one whose creator was deleted before v0.65.0. An administrator revokes it in the
  **Share** dialog of what it opens, which lists every link to it, whoever created it.
- The rendered page is sandboxed into a unique origin and served with `noindex` and `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`,
  so it cannot read dashboard cookies, call the API with credentials, or leak the URL through outbound links. The
  page is never cached; the two images may be, for five minutes.
- A share URL is a capability: anyone holding it can view the page, and it can end up in browser history or proxy
  logs like any URL. Prefer short expiries, and revoke links when an investigation closes.

## Related

- [Access, roles and groups](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do) — the project roles that can mint or revoke
- [Storage & retention](/operate/storage#data-retention) — retention, and how it interacts with long-lived links

# Is this test failing because of my change, or is it flaky?

The most common question in a red CI run, and the most expensive one to answer wrong: re-run a real
regression and you ship the bug; chase a flake and you lose an afternoon. Piwi answers it from history
you already have, in about a minute.

## 1. Open the run's Changes tab

A run compares itself against **one baseline**, an earlier passing run picked by the
[baseline rule](/features/run-changes#the-baseline), and sorts the failures for you. The distinction you want is
right there in the headings:

- **New failures** — this test was passing on the baseline and is failing now.
- **Still failing** — it was already failing before your change.
- **Newly flaky / passed on retry** — it passed after an earlier attempt failed.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-changes.png" alt="Run Changes tab showing the baseline selector, new failures, newly flaky tests, slower and faster tests, and the commits landed since the baseline">
  <figcaption>The Changes tab — read against one baseline, with new failures separated from tests that only passed on retry.</figcaption>
</figure>

If your test is under **Newly flaky / passed on retry**, its failure did not survive a retry: that points at
flakiness, not a regression that breaks it every time. It does not clear your change, which can have made the test
flaky ([what newly flaky says](/features/run-changes#what-newly-flaky-says-about-your-change)): its history (next
step) tells a new flake from an old one. A long-standing flake belongs in [cutting flakiness](./flaky-cleanup).

## 2. Check the test's own history

A single run can lie — a flaky test lands in **New failures** whenever the baseline happened to be
green. Open the test case and read its **status history** and **stability trend**: pass rate, flaky
rate, and duration bucketed over time.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/tour-test-history.png" alt="A test case page: run stats, the duration trend with a status strip under it, and the recent executions">
  <figcaption>Test case history: the status strip is what separates "this has always been shaky" from "this broke on Tuesday".</figcaption>
</figure>

Read it like this:

| History looks like | Verdict |
|---|---|
| Solid green, then red from one run onward | A regression. Find the commit in that gap. |
| Red/green alternating for weeks | A flake that happened to fail on your run. |
| Green, then red, and the failing execution **passed on retry** | A flake: its status reads *Passed on retry*, and its headline is the failed attempt's error. |
| Newly red *and* the failure is shared with other tests | Probably neither — see [triaging a mass failure](./mass-failure). |

## 3. Find what changed around it

Once you know it's a real regression, narrow the window:

- The failing execution's **History** section links back to the **last green run** ("Last passed in run
  #N"), so you have two commits to diff between.
- If the drop lines up with a deploy or an infrastructure change, a
  [timeline marker](/features/timeline-markers) draws it as a vertical line on the trend chart — "it started
  the day we switched CI runners" is a much faster answer than a bisect.
- With [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) configured, the cluster's explanation is read against your actual
  git diff since the last green run, and any suggested patch is checked against your source before you
  see it. Optional, off by default.

## Other ways to get the same answer

Not everyone wants to click through a dashboard mid-review.

**Ask your coding agent.** The [MCP server](/features/mcp) is built into the running instance — nothing to
install. `get_run_insights` returns the same new failures / fixed / newly flaky split this page walks
through, and `get_test_stability_trend` answers "is this getting flakier?" for one test.

**Wire it into CI.** The [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) already knows the difference: a test in
[quarantine](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) keeps running and keeps reporting, but doesn't
block the merge — and the gate reports how many failures it excluded.

**Get told instead of looking.** [Notifications](/features/notifications) let you subscribe to
`run.failed.default_branch` rather than `run.failed`, so you hear about main going red instead of every
red branch build — the difference between an alert people read and one people mute. `flakiness.spike`
fires separately for any run with flaky tests; a subscription's flakiness threshold (set through the API)
narrows it.

- [Flaky tests](/features/flaky-tests) — how the composite score and root-cause categories are computed
- [Core concepts](/guide/core-concepts) — *test case* vs *execution*, the distinction this recipe leans on
- [Timeline markers](/features/timeline-markers) — correlating a drop with a deploy

# Why does my Playwright test fail on CI but pass on my machine?

Something differs between the two machines, and when the test reads a date, a price or a sorted list, it is often
the time zone or the language. A CI runner usually runs in `UTC` with `en-US`, your laptop in its own, and a browser
takes both from its machine unless the Playwright config sets them.

Piwi records where each run executed, so you can read what differs and prove it before changing anything.

## 1. See what differs

The run page's **Environment** line names the runner's time zone, locale, OS and Node.js version. Click it for every
snapshot, shard by shard: the runner, each browser, each server under test
([what each records](/features/run-environment)).

Then put the failure next to a pass:

- **Your machine's run.** Report a run of the test from your machine to the same project, select it and the CI run
  on the project's **Runs** tab, and **Compare**: the **Changes** tab's **Environment changes** section lists the
  fields that differ ([comparing two runs](/features/run-changes#picking-another-baseline)).
- **The test's last pass.** The failing execution's **State** tab diffs its environment against the test's last
  passing execution ([which one](/features/run-changes#one-execution-s-baseline)).

The runner's fields need only the reporter. A browser's own time zone and locale need the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures): without them, the diff infers them from the config, else the runner, and
labels them so. A server under test answers only through an
[instrumentation package](/guide/backend-logs#server-environment). Nothing recorded, from an older reporter or with
collection off? Print the time zone and locale in a CI step and in your terminal:

```bash
node -e "console.log(Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions())"
```

## 2. Check whether it is the cause

A test that has ever passed on a retry has a **Flakiness** tab. Its suspects include the runner's time zone or
locale when the test's failures share one value and its passes another, which takes both sides in its
default-branch history: CI's failures, and passes reported from somewhere else, such as your machine
([how suspects are found](/features/flaky-tests#suspects)).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/flakiness-tab.png" alt="A flaky test's Flakiness tab: two suspects with their counts among failures and passes, the lab condition and result of each, the context a lab cannot apply, and the experiment that reproduced the flake">
  <figcaption>A test's suspects, each with the condition the Flake Lab applies to test it.</figcaption>
</figure>

A suspect is a correlation. The [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab) turns it into a verdict: it runs the test with the
browser in the suspect's time zone or locale, next to a control run, and says whether the failure reproduces.
**Copy command** on the tab gives the command, with the test's id:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter flake 1842
```

It needs the capture fixtures, which apply the condition inside the page, and the reporter's `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and
`PIWI_API_KEY`; the [desktop app](/features/flake-lab#in-the-desktop-app) runs it for you. The lab sets the browser
only, so a date your test code computes in Node.js does not follow it. Without the fixtures, for a test that fails on
every CI attempt and so has no Flakiness tab, or for a date computed outside the browser, the
[next step](#_3-reproduce-it-on-your-machine) is the same check by hand.

## 3. Reproduce it on your machine

Run the test with CI's time zone and `LANG`, as its runner snapshot shows them.

From Piwi, make them the project's [run variables](/features/run-variables): a project admin adds a `TZ` row and a
`LANG` row in **Project → Settings → Run variables**. Every run Piwi starts for the project then gets them:
[Run on my machine](/features/run-on-my-machine) from the desktop app or [Piwi Runner](/features/piwi-runner), and the
editors' runs. Every command Piwi gives to copy, such as a run's retry command, starts with them. Run on my machine
is experimental and off until an administrator turns it on; a copied command needs no app. Run variables apply to
everyone on the project, so remove the rows when you are done, unless CI's values should be everyone's.

Not a project admin, or not running it through Piwi: set them in the terminal.

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
TZ=UTC LANG=en_US.UTF-8 npx playwright test
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:TZ='UTC'; $env:LANG='en_US.UTF-8'; npx playwright test
```

:::

An `LC_ALL` set on your machine wins over `LANG`. On Windows, `LANG` changes the locale of neither Node.js nor the
browser, and a browser may not follow `TZ`: the PowerShell command reproduces neither reliably. Pin
`use.timezoneId` and `use.locale` in the config instead, the next step.

## 4. Fix it for good

Pin the browser's time zone and locale in the Playwright config, so the browser runs the same on every machine,
Windows included:

```ts
// playwright.config.ts
export default wrapConfig(
  defineConfig({
    use: { timezoneId: 'UTC', locale: 'en-US' },
  }),
);
```

They reach the browser only. A date your test code computes still follows the machine's `TZ`, and so does a server
the config starts: give that date an explicit `timeZone`, and set `TZ` in `webServer.env`.

If the failure is a bug your users in other time zones would meet, pinning hides it: test that zone on purpose, with
a Playwright project of its own. If the lab reproduced the failure, [`piwi flake verify`](/features/flake-lab#verify-a-fix)
proves the fix under the same condition.

## 5. When it is not the environment

If nothing differs, or running with CI's values still passes on your machine, the cause is elsewhere:

- **A server under test restarted during the run, or its clock is off the runner's.** The run's **Environment** line
  warns, and so does the State tab's diff ([the rule](/features/run-environment#where-it-shows)). A clock offset
  breaks token expiry and "created just now" checks. Both need the instrumentation package; without it, read the
  server's own logs.
- **The app under test was down.** Everything fails at once, fast, on a navigation or connection error. Piwi flags
  such a run as an [environment incident](/features/environment-incidents), and
  [Forty tests are red](./mass-failure) is the recipe.
- **CI is slower or busier.** A slow route, the load of the shard and a test running alongside can be suspects on
  the same Flakiness tab, and [Regression or flake?](./regression-or-flaky) tells a new failure from an old flake.

## Related

- [Run environment](/features/run-environment): what each snapshot records, and where it shows
- [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab): confirm a suspect by experiment, then verify the fix
- [Run variables](/features/run-variables): what they apply to, and the names they refuse
- [Regression or flake?](./regression-or-flaky): when the question is your change, not the machine

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/recipes/mass-failure -->

# Forty tests are red — where do I start?

Almost never with forty bugs. A run that goes broadly red is usually two or three causes wearing forty
costumes: an environment that didn't come up, an auth change, one shared component, one bad worker.
The job is to collapse the list before reading any stack traces.

## 1. Read the clusters, not the tests

Failures sharing an **error fingerprint** are grouped automatically, so the run tells you
*"forty failures, three root causes"* before you open anything.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/failure-clusters.png" alt="A red run's Tests tab grouped by cluster: one group per root cause with its test count, triage status and an Open cluster link, and the passing tests folded away">
  <figcaption>A red run's <strong>Tests</strong> tab opens grouped by <strong>Cluster</strong> — one group per root cause, with its triage status and a link to the cluster page.</figcaption>
</figure>

The grouping is always on and needs no configuration; [How failures are
grouped](/features/failure-clusters#how-failures-are-grouped) explains what the fingerprint masks.

## 2. Rule out the boring causes first

Before treating any cluster as a product bug, check the two flags on the run's failure groups. They come
from `get_failure_groups` over MCP or from the REST API; the dashboard doesn't show them.

- **Worker correlated** — two or more of the cluster's failures, all on one worker (one lane of one shard,
  whichever processes Playwright started in it), in a run that used several: you're looking at a misbehaving
  worker, or state a worker-scoped fixture holds, not forty broken tests. An account picked by `parallelIndex` is
  shared by that lane in every shard, which the flag doesn't join.
- **Flaky** — a test in the cluster passed on retry in this run: part of the cluster is noise riding on a
  bad run.

An environment that never came up has a signature of its own: everything fails, fast, on a navigation
or connection error. That's one cluster, one fix, and no test code involved.

## 3. Triage each cluster once

A [cluster page](/features/failure-clusters#the-cluster-page) puts the whole investigation on one screen, and its
**Triage**, beside the [state line](/features/failure-clusters#the-state-line), sets one status, note and assignee for
the entire group. Forty tests, three decisions.

Clusters stay open across runs, so the next red build attaches to the same row rather than starting the
conversation over.

## 4. Confirm the fix actually landed

When a later run executes every test a cluster covers and they all pass, Piwi records the fix; re-running just the
affected tests is enough. What counts as a fix, and its verdicts: [Did the fix
work?](/features/failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work).

## Optional: let a model do the first pass

With [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) configured, each cluster gets an explanation read against your
actual git diff since the [last green run](/features/run-changes#the-baseline), and any suggested patch is validated against your source
before it's shown. It's off by default and works with a local model — the point is that clustering has
already decided *what* is worth diagnosing, so the model runs a few times per run, not forty.

Configuring an **embedding** role also [merges clusters](/features/ai-diagnosis#semantic-merging-optional) that are
one root cause phrased differently. Without one, clustering stays deterministic.

## Other ways in

**From your agent.** `get_failure_groups` over the [MCP server](/features/mcp) returns a run's failures grouped
by cluster with the worker correlation included, and `get_test_case_context` pulls the evidence behind a
single failure — steps, console, network, SCM diff. No install; the server is part of the dashboard.

**From a script.** The same grouping is available over the REST API if you'd rather post a summary into
your own channel — see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api).

**Before anyone opens anything.** Subscribe to the `cluster.new` [notification](/features/notifications) event
instead of `run.failed`: you hear once when a genuinely new root cause appears, not on every red build,
and the payload carries a sample error excerpt and how many tests it affects.

## Related
- [Failure clusters](/features/failure-clusters): how failures are grouped, and whether the fix worked
- [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis): semantic merging and the explanation of a cluster
- [Regression or flake?](./regression-or-flaky) — when it's one test rather than forty
- [Core concepts](/guide/core-concepts) — *cluster*, *fingerprint*, *baseline*

# Our suite is unreliable and I have one afternoon

Flaky-test cleanup usually stalls for the same reason: the list is long, every entry looks equally
annoying, and there's no obvious first move. Ranking by flakiness score doesn't help much either — a
test that flakes constantly but finishes in milliseconds costs almost nothing.

Rank by what it *costs* instead, fix three, and leave the rest running.

## 1. Work by impact, not by score

The **Flaky** view of the project's **Failures** tab gives each test a [flakiness score](/features/flaky-tests#flaky-test-detection),
but lists the tests by **[impact](/features/flaky-tests#impact-ranking)**: what their retries cost in CI minutes.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/flaky-detection.png" alt="The Flaky view listing intermittent tests with wasted CI minutes, score, failure rate, top suspect, root cause, retry passes or flips and last flake, under root-cause filter chips and a runs-window selector">
  <figcaption>The Flaky view — ranked by impact, filterable by root cause, over a window of recent runs.</figcaption>
</figure>

Start at the top and work down. Each row's dot colors those minutes, and in a suite carrying real flake debt a few
red rows usually account for most of the total.

## 2. Filter by root cause and fix a class at once

Every flaky test carries a [root-cause category](/features/flaky-tests#root-cause-classification) (`timing`,
`network`, `assertion`, `environment`, `order` or `other`).

Filtering by category is the trick that makes an afternoon enough, because a class usually shares one fix: eight
`timing` flakes usually share one bad wait helper to replace with a real wait condition, a `network` class wants a
stub or a retry on the fixture rather than the test, and an `environment` class is a browser-specific guard or a real
compatibility bug.

## 3. Narrow the window before you conclude anything

Two filters change the answer, and both are worth setting deliberately:

- **Runs window**: one of the [lookback windows](/features/flaky-tests#flaky-test-detection), recent behavior or a
  longer history. A test fixed last week still looks awful over the longest.
- **Environment**: pick one in the project's **Filters** block and the analysis reads only its runs, so `staging`
  noise doesn't inflate a test that's stable in `production`.

## 4. Quarantine the rest — with an exit

You will not fix them all today, and disabling them is how suites rot. The usual
`--grep-invert @quarantine` approach stops the test running, so nothing ever proves it recovered and the
list only grows.

[Quarantine in Piwi](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) keeps the test running and reporting while it
stops blocking merges. Its passes build a streak that flags it **ready to release**, the Flaky view proposes the
**candidates** worth quarantining, and the gate can cap how many tests are in, so the list can't grow unbounded.
Promote the proposed candidates, and release the ready ones as they come.

## 5. Check the fix held

A flaky fix is easy to believe and hard to confirm. Each test case has a **stability trend** — pass
rate, flaky rate, and average duration bucketed over time — which is the honest answer to "did that
help?". If the suite-wide picture is what you need, [Analytics](/features/analytics) lifts the same signals
across every project, including wasted CI minutes and a global flaky leaderboard.

## Other ways in

**Ask your agent.** `list_flaky_tests` over the [MCP server](/features/mcp) returns each test's score, impact,
wasted CI minutes and root-cause category, highest score first; `get_test_stability_trend` answers whether one test is getting worse. Useful
for "what should I fix this sprint?" without opening a browser.

**Script it.** Quarantine is a REST resource, so promoting candidates or releasing ready tests can
be a scheduled job. Shapes are in the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api).

**No server at all.** If this is your own laptop suite rather than a team's, the
[desktop app](/features/desktop) runs the same analysis with no Docker and no Node, on the
[systems it is built for](/features/desktop#where-it-is), and the installers aren't signed yet.

## Related
- [Flaky tests](/features/flaky-tests) — the full scoring, quarantine, and performance reference
- [Analytics](/features/analytics) — the same signals across every project
- [Regression or flake?](./regression-or-flaky) — deciding whether one red test belongs on this list

# Failure evidence

Everything Piwi captured about a failing attempt lands on one screen, the **execution page** (`/test-run-cases/:id`).
This page covers its evidence: the card, clues, attempts, page diff and trace views. Its situation block is read on
[Your first failure, explained](/guide/first-failure); the test's history, on the
[test case page](#the-test-case-page) ([the two](/guide/concepts#execution)).

## One execution, diagnosis-first

A failing execution reads top to bottom in one column. It opens on the **situation block** (headline, most likely
cause, next step, cluster), described on [Your first failure, explained](/guide/first-failure).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/evidence-card.png" alt="The evidence card of a failing execution on its Timeline tab: the page's screencast as a Screen lane, then calls, steps, network, console and dialogs on one axis, then each step with its offset and duration, the failing click with the page at the failure">
  <figcaption>The evidence card on its Timeline tab: the page, every step, request, console entry and dialog on one axis, the failure marked.</figcaption>
</figure>

Below the block, one **evidence card** holds tabs, a count on those that list items, empty ones dimmed. It opens on **Source** or
**Performance** when a strong or medium leading clue cites it, else on **Timeline** when it can place two or more steps,
requests or console entries, else on the tab such a clue cites, else on **Screen** when a screenshot or video exists,
else on **Source**; a weak clue never picks it, and it never opens on **State**. A test that passed on retry opens on
**Attempts**, another passing one on **Timeline**; a link can name the tab (`?evidence=source`).

- **Timeline**: one time axis for the steps, console entries, requests, their backend logs and browser
  dialogs, with the failure marked, over a table giving each step's and request's offset (`t-1.1s`) and
  duration, colored only when it lasts at least 1 s and a third of the test, or twice its time in recent passing
  runs and 1 s more. **Around the failure** / **Whole test**, a drag across the axis and one chip per item type
  filter both. A trace adds a **Screen** lane per page: hover for the page then, click for its frames. **Show the
  page** puts it beside the steps for the hovered or picked row, in a card on hover, or as thumbnails; without a
  panel, a row's time opens it below. Hooks and fixtures fold into
  **Setup** and **Teardown** rows, open when the failure is there; what passed before the failure, but for the last
  three steps and any problem, folds into a **Passed** row; a `test.step` holds its steps; the failing step
  shows its error and its page's Screenshot, DOM and Accessibility tree; a caught error is greyed out; a
  [breakpoint](./editor-breakpoints)'s stop is a **Paused** band.
- **Attempts**: shown when a test ran more than once, see [below](#attempts).
- **Screen**: the page at the failure as views (**Screenshot**, **DOM**, **Accessibility tree**, **Visual diff**,
  [**Page diff**](#page-diff), **Video**) over the trace and attachments. **DOM** renders it as recorded (field values
  with passwords masked, scroll, dialogs, shadow DOM, focus, the mouse), with the action's target outlined. **Open in picker** finds a
  locator on that DOM. Enlarged, a screenshot's details give its attached name in full, with the expected result
  on a line of its own.
- **Source**: the test source as a call stack (the line that threw, with [Debug in my editor](./debug-in-editor), plus its callers), deepened
  [with a trace](#trace-powered-deep-views), then, with [coverage](./code-reach#on-the-execution-page), what the test
  ran.
- **Locators**: each locator the test used, in step order, with how many tests share it
  ([Locator usage](./locator-usage#the-locators-tab)).
- **Network**: the requests, API calls through Playwright's `request` fixture included, with inline
  [backend logs](/guide/backend-logs); one with no response shows the browser's error (`net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`). **Console**: the console output.
  **State**: the app state at test end and the [environment diff](./run-environment) against the [last green run](./run-changes#one-execution-s-baseline). **Performance**:
  performance hints and Web Vitals. **Output**: what the test wrote to stdout and stderr
  ([Test output](/reference/test-metadata#test-output)).

A test that **passed on retry** leads with its failed attempt's error and keeps its
next step; any other passing execution shows identity and facts. A test that **did not run** gives its reason as Most likely, with no evidence card. Network, console,
Web Vitals, ARIA, focus and alternative-locator data come from the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures).

### Clues

A **clue** is a one-line finding a deterministic rule draws from the evidence already captured, with no model
involved. Each carries a **strength** (strong, medium or weak) and a **citation** that opens and marks the evidence it
came from; the **Most likely** line marks the rows and tabs it cites. [Clue rules](/reference/clues) gives every rule
and [how **Most likely** picks](/reference/clues#most-likely) among the clues, the stories and the diagnosis.

### Attempts

When a test passed on retry, the **Attempts** tab lists every attempt (status and duration), then **what differed** between the failing and passing attempts, most diagnostic first:

- the **error** present on the failing attempt and gone on the pass;
- a **request**, keyed by route (`GET /api/cart/:id`), that failed (5xx or no response) on one attempt only, or took
  at least 1 s and twice as long on the failing one;
- a **console** error, warning or page error on one attempt;
- a **step** that errored, ran much slower, or ran with different **params** on one attempt;
- a **page-state or URL** difference, including storage keys and cookies;
- an **ARIA structural** difference at the landmark and heading level.

Each difference links to its evidence tab, a request that is one of the test's [suspects](./flaky-tests#suspects) to
it. The comparison feeds the [root-cause classifier](./flaky-tests#root-cause-classification).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/attempt-diff.png" alt="An execution's Attempts tab: the failed and the passed attempt, then what differed between them: an error only on the failing attempt, a request taking 1.8 s on the failing attempt against 97 ms on the passing one, a step that errored only there">
  <figcaption>What differed between a failing attempt and the passing retry.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Page diff

Where the visual diff compares pixels, the Screen tab's **Page diff** view compares *structure*: it parses the failing
page's [ARIA snapshot](/guide/capture-fixtures#what-gets-captured) and the same test's last passing snapshot into trees
and reports nodes **added**, **removed**, **renamed**, **changed** (an attribute such as `[disabled]` flipped) or
**moved**. The element the failing locator names
is highlighted: a broken `getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })` lands on the button renamed `"Pay now"`.

The baseline is the same test's latest passing snapshot on the same browser, preferring the same environment, then
Playwright release, then branch. Green snapshots come from
[sampling on pass](/guide/capture-fixtures#green-page-sampling-on-pass), about once a day per test; until one exists the
view says why (*not captured*, *no green sample yet* or *not applicable*). The page-diff summary reaches the
`explain_failure` [MCP tool](/features/mcp).

When the trace carries [aria snapshots](#aria-and-screen-snapshots), the view adds an **in-execution** page diff
that needs no green baseline: the structure at the failure against the last different page before the failing action.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/page-diff.png" alt="The Screen tab in its Page diff view: against the last green run, the Pay button of the Checkout form was renamed Pay now and became disabled, and the failing locator points there">
  <figcaption>Page diff: the failing page against the last green run, one changed button.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Trace-powered deep views

::: tip Where screenshots come from
Failure screenshots come from Playwright's `screenshot: 'only-on-failure'` [option](/guide/reporter#basic-configuration), one per page. The failing step shows the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures#what-gets-captured)' screenshot of the failing page, else the only one.
:::

With an uploaded trace (`trace: 'retain-on-failure'` or `'on-first-retry'`), these views go deeper:

- **Source → Full stack**: the failing action's whole call stack, each frame with its source,
  dependency frames folded, Open in editor on your project's frames.
- **Network → Full trace**: every request the page made, on a waterfall with the failing action's window shaded, with
  timing phases, headers and a capped body preview. Sensitive headers and token-shaped strings are masked on the server.

### Aria and screen snapshots

A Playwright 1.63 trace can record the page's **aria tree** and a **screenshot** before and after every action
(`trace.snapshots.aria` and `.screen`), both off in [`wrapConfig`](/guide/reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig)'s trace
([their cost](/reference/reporter-options#defaultcapture)). Screenshots set the page **before the failing
action** beside the one at the failure in the Screenshot view, and add a **filmstrip** of the page before each step to
the Timeline tab where no Screen lane shows. Aria trees show the page at the failing action in the Accessibility tree view, and add the
[in-execution page diff](#page-diff).

### Recovered from the trace without the fixtures

With the reporter alone and a trace uploaded, the dashboard recovers the **console** entries, the **network requests**
(failed and aborted included) and the failure-time **ARIA snapshot** at ingest. Cards showing
it carry a **derived from the trace** chip; fixture-captured data is never replaced.

## Trace viewer

**Open trace**, atop the evidence card, opens the Playwright trace viewer; the Screen tab lists each trace with **Open trace** and **Download**. The dashboard serves the viewer at `/trace-viewer/`, so traces stay on your
server, with or without [authentication](/operate/authentication). The hosted
`trace.playwright.dev` can't send your session cookie, so it needs authentication off.

## The test case page

`/test-cases/:id` covers the test's whole life: total [runs](/guide/concepts#test-case), [pass rate](/guide/concepts#pass-rate), average duration
and last run, a duration trend, a status-history strip, and the recent executions, each linking back to its execution.
A flaky test adds a **Flakiness** tab with its [suspects](./flaky-tests#suspects).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/tour-test-history.png" alt="A test case page: run stats, the duration trend with a status strip under it, and the recent executions">
  <figcaption>The test case page: stats, a duration trend over the status strip, and every recent execution.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › should complete checkout with credit card](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-run-cases/37): Every tab of the evidence card filled: the timeline marks the failing click, the Page diff shows the Pay button renamed and disabled.
