# Run video

A finished run has a **Video** tab, labelled with the number of tests that have a video (**Video (12)**). It plays the
videos Playwright recorded for the run, one test after another, beside a checklist of the tests. A test is ticked as its
video passes the end of the test, so you can follow a worker's run as it happened. The bar under the video has one block
for each test, colored by its result. Click a test or the bar to jump there: while the video is paused it shows that
frame and stays paused, and while it plays it keeps playing from there. The video, the bar and the marks under it fit
the screen without scrolling the page; only the list of tests scrolls.

## Group by Worker or File

- **Worker** plays one worker's tests in the order they ran. Pick the worker above the video.
- **File** plays every test in the order its file declares it, each marked with the worker it ran on. The tests ran in
  parallel, so this order is not the order they ran in.

Only the final attempt of a test is listed. A test that has no video stays on the checklist and takes a small block on
the bar. It is ticked as the reel moves on. The tab is off while the run is live.

## Search the checklist

The box above the checklist finds tests by their title, the way the **Tests** tab's search reads words (case and accents
ignored, `"…"` for a phrase, `*` for anything, `-` to leave a word out). The list keeps the tests that match, with the
matched words marked, and the line above it says how many match. Searching only hides rows: the video, the bar, the
ticks and the marks stay as they were, and a click on a test still jumps there. The search stays when you pick
another worker or group by file. The **x** in the box clears it.

## Maximize the video

**Maximize**, beside the Worker and File switch, opens the same video review window the Evidence uses, with the switch,
the worker picker, the search and the checklist. They are the tab's own: what you pick there is still picked when you
close the window with **Esc** or the close button. Only one video plays, and each side starts on the test the other
was on. On a narrow screen the window fills it.

## Open a video review from Evidence

On a finished execution that has a video, the Evidence header has an **Open video review** button, beside **Open trace**.
It opens the video with the same bar and checklist as the Video tab, in a window that fills a narrow screen. The window's
switch picks what plays, and it starts on **This test**:

- **This test** plays only that test, from the start of its video to its end, and stops. The file's other tests stay on
  the checklist, dimmed, and are not played.
- **Whole file** plays the file's final attempts in declared order, each marked with its worker, and starts on this test.
- **Its worker** plays the tests of this test's worker, in the order they ran, and starts on this test. A sharded run
  keeps each shard's workers apart.

In these two modes only the tests that play are ticked, and **Play** after the end starts again from this test. The
opened test is marked **This test** in every mode. Closing the window stops the video.

Only final attempts that ran are in the file and worker reels. On an earlier attempt or a skipped test, This test plays
its own video and the other two modes are off, with the reason shown under the switch. A run lists at most 2,000 tests
with a video, so a test past that limit also keeps only This test.

## Actions under the video

Under the bar, a lane of marks shows what the playing test did and when: one mark for each click, double click, fill,
type, key press, check, uncheck, select, hover and navigation, placed on the video where it happened. It shows on the
Video tab and in the Evidence video review.

- Point at a mark, or move to it with the keyboard, to read the action and its locator, for example
  `Click getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })`. Choose a mark to go there; it plays on only if the video was playing.
- An action that failed has a red mark.
- Marks less than 28 px apart merge into one mark with a count, so every mark keeps its own hit area. Its tooltip lists them.
- An action outside the video is shown at the nearest edge of the lane, with a note in its tooltip.
- A test with more than 500 actions shows the first 500, and the lane says how many there are.

The marks come from what the project already stores. A test with a [trace](./evidence) uses the trace's actions, and any
other test uses its step list, so there is nothing to switch on. A test with neither shows "No recorded actions for this
test". A test that recorded actions but not when it started shows "This test did not record when it started, so its
actions cannot be placed in the video", since there is nothing to place them by. A failed load is one muted line; the
video plays either way.

Piwi does not show what a test typed. The server masks each action before it sends it, and a locator is shown as the test
wrote it:

| Action | Shown |
|---|---|
| Fill, type | The locator and "typed N chars", never the text. "typed text", with no count, for a password, card or code field, or when no field is named |
| Press | A named key or a shortcut, such as `Enter` or `Control+A`; a single character, alone or behind Shift or Alt, shows as "a key" |
| Navigate | The origin and path, without the query string, fragment or credentials; a path segment shaped like a token is hidden |
| Check, uncheck, select | The locator only, never the chosen option |

## When there are no videos

Most suites record video only for failing tests (`video: 'retain-on-failure'`), so a run where nothing failed often has
none. The tab is then disabled, with the tooltip "no videos in this run". Set `video: 'on'` in Playwright's `use`
options to record every test. Playwright 1.61 adds `retain-on-first-failure`, `on-all-retries` and
`retain-on-failure-and-retries`, for a video of the first failure or of the retries alone, and 1.64 an `fps` option
(`video: { mode: 'retain-on-failure', fps: 30 }`) for smoother animations and scrolling, at more CPU. Videos can be
large, so read [storage cleanup](/operate/storage#storage-management) first.

## Related

- [Failure evidence](./evidence): one failing execution, with its trace, screenshots and video
- [Storage](/operate/storage#storage-management): how long videos are kept

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/failure-clusters -->

# Failure clusters

How Piwi groups failures by root cause into **failure clusters**, where a cluster stands and whether its fix worked.
Triaging the open ones from Home is on [Failure inbox](./failure-inbox), a model's explanation on
[AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis), fixing on [Fix plans](./fix-plans).

## How failures are grouped

Failed executions sharing an **error fingerprint** join one cluster: *"20 failures, 3 root causes"*. Always on, the
fingerprint hashes the error type, message and locator, **masking what varies**:
numbers, UUIDs, hashes, ids glued to an underscore (`order_5f3a9c1e2b`), URLs, emails, timestamps, the folders of a
path under a home folder, CI workspace or Windows drive, a temporary folder's random suffix, an assertion's *expected*
and *received* values, the elements a strict-mode violation lists, and dynamic locator options such as a row's
`{ name: '…' }`. The locator's target (test id, role) still tells failures apart: the first call of its chain, or for
a locator inside a frame, the chain up to the first locator in the frame
(`locator('iframe').first().contentFrame().getByLabel('Card number')`, with `frameLocator()` for any frame).
`frameLocator('#pay')` and `locator('#pay').contentFrame()` are one frame.

It **ignores the failing stack frame** when the error says what failed, so one root cause reached from several spec
files, through a helper or page object, stays one cluster. A **generic** error says nothing of its own: it names no
locator, and its message is an `expect(…)` matcher whose values are all masked, a test timeout, or a bare `TypeError`
or `ReferenceError` line. Its fingerprint also hashes the file of its failing stack frame (the spec, or the helper).

A cluster keeps its first error, so an improved normalization **regroups clusters in place** with their triage,
notes, diagnoses and merges. A run's **Tests** tab groups failures by cluster;
[`get_failure_groups`](/reference/mcp-tools#get_failure_groups) adds a **worker-correlation** flag ("worker 3 is
misbehaving").

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/failure-clustering-fingerprint.svg" alt="The fingerprint pipeline: a raw error is normalized, hashed and routed to one cluster">
</figure>

With an embedding model, near-duplicates the fingerprint keeps apart are merged too
([semantic merging](./ai-diagnosis#semantic-merging-optional)). **A merge never buries a live failure**: the survivor
ends open when either cluster was open and not snoozed, takes the other's assignee when it has none, appends its note,
and inherits its tickets, fix attempts, tracker history and the merges decided against.

### Split a cluster by hand

When some tests fail with the same error for another reason, select them in **Affected tests** and choose **Move to a
new cluster** (Maintainer or above; no AI). Their failures move to a new cluster with your note, the old one gains a
line naming the move, their later failures with that error join the new one, and the two never merge automatically.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/failure-clusters-tab.png" alt="A project's Failures tab: its open clusters with type, triage, tests and occurrences">
</figure>

## The failure inbox

Home's failure inbox lists the open clusters you still owe a decision, in queues: [Failure inbox](./failure-inbox).

### Queues

What puts a cluster in each queue of the inbox: [Failure inbox → Queues](./failure-inbox#queues).

### Triage from the row or the keyboard

The inbox's row actions, keys and bulk bar:
[Failure inbox → Triage from the row or the keyboard](./failure-inbox#triage-from-the-row-or-the-keyboard).

## Owners and assignees

A cluster's **owner** is derived: the failing test's `piwi:owner` annotation, else, on the cluster and execution pages
(not the inbox), the repository's `CODEOWNERS`. An **assignee** overrides it. **Mine** matches either against your
name, username or email.

## The cluster page

Top to bottom:

1. The [situation block](/guide/first-failure) across every test sharing the failure, headed by the latest failure's
   headline when it says more than the cluster's name. Its own lines:
   - **the state line**, right above **Next**;
   - **the occurrence sparkline**: *N occurrences in M tests over D · last X ago*, naming a single test,
     *quarantined* if it is ([quarantine](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out));
   - **What changed**: commits and files since the last passing run (or your baseline), the diff, and with
     [coverage](./server-coverage) the first [suspect line](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines). Missing setup shows what to
     set up ([troubleshooting](/guide/source-control#troubleshooting)); **Browse commits** picks a baseline when none
     passed. One commit on both sides: the change is not in the code. A cluster first seen in a
     [deployed environment](./deployed-environments#the-first-failing-deploy) leads with its first failing deploy.
2. The [occurrence chart](#occurrences-over-time) and the activity, folded.
3. The section **Next** points at (the AI diagnosis, the locator fix…) as its own card, then the one line of
   [**More ways to fix**](./fix-plans#more-ways-to-fix), each other way to fix opening in a side panel.
4. **Affected tests**, picking whose evidence shows, then that evidence, last: nothing follows it.

### The state line

**One sentence with one verb**, beside a colored dot: *still failing*, *not seen for N runs*, *fixed and verified,
still open*, *fixed, but the diagnosed patch still applies at the fix's commit*, *stopped failing*, *regressed, the fix
did not hold*, *resolved*, *ignored*, *snoozed* or *all tests quarantined*. It reconciles the triage status with the
[verdict](#did-the-fix-work), offering **the one action** closing a gap unless **Next** does:
*Mark resolved* (an open cluster stopped failing, or its ticket is Done and the failure stopped; a fix whose patch
still applies keeps it in the **Next** menu), *Unsnooze*, or *Release* (all tests quarantined). **Triage** sets the
status (open / resolved / ignored), note and assignee, and [snoozes](#snoozing); a status change keeps the note, a
note edit the status.

#### Which runs count

*Not seen for N runs* counts finished runs since the last failure, on its branch or the default branch, that ran the
cluster's tests without that failure: never a Flake Lab run, bisect step, reproduction or
[environment incident](./environment-incidents). A skipped, not-run or interrupted test was not run. A whole-suite run
that reached its end counts even when a cluster test no longer exists; one stopped early (interrupted, cancelled, timed
out, `maxFailures`) only if it ran the cluster's tests. A Done ticket's failure has stopped once such a run follows.

### Occurrences over time

A chart of failures per day, week or month since first seen, marking the **fix landed**; the sparkline opens it.

## Did the fix work?

When a run executes every test of a cluster and all pass, Piwi records the fix (run, commit, time open) and a verdict:

- **Stopped failing**: the tests pass again, which a flaky test can do by accident.
- **Diagnosis verified**: the commits since the last failing run touched a file the
  [suggested patch](./ai-diagnosis#validated-patches) named.
- **Regressed**: a fix was recorded, and the cluster fails again.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/ci-rerun-last-run.png" alt="A cluster's Verify section: its last re-run, dispatched to Jenkins, links the run that answered it, which passed">
  <figcaption>The Verify section: the last re-run in CI and the run that answered it.</figcaption>
</figure>

**A fix needs every affected test to pass** in the Playwright projects it last failed in that the run ran (a `--grep`
over them is enough), in a run started after the last failing run, at another commit (a pass at the failing commit,
such as a CI retry, is flake evidence the state line names), on the cluster's last failing branch or the default
branch: a green pull-request branch leaves a cluster failing on `main` open. **A regression needs a run started after
the fix landed**, failing on its branch or the default branch.

**Projects.** A project the run left out but its config lists (another CI job runs it) says nothing; one the config
no longer lists (removed, renamed) does not count, and a test that last failed only there is answered by a pass in any
project. CI jobs loading different project lists (a config per job, a list from a variable) thus record a fix from any
job where the tests pass: give them one list, and pick each job's projects with `--project`.

Only strong evidence moves the status. *Diagnosis verified* resolves an **open** cluster at once, so *fixed and
verified, still open* reads only once something reopened it (a person, or a merge with a live cluster). *Regressed*
reopens a **resolved** cluster, as does a new failure after a person resolved one with no fix on record; each adds a
note line. *Stopped failing* changes nothing; an *ignored* cluster is never touched. The `cluster.fixed` and
`cluster.regressed` [notifications](./notifications) follow the verdict, and the [pull-request](./pr-feedback)
comment gains **Fixed by this change**, even with *only comment on failures*.

## Snoozing

**Snoozing** hides a cluster from every [inbox queue](./failure-inbox#queues), status untouched. **1 day** and
**1 week** return it then; **Until it recurs** returns it to **New** when a run fails it, badged **snoozed, back**
until your next visit.

## From an AI agent

Over the [MCP server](/features/mcp), `list_open_clusters` lists the open clusters by
[inbox queue](./failure-inbox#from-an-ai-agent), and each action above has a [tool](/reference/mcp-tools):
`triage_cluster`, `decide_merge_suggestion`, `move_tests_to_new_cluster`, `rerun_cluster_in_ci`, `link_issue` and
`unlink_issue`.

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › the Pay button times out](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/1): Two checkout tests failing for one reason, in one cluster with its owner; a fix landed once and did not hold.

- [Triage a run gone red](/recipes/mass-failure): a red run collapsed into causes
- [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis): a cluster explained against your diff

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/failure-inbox -->

# Failure inbox

The **Failure inbox** on Home lists the open [failure clusters](./failure-clusters) you still owe a decision, sorts
them into queues, and lets you triage each one from its row or the keyboard. What a cluster is, how failures join one
and whether its fix worked is on [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters).

## What it lists

The inbox lists up to 50 open clusters of the projects you can see, most recently seen first. Each row shows the
cluster's **headline**, its **top clue**, its **owner or assignee**, the **affected tests**, when it was **last
seen**, and exceptional **badges** only (a regression on the default branch, *snoozed, back*).

- **Local runs.** A cluster seen only in developers' local runs, in a project that runs in CI, stays out; **Show
  them** lists them, marked *local runs only*.
- **Environment incidents.** The clusters a run flagged as an
  [environment incident](./environment-incidents#what-a-flagged-run-changes) opened are one row for that run.
- **Snoozed clusters** are out of every queue until their [snooze](./failure-clusters#snoozing) ends.

### Queues

Each queue has a live count and is shareable as `?queue=`:

- **All open**: every open cluster not snoozed.
- **New**: first seen, or seen again, since your previous browser session (kept per browser).
- **Mine**: assigned to you, or owned by you ([owners and assignees](./failure-clusters#owners-and-assignees)).
- **Needs ticket**: untracked default-branch clusters older than the binding's age (2 days by default; see
  [issue tracking](./issue-tracking)).
- **Regressions**: regressed on the default branch, failing there still.
- **Fix didn't hold**: a fix landed, then [regressed](./failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work).
- **Quarantine ready**: [quarantined](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out), and the tests stopped failing.
- **Merge suggestions**: in a pending [merge suggestion](./ai-diagnosis#semantic-merging-optional).

### Triage from the row or the keyboard

Open, resolve, ignore, quarantine, assign, snooze, link a known issue or create a tracker issue from the row, by mouse
or [key](/reference/keyboard-shortcuts#failure-inbox); `x` selects rows for a **bulk bar**. Resolve, ignore,
quarantine, assign and snooze need the Maintainer role or above on the project; linking a known issue and creating a
tracker issue need Contributor.

Resolve, ignore, snooze and assign on one row can be undone for a few seconds. A known issue pins a URL; with an
[issue tracker](/operate/integrations) bound, Jira links unfurl and stay in sync ([issue tracking](./issue-tracking)).

## From an AI agent

Over the [MCP server](/features/mcp), `list_open_clusters` takes the same `queue`, and each triage action has a
[tool](/reference/mcp-tools): `triage_cluster`, `decide_merge_suggestion`, `link_issue` and `unlink_issue`.

## Related

- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters): how failures are grouped, the cluster page, and whether the fix worked
- [Triage a run gone red](/recipes/mass-failure): a red run collapsed into causes
- [Keyboard shortcuts](/reference/keyboard-shortcuts#failure-inbox): every key of the inbox
- [Issue tracking](./issue-tracking): the tickets behind **Needs ticket** and a known issue

# Environment incidents

When the environment under test is down, every test fails at once: staging refuses connections, a DNS name stops
resolving, the browser crashes on a starved runner. None of those failures says anything about the tests or the code.
Piwi recognizes such a run as an **environment incident**, says so on the run page, and keeps it out of every verdict
that compares runs.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/environment-incident.png" alt="A run flagged as an environment incident: the reason, the rule that decided, and the action to clear the flag">
  <figcaption>A run flagged as an environment incident, with the rule that decided.</figcaption>
</figure>

## How a run is recognized

When a run finishes, Piwi reads what it already stored: how many tests failed, what each failure was doing, and the
host of the run's Playwright `baseURL`. A run is flagged by one of three rules:

| Rule | Flags the run when |
|---|---|
| `host-unreachable` | At least 80% of the executed tests failed, and at least 70% of the failures were navigating or connecting to the app's host |
| `browser-crash` | At least 80% of the executed tests failed, and at least 70% of the failures were the browser crashing or closing |
| `cross-project` | At least 50% of the executed tests failed, most failures reached the app's host or share one error, and the same host or error failed in another project's run that started within 30 minutes |

A failure counts as reaching the host when it is a network error (`net::ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`, a name that does not
resolve, a reset connection, `ECONNREFUSED` from a request fixture) or a `page.goto` that timed out, and the address
it names is the host of the run's `baseURL`. With no `baseURL` recorded, the host most failures reached stands in for
it.

A failure whose error names no such address also counts when the network capture of its execution (recorded by the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures)) holds a request to the `baseURL` host that got no answer: a network error
such as a refused connection, or a `502`, `503` or `504` from a gateway in front of the app. That catches an API that
is down behind a page that still loads, where the tests fail on assertions. A `500` is the app answering, and an
aborted route (`net::ERR_FAILED`) is the test's own doing, so neither counts. Piwi reads the capture of at most 500
failing executions per run, and a failure whose capture it did not read counts as not reaching the host.

A third-party host going down (a CDN, an analytics script) does not count, and neither does a failing assertion whose
requests were answered, however many tests it breaks: a login page broken by a commit is a regression, not an
incident. A run with fewer than three failing tests is never flagged.

A [probe](./probes) or [Flake Lab](./flake-lab) run is never judged: it injects its failures on purpose.

## What a flagged run changes

- **The run page** says *Environment incident · not counted*, the reason (*41 of 44 tests failed, 39 of them
  navigating or connecting to staging.example.test (connection refused)*), and which rule decided.
- **Flaky scores, baselines, fix verification, the selection catalog, the editor's CI failures and auto-heal** leave
  the run out. A test that failed only in the incident does not become flaky, does not lose its last green run, and
  does not count as a regression. The run gets no regression signals.
- **One timeline marker** in the `incident` category, labeled *Environment incident: staging.example.test* and linked
  to the run, so the gap on the trend charts has a visible cause (unless `PIWI_AUTO_MARKERS=false`). See
  [Timeline markers](./timeline-markers).
- **One notification**, [`environment.incident`](/reference/notification-events), in place of the run's failure,
  flakiness, performance and new-cluster events. It goes to the project's subscribers, not to a subscription scoped to
  test owners. `run.finished` still fires. When one outage flags runs in several projects, a channel that hears from
  all of them receives one message.
- **The [failure inbox](./failure-inbox)** on Home shows one row for the run instead of one row per new cluster it opened. Clusters that
  were already open before the incident keep their rows, and a cluster it opened gets its own row once a run that is
  no incident fails it again.
- **No AI diagnosis, no pull-request comment and no issue tracker write** are produced for the run
  ([which runs send nothing](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin)).

The run's history stays: its executions, evidence and clusters are kept like any other run's, and analytics still
count it as a failed run.

## The CI gate

The [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-it-leaves-out) gives a flagged run the verdict **inconclusive**,
whatever the policy says, and exits with code `3`, so a pipeline can tell "the environment was down, re-run" from
"the change broke something" (`1`):

```text
? Piwi gate inconclusive — checkout run #930
  44 tests, 41 failed, 0 new, 0 newly flaky, 0 flaky
  ? The run is an environment incident: 41 of 44 tests failed, 39 of them navigating or connecting to staging.example.test (connection refused).
  Re-run once the environment is back, or clear the flag on the run page if it is wrong.
```

## Stopping a run before it starts

With the reporter option [`checkBaseUrl`](/reference/reporter-options#checkbaseurl), the reporter checks that each
`baseURL` of the run's projects answers before any worker starts. When one does not (a refused connection, a name
that does not resolve, no answer in 10 seconds, or a `502`, `503` or `504`, on each of three tries), the run stops
with a message naming it and Playwright's failure exit code. No test runs, so the outage costs no CI time, and no run
reaches the dashboard. The option is off by default, and the check runs before the config's own `globalSetup`, so
leave it off when that setup is what starts the app.

The check runs from the machine that runs Playwright. A browser on a grid (`connectOptions`) reaches the app from the
grid's network instead, unless the `exposeNetwork` rule covers the app's host and port. For such a base URL, the reporter says
so: in the stop message when the check fails, and in a line of the run's output when it passes. A run whose tests then
fail to navigate may have hit a gap between the two networks rather than an app that is down.

## Marking and clearing by hand

The rules can miss an outage or flag a real regression. Anyone who can upload or control the project's runs
(Uploader, Maintainer and above) can decide instead:

- **Mark as an environment incident**, in the run header's **Details**, for a run the rules did not flag (the payment
  sandbox was down, a shared account was locked). The run is left out of the same verdicts and gets its marker.
- **Clear the flag**, on a flagged run, when its failures are real. The incident marker is removed and the run counts
  again: its regression signals are computed, and it feeds flaky scores and baselines from then on.

Either decision is kept on the run, and finalizing the run again (a late shard, a report upload) never overrides it.
The run page says who decided. The same action is in the [API reference](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api), and an
agent makes it with the MCP tool [`set_run_incident`](/reference/mcp-tools#set_run_incident), which needs a key whose
owner may make the same change in the dashboard and is kept in the [write log](./mcp).

## Limits

- The check runs once, when the run finishes. A run in another project that finishes later is compared with this one
  and names it, but this run's flag is not revisited.
- An incident that hits only part of the suite (one service down, 30% of the tests failing) stays below the
  thresholds: mark it by hand.
- Clearing or marking a run after it finished does not send the notifications it skipped, or withdraw the ones it
  sent.

## Try it in the demo

The [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) holds an incident run, and its run simulator streams one: pick
**Staging down** in **Simulate a test run**, and the run is flagged as it finishes.

- [E2E Checkout › a run against staging while it was down](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-runs/14): Ten of eleven tests failed navigating to staging, so the run is an environment incident: not counted, with one incident marker.

# Run environment

Piwi records where each run executed, so "it fails on CI but not on my machine" and "it broke when the runner image
changed" become facts the dashboard shows. The reporter records three kinds of snapshot, each a closed list of fields:
no environment variable is copied whole.

| Snapshot | One per | Fields |
|---|---|---|
| **Runner** | shard | time zone, `TZ`, locale, `LANG` / `LC_ALL` / `LC_TIME`, OS and distribution, architecture, Node.js and ICU versions, CI runner image, container; host name, CPU and memory |
| **Browser** | shard and project | browser version, time zone, locale, languages, how it formats a number and a date, color scheme and reduced motion, headless; screen and user agent |
| **Server** | instrumented origin | runtime, OS, time zone, culture, globalization mode, environment name, app version; app commit, host name, process, start time, clock offset from the runner |

The browser snapshot needs the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures): it is read from the test's page before the
test navigates. The server snapshot needs an [instrumentation package](/guide/backend-logs#server-environment). The
last fields of each row (after the semicolon) change by nature between runs and are never shown as a possible cause.
`collectEnvironmentInfo: false` in the reporter options, or `PIWI_COLLECT_ENVIRONMENT_INFO=false`, turns it all off.

## The application's commit

A server snapshot names the version of its application (`appVersion`) and the commit it was built from (`appCommit`,
7 to 40 hexadecimal characters, else nothing), which tell a run of a [deployed environment](./deployed-environments) which code
it tested:

- **ASP.NET Core**: `appCommit` from the `PiwiTestLogsOptions.AppCommit` option, else `PIWI_APP_COMMIT`, else the full
  commit the .NET SDK writes into the entry assembly's informational version (`1.4.0+4e6f516…`), which is `appVersion`.
- **Nitro**: the options of `piwiPlugin({ appVersion, appCommit })`, exported from the server plugin file in place of
  the default export, else `PIWI_APP_VERSION` and `PIWI_APP_COMMIT`, else, for the commit, the hosting platform's
  variable (`VERCEL_GIT_COMMIT_SHA`, `RENDER_GIT_COMMIT`, `RAILWAY_GIT_COMMIT_SHA`, `SOURCE_COMMIT`).

Instrumentation is off in production by default, so no server snapshot names production's commit: its deploy pipeline
records it with a [deploy marker](./timeline-markers#recording-deploys-from-ci) instead.

## Where it shows

- **Run page**: the **Environment** line under the versions opens every snapshot, shard by shard. It warns when the
  shards disagree (two runner images, two time zones), when a server restarted during the run, and when a server's
  clock is more than 2 s off the runner's, enough to break token expiry and "created just now" checks.
- **Changes tab**: the runner, browser and server fields that changed against the baseline run, grouped, with every
  value of a field the shards disagree on.
- **Execution page**: the environment diff of the **State** tab, against the test's last pass. A browser time zone or
  locale the page did not report is _inferred_ from the declared value, else the runner's, and labeled so.
- **Trend charts**: an automatic marker on the run where the runner, a browser or a server changed, against the
  previous run on the same branch and environment label.
- **Flakiness tab**: the runner's time zone and locale become [flake suspects](/features/flaky-tests#suspects) when the failures
  share one and the passes another; the [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab) runs the browser in it to confirm. The runner
  image and the browser version are listed as context.
- **MCP**: `get_run` returns the run's `environments`.

A run from an older reporter, or with collection off, shows nothing: it was never recorded, and is never read as a
change. Host names are left out of exports and share links.

## Fails on CI, passes locally

A CI runner usually runs in `UTC` with `en-US`, a laptop in its own time zone and language, and a browser takes both
from the machine unless the config sets `use.timezoneId` and `use.locale`. To reproduce a CI failure locally, run with
CI's values:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
TZ=UTC LANG=en_US.UTF-8 npx playwright test
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:TZ='UTC'; $env:LANG='en_US.UTF-8'; npx playwright test
```

:::

On Windows, `LANG` changes the locale of neither Node.js nor the browser, and a browser may not follow `TZ`, so the
PowerShell command reproduces neither reliably: set `use.timezoneId` and `use.locale` in the Playwright config
instead.
[Fails on CI, passes locally](/recipes/fails-on-ci) walks through it from the run page to the fix.

- [Flake Lab](./flake-lab): confirm a time zone or locale suspect by experiment.

# Flaky tests & quarantine

A single run tells you what failed; a few dozen tell you what's *unreliable*. This page covers what Piwi computes
for one project from its history: the flaky score, its ranking and suspects, quarantine and the regression signals.
Testing a suspect by experiment is on [Flake Lab](./flake-lab); the same signals across every project, on
[Analytics](./analytics).

## Flaky test detection

A test is flaky when its result isn't deterministic. Piwi computes a **flakiness score** (1–100) per test from two signals, weighted 60/40:

- **Retry passes** — failed, then passed on retry (each `--repeat-each` repetition on its own).
- **Status alternation** — flips between pass and fail; other outcomes ignored.

The **failure rate** is shown but not scored. Only runs where the test passed or failed count, and a test is listed
once it has 3 of them in the window, with a retry pass or two flips.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/flakiness-score.svg" alt="A test's last 10 runs with 2 retry passes and 4 flips give a score of 30; its impact is 0.7 times 3 wasted CI minutes plus 0.3 times a fixed weight of 30 times 2 retry passes, 20">
  <figcaption>The score and the impact ranking, computed for one test.</figcaption>
</figure>

The project's **Failures** tab has a **Flaky** view with a **lookback window** of 20, 50 or 100 runs. Each flaky test links to its history and, unless already quarantined, offers **Quarantine**.

**Scoping**: only runs within the project's **Filters** count: environment (the [default environment](./environments#default-environment) unless picked), branch (the [default branch](./branches#the-default-branch) unless picked) and full runs only.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/flaky-detection.png" alt="The Flaky view of a project’s Failures tab, listing tests with composite score, failure rate, retry passes, and flip counts">
  <figcaption>The Flaky view: each intermittent test scored and ranked by impact, with its top suspect.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Root-cause classification

Every flaky test is tagged with one of six categories, using keyword and distribution heuristics over its errors, steps, and browser spread, sharpened by the failed requests actually captured and by the [attempt diff](./evidence#attempts). It reads the test's last 100 failed attempts and its last 100 passes from any run, green or red, so the failed attempt of a test that passed on retry counts, and a rare flake keeps its failures however many passes came since:

| Category | Typical signals |
|----------|-----------------|
| `timing` | Timeouts, "to be visible", `waitFor`, element-not-found-within |
| `network` | `net::` / `ERR_` errors, 5xx responses, `ECONNREFUSED`, `waitForResponse` — plus the count of failed and 5xx requests captured on the failing attempts, and any request that failed on the failing attempt but not the passing one |
| `assertion` | `expect(...)`, "Expected:", snapshot/screenshot comparison — with no timing/network noise |
| `environment` | Fails at least 3 times on exactly one browser, or one runner time zone or locale, while another passed at least 3 times without failing |
| `order` | Its code path changes with whether another test ran before it in the run, and its failures follow that change ([coverage insights](./coverage-insights#a-path-that-depends-on-the-tests-before-it)) |
| `other` | No clear signal |

A test is classified when it passes on retry in a finished run, and a listed test still without a category when the
list opens.

Filter the flaky table by category to triage a class of failures at once.

### Suspects

A flaky test's **Flakiness** tab lists its **suspects**: what its failures share and its passes do not,
over its last 30 days (at most 200 attempts, from the runs the flaky list reads).

| Factor | Measured per attempt |
|--------|----------------------|
| Slow route | a request's slowest duration, over the threshold that best separates failures from passes |
| Failed route | a request answering 5xx, or with no response |
| Load | other tests of the same shard running at once, over a threshold |
| Time zone, locale | the runner's, when it varied |
| Alongside | another test overlapping it |
| Before | the test just before on its worker |
| Browser | its Playwright project |

Each factor becomes a [lab condition](./flake-lab#the-conditions).

Each shows its raw counts: `GET /api/cart slower (≥1.6 s)`, 7 of 8 failures, 3 of 44 passes. It needs 3
failures and a lift of at least 2, `(fw+1)/(f+2) ÷ (pw+1)/(p+2)`; at most 5 are listed, ranked by lift ×
those failures. A neighbor names the paths both tests write, marked approximate when the overlap crosses shards,
whose clocks agree only roughly. First attempts, the UTC hour, other runs on the same environment, the runner image and
the browser version are context, without a condition. Nothing is stored.

The flaky list names each test's top suspect (a reproduced one first), the [Attempts](./evidence#attempts) tab links
requests to suspects, the clue `known-flake-suspect` marks failures showing one, and MCP's `get_flake_profile`
returns it. The [Flake Lab](./flake-lab) tests each suspect against a control run.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/flakiness-tab.png" alt="A flaky test's Flakiness tab: two suspects with their counts among failures and passes, the lab condition and result of each, the context a lab cannot apply, and the experiment that reproduced the flake">
  <figcaption>A flaky test's suspects, and the experiments run on them.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Verified fixed

When a [`piwi flake verify`](./flake-lab#verify-a-fix) experiment holds, the test reads **verified fixed on
`<commit>`** on its Flakiness tab and leaves the ranking, and with it the MCP `list_flaky_tests` tool, quarantine
candidates and the analytics leaderboard. The Flaky view lists it apart, under **Verified fixed**. The first
retry-pass in a run that started after the verification brings it back. A `still-fails` verify, or a later
reproduction, removes the mark; an `inconclusive` one changes nothing.

### Impact ranking

The list is ranked by **impact**, `wasted CI minutes × 0.7 + retry passes × 30 × 0.3`, so the tests that cost the most
come first. Here **wasted CI minutes** are the test's retry-pass runs times the average duration of its failed
attempts in the window: what its retries cost, not the [wasted time](./slow-tests#wasted-time) of Analytics. Ties go
to the higher score, then more retry passes, and the top 50 are listed. A dot colors the wasted minutes:

- 🟢 green — under 5 wasted minutes
- 🟡 amber — under 30 minutes
- 🔴 red — 30 minutes or more

### Per-test stability trend

The **Trend** tab of a test's page draws its pass rate, [flaky rate](/guide/concepts#flaky-rate) and average duration over its
[runs](/guide/concepts#test-case) of the last 30, 90 or 365 days, one point per UTC day, week or month, with the project's timeline markers, to
see whether a fix stuck. The same series is the MCP `get_test_stability_trend` tool.

## Quarantine, with a way out

Detecting a flaky test doesn't stop it blocking merges. Quarantine does — without hiding it.

The usual approach is `--grep-invert @quarantine`: the test stops running, nothing ever proves it's fixed, and the
list only grows.

**A quarantined test in Piwi keeps running and reporting.** It is excluded from the [gate](./merge-gate#what-it-leaves-out)'s
`--max-failed`, `--max-new-regressions`, `--max-new-flaky`, `--require-tag` and `--require-selection` checks and the
[commit status](./pr-feedback#what-gets-posted). That makes the exit possible:

- Each run started after the quarantine counts once toward a **streak**: a pass adds one, a failure or a pass on retry
  resets it, a skip does neither.
- After five consecutive passes the test is flagged **ready to release**: you're told, not asked.
- A fix [verified](#verified-fixed) after the quarantine flags it at once, until the test fails again. Release stays
  yours to click.
- **Candidates** (**Proposed for quarantine** in the Flaky view) are flaky tests wasting 2+ CI minutes with a score
  of 40+, ranked by impact; a high-confidence AI diagnosis calling the test flaky adds a reason. A 200 ms flake
  costs nothing; one burning a four-minute timeout weekly hurts.
- **Debt** is reported in aggregate: how many are quarantined, ready to release or failing in their latest run, and how
  long the oldest has been in.

**Dismiss** turns down either proposal, with an optional reason, and moves no test: a dismissed release stops counting
as ready, and a dismissed candidate returns once the flaky analysis reads a newer run. Agents call [`dismiss_quarantine_proposal`](/reference/mcp-tools#dismiss_quarantine_proposal)
and [`set_test_quarantine`](/reference/mcp-tools#set_test_quarantine).

The gate always states how many failures quarantine excluded, and `--max-quarantined` sets a ceiling on the list.

Manage it from the **Quarantine** view of the project's **Failures** tab, or over the REST API (see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api)).

## Regression signals

A run's tests carry badges:

- **New regression** (red): failing here, passing in the [baseline](/guide/concepts#baseline-last-green-run), the same
  Playwright project in the last complete passing run
- **Newly flaky** (fuchsia): flaky here, passed with no failed attempt in the baseline
- **Passed on retry** (fuchsia): failed at least once in this run, then passed

Filters on the run's test-case list show only the **New regression** or the **Newly flaky** tests.

An [execution](./evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) shows them in its status chip and the line under its headline.

## Spec health by file

With **Group by: File** on the project's **Tests** tab, each spec file's header carries its tests' pass rate, flaky rate, failure count, run count and average time over the list's window (the last 30 days by default), so an unhealthy file jumps out. The **Spec health** [Analytics](./analytics) widget gives them per spec directory.

## Across every project

[Analytics](./analytics) lifts these signals across every project.

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › Flaky tests](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/1?tab=flaky-tests): The project’s flaky tests, each scored, with its root cause, top suspect and Quarantine button.
- [E2E Checkout › should apply discount code](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-cases/9?tab=flakiness): A flaky test’s suspects: a slower cart request in all 7 failures, and the experiment that reproduced it.

# Flake Lab

A flaky test costs the most when nobody can make it fail: the fix is a guess, and "it passed ten times in a row"
proves nothing about a failure that happens one time in twenty. The [Flakiness tab](./flaky-tests#suspects) ranks
**suspects** from the test's history, such as a request that is slower when it fails. The **Flake Lab** tests them:
`piwi flake` replays each suspect as a condition on your machine or in CI, next to a control run, until the failure
reproduces. A reproduced condition proves the cause, and the same condition later proves the fix.

## Run an experiment

From the project root, name the test by its test case id (the number in its dashboard URL) or its spec file and
line:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter flake 1842
npx @piwitests/reporter flake tests/checkout.spec.ts:42
```

The command reads the test's plan from the dashboard, so it needs the reporter's `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and
`PIWI_API_KEY` (or the project's `.env`). The specs must use the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures), which apply the conditions inside the page. The
[desktop app](#in-the-desktop-app) runs it for you.

It runs, one after the other:

1. **The control**: the test alone, 10 times, with no condition.
2. **One arm per suspect**: the test under that suspect's condition, up to 10 times, stopping at 3 failures with the
   same error as in CI. Suspects no experiment tested run first, most likely first; one that did not reproduce runs
   last, never dropped.

Every repetition has retries off, on your current checkout. Before it starts, it prints an estimate from the test's
median duration; `--budget` (15 minutes by default) stops it from starting another arm once spent.

```text
  control                            0/10
  1  delay GET /api/cart 1.8 s       3/4    stopped at 3 · same error as in CI          reproduced
  2  run with admin › resets catalog 1/10   same error as in CI                         not reproduced
Verdict: reproduced by delay GET /api/cart 1.8 s (3/4 against 0/10, p = 0.011)
```

## The conditions

Each [suspect factor](./flaky-tests#suspects) becomes one condition:

| Factor | Condition | How the arm applies it |
|---|---|---|
| Slow route | delay it to the failures' median duration | the fixtures hold each response until that long after the request started |
| Failed route | fail it with the same status, or abort it | the fixtures answer with the status, or reset the connection |
| Load | throttle the CPU ×4 | a DevTools session, so Chromium only |
| Time zone, locale | run the browser in the runner's | `timezoneId` or `locale` of each context the test opens |
| Alongside | run both tests together | both tests on two workers; only rounds where they overlapped count |
| Before | run that test first | both tests on one worker; only rounds where it ran just before count |
| Browser | pin the Playwright project | `--project` |

`--suspect <n>` runs only suspect `n`'s arm. `--all` also runs every condition at once when none reproduces alone.

## Reading the verdict

A failure counts toward an arm only when its error matches one of the test's failures in history (the same masked
error message, so a different timeout or id still matches). A condition that breaks the test some other way, such
as a delay that trips a timeout the test never hit in CI, is shown apart and has not reproduced the flake.

| Verdict | When |
|---|---|
| **Reproduced** | at least half the arm's repetitions failed with a matching error, and a one-sided Fisher exact test against the control gives p < 0.05 |
| **Amplified** | p < 0.05, but under half the repetitions failed |
| **Not reproduced** | anything else |

The command prints the commit it tested next to the commit of the test's latest failure, and warns when they
differ: a condition that reproduces on today's code says little about last month's failure. The control catches a
test that simply fails on this machine.

**Not reproduced is not ruled out.** Ten clean repetitions only show the condition fails in under about 26% of them (95%
confidence): a one-in-twenty flake can still come from it, so the next experiment runs it after the untested ones.

## Verify a fix

After the fix, rerun the condition that reproduced it:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter flake verify 1842
```

It reruns the reproducing arm and its control for enough repetitions that a failure at the rate it reproduced would have
shown with 95% confidence (`⌈ln 0.05 / ln(1 − rate)⌉`, at least 5), and stops at the first matching failure. With
none, the fix is **verified**. The verify experiment appears on the Flakiness tab next to the one it verifies, and the
test reads [verified fixed](./flaky-tests#verified-fixed): off the flaky ranking until it retry-passes again, and a
quarantined test is proposed for release at once, until it fails again.

**Exit codes:** `0` an arm reproduced the failure (`verify`: the fix held) · `1` nothing reproduced (`verify`: it
still fails, or too few repetitions passed to say) · `2` error.

## Where results show

- The project's **Flake Lab** tab lists every flaky or tested test with where it stands and the
  command it needs next, then the project's newest experiments.
- The test's **Flakiness** tab lists its experiments and each suspect's latest result, with buttons that copy both
  commands.
- The **flaky list** marks a test whose latest experiment reproduced it.
- The [clue](/reference/clues) `known-flake-suspect` turns strong on a failure showing a reproduced suspect.
- Over [MCP](/features/mcp), `get_flake_profile` and `plan_flake_experiment` give an agent the experiments and the
  arms to run; the `stabilize-flaky-tests` [agent skill](/features/agent-skills) follows this loop.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/flake-lab-tab.png" alt="A project's Flake Lab tab: counts of flaky, untested, to-verify and verified-fixed tests, each test with its lab state and the command to run next, then the newest experiments with their verdicts">
  <figcaption>The Flake Lab tab: each flaky test's lab state and next command, then the newest experiments.</figcaption>
</figure>

The lab's own runs are stamped as flake-lab runs, kept out of the flaky score, clusters, notifications, quarantine
and every other comparison between runs.

## From the editor and the failure pages

- **In the [editor](./editors#the-tests-behind-each-line)**, a flaky test's line shows the share of its recent passed or
  failed runs in which it failed or passed on a retry, and its top suspect ("flaky 18% · top suspect: GET /api/cart slower (reproduced
  7 of 10)"), with **Reproduce this flake** and, once reproduced, **Verify the flake fix**, run in a terminal against
  the instance the editor reads. Beside a team instance, **Reproduce this flake in the desktop app** (a failure's node
  has it too) runs the instance's plan in the [desktop app](./desktop#jobs-from-your-editor) once you confirm it; **Share on …** records the results on the instance, as run from `desktop`.
- **On a flaky failure's execution or cluster page**, the [next step](./fix-plans#the-next-step) reproduces it under the top untested suspect, then verifies the fix.
- **Home** lists the tests waiting for a verify, then those whose top suspect is untested.

## In the desktop app

On a flaky test's Flakiness tab in the [desktop app](./desktop), **Reproduce this flake** checks out the commit of the
test's latest failure in a throwaway worktree, installs, and runs `piwi flake` there. Its options pick the arms (every
suspect, all at once, or one), the runs and the budget. The experiment lands on the tab, recorded as run from
`desktop`.

Once an experiment has reproduced a test, **Find the breaking commit here** on its failure is flake-aware: each step
runs the reproducing arm (`piwi flake verify --bisect`), bad at a failure with the same error as in CI, good after
enough clean repetitions, which tells when a flake started.

## Run it in CI

A local machine is not CI: a delay reproduces a race anywhere, but load and interference depend on the machine. Run it
where the flake lives with a manual workflow, started with the test case id:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/flake-lab.yml
name: Flake Lab
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      test:
        description: Test case id, or file:line
        required: true
jobs:
  flake:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx @piwitests/reporter flake "${{ inputs.test }}"
        env:
          PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: ${{ vars.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL }}
          PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

The experiment is recorded with the source `ci`. Exit code 1 (nothing reproduced) fails the job; add
`continue-on-error: true` to the step when you only want the result on the tab.

To start it from a failure's next step (**Reproduce in CI**, **Verify in CI**), make the input the command's arguments
(<code v-pre>npx @piwitests/reporter ${{ inputs.piwi_flake }}</code>) and add the workflow as a CI action that accepts
**Flake Lab**, in the project's **CI** settings ([CI actions](./ci-actions)). It receives `flake 1842` or
`flake verify 1842`.

## Without the dashboard

`--no-upload` keeps the results off the dashboard, but the plan still comes from it. When the dashboard cannot be
reached, pass a plan saved earlier with `--plan <file>`: the response of the plan endpoint, or the `plan` the
`plan_flake_experiment` MCP tool returns. The verdict is computed locally the same way.

## Limits

- `cpu` needs Chromium; on another browser the arm is skipped.
- A failure that depends on another team's run on a shared environment has no condition; it stays context on the
  Flakiness tab.
- Order across whole files is not controlled: an `after` arm counts only the rounds Playwright happened to run in
  the order it asked for.

## Try it in the demo

The [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) cannot run the lab but holds experiments:

- [E2E Checkout › should apply discount code](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-cases/9?tab=flakiness): A cart delay reproduced it 3 times in 4 against a clean control.
- [UI Components › Table pagination works correctly](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-cases/35?tab=flakiness): One suspect reproduced it and one did not, a first fix still failed and the second is verified, so its quarantine is proposed for release.
- [UI Components › Flake Lab tab](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/3?tab=flake-lab): Where each flaky test of the project stands in the lab, and the command it needs next.

# AI diagnosis

An LLM you configure explains why a [failure cluster](./failure-clusters), or one execution, broke, against the code
that changed. This page covers the diagnosis (its content, when it runs, what the model receives, how it fares) and
the model's two clustering jobs: titles and semantic merging. Setting up the model is on
[AI provider](/guide/ai-provider); acting on the result, on [Fix plans](./fix-plans).

## Enabling AI diagnosis

It needs an [AI provider](/guide/ai-provider), where providers, model roles and auto-diagnose are set up.

## Response language

A diagnosis comes back in the [response language](/guide/ai-provider#response-language) set for the instance or the project.

## What a diagnosis contains

- **Category** and **confidence**
- **Root cause**: the most likely explanation
- **Evidence**: the signals relied on, each citing a section of the page
- **Suggested fix** and **prevention tips**

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/ai-diagnosis.png" alt="The AI diagnosis of a failure cluster on the cluster page">
  <figcaption>The AI diagnosis of a failure cluster.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Diagnosing automatically

With **auto-diagnose** on ([AI provider](/guide/ai-provider#enabling-ai-diagnosis)), a finished run's clusters with
no completed or running diagnosis, not ignored, are diagnosed up to a per-run budget, ordered by their representative
execution's top [clue](/reference/clues): **no clue** first (the model reasons from scratch), then a weak clue only,
then a failure a strong clue explains, newest cluster first on ties. A diagnosis you rated unhelpful takes a slot again once the evidence changed since it ran, once per
rating. New clusters also get a short **title** from one batched call per run; otherwise a cluster is named from its error
kind, locator, route and spec file, such as `Timeout on getByLabel('Email address') in
checkout.spec.ts`.

## Watching it stream

The model's reasoning streams into a live panel with a stage indicator (*Researching patterns*
while a [research model](/guide/ai-provider#model-roles), when one is configured, pre-analyzes the failure, then
*Diagnosing root cause*), and turns into the result card when it completes. The
[API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) (`/settings/api` on your instance) describe its protocol.

## Diagnosing one execution

On an [execution page](./evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first), the **Diagnosis** section of **More ways to fix**
shows the cluster's diagnosis summary and patch with an **Open** link; without one, it diagnoses that execution alone,
with the same panel and model. Execution and cluster diagnoses are stored apart; one never overwrites the other. A
stored diagnosis stays on screen with no provider configured; with no result and no provider, **Copy prompt** copies
the exact request, trimmed to the [context limits](/guide/ai-provider#context-limits-and-token-cost), for your own AI
tool.

## SCM-grounded context

The diagnosis is fed the code that changed. On a cluster page, **pin a baseline commit** (the diff from it to the
run), **cherry-pick commits** (their full diffs), and **preview the exact context** before running it. Unpinned, the
diff starts at the last green run before the cluster first appeared, else the last run before it where this test
passed; the preview names which. When the host lists only part of a large diff (its newest commits, its first files),
or the patches are cut to budget, the section is marked truncated. With the repository reachable
([Source control](/guide/source-control)), the **full current content** of the most suspect changed files and of the
failing test's local imports (page objects, helpers, fixtures) is sent too, capped by `PIWI_AI_MAX_SOURCE_FILES`
(default 4) and `PIWI_AI_MAX_SOURCE_FILE_CHARS`.

When the failing tests recorded [coverage](./server-coverage), the context lists their
[suspect lines](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines), the changed lines they ran, ranked by how many passing tests of the run
ran them too; their files' patches come first within the budget.

### Validated patches

Every suggested patch is dry-run, hunk by hunk, against the source files the model was shown, and carries one badge:
**Applies cleanly**, **Applies with offset** (`git apply` should still succeed), **Does not apply** (the file
diverged), **Invalid diff**, or **Unverified** (the file was not in the context). When a fix is
[verified](./failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work), the patch is checked again at the fix's commit. The model is told to
return no patch unless it can quote the lines it changes. Applying one is always yours
([the actions](./fix-plans#the-next-step)); only [auto-heal](./auto-heal) writes to your repository, with deterministic
locator edits.

## Diagnoses written by an agent

A coding agent can record its own diagnosis on a cluster or one failure with the MCP tool `record_diagnosis` (on one
failure, the [REST API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) too), in the JSON a model returns here. It needs no
provider, its patch is validated against the failing commit's source when [source control](/guide/source-control) is
connected, and the panel shows it **written by an agent** with the model it named. It replaces the current diagnosis (kept in the
history). Declining the **Agent diagnoses** capability refuses them; declining AI diagnosis does not.

For one failure, `run_execution_diagnosis` runs the page's diagnosis and `get_execution_diagnosis` reads the stored
one, whoever wrote it.

## Locator healing

For a broken locator, the context holds [Locator healing](./locator-healing)'s ranked replacements and recommended
fix, which the model is told to use rather than invent one.

## Fix plans

The diagnosis, its patch, the locator fix, the top five suspect lines and the verify command form a
[fix plan](./fix-plans).

## Diagnosis history

A re-diagnose keeps the previous result; a nightly sweep keeps the newest 20 per cluster
(`PIWI_RETENTION_DIAGNOSIS_VERSIONS`, `0` keeps all). **History** in the panel header lists them newest first, with
model, category, confidence and token cost, and what changed since each. A re-diagnose sends the model the previous
category, confidence, summary and root cause, the triage note, and, when you rated it unhelpful, your note and an
instruction not to repeat it without new evidence. The new diagnosis starts unrated; the history keeps the old one's
thumbs.

A diagnosis is flagged **may be stale** only when the evidence changed since it ran **and** the cluster is still
failing; the banner says whether new occurrences or new evidence caused it.

## How diagnoses fare

**AI usage** in Settings → AI ([what it counts](/guide/ai-provider#usage-and-quality)) also says how each model's
diagnoses fared:

- **Rated helpful**: thumbs up over every rating, from 10 ratings (below, the panel says the sample is too small);
- **Patches that apply**: suggested patches that [apply](#validated-patches), over every patch that could be checked;
- **Verified by the fix**: diagnoses whose cluster a change to the files they named fixed;
- **Regressed**: verified diagnoses whose failure came back.

Agent diagnoses get their own row, under the model the agent named. Each diagnosis stores a hash of the instructions
it was written under (`promptSha` in its details), telling apart diagnoses before and after a change to the custom
instructions or the language. Piwi never switches models on these numbers;
[Analytics](./analytics#hand-back-outcomes) shows the ratings across projects.

## Custom instructions

**Global** instructions (Settings → AI) and **per-project** ones (Project → Settings → AI diagnosis) describe your
architecture, common false positives or house style for fixes.

## Context limits (and token cost)

Each input sent to the model is capped to keep diagnoses fast and affordable; the caps are set on the [AI provider](/guide/ai-provider#context-limits-and-token-cost) page.

## Privacy

API keys are encrypted at rest with [`PIWI_SECRET_KEY`](/reference/configuration#general). A diagnosis sends the
bounded context above to your provider; for local analysis, use Ollama or another self-hosted OpenAI-compatible model.

## Semantic merging (optional)

With **Semantic clustering** on (Settings → AI) and an embedding model, a semantic layer sits on top of the
[fingerprint](./failure-clusters#how-failures-are-grouped). After a run, its new clusters are embedded and compared (cosine similarity) with the project's other open
clusters; near-duplicates above `PIWI_CLUSTER_SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD` (default `0.92`) are merged
into the longest-lived cluster ([what the survivor keeps](./failure-clusters#how-failures-are-grouped)), and a
fingerprint alias sends future occurrences to it. This catches one root cause phrased differently enough to dodge the
fingerprint. The text is cleaned first (ANSI codes, framework stack frames, volatile tokens), and older clusters are
embedded a few at a time over the runs that follow.

Pairs in the **ambiguous band**, between `PIWI_CLUSTER_SUGGEST_THRESHOLD` (default `0.80`) and the merge threshold,
go to a model, which judges the error text, locators, most-affected tests and overlap: a confident yes merges, a less
confident yes becomes a **merge suggestion** (Clusters view of the project's Failures tab) for a Maintainer or above to
approve or dismiss, and a no stays apart. Without AI, or past five model calls in a run, the pair becomes a
suggestion. This runs after every run that [sends notifications](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin), independently
of auto-diagnose.

Each pair is judged once: the model's no is kept. A pair someone dismissed, or [split by hand](#split-a-cluster-by-hand),
is never merged automatically, however close the score.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/failure-clustering-semantic-merge.svg" alt="Diagram of the semantic merging flow: clusters are embedded, compared by cosine similarity, and kept apart, adjudicated by a model, or merged depending on the score">
  <figcaption>The cosine score decides between keeping two clusters apart, asking a model (or a person), and merging them.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Split a cluster by hand

Moving tests out of a cluster needs no AI: see [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters#split-a-cluster-by-hand).

## Try it in the demo

The [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) needs no provider: some clusters carry a diagnosis with a validated patch,
the others stream a simulated one.

- [Web Dashboard › Users table paginates 25 rows per page](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/10): A stored diagnosis traces the 50 user rows (51 with the header) to the API’s default page size and suggests a patch; the fix has since landed.
- [Web Dashboard › Users table paginates 25 rows per page](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/10): The dashboard’s ASP.NET Core API records server coverage by line: of the 13 lines changed in the range, the failing test ran 3, the statements of UsersEndpoints.cs that size, fetch and return the page, which two passing tests ran too; the What changed line names them, the diff marks them, and the diagnosis context and the fix plan list them.
- [UI Components › Modal opens and closes correctly](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/5): Browser coverage names files: of the two files changed in the range, the failing modal tests ran the modal controller and no passing test did, so its whole hunk heads the suspect lines on the What changed line, its card and the diagnosis context.
- [E2E Checkout › should complete checkout with Apple Pay](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/2): No stored diagnosis: the Diagnose with AI button streams a simulated one, built from the cluster’s own data.

# Assistant

The assistant answers questions about this instance: why a run failed, which tests are flaky, what a setting does,
whether a capability is on. Your AI model writes the answer from the same read tools the [MCP server](./mcp) gives
coding agents, called with the access of the person asking, and from Piwi's documentation bundled with the server,
so it can say only what the data and the docs say. It changes nothing until you click **Apply** on a change it
proposes.

## Asking a question

Click **Ask Piwi** in the sidebar, under the search, press `Ctrl` + `I` (`⌘` + `I` on macOS), or type a question in
the command palette (`Ctrl` + `K`) and pick **Ask Piwi**. The palette, and an empty conversation, also offer a few
**Ask about this page** questions. The panel keeps its conversation while you move between pages.

From 1280 px wide the panel docks on the right and the page narrows beside it; below 1536 px it folds the sidebar to
its icons until it closes. Drag its left edge to widen it, or float it over the page with the panel icon in its
header; the browser remembers both. Narrower, it opens over the page, full screen on a phone.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/assistant-docked.png" alt="The assistant docked beside Home, the field offering the next question">
  <figcaption>The assistant docked beside Home.</figcaption>
</figure>

Each question carries the page it was asked on: its address, tab, filters, project and the parts a guide can point
at, so "Why did this fail?" on an execution needs no ids. The clock lists your conversations; the pen starts a new
one.

The answer streams in, with a line for each tool it calls. **Stop** ends it, keeping what it wrote; an answer that
stopped or failed offers **Try again**. In the question field ([keys](/reference/keyboard-shortcuts#assistant-panel)),
`↑` brings back earlier questions and `→` takes the suggested one: the model's (a few dozen tokens), else the
page's. What you type stays when the panel closes.

The [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) has no model: it answers the prepared questions **Ask about this page**
lists, computed from its sample data in your browser, and offers them and the authored guides for any other question.
With no AI provider configured, the panel says so and links Settings → AI.

## What an answer contains

An answer is text and blocks, each drawn by the dashboard's own components; the model sends no HTML.

- **Text**: Markdown with headings, lists, tables and code. A run, execution, cluster, test or project links to its
  page only when a tool result of the conversation named it, so the model cannot link to something it never read.
- **Code and commands**: a snippet with a copy button, and a shell command in bash and, when it differs, PowerShell.
- **A patch**: a unified diff checked against the files at the run's commit, as on a [diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis), with
  download, apply and copy buttons.
- **A card** for a run, an execution, a cluster or a test, in its outcome's color, drawn from the tool result.
- **Options**: two to four ways to solve the problem, each with its trade-off and effort, one marked recommended.
  **Choose** sends your pick as the next question.
- **A question** with radio buttons or checkboxes and an **Other** field. **Answer** sends your picks back in words and
  by id.
- **A checklist**: steps to do in order, some with their command. Your ticks are saved with the conversation.
- **Show me**: a guide on your own screens. A popover walks you through the parts of the dashboard the answer is
  about, each linking its docs page: only parts Piwi lists and tests for guides, never an element the model picked.
- **A link** to the page to open next.
- **A proposed change** to apply with a click ([below](#proposed-changes)).

Under each answer, **What it read** unfolds the tools it called and names the model. The line under the question field
names it too, and says what is sent to it.

## Proposed changes

Asked to do something ("resolve this cluster"), the assistant answers with a card per change, with **Apply** and
**Dismiss**. Nothing runs until you click **Apply**: the dashboard sends its own button's request, with your session,
and reloads the page. The card keeps what became of it, or why it was refused. A card can resolve, ignore or
reopen a failure cluster, [quarantine](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) or release a test, start a diagnosis, keep a run or decline a capability, and
shows only when you hold the permission it needs; to act on several tests, it first lets you tick them.

<figure>
  <div class="figure-pair">
    <img src="/screenshots/assistant-proposal-wide.png" alt="An answer in the assistant panel proposing to resolve the cart cluster once the fix is in, with Dismiss and Apply">
    <img src="/screenshots/assistant-proposal-wide-applied.png" alt="The same proposal after Apply, marked Applied">
  </div>
  <figcaption>A proposed change, before and after Apply.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What it reads

Each question is offered core read tools (search, projects, runs, failure clusters, a failure's evidence, flaky
tests, fix plans, the documentation), the tools of its page, and any it adds with `find_tools`. `get_instance_config` tells it how this instance is set up: the capabilities' states, the AI roles'
providers and models (never a key), the connected issue trackers and whether authentication is on. Storage and
retention are shown to administrators only. `explain_setting` explains a settings field and its `PIWI_*` variables;
which are set, and its value, go only to those who can open its page, a secret only as set or not.

- **Your access.** The tools run as you: a Member reads only their projects.
- **No writes.** No tool that changes anything is offered; you apply a change yourself ([above](#proposed-changes)).
- **Tool results are data.** Test titles, error text, console lines and commit messages reach the model as data,
  never as instructions, and each result is cut to 12,000 characters.
- **Sources.** The answer names the tool results and docs sections it used; each stored answer lists the tools it
  called, with their arguments.

## The model

The assistant uses the model of **Features → Assistant model** in Settings → AI ([model roles](/guide/ai-provider#model-roles)).
Left unset, it uses the diagnosis model, so an instance with AI configured needs no further setup; set it to a faster,
cheaper model while diagnosis keeps the strong one.
The response language and the global and project instructions apply as they do to [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis).

Anthropic models and most OpenAI-compatible servers call tools natively. With the Claude Code CLI (the desktop app, or
a server with `PIWI_CLAUDE_CLI_PATH`), one Claude Code run writes the whole answer: its only MCP server is this server's
endpoint for that answer, offering the assistant's tools through a token valid for that answer only; the desktop
app's own token never goes to the CLI. A server that refuses tools, or an older Claude Code, answers in a JSON action
mode: one tool call or the answer per reply.

In the desktop app it can also read a file's current code inside the project's linked folder; it never changes a file
or imports a run.

## What leaves the instance

Only the calls to the model endpoint you configured, as for AI diagnosis: the question, the page it was asked on, the
earlier exchanges of the conversation and what the tools return. A local model through the OpenAI-compatible provider
keeps everything on your network.

## Privacy

A conversation belongs to the person who started it: no route returns it to anyone else, administrators included.
With authentication off every visitor is the same administrator and shares one list. Deleting a user deletes their
conversations, and the nightly sweep deletes a conversation `PIWI_ASSISTANT_RETENTION_DAYS` after its last message
(90 days by default).

## Limits

| Limit | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Tool calls for one question | 8 |
| Output tokens of one model call | 2,048 |
| Time for one question | 180 seconds |
| Tokens per user in 24 hours | 1,000,000 |
| Tokens for the instance in 24 hours | 5,000,000 |

A daily cap reached stops the answer before its next model call, with an error that names the cap; at the tool-call
limit the model is asked to answer with what it has. Deleting a conversation does not give its tokens back. The
`PIWI_AI_ASSISTANT_*` variables in the [configuration reference](/reference/configuration#assistant) change the
limits, and **AI usage** on Settings → AI counts the assistant's answers apart from diagnoses.

The gauge under the question field opens the cap that binds first, yours or the instance's, with when it frees up,
and with the Claude Code CLI on a Claude subscription its 5-hour or weekly window. A line warns from 80%; a spent cap
stops the field from asking.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/assistant-input.png" alt="The question field warning at 85% of the daily allowance">
  <figcaption>The question field warns at 85% of the daily allowance.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Turning it off

Decline **Assistant** in **Settings → Capabilities** ([Choose what you use](/operate/capabilities#declining-a-capability)) and its
routes answer as unavailable for everyone; **Ask Piwi** leaves the sidebar and the command palette. Declining AI turns it off too. [Suggestions](./guides#suggested-on-a-page) that offer a guide stay.

- [AI provider](/guide/ai-provider): configure the model roles
- [MCP server](./mcp): the same tools, for coding agents
- [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis): what the diagnosis model sends and stores
