# Follow a run

This page follows a run while it goes, in the same words in every tool: its number and page on the instance, how far
it is, where a test stopped and why, and when a failing test is held. To see a test's page:
[Watch a local test](./watch-running-test) in your tools, [Live view of a run](./live-view) on the team instance.

## The run's number and page

A run has one number on the instance it reports to, `#78`, and one page. The reporter learns the number as the run starts: from the global setup that registered it, else as its stream
to the instance opens. It prints the page once, and tells it to the editor or the desktop app that follows the run.
The page is under the instance's public address when the instance sets `PIWI_SITE_URL`, else under the address the
reporter reached it at. A tool links it only on this machine or under an instance it connects to itself: in an editor,
the instance of a Playwright config of the window; in the desktop app, the team instance whose run requests it takes. A
page elsewhere, which the test's own code could name, is not shown, and the run reads as one with no number.

| Where | What it shows |
|---|---|
| The terminal | `[Piwi Dashboard] View live progress: https://piwi.example.com/test-runs/78`, once, at its start |
| VS Code | The run-control item: `#78 · 3 of 9`, its tooltip **Open run #78**; while your run goes, **Open run #78 (running)** first in the status bar item's tooltip; **Piwi: Open the page of a run of this window** and **Piwi: Open the branch's run in progress** in the palette |
| JetBrains IDEs | The status bar item: `Piwi: run #78 · 3 of 9`, kept beside a stop or a share; **Open run #78** in its menu; **Open run #78 (running)** in place of **Open the latest run** while it goes |
| Piwi Picker's [Runs window](./runs-window) | **Run #78**, **Open** and **Copy link** on the run's card, while it runs and after it ended, with its progress and how it ended |
| The desktop app's [Local runs tray](./desktop-runs) | **Run #78 · Open** under each run of its hub, a run a team instance asked for included, whose page opens in the browser; **Open run #78** on a run the app's own server holds |
| **Debug in my editor** | Once the editor runs the test: "Following run #81 in VS Code · Open" beside the button |

A run that reports to no instance, or with `streaming: false` and no global setup, has no number until its results
are sent.

## How far it is

The reporter's own process tells the editor or the desktop app how many tests the run holds, how many ended and how,
and how the run ended with its first failure. The editors' status bars and the Runs window count it the same way: each
test once, by its last attempt. The desktop tray counts as the run's own process does ([Local runs tray](./local-runs-tray#each-run)).

On the dashboard, Home's **Recent activity**, a project's runs list and the **Projects** page show a running run with
the count bar and how many results are in: `120 of 400 · 2 failed`. Its row moves on by itself as results reach the
instance, at most every 2 seconds, without the page reading the list again. Until the run ends these count each result
as the reporter sends it, a retry again; the run's page counts each test once.

The status bar item's tooltip also says what each worker runs now (`Worker 2 · cart › adds a mug · stopped`). In VS
Code, the Testing view's test run of your run writes in its output each test a worker starts, each stop and why, with
the line it stands at, and each stop answered.

A run in progress that is not yours, a CI run or a teammate's, shows read-only:
[A CI run of your branch](./editor-ci-runs).

## Where a test stopped

A test of a run on your machine stops at a call and waits to be answered: at a breakpoint, after a step, at a Pause,
at the line it was run to, at `page.pause()`, or at a failure [held](#hold-failures) for a look. Every tool says why in
the same words:

- **Stopped at a breakpoint**, **Stopped after a step**, **Paused**, **Stopped at the line it ran to**, **Stopped at
  page.pause()**, and **Stopped** for a reason a newer reporter names;
- **Held at its failure**, then how the test failed (**Failed at** and its place in the Runs window and the desktop
  app's tray);
- at a stop an agent asked for, **Paused by the agent**, **Stopped after the agent's step** or **Stopped at the line
  the agent ran it to**.

The editors show it above the stopped line, the Runs window and the desktop app's tray on the worker, and the
terminal on a line naming the editor, or the desktop app, that steers the run:

```text
[piwi] Stopped at a breakpoint at tests/cart.spec.ts:12 before Click: Resume, Step or Finish in Visual Studio Code.
```

Edit the file at a stop, and the Runs window names the stopped line where it stands now, as the editor does.

**On the run's page**, the test's row says why, at the stopped call, whose place opens in your editor. A shared run
tells it from its [live view](./live-view); a run nobody shares, as text with `@piwitests/reporter` 0.68.0 or later:
the call's title, its file and line, the test's title and since when, as each stop shows and ends, never an image, the
row saying for how long once it has stood a minute. A stopped test is never marked [**Stuck?**](./stuck-tests).

At a stop of a headed run, every tool offers **Show the browser**, which brings the test's window to the front where
your system allows: **Piwi: Show the stopped test's browser** in VS Code and the stop's hover, **Tools → Piwi → Run
control** in a JetBrains IDE, and a button in the Runs window and the desktop app's tray. A
headless run has none to show, nor does an older reporter.

### Hold failures

**Hold failures** decides, for one run, whether a failing test waits at its line. Held, the test keeps its page once
its function, hooks and fixtures are done, at the line where the error entered its code, else the failing locator's,
else the call a test timeout cut short. **Resume**, **Step** and **Finish** let it end as it failed; **Pick** and
**Record** fix it there ([Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code#a-failure)). Each failing attempt is held once, an
expected failure never. Piwi's evidence is the page at the failure: the requests, console entries and dialogs of the hold
are not recorded, while Playwright's trace and video go on.

Headed or headless, it is off unless turned on; off, a failure goes on at once, as without Piwi:

- **From the run's start** in a run with the editor's breakpoints or a spec's `page.pause()`, a
  [debug run](./debug-in-editor), a desktop app's reproduction, a run an agent starts (`run_start`, until two minutes
  after its last call), or one whose start options choose it ([editor](./editor-runs#how-a-run-starts),
  [desktop app](./desktop-runs#each-worker)).
- **While it runs**, from any tool that follows it: the editors (**Piwi: Turn hold failures on or off for the run**,
  **Tools → Piwi → Run control**), the switch on each run of the Runs window, the desktop app's
  tray and Piwi Runner, or an agent (`run_follow`). Each tool shows it as the last one set it. Turned off, a held
  failure no pause bar shows goes on.
- **Never** in a run nobody attends: a Flake Lab run, a bisect, a lab job, **Verify ×3**, a fix plan's verification, a
  Flake Lab line, a terminal run whose output goes to a file or a pipe, `--repeat-each` above 1 without
  `--max-failures=1`, and UI mode. Their switch says why.

A run [started in a terminal](./terminal-runs) holds a failure only once you turn it on, and a held failure goes on
once no tool is left to show it.

## Share with Playwright tools

At a stop, **Share with Playwright tools** binds the test's browser for Playwright's own tools: [Pause and step from
the editor](./editor-run-control#share-with-playwright-tools).

## The terminal's lines

What a run prints in its terminal (its page, the editor or the desktop app it follows, its progress):
[Runs started outside Piwi](./terminal-runs#the-terminal-s-lines).

## When the run does not reach the instance

What the editor says of a run it started that sent nothing: [Runs from the editor](./editor-runs#after-a-run).

## Related

- [Watch a local test](./watch-running-test): a test's page, in your tools
- [Live view of a run](./live-view): a test's page, on the team instance
- [Share a local run live](./share-live): a teammate watches a run on your machine
- [Runs window](./runs-window): follow and steer your runs from Piwi Picker
- [Pause and step from the editor](./editor-run-control): the controls at a stop

# Live view of a run

In a project that turns the live view on, a running test of a CI run, or of a run a developer
[shares from their machine](./share-live), gets **Watch** on its run page on the team instance: the page that worker
is on, a few images a second, each with the call it was taken at, for a CI run that seems [stuck](./stuck-tests) or a teammate's
paused test. Nothing you do in the view reaches the test.

## Where to watch a run

A CI run, or a shared run, is watched here. A run you start yourself shows in its browser when headed, and in your
editor, Piwi Picker's Runs window and the desktop app's tray, running or stopped:
[Watch a local test](./watch-running-test). A run that reports to the desktop app gets no live view key, so no team
**Watch**.

## Turn it on

The live view is off in every project. A Project admin turns it on in **Project → Settings → Live view**, or from a running run's status. It applies to
each CI run that starts after, as the reporter's global setup registers it: [`wrapConfig`](/guide/reporter) adds that
setup. A CI job is told by its provider's variable (`GITHUB_ACTIONS`, `GITLAB_CI`, …) or by `CI` set to anything but
`false` or `0`. Such a run's log then says:

```txt
[Piwi Dashboard] Live view on for the specs that use Piwi's fixtures: people who may open this run can watch their tests' pages on the dashboard while it runs. Nothing is stored.
```

A spec file that imports `test` from `@playwright/test` instead of your [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures)
has no view: the log names the first one. A CI run without a view logs why instead, for a reason
[Check availability](#check-availability) lists, with the error the instance answered.

Turning it off ends every view at once. Turned on again, a run that had a view and still runs gets it back within a
minute.

## Check availability

A running run's **Tests** tab says **Live view available**, or what is missing, its help giving the step:

| It says | Why, and what to do |
|---|---|
| **Live view off** | A Project admin turns it on for the next runs, from its help. |
| **Live view unavailable** | The run has no key: it started before the setting was on, without `wrapConfig`'s global setup, while the instance did not answer that setup, or with `streaming` off. Start a new run. |
| **Live view waiting** | No worker is connected yet: they are starting. |
| **No worker connected** | Tests run without one: the specs import `test` from `@playwright/test`, not the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures). |
| **Not shared live** | The run is on a developer's machine: they [share it](./share-live). |
| **Watch** says nothing has come for 35 seconds | A reverse proxy buffers the live view's streams: turn its buffering off ([Reverse proxy](/operate/deployment#reverse-proxy-https)). |

## Watch a worker

On the run page's **Tests** tab, **Watch** at the end of a running test's row opens its worker's view, docked beside
the page (a sheet on a smaller screen): the test's page as the browser paints it, under it the call the image was
taken at (`Click getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' }) · checkout.spec.ts:30`). A still page shows as the view opens,
then sends no new image, so the caption names the step the test began since. Widen the panel or open it full
screen; a click on the image zooms.
Under it, the page's [events, text and filmstrip](./live-view-layers) and [Inspect](./live-inspect); [Watch all](./watch-all)
shows every worker at once.

The view follows that call: how long it has run (while its test stands at a [stop](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped),
the stop in its row's words, **Paused**), Playwright's log of it as a failed call's error prints it, and while it
waits, what its locator matches (no element yet, several, or one not enabled), outlined on the image, with the point a
click acts on; **Zoom to the element** crops the image around it. In a CI run this needs Playwright 1.64 (1.63
shows the log without the matches, an older one the call alone); a shared run reads it inside the worker, pausing
nothing.

A view follows its worker's lane: it says how each test ended, lists the lane's earlier tests and goes on, across
worker restarts; untick **Follow the worker's next test** to end it with its test. The page's address names the lane
(`?watch=2`; `?watch=3.2` for worker 2 of shard 3) for a link. It ends with the run, saying how it went, 30 s after its
lane's worker left, as the live view turns off, or as you close it. A view that cannot open says why.

## What is sent, to whom, and what is kept

- **No image from a run on your machine until you share it.** Its workers open no connection; its
  [stops](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped) show as text. Shared, its worker sends the team the images of the one
  view its own tools watch.
- **Nothing while nobody watches.** Each worker of a CI or shared run keeps one connection to the dashboard and says
  only when its test stops and goes on. No image is taken.
- **While someone watches a worker**, that worker sends JPEG images of its test's page at quality 50, at the size the
  view shows them in device pixels, 1280 by 800 at most: four a second to a view,
  one to a [Watch all](./watch-all) tile, and about 256 KB a second, a heavier image holding the next one back longer.
  A test whose trace or video already films the page shares that recording's images, 800 pixels wide at quality 90.
  The recording stays whole. A test that starts its own `page.screencast` gets it, and the view
  goes on with an image a second. A view also gets the call's log. Nothing of the view is a step of the test or an
  action of its trace.
- **Only to people who may open the run**: watching needs what opening the run needs, the project's
  [roles](/operate/project-access). On an instance with authentication off, that is anyone who can reach it. A CI
  lane watched [in your editor](./editor-ci-runs) comes from here, read with the editor's
  key, and counts among the run's watches for the key's owner, as a dashboard tab does; the editor keeps none.
- **Nothing is kept.** The dashboard relays each image to the people watching that worker and drops it: never written
  to the database, the logs or an export. A viewer that reads slowly gets the latest image alone. The run's trace stays
  the record.

**Masked in the worker**, with `@piwitests/reporter` 0.64.0 or later (an older one masks nothing): before an image
leaves it, the worker paints over password fields, fields whose `autocomplete` asks for a one-time code or a card's
number or code, and the project's **Masked elements** (Playwright locators). While one shows, two images a second go at
most. A zoomed-in page sends no image. A secret in the page's own text still shows; the caption and the log hide
credentials and typed text. The workers reach the dashboard with a key
the run got as it registered: it opens this run's live view and nothing else, ends with the run, and is never in the
environment of the tests, their hooks or their fixtures. The dashboard keeps the key's SHA-256 digest with the run,
never the key, so a dashboard that restarts takes it back from the workers while the run lasts.

## Limits

- **Watch only.** No input, and no control but **Let it go** on a [held CI failure](./hold-ci-failure) and, where
  the project allows it, [Pause a CI test](./pause-ci-test): a test is stepped from the [editor](./editor-run-control) or the
  [Runs window](./runs-window).
- **One page at a time**: the `page` fixture's, else the page of the test's latest call
  ([which](/guide/capture-fixtures#where-capture-works)).
- **Sixteen pages watching a run at a time**, four of them one person's with authentication on: a fifth closes
  that person's oldest. Its workers send 4 MB of images a second at most together.
- **One dashboard server.** The view is relayed in the memory of one server, so it needs a deployment of one server
  ([Resource requirements](/operate/deployment#resource-requirements)), which sticky sessions do not make up for.

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/watch-all -->

# Watch all workers

**Watch all**, on a running run's **Tests** tab, shows a tile for each worker in the run's
[live view](./live-view): the page its test is on, one image a second, with the worker's number, its test and the step
it is on. A click on a tile shows that worker in full, in the panel **Watch** opens. It is for a run of many workers
where you do not know yet which one to look at. It needs what the live view needs: the project's live view on, and a
CI run or a run [shared from a developer's machine](./share-live).

## What a tile shows

- **The page**, as the worker's test sees it: one image a second, 320 pixels wide, the latest alone. A still page shows
  as the tile opens, then sends none until it changes.
- **The worker**, by its lane (`Worker 2`, as the rows and the Timeline name it), the test it runs and its step.
- **What its test needs attention for**: where it stands [stopped](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped)
  (`Stopped at a breakpoint`), or **Stuck?** once the dashboard marks it ([Stuck tests](./stuck-tests)).

The tile of the worker shown in full is outlined. A worker that leaves the run's live view leaves the grid; the one
Playwright starts in its lane after a failure takes its place.

## Follow what needs attention

In the full view, **Follow what needs attention** moves the view on its own to a worker whose test failed, was marked
**Stuck?**, or [stopped](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped), and says why it moved:
`Moved to worker 3: “pays with a saved card” failed.` It follows these rules:

- It goes where the newest of them happened, in another worker of the run's live view.
- It stays at least 5 seconds after it moved or you chose a worker yourself (a tile, a row's **Watch**).
- It stays on a worker that needs attention itself: one stopped or marked **Stuck?**, for as long as it lasts, and one
  whose test failed, for 10 seconds.
- A failure from before you turned it on, or that the run page saw more than 30 seconds ago, the view open or closed,
  moves nothing; nor does anything from before you last chose a worker yourself.

After a failure, Playwright starts a new worker in the lane: the view shows its next test, and the line under its
checkboxes says which test failed. The view moves within its panel, which stays in full screen if you put it there.

## One connection

The run page holds one connection to the dashboard for everything it watches: the tiles and the full view travel
together, and showing another worker or resizing the panel changes what it carries without opening another. The full
view's images come at the size the panel shows them, up to 1280 by 800 pixels; a worker shown in full and as a tile
sends the larger. Each worker sends images only while a page shows it, in full or as a tile, and nothing is stored:
[what is sent, to whom, and what is kept](./live-view#what-is-sent-to-whom-and-what-is-kept) applies to every tile.

A run takes 16 such pages at a time, whatever each shows, and its workers send 4 MB of images a second at most together.
Each page gets 1 MB of images a second at most, the latest of each worker waiting for the next second, and a page that
reads nothing for 5 seconds is cut off, then connects again. A tile carries no call log, nor the
[events, text or filmstrip](./live-view-layers) of the full view, and an image of 48 KB at most:
a worker someone else watches in full at a large size says so in its tile. In a tab hidden for 10 minutes, the page
stops asking for tiles, and asks again as you come back. An older reporter sends its images at 640 by 400 pixels, four a
second, whatever the view asks; the dashboard passes one a second of them to a tile.

A CI run's workers keep their own connections through an outage or a restart of the dashboard: each tries again after
1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, then every 30 to 60 seconds while the run lasts. A worker whose view stays out says so once
in the run's log, with the cause, and once more as it is back.

## In the demo

The live demo runs no browser: **Watch all** on a simulated run shows each running worker's step where its image
would be, and its stops and **Stuck?** marks. A click on a tile opens its worker's panel with no image: the call its
test is in, with its log, and [Inspect](./live-inspect#in-the-demo) on the checkout page from a recorded trace. Its
page events, text and filmstrip stay empty.

## Related

- [Share a local run live](./share-live): let a teammate watch a run on your machine

# Page events, text and filmstrip

Under the image of a worker's [live view](./live-view), the panel also shows what the image cannot: what the page and
the test's requests said, the page as text, and a filmstrip of the test's calls. It is for a test that fails or waits
for a reason the pixels do not show: a console error, a request that never answered, a 500 and the exception the
backend logged for it. Each part comes from the worker only while the panel shows it, in a CI run or a run
[shared from a developer's machine](./share-live), and the dashboard stores none of it. Your editor, Piwi Picker's
Runs window and the desktop app show the same beside a test they watch: [in your own tools](#in-your-own-tools).

## Page events

**Page events**, open by default, lists as they happen, newest first:

- **Console errors** and **uncaught errors** the page threw;
- **failed requests**: no answer, or a status of 400 or more;
- **pending requests**, once one has waited 5 seconds for its answer: one line whose time grows
  (`POST /api/checkout`, pending for 17 s), then says how long it took;
- what the backend **logged** while it answered, errors and warnings, under the request it answered, from its
  [backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs);
- the test's **API calls** through Playwright's `request`, with their status and time: a test with no page shows these.

Addresses and texts reach the dashboard with their credentials hidden. A worker sends 20 events a second at most and
counts the others, the dashboard counts those a page reading too slowly could not take, and the list keeps the latest
100; each says how many it left out. Folding the section stops them coming.

## Page text

**Page text**, folded by default, shows the page as roles and names when you open it, as Playwright's ARIA snapshot
writes it (`- button "Pay €84.90" [disabled]`): what a screen reader would read, searchable and selectable at any width.

- **Where it comes from**: the test's own trace, when the project's trace takes ARIA snapshots (`snapshots.aria`;
  `wrapConfig`'s does not), a new one after each call. Otherwise the worker reads the page as you open the section or
  choose **Read again**: about 8 levels deep, which can hold a heavy page's test up for 120 to 300 milliseconds.
- **Find in the text** ignores case and accents, and says how many matches it has.
- **The element the call waits on**, when its locator names it by role and name, label, placeholder or text
  (`getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })`), is marked in the text.
- **Masked in the worker**: the value of a password, PIN, one-time code or card field, anything that reads as a card's
  number, the values the page's secret fields hold, and the project's **Masked elements** read `<hidden>`. A masked
  element the snapshot cannot name sends no text, and the section says why.

A text is 96 K characters and 192 KB at most, and says so when it is cut.

## Filmstrip

Under the image, the **filmstrip** shows the page after each call of the test that ended, one small image a call; a
click on one shows it larger, with its call's title. The worker takes them from the view's own images, masked as its
frames are, 320 by 200 pixels at most, only while someone watches, and keeps the current test's strip in its memory,
40 images at most. A view that opens later gets that strip at once: from the test's start, when someone watched it all
along.

## What is sent, and what is kept

- **Only what a panel shows.** The worker sends events while a panel shows **Page events**, the text as one opens
  **Page text**, and the filmstrip while a panel shows the worker; to those panels alone.
- **Bounded.** The dashboard relays at most 40 events, 4 texts and 16 filmstrip images a second of a worker; the images
  count against the [bytes](./live-view#limits) a run's workers and each page may send, and a page past its bytes gets
  the filmstrip's images a little later, in their order.
- **Nothing is kept.** As with the images, the dashboard relays each part and drops it: never written to the database,
  the logs or an export. The panel holds the parts of the test it shows in the browser's memory, until the view moves
  to the next test or closes.

A worker of an older reporter sends none of them: the sections stay empty, and **Page text** says no text came.

## In your own tools

Under a watched page in your editor's view, a CI run's lane included, and, with a reporter newer than 0.68.0, in
Piwi Picker's Runs window and the desktop app's tray ([Watch a local test](./watch-running-test)):

- **Why it waits**: the call the test is in, how long it has run, how many elements its locator matches and whether
  the first is enabled, and the last lines of Playwright's log.
- **Events**: console and uncaught errors, failed requests, requests pending long (`POST /api/checkout pending 17 s`)
  and the errors the backend logged, newest first.
- **Text**: the page as roles and names, its secret fields hidden, read at each test (**Show the page's text** in the
  Runs window and the tray), then followed through the test's trace. Find searches it.
- **Filmstrip**: one image per call the test finished; a click shows it larger, with its call.

The text and the filmstrip are read only while open, and kept in memory alone, on your machine. The view says when an
older reporter, or team instance, may send none of them.

## In the demo

The live demo runs no browser. **Watch** on a simulated run's running test, or a tile of
[Watch all](./watch-all#in-the-demo), opens its worker's panel with no image: the call its test is in, with its log,
and [Inspect](./live-inspect#in-the-demo) on the checkout page from a recorded trace. The page's events and the
filmstrip stay empty; the panel says why no image comes, and **Page text** why no text does.

# Inspect a worker's page

Under a worker's [live view](./live-view), **Inspect** shows its test's page as a document rather than an image: the
DOM Playwright's trace takes at each call (before the call, at its action and after it), rendered by the dashboard
with its stylesheets and images, and the locator picker on it. It is for a CI test that waits on an element: you see
the page as the test sees it, at the call it is stuck on, and pick the locator to use while the test still waits. It
works in a CI run or a run [shared from a developer's machine](./share-live), and the dashboard stores none of it. The
[desktop app](./desktop-runs#watch) shows the same view of its own runs, from the test's own trace.

## Use it

In the lane panel of a running test, open **Inspect** under the image.

- **The latest call.** The view opens on the page at the latest call the worker sent, and shows each new call as it
  comes while **Follow the latest call** is on: about three a second at most while they keep coming, the latest
  each time.
- **Before, Action, After.** The page before the call ran, at its action (where a click or a fill acts, for an input
  action) and after it. A moment the worker sent no page of stays greyed out.
- **The calls.** Under the page, each call whose page came, the latest last. Choosing an older one turns following
  off, so the view stays on it as the test goes on; tick **Follow the latest call** to go back to the newest.
- **Pick a locator** opens the [snapshot picker](./evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) on the page shown: click an
  element to get the locators that target it, ranked, to copy. Picking turns following off. Nothing is saved: the
  test is still running.

As the test ends, the dashboard lets its pages go: the page shown stays, but no other call's page opens and Pick a
locator is off. The view goes on with the lane's next test, as the image does, following its latest call. When no
page comes, Inspect says why, in place of the page or above the calls it already lists.

## Where the pages come from

- **The test's own trace**, when the project's `trace` option records this attempt: the worker reads the snapshots
  the trace takes as it grows. Nothing in the trace changes, and the archive the runner keeps is the same.
- **Otherwise, a trace of the worker's own**, started when the first viewer opens Inspect, taking DOM snapshots alone,
  and stopped unsaved when the last closes it: its files are deleted, and so are the response bodies it wrote to the
  trace folder's `resources/` that no other trace there names, then or as the test's context closes. A test that
  starts or stops tracing itself meanwhile, even while the worker's trace starts or stops, waits for the worker's
  trace to stop, then goes; the worker starts none again until the test's own stops. That trace sees only what the
  page loads from then on, so a page loaded before Inspect opened may show unstyled until the test loads it again.
  Playwright's snapshot script stays in the pages that context opens later.

## What is sent, and what is not

- **Nothing until someone opens Inspect.** The worker sends pages only while a viewer of it has Inspect open: first
  the page's snapshots since its last navigation, 16 MB at most, then each new one, 12 a second at most. Past 16 MB,
  the oldest snapshots after a frame's full one are left out, never the full one, which the others build on; a large
  trace starts from the page's last navigation. A snapshot is 4 MB at most. Each waits once, a second at most, behind
  the view's images, then goes, and its bytes space the images after it: the image can slow while Inspect sends.
- **The stylesheets, fonts and images a page names**, once per run, 2 MB each at most, each sent only when its bytes
  are of the kind its type says; fonts are WOFF, WOFF2, TTF, OTF, font collections and EOT alone. Never a script, a
  document, an SVG or an SVG font.
- **Secrets.** Before a page leaves the worker, the value of each field that holds a secret is removed: a password, a
  one-time code, a card's number or code, a field whose name, label (an `aria-labelledby` one too) or `autocomplete`
  names one. So is any text equal to a value the test's secret fields held or its calls typed into one, and anything
  that reads as a card's number: each reads `<hidden>`. Each address in the page (its links, sources, forms, its own
  and its stylesheets') and each text and attribute value has its credentials hidden, as the
  [page's events](./live-view-layers#page-events) do: a URL's password, a query value named or shaped like a token, a
  key's or a JWT's shape anywhere. A `meta` named for a token, a key or a secret has its content hidden. The dashboard
  hides fields, credentials and those `meta` again before it renders a page: a secret field shows empty.
- **No page the worker could not clean**: one whose secret fields it could not read, or whose snapshot it could not
  read whole (deeper than 512 levels, more than 500,000 nodes, or naming one it no longer holds).
- **A project with Masked elements gets no page.** Its masks are locators, which a snapshot cannot apply. As a project
  starts masking elements, the dashboard lets go of every page it kept of its live runs and takes no more.
- **No script of the page runs.** The worker empties a script Playwright kept (an SVG's) and leaves out an attribute
  whose address runs one. The dashboard renders each page itself, its scripts, inline handlers and `javascript:`
  links left out, in a sandboxed frame that loads nothing from the network.

## What the dashboard keeps

The pages and their resources stay in the dashboard server's memory, for the run alone, and only those of each
worker's running test: a worker's pages go as its test ends. It keeps each worker's latest 32 MB of pages (8,192 at
most), 128 MB for the run's workers together (32,768), the resources they name, the 64 MB used last (4,096), and the
8 rendered pages read last, until one they are built from goes. Every live run's together take 512 MB at most:
past it, no new page is kept until runs end. Nothing goes to the database, the disk, the logs or an export, and it all
goes when the run ends.

Who sees them: who may open the run, each from their own view, as for the [images](./live-view#what-is-sent-to-whom-and-what-is-kept).
The dashboard takes pages only from a worker someone inspects: 24 a second from each worker, 8 MB of resources a
second, and 16 MB of pages and resources a second from the run's workers together, apart from their images.

## When no page comes

Inspect says why:

- **The project masks elements.** When the worker's reporter cannot read the masks, Inspect asks to update it.
- **The trace takes no DOM snapshots** (`snapshots` off, or from Playwright 1.63 an object without `dom`), the browser
  keeps no trace folder, or the test traces itself: open Inspect again once its trace stopped.
- **A page not sent**: its secret fields or its snapshot could not be read, it passes 4 MB, Inspect fell behind the
  test's calls (16 MB waiting), or the page's full snapshots alone pass 16 MB. Most say Inspect sends it again from
  its next navigation.
- **A page no longer kept**: let go at the bounds above, of a test that ended, or as the project began masking
  elements; built on a page the worker did not send; or one the dashboard cannot read whole or render in time.
- **The view ended**: the run ended, the live view was turned off, the test ended, or the view closed.

## Limits

- **The test's `page`, its main frame.** An iframe's content is not shown, nor another page of the test.
- **A worker of an older reporter** sends no page: Inspect waits for one.
- **A trace's snapshots, not the live page.** A page shows what Playwright recorded at a call: an element that
  appears between two calls shows at the next.

## In the demo

The live demo runs no browser: its Inspect shows a recorded trace's checkout page
([Stuck tests](./stuck-tests#try-it-in-the-demo)).

- [Live view of a run](./live-view): turning it on, and the image and call of one worker

- [Failure evidence](./evidence): the DOM snapshot and the snapshot picker of a finished test

# Hold a failing CI test

A CI test that fails is gone a second later: its page closes before anyone can look at it. With this setting on, a CI
test that fails while a Maintainer or a Project admin watches its worker in the [live view](./live-view) waits at its
failure, its page open, so they can [inspect](./live-inspect) the page as it failed, read its events and text, and pick
the locator it should have used. **Let it go** ends the wait; the test then ends as it failed.

## Turn it on

A Project admin turns on **Hold a failing CI test for its controllers** in **Project → Settings → Live view**, with the
project's live view on, and sets the **Longest hold**: 1 to 15 minutes, 5 by default. It is off in every project.
It needs `@piwitests/reporter` 0.75.0 or later: an older one never holds, and gets no **Let it go**. With it on, the
same people may also [pause a CI test](./pause-ci-test) they watch, once a Project admin turns that on too.

The CI workers of the runs going on hear the change at once: turned off, a test that is held goes on.

## When a test is held

A CI test is held only when all of these stand as it fails:

- the project's setting is on;
- someone with the `run:control` permission on the project (a Maintainer or a Project admin:
  [roles](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do)) watches that worker's lane in full: in the run page's lane
  panel, in an [editor's worker view](./editor-ci-runs#a-failure-held-for-you), or in
  [Piwi Picker's Runs window](./runs-window), each with that person's sign-in or key. A tile of [Watch all](./watch-all) does
  not count, nor does a Viewer or a Contributor watching;
- the test failed or timed out, and was not expected to.

With authentication off, everyone who opens the run may control it, so anyone watching counts. Who may control the
run is read as a watch opens and again at each change of it (another worker, the panel's size, its layers): a role
taken away counts from then.

The page held is the one the test used last: the `page` fixture's, or one it opened itself (`browser.newPage()`, a
page a `beforeAll` hook opened).

A test that fails while nobody who may control the run watches goes on at once, as it always did: a wait nobody looks
at only costs CI minutes.

## While it is held

The test's row and its lane panel say **Failed, held at its line**, then for whom and until when:
**Held for Ana · until 12:05**, naming the people watching it as it failed. The lane panel shows the failure and its
place, and the live view goes on as for any watched test: the image, the call's log,
[page events, text and filmstrip](./live-view-layers), and [Inspect](./live-inspect) on the failing page. Nothing
reaches the page: no click, no key, no code.

The test's own timeout stops while it waits, as at a breakpoint, so Playwright does not fail the wait itself. **The
CI job's own timeout still runs**: the lane panel says so beside the hold. A job that reaches its timeout during a
hold fails as it would have, later.

### Where it shows

Every surface that watches the lane shows the hold in the same words: the run page's lane panel, VS Code's worker
panel, the JetBrains **Worker** tab and the Runs window's CI run, whose test list marks the lane **Failed, held at its
line** too. **Let it go** shows on a surface whose own watch of the lane counts as a controller's: the instance says so
to that watch as it opens, so an editor or Piwi Picker connected with a Maintainer's key offers it, and one connected
with a Viewer's key shows the hold without it. A refusal is said in the instance's words.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-runs-ci-held.png" width="488" alt="The Runs window watching worker 2 of CI run #78: the test list marks it Failed, held at its line, and above its live page a box says Failed, held at its line, Held for Ana until a time, the expected and received text, tests/checkout.spec.ts:42, The CI job’s own timeout still runs, and a Let it go button">
  <figcaption>A held CI failure in the Runs window, with Let it go.</figcaption>
</figure>

The run's log says that the test is held, and until when, in UTC:

```text
[piwi] The test failed at tests/checkout.spec.ts:42: held for the people watching it on the run page, until 12:05:00 UTC at the latest.
```

## When it ends

The hold ends at the first of:

- **Let it go**, on a surface watching the lane, which only someone with `run:control` sees;
- the longest hold the project set. A new length set during a hold applies to it: the hold ends that long after it
  began, at once when that is past;
- nobody with `run:control` watching the lane in full any more: the last one closed the panel or moved to another
  lane. A Runs window hidden or minimized lets go of its watch, so it stops counting;
- the project's setting turned off, or the run's live view ending (the run ended or interrupted, the project's live
  view turned off).

The test then tears down as it would have: its result, its error and its trace are those of the failure, and its
`piwi-pauses` attachment records the hold. Its reported duration leaves the wait out.

**Let it go** is logged by the instance at info level, with the run, the worker and who asked. Nothing is stored.

## What it costs, and what it never does

- **CI minutes.** A held test holds its CI job's runner for the longest hold at most, each time. One lane waits; the
  run's other workers go on.
- **No new reach.** The worker already holds its live view stream to the instance; nothing listens on the CI machine.
  The instance checks the setting and the permission of the person who asks, and the worker takes **Let it go** only
  on its own stream, and only while its project's setting is on.
- **No input.** The page takes no click, key or text from a viewer, and nothing is run in it: the CI page may be
  signed in to real systems.

# Pause a CI test

A CI test that waits on an element goes past the moment worth seeing before anyone can look at it. With this setting
on, a Maintainer or a Project admin who watches a CI worker in the [live view](./live-view) can **Pause** its test
before its next call, look at the page as it stands, [inspect](./live-inspect) it, then **Resume** it or **End the
test**: a local run's controls, on a test running in CI.

## Turn it on

A Project admin turns on **Let controllers pause a CI test** in **Project → Settings → Live view**. It needs
[Hold a failing CI test](./hold-ci-failure) on: the switch stays off until the hold is on, the API refuses it alone, and
turning the hold off turns it off too. A pause lasts the **Longest hold or pause** at most: 1 to 15 minutes, 5 by
default. It is off in every project, and needs `@piwitests/reporter` 0.75.0 or later: an older one never pauses, and
its lanes offer no **Pause**.

The CI workers of the runs going on hear the change at once. While it is on, a CI worker follows its test's calls
through Playwright's in-process instrumentation, as a local run that may pause does, so a pause stops a call before it
waits for its element, where a local run's would. A test whose page was watched before the setting was turned on was
followed through Playwright's own call stream, which would stop the call only after that wait: it takes no Pause, and
says so; the worker's next test can pause.

## Pause, Resume, End the test

In the run page's lane panel of a CI lane, someone with the `run:control` permission on the project
([roles](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do)) sees **Pause** while the lane's test runs. The test stops
before its next call, the way a local run's **Pause** stops it: a test waiting in a long call stops once that call
ends. Until then the lane panel says **Pause asked by Ana**, and **Resume** takes the Pause back. One Pause at a time:
a second one, from anyone, is refused naming who asked the first.

The worker drops a Pause it cannot take, and the lane panel says why, with **Pause** offered again: no test runs (the
worker is between tests, or in a `beforeAll` hook), the test's function ended first (its `afterEach` hooks and
fixtures never stop, and a failure is then [held](./hold-ci-failure) as any other), nobody with `run:control` watches
the lane in full any more, or the setting went off.

While it is paused, the test's row and its lane panel say by whom and until when: **Paused by Ana · until 12:05**,
or **Paused · until 12:05** when the instance knows no name. The lane panel shows the call the test stopped before and its place, and the live
view goes on as for any watched test: the image, [page events, text and filmstrip](./live-view-layers), and
[Inspect](./live-inspect). The lane panel offers:

- **Resume**: the test goes on from where it stopped;
- **End the test**: the test fails there, at once, with the error `Ended from Piwi by Ana` (`Ended from Piwi` when the
  instance knows no name), so the CI job stays red and the test's retries run as after any failure. The call it
  stopped before never runs, nor does anything after it in the test or its `beforeEach` hook: the call stays held
  until its page closes, then fails, which the result may list as a second error. The `afterEach` hooks and fixtures
  tear down as after any failure. On a Playwright runner whose internals Piwi does not recognize, the test fails at
  its next locator call or as its function ends instead, and the call it stopped before runs first unless it is a
  locator call on Playwright 1.62 or later.

A Viewer or a Contributor watching sees the pause, and no control. A refusal is said in the instance's words, such as
"The project's setting is off" or "You may watch this run, not control it".

The test's own timeout stops while it waits, as at a breakpoint. **The CI job's own timeout still runs**: the lane
panel says so beside the pause. A paused test that resumes passes or fails as it would have, and its reported
duration leaves the wait out.

### Where it shows

Every surface that watches the lane shows the pause and the Pause asked in the same words: the run page's lane panel,
VS Code's worker panel, the JetBrains **Worker** tab and the Runs window's CI run, whose test lists mark the lane
**Paused**. The controls show on a surface whose own watch of the lane counts as a controller's, as **Let it go** does
([Where it shows](./hold-ci-failure#where-it-shows)): an editor or Piwi Picker connected with a Maintainer's key
offers them, one connected with a Viewer's key shows the pause without them. Each is asked once in each state of the
lane, a refusal said in the instance's words.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-runs-ci-paused.png" width="488" alt="The Runs window watching worker 2 of CI run #78: the test list marks it Paused, and above its live page a box says Paused by Ana until a time, the call it stopped before, tests/checkout.spec.ts:31, The CI job’s own timeout still runs, with Resume and End the test">
  <figcaption>A CI test paused for you in the Runs window, with Resume and End the test.</figcaption>
</figure>

The run's log says that the test is paused, and until when, in UTC:

```text
[piwi] The test is paused at tests/checkout.spec.ts:31 for the people watching it on the run page, until 12:05:00 UTC at the latest.
```

## When it ends

A pause ends at the first of:

- **Resume** or **End the test**;
- the longest pause the project set. A new length set during a pause applies to it;
- nobody with `run:control` watching the lane in full any more: the last one closed the panel or moved to another
  lane, as for a [hold](./hold-ci-failure#when-it-ends);
- the project's setting turned off, the hold's included, or the run's live view ending.

A **Pause** that no call took yet is dropped at the same ends, and as its test's function ends: it never stops the
next test.
Each command is logged by the instance at info level, with the run, the worker, the command and who asked. Nothing is
stored.

## What it costs, and what it never does

- **CI minutes.** A paused test holds its CI job's runner for the longest pause at most, each time. One lane waits;
  the run's other workers go on.
- **No new reach.** The worker already holds its live view stream to the instance; nothing listens on the CI machine.
  The instance checks the settings, the permission of the person who asks and that their own watch shows that worker
  in full, and sends the command on that worker's stream alone; the worker takes it only on its own stream, and only
  while its project's setting is on.
- **No input.** The page takes no click, key or text from a viewer, and nothing is run in it. **Interact**, the
  picker acting on the page, **Show the browser** and **Stop the run** stay with local runs: cancelling a CI job
  belongs to CI.

# Share a local run live

A run on your machine sends the team instance nothing of its pages until you share it. Shared, it gets the
[live view](./live-view) a CI run gets: a teammate opens its page and watches each worker, and its stops show on its
rows. Sharing changes nothing for the run itself, and stops as you choose, or as the tool that shared it closes.

## Share and stop

Choose **Share live** while a local run executes to let a teammate watch it. The run must report to a team instance
whose project enables live view, and connect to an editor or the desktop app for controls.

| Where | Share | Stop |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code | **Piwi: Share the run live on the team instance**, or the Piwi item's menu | **Piwi: Stop sharing the run live**, or **Stop sharing** in the Piwi item's menu under **Shared live**, beside **Open the run page** and **Copy the run page's link**, which **Piwi: Shared live: open the run page, copy its link or stop sharing…** also lists, after a confirmation |
| JetBrains IDEs | **Tools → Piwi → Run control → Share the run live on the team instance** | **Tools → Piwi → Run control → Stop sharing the run live**, or **Stop sharing the run** in the status bar item's menu, after a confirmation |
| Piwi Picker's [Runs window](./runs-window) | **Share live** under the run's name | **Stop sharing**, after a confirmation |
| The desktop app's [Local runs tray](./desktop-runs) | **Share live** above the run's workers | **Stop sharing…**, after a confirmation |

The first share asks for confirmation; in an editor, and in the Runs window for an editor's run, it also asks whether
to share this run or [the window's runs](#a-window-s-runs). The shared run shows its destination, viewer count and a link to copy.

Until then, its workers send nothing, and the run's **Tests** tab says **Not shared live** once, beside its search,
with [**Ask to watch**](#ask-to-watch) for a teammate who may ask; its running tests say where they
[stopped](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped). Once shared, images go only to those watching. **Stop sharing** closes the views
within seconds. Closing the editor or the desktop app stops it too.

A run that cannot be shared says why: it reports to no instance or to the desktop app, it does not stream its results,
its project has the live view off, the reporter's global setup did not register it, or the instance did not register the run
as it started. A sharing that stops on its own says why (the live view turned off, or the instance stopped answering), and **Share live** shows again: shared again, the run streams once the instance answers with its live view
on, a restarted instance taking the run's key back. A run the instance no longer holds live cannot be shared again. A [requested run](./run-on-my-machine#a-requested-run-is-yours-alone)
gets no live view key from the instance, so it cannot be shared.

### From a terminal

A run you start in a terminal that no editor or app follows has no **Share live** to choose: set `PIWI_SHARE_LIVE=1`
to share it from its start. The reporter prints what goes out and where before any image does, or why the run cannot
be shared. A tool that follows the run can still stop it.

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
PIWI_SHARE_LIVE=1 npx playwright test
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:PIWI_SHARE_LIVE='1'; npx playwright test
```

:::

### A window's runs

**Piwi: Share this window's runs live until I stop** in VS Code, **Tools → Piwi → Run control → Share this project's runs live
until I stop** in a JetBrains IDE, and **Share this editor window's runs** under an editor's run in Piwi Picker's Runs
window share each run the window starts from then on, each one said as it is shared, until you stop (**…Stop sharing
this window's runs live**, **Shared live** in the Piwi item's menu, or **Stop sharing this window's runs**
on the Runs window's line that says the window shares its runs, whatever runs it lists) or close the window. A run's
own **Stop sharing** in the Runs window stops that run alone.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-runs-share-window.png" width="488" alt="The Runs window under its heading saying Visual Studio Code's window shares its runs live until you stop, with Stop sharing this window's runs under that line, and a run shared as one of them, with its own Stop sharing">
  <figcaption>An editor window's runs, shared from the Runs window.</figcaption>
</figure>

On the team instance, the page of the run before says **Continued in run #78**, linked, and a teammate who
has it open is taken to the new run, on the worker they were watching.

## Ask to watch

A teammate who opens a running run of yours that is not shared can ask you to share it: **Ask to watch**, beside
**Not shared live**. The tool you launched the run from asks you, naming the person who asks, and offers
**Share live** and **Not now**; a run that no tool follows prints the ask in its terminal. Their page shows your answer:
**Asked to watch** while it waits, **The developer answered Not now**, or the live view once you share.

- **Who** — anyone signed in who may open the run. With sign-in off on the instance, nobody is named, and asking is
  not offered.
- **How often** — one ask per person and run every 5 minutes; their page says when they may ask again.
- **Which runs** — a running run from a developer's machine that holds a live view key, never a CI run, whose
  workers stream as they start.
- **Turn it off** — a Project admin turns off **Let signed-in readers ask to watch a run nobody shares** in the
  project's **Live view** settings; it is on by default. Turning it off, or the live view, drops the asks that wait.

Asks are kept in the instance's memory, never stored, and end with the run.

## Stops, shared or not

A stopped test's row on the run's page says why and where, from the live view of a shared run, else as text, never an
image: [where a test stopped](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped).

## From the desktop app

A **Re-run** in a folder whose `.env` or Playwright config names your team's instance reports to it, and can be
shared: **Share live**, above the run's workers, asks first the first time since the app started.

A run that reports to the [desktop app](./desktop-runs) itself (a reproduction, a bisect, a **Re-run** in a folder
that names no instance, a run your editor started) cannot be shared: the app hands out no live view key, since no
teammate reaches it. Its tray offers no **Share live** for it, the app's project settings have no **Live view**
section, and on the run's page its running tests offer [**Watch** and **Pause and watch**](./desktop-runs#watch),
shown in the app's tray from the app itself. A run your editor started says **See its page at a stop** there: its page
shows where the editor steers it.

## Related

- [Live view of a run](./live-view): what a teammate sees, what is sent and what is kept
- [Editor run control](./editor-run-control): the controls of a run your editor starts
- [Runs window](./runs-window): Piwi Picker's view of your runs
- [Desktop app runs](./desktop-runs): the desktop app's runs and its tray

# Stuck tests

A CI run that never ends is often one test waiting on something that will not come: a button that stays disabled, a
page that never loads, a lock never released. Piwi says so while the run is still going. A running test that has run
far longer than it usually does is marked **Stuck?** on its run page, and a `test.stuck` notification goes to the
project's channels. Nobody needs to have the run open, and the [live view](./live-view) does not need to be on.

## When a test is stuck

The dashboard checks the running tests of its live runs every 15 seconds. A test is stuck when its current attempt has
run longer than both:

- two minutes, whatever the test usually takes;
- three times its longest duration among its last ten passing executions on the same browser.

A test needs two passing executions on that browser before any attempt of it can be stuck: a new test is never
flagged. The executions read are the ones a baseline reads, so no Flake Lab or investigation run and no environment
incident. The time counts from the start the attempt's begin event names, else from when the dashboard heard it begin; the
reporter's begin events name none.
Each attempt is said to be stuck once; a retry is a new attempt.

A test of a run on a developer's machine may stand stopped at a breakpoint or a `page.pause()`. With
`@piwitests/reporter` 0.68.0 or later its run tells the dashboard so: the test is never said to be stuck while it
stands stopped, and the time it stood stopped is left out of how long it ran.

The question mark is meant: a test can be slow for a good reason, a large import or a cold cache. The rule says only
that this attempt is far outside what its passing runs took.

## On the run page

A stuck test's row on the run page's **Tests** tab carries a **Stuck?** badge, how long it has run and the longest
its last passing runs took: `Running for 7 minutes, usually 41.2s at most`. The row's live step names the step it is
in. With the project's [live view](./live-view) on, **Watch** shows its page and, in a CI run, what its current call
waits for. The badge leaves the row when the attempt ends. A test that stands stopped says where in its place:
`Stopped at a breakpoint · Click getByRole('button') · tests/checkout.spec.ts:18 · for 3 minutes`.

A page opened after the test was said to be stuck shows it too: the dashboard keeps it with the running test.

## On the Timeline

While a run runs, its **Timeline** tab shows each worker's lane, grouped by shard, with a bar for every attempt. A
running attempt's bar grows to now over a pale bar of its test's usual time: the longest of the last passing runs this
rule reads. Once it runs past that time, a white tick marks where it would usually have ended, and it turns amber once
the test is marked **Stuck?**. A test with too few passing runs has no pale bar. The header counts the stuck tests, and
a sharded run's says which of its shards have started: `shards 1 and 3 of 4 started`.

On the **Tests** tab, `is:stuck` lists the stuck tests, and `worker:` and `shard:` narrow the list to one worker or one
shard ([Test search](/reference/test-search)).

## In your editor

In VS Code and a JetBrains IDE, the [editor extensions](./editors) say it of the run they follow: the test's line
reads `Stuck? running over 7 min, usually 41 s, in your run #130`, VS Code's Testing view writes that line in the output of
a run you started, once, and the [status bar item](./editor-status-bar) counts them (`Piwi: run #130 · 4 of 9 · 1 stuck?`). A test
that stands stopped is not counted until it goes on.

## The notification

`test.stuck` fires once per attempt, through the channels of the project's
[subscriptions](./notifications#subscriptions) that chose it. Its message names the test, how long it has run against
its usual time, the run with its branch and environment, the browser and worker, and the test's owner. Its button opens
the run with its **Tests** tab searched for the test, and the [live view](./live-view#watch-a-worker) of its worker
where the project has it on. The payload is on
[Notification events & webhooks](/reference/notification-events#payload-fields-by-event).

The branch, environment, owner and **Default branch only** filters apply to it. A run started on a developer's machine
sends none, complete or not: a run from a terminal, the desktop app, an editor, `piwi preflight --run` or
`piwi bug --write` is marked **Stuck?** on its run page and notifies nobody, since its test may be stopped at a
breakpoint. A bisect step or a reproduction sends none either. A CI job the reporter does not detect as CI records its
runs as `local`: set `PIWI_ORIGIN=ci` on it ([run origin](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin)).

## Limits

- **A live run on this dashboard.** The running tests are kept in the memory of the server the run reports to, as the
  run's live events are. A dashboard that restarts forgets them until each test's next attempt begins, and it needs one
  dashboard server ([Resource requirements](/operate/deployment#resource-requirements)).
- **Fixed thresholds.** Two minutes and three times the longest pass are the same for every project.
- **No history, no verdict.** A test with fewer than two passing executions on its browser is never said to be stuck.

## Try it in the demo

In the [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/), pick **Stuck test** in **Simulate a test run**: the PayPal checkout
waits on a **Pay** button that stays disabled, and its row carries the **Stuck?** badge once it runs past its usual time; on
the **Timeline** tab its bar turns amber past the pale bar of that time. Its row's **Watch** shows the click it waits
on, its call log retrying a disabled **Pay** button, and [Inspect](./live-inspect) the checkout page at that click, as
a recorded trace holds it, with the locator picker.
**Stopped at a breakpoint** plays a run from VS Code whose PayPal test stands at a breakpoint for five minutes: its row
says where, and never reads **Stuck?**.

## Related

- [Live view of a run](./live-view): watch a stuck test's page and what it waits for
- [Test search](/reference/test-search): `is:stuck`, `worker:` and `shard:`
- [Notifications & alerts](./notifications): channels and subscriptions
- [Notification events & webhooks](/reference/notification-events)

# Our suite takes too long — where is the time actually going?

The instinct is to look for slow tests. That is usually the smallest part of the bill. A suite's wall
clock is mostly made of four things, and only one of them is "the app is slow":

1. **Waits somebody wrote** — `waitForTimeout` sleeps that were a workaround once.
2. **Timeouts nobody revisited** — a thirty-second budget on a three-second test costs twenty-seven seconds *every time it fails*.
3. **Retries of flaky tests** — paid on every run, and they buy no signal.
4. **The application itself** — the only part that needs a real fix.

Piwi measures all four separately, so you can spend effort where the minutes are. It does not make your
app faster; it tells you whether that is even the problem.

## 1. Split the bill before optimizing anything

[Analytics](/features/analytics) has two widgets that belong side by side: **CI time**, the minutes your runs
consumed, and **Wasted CI time**, the part that produced no signal ([what counts as wasted](/features/slow-tests#wasted-time)).

If wasted time is a small slice, your suite is just big: look at [the application](#_5-ask-whether-the-app-is-slow-not-the-test) and
[parallelism](#_6-spend-the-parallelism-you-already-have). If it is a large slice, start with [the waits](#_2-reclaim-the-waits-you-wrote),
[the timeouts](#_3-tighten-the-timeouts-that-only-bill-you-on-failure) and [the flaky retries](#_4-stop-paying-for-flaky-retries).

## 2. Reclaim the waits you wrote

The sleeps somebody wrote are wasted time Piwi totals per execution and per run, and which waits count is yours
to tune ([wasted time](/features/slow-tests#wasted-time)). Turn on **Show waits** on a run's **Timeline** tab and each
sleep is a bar that opens its test.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-timeline.png" alt="A run's Timeline tab: one horizontal lane per worker, tests as bars with their setup and teardown hooks hatched at each end, the fixed-wait sleeps highlighted as wasted-wait spans, and the Show hooks and Show waits switches above">
  <figcaption>The Timeline tab: one lane per worker, hook time hatched at each end of a test, and the fixed-wait sleeps highlighted as their own span.</figcaption>
</figure>

Count every wait once to see how much of the suite is waiting on something, then set the patterns back.

## 3. Tighten the timeouts that only bill you on failure

An oversized per-test timeout bills you only when the test fails. The **Performance** tab's
[**Timeout opportunities**](/features/slow-tests#timeout-opportunities) lists the tests whose timeout dwarfs their real
duration, and the outgrown `test.slow()` marks, each with a tighter value and the time it reclaims.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/performance-trends.png" alt="Project Performance tab showing the duration trend chart with total, average and percentile series and timeline markers, above the slowest-tests table">
  <figcaption>The Performance tab: average and percentile duration over time, then the ranked slowest tests.</figcaption>
</figure>

Read the [percentile line](/features/slow-tests#duration-trends), not the average.

## 4. Stop paying for flaky retries

A flaky test bills you twice, for the failed attempt and for the retry, on every run where it misbehaves. That is
why Piwi ranks flaky tests by what their retries cost ([impact](/features/flaky-tests#impact-ranking)) rather than by
flakiness score.

[Cutting the flakiness that costs the most](./flaky-cleanup) is the whole recipe for this. The short
version: work down the impact order, fix the red dots, and
[quarantine](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) the rest so they stop blocking merges while
still running.

## 5. Ask whether the app is slow, not the test

Everything above shaves time off the harness; this step finds a real performance bug.

- **[Slow endpoints](/features/slow-tests)**: on a run, network requests grouped by normalized route with their
  duration and error rate; [Analytics](/features/analytics) lifts the same view across every project.
- **Web Vitals**: TTFB, FCP, LCP, CLS and the rest per execution. LCP, CLS and INP are Chromium-only.

Both require the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures): the reporter alone cannot see the network.
Without them you still have the trace: its network waterfall shows the same requests for one execution,
just not aggregated across the suite.

## 6. Spend the parallelism you already have

- **Worker imbalance** is called out in a run's [Timeline](/features/slow-tests#the-run-s-timeline) tab, under the worker
  distribution: if one worker finishes long after the others, the suite is as slow as its unluckiest shard, and no
  amount of per-test tuning fixes that.
- **Sharding** is Playwright's own `--shard`; Piwi merges the shards back into [one
  run](/guide/concepts#test-run), so you can raise the shard count without turning your history into
  fragments. See [CI & sharding](/guide/ci#sharding).

## Other ways in

**Ask your agent.** Over the [MCP server](/features/mcp), `get_slow_tests` returns the ranked slowest tests,
`get_performance_trend` the duration history, and `get_run_insights` the worker imbalance of one run.

**Script it.** The same numbers are on the REST API: see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api).

**Watch it drift.** Rather than auditing periodically, subscribe to the `perf.regression`
[notification](/features/notifications) event and let it tell you when a duration trend breaks.

## Related
- [Slow tests & wasted time](/features/slow-tests) — the full reference for trends, slowest
  tests and timeout hygiene
- [Cut the flakiness that costs the most](./flaky-cleanup) — the flaky-retries step in full
- [Analytics](/features/analytics) — CI time and wasted CI time across every project
- [Capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) — what unlocks the network and Web Vitals views

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/slow-tests -->

# Slow tests & wasted time

The test list tells you what failed; it doesn't tell you where the **minutes** go. This page covers the project's
**Performance** tab (duration trends, the slowest tests, timeout opportunities, slow endpoints), a run's **Timeline**
and the time Piwi counts as **wasted**. What the run cost the machine is on [CPU, memory & disk](./cpu-memory-disk); flaky tests ranked
by the time their retries cost, on [Flaky tests](./flaky-tests#impact-ranking).

## Duration trends

Average and **P90** duration over time, so a few slow outliers don't hide a real regression (a rising P90 with a flat
average is a tail getting worse). Read the percentile, not the average: a handful of slow outliers move it and barely
move the mean, and the outliers decide how long a shard takes. **Slowest tests** ranks the top offenders by duration.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/performance-trends.png" alt="Performance tab showing the duration trend chart and slowest-tests table">
  <figcaption>The Performance view — average and P90 duration trends over time, followed by a ranked table of the slowest tests.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Timeout opportunities

Tests whose configured per-test timeout dwarfs their real p95 duration — so a hang or failure waits far longer than it needs to — plus tests still carrying a stale `test.slow()` mark they no longer need. Each row suggests a tighter timeout (or removing the mark) and the time reclaimable per failing run, ranked by impact.

An oversized timeout costs nothing while the test passes and its whole budget each time it fails: a thirty-second
timeout on a three-second test burns twenty-seven seconds on every failure before anyone learns anything.

This reads the per-test timeout the [reporter captures](/reference/test-metadata#per-test-timeout); runs reported before that shipped still surface stale `test.slow()` marks from annotations and durations alone. The thresholds are set in **Settings → Performance**.

## Wasted time

**Wasted time** is time that produced no signal. Piwi counts two kinds:

- **Waits**: the time inside wait steps that match the wasted-wait patterns. By default only explicit sleeps count
  (`waitForTimeout` and friends), since framework-injected waits (load-state, wait-for-function) are usually
  unavoidable. Tune the patterns in **Settings → Performance**, or lock them with
  [`PIWI_WASTED_WAIT_PATTERNS`](/reference/configuration#wasted-time); `*` counts every wait, which shows once how
  much of the suite is waiting. They are applied when a run is viewed, so a change re-classifies the whole history
  with no re-run.
- **Failed attempts**: the time spent running attempts that ended failed or timed out.

A run's test list and an execution's **Details** popover show each test's fixed-wait time, and the run's **Timeline**
tab draws the sleeps as bars with **Show waits**. The **Wasted CI time** [Analytics](./analytics) widget adds waits and
failed attempts over time and per project, beside **CI time**, the minutes the runs consumed, and states how much is
**reclaimable** by tightening timeouts and dropping stale `test.slow()` marks. With a
[cost per CI minute](/reference/configuration#wasted-time) set, each wasted-time number carries its cost.

The flaky list's **wasted CI minutes** are a narrower number, a test's retries times its average failed attempt:
see [Impact ranking](./flaky-tests#impact-ranking).

## The run's Timeline

A run's **Timeline** tab draws each worker's tests on one time axis, with waits, locks and
[breakpoint](./editor-breakpoints) stops. Under the lanes it ranks the run's **Slowest tests**, sums each named lock's
held and serialized time in **Locks**, and shows the **Worker distribution**, how the tests spread across the workers:

- **Hooks**: hatched over each test's bar, setup (`beforeAll`, `beforeEach`, fixtures) at the start,
  teardown (`afterEach`, `afterAll`, worker cleanup) at the end. A failed hook is dark red and counted in
  the header, even with **Show hooks** off; hover it for the hooks, times and error,
  click it for the test's steps on that hook. Playwright leaves `beforeAll` and `afterAll` hooks and worker
  fixtures out of a test's duration; the bar spans them, and its tooltip gives Playwright's duration.
  Older reporters send no hook list.
- **Gaps**: a lane is one [worker](/reference/test-metadata#worker-lanes). Playwright replaces a worker process
  after a failed test, so a lane can hold several processes in turn: **↻** marks where a new one took
  over, and the stretch before it is that replacement. A dashed line is time the
  worker ran no test; hover either for details.
- **Retries**: a retried test has one bar per attempt, the last solid, the earlier ones pale. Hover one to join
  them with arrows.
- **Resources**: the run's CPU, memory and open pages, above the worker rows and under each of them.

## Time paused at a stop

When a test stands [stopped](./watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped) at a breakpoint, a Pause or a held failure, its
duration leaves the time paused out, while every step keeps its clock time: the timelines draw each stop as a
**Paused** band, and the step statistics (the slowest step, wasted time) leave it out.

The test timeout stops while a test is paused at a breakpoint, and so does the paused call's own budget
(`actionTimeout`, or `expect.timeout` for an assertion on that line). A wait the test started before the stop keeps its
own deadline: `expect.poll`, `toPass`, or a `waitForRequest`, `waitForResponse` or `waitForEvent` around the paused
call can run out while you look and fail the test. The pause bar then goes away, before Playwright's failure
screenshot and the `afterEach` hooks.

## Network and Web Vitals

- **Slow endpoints** — slow API calls grouped by method and normalized route (e.g. `/users/:id`), for a run picked from the tab.
- **Browser Web Vitals** — TTFB, DOMContentLoaded, FCP and more, with color-coded thresholds, shown per execution in the **Performance** tab of the execution page's evidence rather than on the project.

Both require the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in your test setup — without them the reporter has no network timings or Web Vitals to aggregate.

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › Performance](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/1?tab=performance): Duration trends with their markers, the slowest tests, and the timeouts worth tightening.

## Related

- [Cut the time it costs](/recipes/faster-suite): the slowest tests and wasted time, cut in order of cost
- [Capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) — the test-side setup behind network analysis and Web Vitals
- [Flaky tests](./flaky-tests): the time a flaky test's retries cost
- [Analytics](./analytics): wasted time and slow endpoints across every project
- [Reporter](/reference/test-metadata#per-test-timeout) — how the per-test timeout is captured
