# Re-run in CI

A [filtered run that passes every affected test closes a cluster](./failure-clusters#did-the-fix-work). Piwi can start
that run in CI, and others: a page's **run button** opens a dialog whose **Where** lists the project's
[CI actions](./ci-actions) beside your own apps ([Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine)). It reads **Run on CI**,
**Run on my machine** or **Run on my machine or CI**, after what you may use there; in the desktop app, it says what it
runs on [this computer](./run-on-this-computer):

| Page | What CI runs |
|---|---|
| Project | The whole suite, or the [tests carrying some tags](#tagged-tests), on the project's default branch |
| Run | Its failed tests, or the action's whole suite on the run's branch |
| Execution | The test, or every test of its cluster |
| Test | The test, or a [Flake Lab](./flake-lab#run-it-in-ci) experiment |
| Failure cluster, and its Verify section | Its affected tests |

A re-run sends each test's `file:line` from its latest failure and the projects it failed in, at most 100 tests, on
the branch of the run it comes from. The **Re-run in CI** next step, and a Flake Lab one, open the dialog on CI.

CI is **off by default**: a project starts it through the [CI actions](./ci-actions) of its **Settings**, each saying
where Piwi starts CI and what it sends. The dialog, MCP and the API can name another action than the default, a branch
and a value for each choice input.

CI shows to people with [`run:control`](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do) once an action that takes the
page's tests can be sent: it serves the run's repository with a credential, and a re-run's tests have a path
Playwright takes.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-dialog.png" alt="The run dialog of a failed run: its failed tests or every test, three CI actions, one disabled because it takes no re-runs, and the picked action's branch and input">
  <figcaption>A failed run's dialog: an action that takes no re-runs is disabled, with the reason.</figcaption>
</figure>

## The run dialog

- **Where** opens on the one you last sent to in this project, from this browser. Otherwise a re-run picks the action
  that started its run, else the one of its environment, else the default for re-runs; the project page picks its
  default for Run on CI, or for tagged tests, and the test page your first online app. In the desktop app, **This
  computer** takes your apps' place and comes first: [Run on this computer](./run-on-this-computer).
- A CI row shows its target and environment. It is disabled, with the reason, when the action does not take the
  chosen **What** or cannot be sent. Picked, the dialog says what a team run is: it counts in the project's history,
  sends notifications and pull-request feedback, and spends CI minutes. A Flake Lab experiment is a lab run instead,
  kept out of the history.
- **Branch**: a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket action offers the branches the project's runs reported, then the
  repository's; a Jenkins job with `{branch}` in its path, or a Custom request naming the branch, takes a typed name;
  any other CI server job runs its configured branch. A name git refuses is not sent.
- Each choice input offers its options; the fixed ones are listed.
- An action on a [per-user credential](/operate/per-user-credentials) says *in your name*, and asks for your own
  token the first time.
- The button's menu sends the page's first **What** in one click, to one action or app, on the branch the dialog
  would pick, with the default choices. In the desktop app, it is This computer's menu, with these runs on CI in it.

After **Send** the dialog follows the dispatch: *waiting for the run to report*, with **Open in CI**, then the run and
its result once [matched](#matching-the-run), which a toast says if you closed the dialog. With no run after 30
minutes, it lists the likely causes. **Run again** sends it again; a CI run is cancelled in the CI. The Verify section
of a cluster and of its executions shows the cluster's last re-run.

*Copy retry command* is the local counterpart: it copies an `npx playwright test` command to run the same tests on your
machine. On a run's page, its menu adds run options the browser remembers (headed, trace, repeat each up to 10 without
retries, workers up to 4), and one project the tests ran in.

An action that accepts **Flake Lab** runs `piwi flake` for one flaky test: [Run it in CI](./flake-lab#run-it-in-ci)
shows the GitHub workflow, and [Flake Lab on Jenkins](./ci-actions#flake-lab-on-jenkins) the Jenkins job.

## Tagged tests

On the project page, **What** also offers **Tests tagged…**. Pick up to 10 of the tags of the tests that ran in the last
30 days, each listed with how many of those tests carry it, spellings that differ only in case counted as one, and, for
two or more, whether a test carrying **any of them** or **all of them** runs. Only an action that accepts **Tagged
tests** takes them; the others are disabled, with the reason. Your apps take no tags: a run request names its tests.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-dialog-tags.png" alt="The project page's run dialog on Tests tagged: @api and @regression picked, All of them chosen, the nightly action picked and the smoke action disabled because it takes no tagged tests">
  <figcaption>Two tags, a test carrying both: the action that takes no tagged tests is disabled.</figcaption>
</figure>

CI gets one `--grep` over what Playwright greps, a test's titles and its tags, ignoring case, so `@smoke` in a title
and in the `tag` option both match. Each tag runs up to a space or the end, after any character, as Playwright reads a
tag from a title (`@example.com` in `emails user@example.com`); one of 60 characters, the most Piwi keeps of a tag,
matches as a tag's start. **All of them** for `@smoke` and `@checkout` sends:

```text
--grep="^(?=[^]*@smoke(?=\s|$))(?=[^]*@checkout(?=\s|$))"
```

It is double-quoted like every argument Piwi sends, and reads the same in bash, PowerShell, cmd and
[`rerun`](/reference/cli#rerun). A tag holding a space, a double quote, or one of `$`, `` ` ``, `\`, `%` and `!` is not
offered.

## Waiting rows

A project's runs list shows each dispatch no run has answered yet as a row above its runs, to everyone who reads the
project: *Waiting for CI*, what it runs, its action and the branch it names, when and by whom it was dispatched, and
**Open in CI**. After 30 minutes it reads *No run reported yet*, with the likely causes under **Why?**. Once a run is
[matched](#matching-the-run) to it, the row reads *Running* with **Open run #N** while that run goes on, since the
list's filters may leave the run out (a re-run is a partial run), and leaves when the run ends. A dispatch no run is
matched to within six hours leaves then.

Your own [run requests](./run-on-my-machine) wait there as well, seen by you alone. A requested run is never in the
list, so its row stays while the run goes on, with a link to it, and leaves once the request ends.

The rows show whatever the filters say, five at a time with **Show all**, but not under **Kept runs only** or a period
opened from Analytics; dispatches show while the project's CI actions are on. The page reads the dispatches with
itself, your requests once it has loaded, and both again on each run event of the project and when the browser tab
shows again; while a row shows, a dispatch every 30 seconds, a request every 5 seconds until its run starts, then every
30.

## Matching the run

Piwi matches each dispatch's run as it starts: by the `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF` the run carries, else by the CI's own run id
(GitHub's run, GitLab's pipeline, Bitbucket's build), and a Flake Lab run by its experiment's test. At its end, a CI
server re-run, or a GitHub one answered without a run, matches by branch, a start within six hours and exactly its spec
files.

A matched re-run's [origin](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin) is `ci-rerun`. The run of a whole suite or of tagged
tests keeps `ci`, and the grep of tagged tests makes theirs a partial run, as any grep does. The last re-run links its
build and run with its result, or reads *no run reported* after six hours. A repeat within ten seconds is refused; dispatches are kept
90 days.

A workflow GitHub answers with its run needs no change; otherwise the dispatch id input, optional since GitHub refuses
undeclared ones and passed on as `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF`, alone matches a whole suite or tagged tests:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      args:
        required: false
        default: ''
      piwi_dispatch:
        required: false
        default: ''
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright test ${{ inputs.args }}
        env:
          PIWI_ORIGIN_REF: ${{ inputs.piwi_dispatch }}
```

## Limits

- A dispatch is one request: Piwi does not poll the CI, it waits for the run to report.
- The demo runs only CI server actions: it records a dispatch without sending it, so its follow-up and its row in the
  runs list keep waiting for the run, and its Check answers as a job that declares the default parameters.

- [CI actions](./ci-actions): the workflows, pipelines and jobs a dispatch goes to
- [Pull-request feedback](./pr-feedback): the result posted on the pull request
- [Source control](/guide/source-control): the SCM credential and its scopes
- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters): the clusters a re-run acts on
- [Flake Lab](./flake-lab): the experiment a Flake Lab action runs in CI

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/ci-actions -->

# CI actions

A CI action is a named way for a project to start CI: the run button's [Re-run in CI](./ci-rerun) and the MCP tool
`rerun_cluster_in_ci` go through one. They are **off by default** and set per project in the **CI** section of the
project's **Settings** tab (under Integrations, beside **Issue tracker**).

## What an action has

A CI action has:

- a **name**, unique in the project, ignoring case;
- a **target**: a GitHub workflow, a GitLab or Bitbucket pipeline, a Jenkins job or a Custom request;
- **inputs**: a *fixed* value (`TARGET_ENV=staging`) or a *choice* with a default and options. They are sent beside the
  Playwright arguments, never inside them: as workflow inputs on GitHub, variables on GitLab and Bitbucket, and
  parameters on Jenkins. A name is letters, digits and `_`, and on GitLab and Bitbucket cannot start with `CI_`,
  `GITLAB_` or `BITBUCKET_`. A Custom request sends none;
- what it **accepts**: re-runs, Run on CI, [tagged tests](./ci-rerun#tagged-tests), Flake Lab;
- an optional **environment**, one of the project's [environments](./environments), which a run of that environment
  picks first;
- the kinds it is the **default** for.

Unless you pick another, a dispatch uses the action that started the run it re-runs, else the one of the run's
environment, else the project's default. A repository action serves only a run whose repository is on that host; a CI
server action serves any run. Settings saved before CI
actions existed were converted when read.

**Check** reads an action's target without starting it and says whether it declares every name a dispatch sends, the
inputs included, and, on GitHub, whether the action sends every input the workflow requires with no default. It reads a
GitHub workflow file, a Jenkins job, and a Bitbucket custom pipeline on the default branch, whose undeclared variables
it names as a warning. GitLab pipelines and Custom requests cannot be checked, and Check says so.

Two actions on one workflow, one per environment, differ only in their inputs:

```yaml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      args: { description: Playwright arguments, default: '' }
      TARGET_ENV: { description: Environment under test, default: staging }
jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright test ${{ inputs.args }}
        env:
          TARGET_ENV: ${{ inputs.TARGET_ENV }}
```

*Smoke · staging* and *Smoke · production* both target `e2e.yml`, each with one fixed input, `TARGET_ENV=staging` or
`TARGET_ENV=production`.

## Picking from what the target declares

The action editor reads the target without starting it and offers what it finds, as the issue tracker binding offers a
Jira project's fields. Any name can still be typed, for a job the listing does not reach.

| Target | The jobs it lists | The fields of a job |
|---|---|---|
| **GitHub** | The workflow files at the ref with a `workflow_dispatch` trigger, by their `name` | The trigger's inputs, with their type, default, options and whether they are required |
| **GitLab** | None: a pipeline runs the CI file of its ref | The variables `.gitlab-ci.yml` sets, at its top level and in each job |
| **Bitbucket** | The `custom:` pipelines on the default branch | The pipeline's `variables`, with their default and allowed values |
| **Jenkins** | The jobs under the base URL, folders three levels deep, a multibranch pipeline as `path/{branch}` | The job's parameters, with their type, default and choices |

The arguments input and the dispatch id input are picked from the job's fields, and **Add a declared input** (a
variable on GitLab and Bitbucket, a parameter on Jenkins) adds one of the others: a choice or a boolean as a choice, any
other field as a fixed value holding its default. Picking a GitHub workflow adds the inputs it requires with no default,
and the editor names what a workflow, a custom pipeline or a Jenkins job does not declare. GitLab takes any variable a
pipeline is created with, so its variables are suggestions; the files a CI file `include`s are not read.

The files are read with the action's credential, else the repository's. A Jenkins listing carries the credential a
dispatch would, whose user needs the Overall/Read and Job/Read permissions, and is logged; read with a credential other
projects share (the instance's, or one shared with several projects), it leaves out a parameter's free-text default and
its description. A branch is read at its latest commit; what was listed is kept five minutes, and the refresh button
beside the listing reads again.

## Repository host

Choose the provider of the action:

| Provider | What the target names | Token scope |
|---|---|---|
| **GitHub** | Workflow file name (e.g. `e2e.yml`), a ref, the `workflow_dispatch` input that receives the arguments, and optionally the input that receives the dispatch id | **Actions: write** (fine-grained), `repo` (classic) |
| **GitLab** | A ref and the pipeline variable name that receives the arguments | `api` |
| **Bitbucket** | The `custom:` pipeline name and the variable name that receives the arguments | `pipeline:write` |

The dispatch carries the action's **Credential**, else the repository's
[SCM credential](/guide/source-control#set-the-credential), with the scope above. **Check** and the editor's listings
carry the same credential to read the repository's files, which takes read access to its contents as well.

On GitLab and Bitbucket, name the variable `PIWI_RERUN_ARGS` and run [`rerun`](/reference/cli#rerun), which reads the
quoted arguments without a shell:

::: code-group

```yaml [GitLab]
e2e: # the job that runs your tests
  variables:
    PIWI_RERUN_ARGS: "" # empty runs the whole suite; a re-run sets it
  script:
    - npm ci
    - npx @piwitests/reporter rerun
```

```yaml [Bitbucket]
pipelines:
  custom:
    rerun: # the custom pipeline name in the Bitbucket block
      - variables:
          - name: PIWI_RERUN_ARGS
      - step:
          script:
            - npm ci
            - npx @piwitests/reporter rerun
```

:::

GitHub answers with the run it started, which the link opens; a server that answers none (an older GitHub Enterprise
Server) links to the workflow's runs page for the branch. GitLab and Bitbucket link to the pipeline.

## CI server

A CI server action is a **preset**, which builds the request from a few fields, or a **Custom request** you write.

**Jenkins** takes the job as Jenkins shows its path (`polaris/e2e`; `polaris/e2e/{branch}` for a multibranch pipeline)
and posts to its `buildWithParameters` with `PIWI_RERUN_ARGS` (the arguments) and `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF` (the dispatch id),
names you can change, plus the action's inputs. The credential is a Jenkins user and their API token, sent as Basic
authentication. The link goes to the job's page. The job declares both parameters and runs `rerun`:

```groovy
pipeline {
  agent any
  parameters {
    string(name: 'PIWI_RERUN_ARGS', defaultValue: '', description: 'Playwright arguments of a re-run')
    string(name: 'PIWI_ORIGIN_REF', defaultValue: '', description: 'The dispatch Piwi matches the run to')
  }
  stages {
    stage('e2e') {
      steps {
        sh 'npm ci'
        sh 'npx @piwitests/reporter rerun'
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Check** reads the Jenkins job as it is in the form, unsaved fields included. Jenkins drops a parameter its job does
not declare, so a re-run would fail or never be matched. A Pipeline job declares its Jenkinsfile's parameters on its
first build: run a new job once, then check it. A multibranch pipeline is checked on its default branch.

### Flake Lab on Jenkins

A Jenkins action that accepts Flake Lab receives `flake 12` or `flake verify 12` in its arguments parameter and hands
it to the reporter, which reads `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and `PIWI_API_KEY`:

```groovy
pipeline {
  agent any
  parameters {
    string(name: 'PIWI_RERUN_ARGS', defaultValue: '', description: 'flake 12, or flake verify 12')
    string(name: 'PIWI_ORIGIN_REF', defaultValue: '', description: 'The dispatch Piwi started')
  }
  environment {
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL = 'https://piwi.example.com'
    PIWI_API_KEY = credentials('piwi-api-key')
  }
  stages {
    stage('flake') {
      steps {
        sh 'npm ci'
        sh 'npx playwright install --with-deps chromium'
        sh 'npx @piwitests/reporter $PIWI_RERUN_ARGS'
      }
    }
  }
}
```

On a Windows agent use `bat` steps and read `%PIWI_RERUN_ARGS%`.

### Custom requests

**Customize the request** turns the preset into a Custom request that sends the same thing, to edit from there. A
Custom request is JSON: `auth` (`none`, `basic`, `bearer`, or `{ "header": "X-Token" }`) and a `rerun` request with a
`method` (`POST` or `PUT`), a `path` relative to the base URL, and optional `query`, `headers`, `body`, `link` and
`buildNumber`. Its values may name these placeholders:

| Placeholder | Value |
|---|---|
| <code v-pre>{{args}}</code> | The Playwright arguments (tagged tests' `--grep`), or `flake 12` for Flake Lab |
| <code v-pre>{{dispatchId}}</code> | The dispatch id the run hands back as `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF` |
| <code v-pre>{{ref}}</code> | The branch asked, else the run's (the project's for its whole suite or tags), else the action's |
| <code v-pre>{{commit}}</code> | That run's commit, else empty |
| <code v-pre>{{branchJob}}</code> | The branch as Jenkins names a branch job (`feature/x` is `feature%2Fx`) |

A placeholder in a path is percent-encoded inside its segment, and a value that would add a `.` or `..` segment is
refused. In a JSON body it fills a whole string value.

### The credential and the hosts

A CI server action names a [credential](/operate/credentials): a user, a secret and the base URL it may be sent
under, saved once, shared with projects, and logged on each use. Its base URL can stay empty to use the credential's. A
request carrying it sends only the inputs it allows; **Check** names the ones left out. With no credential, a preset's
request under `PIWI_CI_SERVER_URL` carries the instance's (`PIWI_CI_SERVER_USER`, `PIWI_CI_SERVER_TOKEN`) and sends
only the inputs `PIWI_CI_SERVER_ALLOWED_INPUTS` lists. A base URL or request path is refused when a segment would climb
once a server decodes it (`..%2F`, `..;`).

A request never follows a redirect, and a link from the answer is kept only as an `http(s)` URL or a path from the
base URL's root. A CI server is reached over `https`; over `http` or on a private address it is reached only when
it is the host and port of `PIWI_CI_SERVER_URL` or is listed in `PIWI_CI_SERVER_HOSTS` (the desktop app reaches any
address). See the [configuration reference](/reference/configuration).

- [Re-run in CI](./ci-rerun): the run button and dialog that dispatch an action, and how its run is matched
- [Source control](/guide/source-control): the SCM credential and its scopes
- [Credentials](/operate/credentials): the credential a CI server action names

# CI merge gate

The CI merge gate fails a CI job on the dashboard's analysis of a run, not on Playwright's exit code. `npx playwright
test` exits non-zero when anything failed; whether the change broke something that was working, whether a critical
test failed or a new root cause appeared needs the run history, so the dashboard evaluates a policy the pipeline
declares and `piwi gate` turns its verdict into an exit code. The reporter never fails a build on its own: the policy
belongs to the pipeline.

## Turn it on in CI

Record which run to gate on, then run the gate after the tests, whatever their outcome:

```yaml
- run: npx playwright test
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE: piwi-run.json

- run: npx @piwitests/reporter gate --require-tag @critical --max-new-regressions 0
  if: always()
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

The full recipe and the output a failed gate prints are in [CI & sharding](/guide/ci#blocking-a-merge); every flag,
default and exit code is in the [CLI reference](/reference/cli#gate). The policy needs at least one rule or one
warn-only flag, or the gate refuses to run.

## What fails it

Each flag is one rule, and the gate evaluates every rule it was given, so a failed verdict lists everything that is
wrong, not only the first rule to trip. The rules bound:

- **Failures**: the tests that failed for good (`--max-failed`), counted once per test however many Playwright
  projects or attempts failed it; a test that passed on a retry did not fail.
- **New regressions and newly flaky tests** (`--max-new-regressions`, `--max-new-flaky`): tests failing now that
  passed in the [baseline](/guide/concepts#baseline-last-green-run), and tests that started passing only on a retry.
- **Required tests**: every test carrying a tag (`--require-tag`) must pass, a pass on a retry included. A tag no test
  of the run carries is a violation in itself, so a misspelled tag cannot pass.
- **A selection** (`--require-selection`): the dashboard resolves the
  [selection](/features/test-selection#guard-it-in-ci)'s current definition and fails when a test it matches did
  not run, was only skipped, or failed. A selection that matches no test fails too.
- **Flakiness** (`--fail-on-flaky`): any test of the run that passed after an earlier attempt failed.
- **New failure clusters** (`--fail-on-new-cluster`): a [cluster](/features/failure-clusters) first seen in this run.
- **Quarantine debt** (`--max-quarantined`): how many tests the project holds in quarantine, whatever this run did.
- **Leaks** (`--max-leaks`, `--max-new-leaks`): the browsers, contexts, pages and API request contexts the run left open, counted per
  opening line (never a server or a process left running), and those no earlier run of the base branch showed ([leak history](/features/leak-history)). A run
  that sent no resource report (the capture fixtures missing, `captureResources` off, or a reporter older than 0.45)
  fails a leak rule rather than passing on silence, and so does a run of a project that
  [declined](/operate/capabilities#declining-a-capability) the Resources capability, whose leaks are not measured.
- **Pass reuse** (`--max-reused`, `--require-executed`): how many tests the run [reused](/features/reuse-forecast#skipping-reusable-tests)
  from earlier passes, by count or share, and the tags whose tests must have executed. In a run that passed with no
  run error, a reused test counts as passed for `--require-tag` and `--require-selection`, unless a
  `--require-executed` tag names it. A run that claimed a plan whose reused tests could not be recorded fails every
  reuse rule.

## What only warns

Two flags report and never fail: they change neither the verdict nor the exit code.

- `--max-uncovered-changes <n>` warns when more than *n* changed files are
  [uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes), naming up to five of them.
- `--min-patch-coverage <percent>` warns when fewer of the change's added and modified lines ran in the head commit's
  [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage), or when that coverage counts none of them.

Either warns too when the run has no source control diff to count, or when reading the change failed. Without them,
the gate ignores uncovered changes.

## What it leaves out

- **Quarantined tests.** A [quarantined](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) test still runs and reports,
  and the gate says how many failing tests quarantine excluded. It counts toward no failure, new regression, newly
  flaky, required tag or selection rule. `--fail-on-flaky` reads the run's flaky count and `--fail-on-new-cluster` its
  new clusters, quarantined tests included.
- **Environment incidents.** A run flagged as an [environment incident](/features/environment-incidents), by its
  rules or by hand, gets the verdict **inconclusive** whatever the policy, with no violation listed: its failures say
  nothing about the change. The gate exits `3`, so a pipeline can re-run instead of blaming the change.
- **Runs it does not judge.** A run still running or in its global setup is refused, and so is a run the caller cannot
  see, such as another person's [run requested from the dashboard](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin): the gate
  exits `2`, as it does when it cannot reach the dashboard, so a broken pipeline never passes. Any other run is judged
  as it is, whatever launched it.

## The verdict

The gate prints one summary line of counts, each violation, each warning and the run's link. With `--json` it prints
the result instead: `verdict` (`passed`, `failed` or `inconclusive`), `passed`, `violations` (each with a stable
`rule` id a pipeline can branch on, its message, and for a threshold the value and the limit), the measured `facts`
and any `warnings`. An inconclusive result carries `passed: false` and the incident under `facts.incident`, so a client
that reads only `passed` still blocks the merge. Evaluating never changes the run.

## On the pull request

An evaluation made with a key that can upload or control the project's runs (Uploader, Maintainer and above, the CI
key `piwi gate` uses) is stored with its policy, its verdict, its violations and warnings, and the pull request it
judged. Any other reader of the project gets the verdict only: nothing is stored or posted.

- **A commit status of its own.** Turn on **Gate status** under **Project → Settings → Source control**, and each
  stored verdict is also posted as your status context plus `/gate` (`piwi/tests/gate`): green with *Gate policy
  satisfied*, red with the first violation. A branch rule can then require the gate rather than the run. It needs
  [pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback#turn-it-on) on, with **Set a commit status**, and `PIWI_SITE_URL`
  set, since the status links the run. An inconclusive verdict posts nothing.
- **Overrides and escapes.** Every ten minutes Piwi asks the host what became of the pull requests a gate failed on.
  One merged while its last evaluation still failed counts as an override; one fixed first, or closed, does not. When
  a cluster that evaluation caught as a new regression fails again on an eligible default-branch run within 30 days
  of the merge, the override also counts as an escape past the gate.

The pull-request comment reports a run's failures; it never blocks a merge. The gate does.

## Related

- [CI & sharding](/guide/ci#blocking-a-merge): the gate in a CI job, and its output
- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli#gate): every flag, default and exit code
- [Pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback): the comment and commit status of a run
- [Flaky tests & quarantine](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out): what quarantine leaves out
- [Environment incidents](/features/environment-incidents): the runs the gate calls inconclusive

# Issue tracking (Jira)

An investigation ends with what a ticket needs: a headline, the affected tests and owners, the diagnosis, a
validated patch, the verify command. **Create issue** makes it a Jira issue, linked back as the cluster's
*known issue*.

It is **off until an [administrator connects Jira](/operate/integrations#connecting-jira-cloud)**.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/create-issue-modal.png" alt="The Create issue modal on a failure cluster: an optional comment, an editable title, the Jira project and issue-type fields, include toggles, and a preview of the fix-plan body">
  <figcaption>The Create issue modal on a failure cluster.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What it does, exactly

- **Create issue** appears on a failure cluster, on a failing execution, on each inbox row (plus the `c` key and the
  inbox bulk bar's *Create issues*), and on a [bug report](./bug-reports#filing-it-in-jira). The cluster's **Issue**
  line and an execution's **Cluster** line offer *Create issue* and *Link an issue* until the cluster has a ticket,
  then name it, its summary on hover.
- **Link an issue** pins an existing ticket: one on the site of the [bound connection](#the-project-binding) shows its
  live status; any other stays a plain link.
- The issue **body is the fix plan**, rendered to Atlassian Document Format: *What happened*, *Most likely*, *Evidence*,
  *What to do* (patch, locator replacement, verify command, reproduce steps), *Related issues* fixed before and *Links*
  back to Piwi. Every section degrades independently.
- Each issue carries the labels `piwi`, `piwi-cluster-<id>` and `piwi-fp-<hash>` and a `Piwi-Cluster: <id>` trailer
  for JQL.
- **Filing is deduped by cluster** — a second click, a duplicate event, a [rule](./issue-automation) or another of its
  executions names the issue already filed; once that link is removed or the issue is Done, the next create files a new one, and a
  Done issue stays linked. Before creating, the modal surfaces any issue that already tracks the failure (a pinned
  link, a matching label, or a *fixed-before* match) and leads with *link it instead*.
- Creating an issue is a **durable outbox action**: attempted immediately, retried with backoff if Jira is down (the
  cluster and execution pages show *Filing queued*, with a retry), and recorded: the cluster's **Activity** lists each
  write Piwi makes to the issue. A create Jira refuses outright (a missing or invalid field) fails at once, with
  Jira's reason atop the modal and on the Issue or Cluster line; creating again replaces it.
- **Comment** places your words first in the issue, or adds them to the cluster's issue already filed. Runs and
  tests: [Issues about a run or a test](./run-issues).

## The key travels

A cluster's **known issue** is its ticket filed or pinned, else one [its tests name](#links-the-tests-declare),
open ones first; others stay among its links, which an execution's *Details* also lists. Its key follows the failure
everywhere:

- the cluster's **Issue** line and a failing execution's **Cluster** line, the **inbox row** and the execution's row in
  the **run's test list** show the key with its status; the **search** (Ctrl K) finds the cluster from the key;
- `cluster.new`, `cluster.fixed` and `cluster.regressed` **Slack** messages name it, as does the `cluster.new` email;
- the **pull-request feedback** comment says *tracked in PROJ-123* on each failure whose cluster has one;
- the **fix plan** lists it under *Links*, and the `get_cluster` / `get_fix_plan` MCP tools return it.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/cluster-issue-line.png" alt="A failure cluster's situation block with its Issue line naming the Jira issue the cluster is tracked in">
  <figcaption>The cluster's Issue line names the Jira issue that tracks it.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Links the tests declare

A failing test's [`piwi:issue`](/reference/test-metadata#issues-the-tests-declare) or
[issue-key tag](/reference/test-metadata#keys-in-test-tags) links its cluster to issues of the bound project. It counts
as tracked, yet Piwi never writes to it and its status never resolves or reopens the cluster itself.

## Keep the ticket honest

A background [status sync](/operate/integrations#status-sync) reads each tracked issue back and caches its status,
title and assignee. Per-project **policies**, all **off by
default**, each a durable deduped outbox action, write back as the cluster evolves:

| When Piwi observes | What Piwi does |
|---|---|
| A cluster's **fix lands** (stopped failing or diagnosis verified) | Comments *Fix landed in run #N …*, and with *transition on fix* moves the issue. |
| A cluster **regresses** | Comments *Regressed in run #N …*, and optionally reopens the issue. |
| **New occurrences** on an open ticket | At most one note a day or a week: *Still failing — +N occurrences in 3 runs …*, with what is new. |
| A cluster is **merged** | With *comment on merge*, notes it on both issues; the survivor inherits the links. |
| The **ticket moves to Done** | With *resolve on close*, resolves the cluster unless its fix regressed. Otherwise, once the latest finished run no longer fails and the fix did not regress, the next step is *Mark the cluster resolved — PROJ-123 is Done*; while it fails, the Issue or Cluster line offers *File a new issue*. |
| The **ticket is reopened** | With *reopen on ticket reopen*, reopens a resolved cluster with a note. |

Both status policies act on a **move** of the ticket, so a person's reopen or resolve stands.

Every comment is written in the [ticket's language](#language); [Issue automation](./issue-automation) adds diagnosis
comments, description updates and [the runs that write](./issue-automation#the-runs-that-write). An optional
[inbound webhook](/operate/integrations#registering-the-inbound-webhook) shows a close or reopen at once. The failure
inbox gains a [**Needs ticket**](./failure-inbox#queues) queue.

## The project binding

A Project admin [binds the project](/operate/integrations#who-can-do-what) under **Project → Settings → Issue tracker**: the connection, Jira project and issue
type, default labels and assignee, the [ticket language](#language), what a ticket carries, the policies above, and
**owner routes** — mapping a cluster's owner (`@acme/checkout`, an email) to a Jira project, component, assignee and
labels. The create-issue draft picks the first matching route.

Tickets linked through a connection the project is no longer bound to keep their last status; the sync and the
policies skip them.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/project-integration-binding.png" alt="The project's Issue tracker settings: connection, Jira project and issue type, labels, the runs that write to the ticket, sync-policy switches, an owner-routes table, and automatic creation with one rule">
  <figcaption>A project's Issue tracker settings.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Title prefix and who filed it

A **title prefix** such as `[Piwi]` starts every summary Piwi files. Set it on the project binding or as the
connection's default; the binding's wins. It is up to 40 characters and counts toward Jira's 255, so a long title is
cut, never the prefix. A title you type is filed as typed; one an agent gives through MCP gets the prefix. A summary
edited in Jira never gets it back.

A ticket ends with *Filed by Priya Shah from Piwi*, naming the person once, as the cluster's **Issue** line does.

## Required Jira fields

Piwi reads the issue type's create screen and asks for every required field it does not fill, such as a
*Severity* or a *Team*:

- The project binding's **Jira fields** block lists them; a value there fills every issue from the project.
- The create modal shows them under **Required by Jira**, prefilled from those defaults, and keeps *Create* disabled
  until each has a value or a Jira default. A search in both adds any other field, custom ones included. An issue
  field, such as the *Parent*, searches Jira; a team is typed as its id.
- The [`create_issue` MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#create_issue) refuses early, naming each missing field, its id and
  what it takes; an agent passes them in `fields`.

Transitions are checked the same way, as [Issue automation](./issue-automation#required-fields-of-a-transition)
explains.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/create-issue-required-fields.png" alt="The Create issue modal's Required by Jira block: Severity Major, from the project settings, Team empty, Found in on Jira's default, and the footer saying Jira still needs Team">
  <figcaption>The Required by Jira block, with where each value comes from.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Requirements

- A connected **Jira Cloud** site — see [Operate → Integrations](/operate/integrations#connecting-jira-cloud).
- A [project binding](#the-project-binding) naming the connection: a project's issues are filed, read and written
  back through that one connection, never through another.
- **`PIWI_SITE_URL`** set, so the issue body's links resolve back to the dashboard.
- The **Contributor** role or above to create or link an issue ([who can do what](/operate/integrations#who-can-do-what));
  anyone who reads the project sees the key and status.

## Enable it

The modal files through the connection of the [project binding](#the-project-binding) and prefills its fields from
the binding, else offers pickers over the bound site; toggles choose what the body carries (diagnosis and patch on, [share link](/features/share-links) off).
A share link needs the **Maintainer** role and is created when the issue is filed.
From an AI agent, the [`create_issue` MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#create_issue) files the same ticket once the
binding names a Jira project and issue type.

## Language

A ticket's language follows its **destination**: the **project binding**'s language, else the **connection**'s default,
else **English**. The create modal has a *Language* select; the `create_issue` MCP tool takes a `locale`.
**English and French ship.**

Only the copy **Piwi authors** is translated: headings, fact labels, policy comments, dates and counts. Your data
(test titles, errors, locators, paths, commands, the patch) is **never** translated. The model's
prose follows the separate [AI response-language setting](/features/ai-diagnosis#response-language).

## Limits

- **Jira Cloud only** (REST v3, email + API token).
- A ticket's body is a **snapshot** at creation, unless [description updates](./issue-automation#comments-and-description-updates)
  are on for an issue Piwi filed.
- The dashboard's deterministic sentences (headline, story, clue, state line) are **English templates**, even in a
  French ticket.
- Attachments honor the [export size budget](/features/offline-export); the trace is never attached.

## Try it in the demo

- [API Integration › POST /auth/login returns 200 with valid credentials](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/3): The login 500 is tracked in DEMO-42, filed from Piwi and In Progress in Jira; its key follows the failure to its executions and the inbox.
- [E2E Checkout › should complete checkout with Apple Pay](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/2): Its test names three DEMO issues with piwi:issue: DEMO-57 and DEMO-61 are linked from the test’s annotation, DEMO-64 is not in Jira, and DEMO-61 is Done, so the known issue is DEMO-57.
- [E2E Checkout › should complete checkout with PayPal](https://piwitests.dev/demo/failure-clusters/1): Its tag DEMO-52 names a Bug, linked with the chip From the tag; the credit card test’s tag DEMO-53 names a Task, which the binding’s issue type leaves out, so it is neither linked nor counted.

- [Issue automation](./issue-automation): tickets filed by rule
- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters): what a ticket tracks

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/run-issues -->

# Issues about a run or a test

Not every finding is a failure Piwi groups: a test that passes but misses a case, a step too slow to be useful, a
suite that passed while the feature is broken. **Create issue** also files those, through the same modal, connection
and [project binding](./issue-tracking#the-project-binding) as an issue about a failure.

## Where it is

- **On a run's page**, the header's **Create issue** files an issue about the whole run.
- **On an execution with no failure cluster** (a passed or skipped test, or a failure not grouped), the **More
  actions** menu's **Create issue** files one about that test. An execution with a cluster files on its cluster, as
  [Issue tracking](./issue-tracking#what-it-does-exactly) describes.

## What the issue holds

- **Comment** comes first: your own words, up to 5,000 characters, under your name. The modal offers it for a
  failure cluster's issue too; when the cluster already has its issue, the comment is added to that issue instead,
  and a later update of the issue's description keeps it first. The modal says whether the comment was added, is
  still queued, or was refused by Jira.
- **A run's issue** lists the run (project, branch, commit, environment, start), its results, its tests with failed
  ones first (25 listed, then a count), the failure clusters of its failures with the issue each one already has
  (the 10 with the most failures, then a count), links back to the run, and who filed it from Piwi. Its proposed
  title counts the failures and names the branch.
- **A test's issue** has the same body for that one test, titled after it, with its error when it failed.
- Each carries the labels `piwi` and `piwi-run-<id>` and a `Piwi-Run: <id>` trailer, for JQL. A run's issue shows in
  the run's **Links**.
- The body follows the [ticket's language](./issue-tracking#language). Only Piwi's own copy is translated, never your
  comment or the test data.

## Several issues, each filed once

A run, or a test with no cluster, **can have several issues**: the modal lists the ones already linked and files a new
one. Each opening of the modal files at most one, so a second click on **Create**, or opening it again while a filing
waits on Jira (after a reload too, or in another tab of the same browser, for a day), never files twice. Create sent
again while that filing is still queued files it with what the modal holds now. Any create, a cluster's too, that Jira
may have received without its answer coming back (a timeout, or the server restarted during the call) fails with
**Outcome unknown** rather than risking a second issue: check Jira for it, then create it again if it is not there.

## Limits

- **Filed by hand only**: [Issue automation](./issue-automation) rules file failure clusters, never a run or a test.
- The body is a **snapshot** at creation; the [write-back policies](./issue-tracking#keep-the-ticket-honest) follow
  clusters, not runs.
- From an AI agent, the [`create_issue` MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#create_issue) files about a cluster, an
  execution in a cluster or a bug report, one issue per cluster: never a whole run, nor a test with no cluster.

## Related

- [Issue tracking (Jira)](./issue-tracking): issues about a failure cluster, the binding and the sync
- [Issue automation](./issue-automation): tickets filed by rule

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/issue-automation -->

# Issue automation

[Issue tracking](./issue-tracking) files an issue when someone clicks **Create issue**. Issue automation does it for
them: after each run, Piwi files an issue for every failure that a project's **rules** say has failed long enough, on
the branches and environments that matter, and keeps the issue's comments and description current as the failure
evolves. Everything is **off by default** and set per project, under **Project → Settings → Issue tracker**.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/project-integration-auto-create.png" alt="The Automatic creation block of a project's issue tracker settings: two rules, one for release branches at the first occurrence and one for the default branch in staging after three occurrences in two runs over a day, the guards, and a preview listing the open failure the second rule files at its next occurrence">
  <figcaption>Automatic creation: the rules, the guards, and a preview of what they would file.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Automatic creation

Switch on **File issues automatically** and give the project one or more rules. After a run finishes, Piwi checks each
[failure cluster](/guide/concepts#error-fingerprint-failure-cluster) that failed in it against the rules, in order.
The first rule the cluster meets files the issue; a cluster that meets none yet waits for its next failure.

A rule counts only the runs it names:

| Field | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Branches** | Branch names or `*` patterns (`release/*`). With **Default branch** on, the project's default branch too, whatever it is named. Nothing named: every branch. |
| **Environments** | The project's [environments](./environments), picked from its list, or typed keys and `*` patterns (`prod*`), each matching an environment's key or an alias, ignoring case. A run whose label has no environment matches by its label. Nothing named: every environment. |
| **Occurrences** | The failing executions counted in those runs. |
| **Runs** | The distinct runs among them, so one run with ten failing retries counts once. |
| **Days** | The days since the first counted occurrence, measured at the run being checked. |
| **Test tags** | Only failures of a test carrying one of these tags (`@critical`). Nothing named: every test. |
| **Extra labels** | Labels added to the issues this rule files, on top of the binding's. |

The run being checked must be one the rule counts: a failure that met a rule on `main` is filed by its next failure on
`main`, never by a run on a feature branch. A failure that stops failing is never filed, whatever its counts.

A fresh binding starts with one rule: two occurrences in two runs on the default branch. Two rules a team often wants:

- **Release branches at once** — branches `release/*`, one occurrence, one run, the label `release-blocker`.
- **The default branch when it persists** — the default branch in `staging`, three occurrences in two runs over a day.

Whatever the rules say, a cluster is **never** filed automatically when it is resolved, ignored or snoozed, when an issue
still tracks it or its filing is queued, or when it looks flaky (one of its tests passed on a retry since it first failed, or every one passed
at the commit it failed at), unless *Leave out failures that look flaky* is off. Two more guards hold:

- **An open issue in the tracker already carries the failure's labels** (`piwi-cluster-<id>` or `piwi-fp-<hash>`):
  Piwi leaves the link to a person. The cluster's Activity and Issue line name the issue it found and offer *Link an
  issue*, beside a Done issue too. An issue the cluster already links is left for the next sync to read back.
- **The daily cap**: at most this many issues filed automatically per project in any 24 hours (default 5).

With [owner routes](./issue-tracking#the-project-binding), an issue goes to the route of the cluster's owner (its
assignee, else the `piwi:owner` annotation, else CODEOWNERS). A failure whose owner matches no route is filed only with
*File owners with no matching route into the default project* on.

The issue is filed through the same path as a click: the same body, labels and [dedupe by
cluster](./issue-tracking#what-it-does-exactly), the same [required fields](./issue-tracking#required-jira-fields). An
issue that is Done, or whose link was removed, no longer tracks the failure, so a rule files a new one. The exception
is a Done issue the [reopen transition](./issue-tracking#keep-the-ticket-honest) is moving out of Done after a
regression: until the next sync reads that issue back, a rule files nothing beside it. An automatic create the tracker
would refuse for a field the binding leaves empty is recorded as a failed action, naming the field.

### Preview

**Preview** evaluates the rules as the form holds them, before you save, against the project's open failures that no
issue tracks yet. It lists the ones a rule files at their next occurrence in a run it counts, the ones waiting on a
threshold (*Waiting on rule 1: 1 of 2 runs*), and the ones left out with the reason, with the issues already filed
automatically in the last 24 hours and any field the tracker requires that the binding leaves empty. Nothing is
written.

## The runs that write

**Runs that write to the ticket** is a second scope, for the writes that follow a tracked issue: the fix, regression
and still-failing comments, the transitions, and the description updates. It takes branches, the default branch and
environments like a rule, and every run when it names nothing. A fix verified on a feature branch then leaves the
issue alone when the scope names `main`.

Some runs never write to a tracker, whatever the scope, such as a run from an editor or one flagged as an
[environment incident](./environment-incidents): [the runs that send nothing](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin).

## Comments and description updates

Each of these is a switch in **Keep the ticket honest**, off by default, and a durable action listed with the others:

- **'Still failing' note** — at most once a day or once a week, and only after the chosen number of new occurrences
  since the last note. It says how many occurrences over how many runs, where the latest one failed, and what is new
  since the last note: a branch or an environment it reached, the tests it now fails in.
- **Comment when the failure is diagnosed** — when a [diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis) of the cluster completes, from Piwi or
  from an agent: the summary, the root cause, and the category with its confidence. It needs the diagnosis switched
  on in what the ticket carries.
- **Keep the description up to date** — Piwi rewrites the description of an issue it filed: at most once a day after
  a run in which the failure failed again, and when a diagnosis completes. The rewrite keeps the language, the toggles
  and the share link the issue was filed with, and changes the title only on an issue a rule filed. Before writing,
  Piwi reads the description back: once someone has edited it in the tracker, Piwi never replaces it again, and the
  activity list says so. A rewrite that would change nothing is not sent. Piwi keeps no copy of a share link's token:
  it takes the link from the issue's description, and skips a rewrite that cannot find it there.

## Required fields of a transition

For *transition on fix* and the reopen transition, the binding suggests the transitions an issue offers and asks for
their required fields, such as a *Resolution*; a move that would leave one empty fails at once, naming it. A requirement
no screen shows, such as a workflow validator, comes back as Jira's refusal naming the field, which the modal then
asks for.

## What an automatic issue says

It opens with why it was filed: *Filed automatically by Piwi after 4 occurrences in 2 runs since Oct 6, 2026. Counted
on main (staging).*, in the [ticket's language](./issue-tracking#language). The rest is the body every issue carries:
what happened (occurrences over runs, every branch and environment it failed on, the latest commit), the affected tests
with their owner and failure count, the most likely cause with the diagnosis category, the evidence, what to do, the
issues of the same kind of failure fixed before, and the links back to Piwi.

## Requirements

- A [connected Jira](/operate/integrations#connecting-jira-cloud) and a project binding that names the Jira project
  and issue type.
- The **Edit Issues** permission on the Jira project for description updates, besides the ones issue tracking needs
  ([permissions](/operate/integrations#permissions-the-token-needs)).
- The **Project admin** [role](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do) or above to change the rules.

## Limits

- Rules file **failure clusters** only: a flaky test or a whole run is filed by hand.
- Rules are checked when a run finishes, not on a timer: *Days* is measured at the next failing run, and a project
  with no new runs files nothing.
- A description edit is told apart by its text, ignoring whitespace: changing only the formatting of a description
  in Jira does not stop the updates.
- Jira Cloud only, like [issue tracking](./issue-tracking#limits).

## Related

- [Issue tracking (Jira)](./issue-tracking) — creating an issue by hand, the body, the key and the sync.
- [Operate → Integrations](/operate/integrations) — connecting Jira and the permissions the token needs.
- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters) — what a rule counts.

# Results in Zephyr Scale

When a CI run of the whole suite finishes, Piwi can write its results to Zephyr Scale Cloud: one **test run** (a test
cycle in Zephyr) holding one result for each test case key the run's tests carry. The test run links back to the
run's page in Piwi, and the run's page shows what was sent.

It is **off until an [administrator connects Zephyr Scale and a Project admin binds the project](/operate/zephyr-scale#bind-a-project)**,
and a new binding starts as a **dry run** that sends nothing.

## When a run is sent

A run is sent once, when it finishes, if all of these hold:

- the project is bound to a Zephyr project, the binding is **Enabled**, and the run is in the binding's branches and
  environments;
- the run came from CI and ran the whole suite to the end. A partial run (a filter, a selection, a rerun of the failed
  tests), a run that was interrupted or timed out, a run from a developer's machine, the desktop app or an editor, a
  lab run, a bisect step or a reproduction, a run requested from the dashboard, a run flagged as an
  [environment incident](./environment-incidents) and an imported run send nothing;
- the project's test case catalog has been read, and at least one test of the run carries a key the catalog holds.

A run split across shards is sent once, after its last shard reports, with the results of every shard. Sending is a
background action, so the run is not held up. Only two failures are retried on their own, with a growing wait: Zephyr
asking Piwi to slow down (a 429), and a failure after Zephyr named the test run, which repeats only the step that
failed. An upload that gets no answer is **Outcome unknown** and waits for **Sync again** (see below).

The binding is read again when the results go out. If it was turned off, became a dry run or names another Zephyr
project since the run finished, nothing is sent and the run's panel says why. If Zephyr already holds the test run by
then, the send fails and names it, so you can find it in Zephyr.

## What is sent

- **One result per test case key.** When several tests carry the same key, or one test runs in several browsers or
  repeats, the worst outcome wins: a failure beats a flaky test, which beats a pass.
- **Only keys the catalog holds.** A key a test carries that is not a case in the project is left out and listed on the
  run's page, so a typo never creates anything in Zephyr. Tests with no key are not sent.
- **Flaky and skipped tests follow the binding.** A flaky test is reported as a pass, as a fail, or with the flaky
  status you name; a skipped test is left out or reported as not executed. See **Result statuses** under
  [Bind a project](/operate/zephyr-scale#bind-a-project).
- **The first line of the error** is added to a failed result only when the binding says so. It is off by default.
- **The test run's name** comes from the binding's [name template](/operate/zephyr-scale#the-test-run-name). Its
  description holds the run's address in Piwi, the branch, the short commit and the counts sent.

Piwi never imports test cases, steps or results from Zephyr: the catalog it keeps holds only each case's key, name,
status and folder.

## On the run's page

A run that was sent, or would be, shows a **Zephyr Scale** panel in its header:

- **A live send** shows the key of the test run, how many results were sent and the counts, for example
  `SHOP-R2`, "12 results sent: 10 passed, 1 failed, 1 flaky, 0 not executed". The key is also listed with the run's
  links.
- **A dry run** says that nothing was sent and shows how many results a live sync would send, with their counts, and
  the keys left out because the catalog does not hold them, so you can check them before you turn the dry run off.
- **A run that was not sent** says why: for instance that the catalog was not read yet or that no test carries a
  mapped key.
- **A send that waits to retry** says that sending failed, at what time the next attempt is due, and the error.
- **A failed send** shows the error, and Maintainers and above get **Sync again**.

The panel keeps itself current: it appears within about a minute of the run ending, follows a send while it runs, and reads
a retry again once it is due.

## Outcome unknown, and Sync again

Zephyr creates a new test run every time results are uploaded, so Piwi never uploads the same run blindly. It records
that an upload started before it begins, and the test run's key as soon as Zephyr names it.

A large upload can take longer than the request is allowed to wait, so Piwi may not know whether Zephyr received it.
The panel then says the outcome is unknown. It does not retry on its own. **Sync again** first looks in Zephyr for the
test run that run's upload may have made, by its name. It reads the test runs that hold the latest results of one of
the run's test cases: those that ended since the upload began, then, when none of them is the one, all of them.
Whether Zephyr gives uploaded results an end date is unchecked, so the search does not depend on it:

- one that is found is linked to the Piwi run and is not made again;
- none found, after every test run was read, uploads the results again;
- when Zephyr gives no answer Piwi can trust (more executions or test runs than it reads, or a test run it cannot
  read), nothing is sent, the send stays failed and the message says why. Check the project in Zephyr before you try
  again.

Two people who press **Sync again** at the same time send the results once: the second is told the sync changed.

A send that failed before the upload, or after the test run was made, only repeats the step that failed. **Sync again**
works on a failed send; a dry run has nothing to repeat. It is refused, and says why, while the binding is turned off,
is a dry run, or names another connection or another Zephyr project.

## Linked back to the run

The test run in Zephyr gets a web link to the Piwi run's page, titled with the run's number, when the server knows its
public address: set [`PIWI_SITE_URL`](/reference/configuration#integrations). The Piwi run lists the Zephyr test run
among its links, as the key, and removing the link there does not delete anything in Zephyr.

## Good to know

- Zephyr Scale **Cloud** only. Zephyr Scale Server and Data Center, Xray and other tools are not supported.
- Piwi writes through the connection's token, one request budget per connection, shared with the catalog.
  See [Request rate](/operate/zephyr-scale#request-rate).
- If you would rather have Zephyr own the test run, Playwright's built-in `junit` reporter writes a file Zephyr Scale
  can import itself. Use one or the other for a project, not both, or the results are recorded twice.

## Related

- [Zephyr Scale Cloud](/operate/zephyr-scale): connect it, bind a project and read the test case catalog
- [Test metadata](/reference/test-metadata): the tags and external IDs a test carries its case key in
- [Issue tracking (Jira)](./issue-tracking): the other integration that writes to an external tool
- [Jira Cloud](/operate/integrations): how connections are managed

# Test selections

A **selection** is a named subset of your suite that Piwi resolves from the run history it already keeps, then hands
back as a command you can run. Instead of a `@smoke` tag convention and a grep pattern in a CI file that drift apart,
you describe the subset once ("critical tests, under 15 s each, not quarantined") and `piwi run` turns it into the
tests to run. A selection is resolved on demand, never frozen, so a renamed file or a newly flaky test is reflected
the next time you resolve it.

## Run one

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter run smoke
```

`piwi run <key>` resolves the selection and runs `playwright test` with exactly those tests. It finds your dashboard
the way the reporter does, through `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `PIWI_API_KEY` (if auth is on) and `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, and
passes anything after `--` straight to Playwright. The run is **stamped** with the selection it came from, so the
[pull-request comment](/features/pr-feedback) names the subset, and the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) can re-resolve the same
definition to check nothing was silently dropped.

If the dashboard is unreachable, `piwi run` falls back to the full suite with a warning (and reuses the last good
resolution from `.piwi/selection-cache.json` when it has one): a reporting problem never breaks the test run. Pass
`--strict` to invert that for CI, where an unresolvable selection should stop the pipeline. Resolving a named selection to
**zero** tests is always an error.

### Print, shard and reorder

`piwi select <key>` resolves and prints the Playwright arguments instead of running them, for a two-step job. Flags
shape a resolution: `--shard i/n` splits it into shards of even duration, keeping every test that shares a
[lock](/reference/test-metadata#test-locks) in one shard, `--fail-fast` puts the least-reliable tests first without
dropping any, and `--budget 5m` caps its total time. Shard with `piwi run --shard` rather than Playwright's own
`--shard`, which would split a lock: `piwi run --shard` jobs merge into one run that still covers the whole selection.
Every flag and the output formats are in the [CLI reference](/reference/cli#select-run).

### Balanced Playwright shards

A suite sharded with Playwright's own `--shard` can be split by duration too: turn on the reporter's
[`balanceShards`](/reference/reporter-options#balanceshards) option. With Playwright 1.62 or later, each shard lists the
suite before Playwright splits it and asks the dashboard for shards of even recorded duration (a test with none weighs
the median), keeping in one shard the tests that share a lock, a serial describe, and a file that is not fully
parallel. The first shard to ask stores the split for 24 hours, keyed by commit, shard count and the tests listed, and
the others read it, so every shard agrees. The option stands aside for `--last-failed`, `--only-changed`, `--test-list`
and `--test-list-invert`, whose selection differs per machine. When the dashboard does not answer within 10 seconds, or
its answer does not cover the listed tests, the reporter logs one line and Playwright splits the run as usual. A
shard that falls back lines up with the others only if they fell back too; otherwise some tests run twice and others
not at all.

## Built-in selections

Two selections exist for every project with no setup:

| Key | What it resolves to |
|---|---|
| `failed` | Tests whose most recent execution failed or timed out. |
| `quarantine-free` | The whole suite minus tests under an active [quarantine](/features/flaky-tests). |

## Defining a selection

Save a selection through the dashboard or the [API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api). The `definition` is declarative
JSON: OR-ed `include` groups, minus OR-ed `exclude` groups, then pins, a budget and a limit — applied in that order.

```jsonc
{
  "include": [
    { "tags": ["smoke"] },
    { "priority": ["critical", "high"], "maxAvgDurationMs": 15000 }
  ],
  "exclude": [{ "quarantined": true }],
  "budget": { "maxTotalDurationMs": 300000, "rankBy": "failureLikelihood" },
  "limit": 200
}
```

Within a group every predicate must hold (AND); a test matches `include` if it matches any group (OR). An empty or
absent `include` starts from the whole suite. The predicates, all optional:

| Predicate | Matches when |
|---|---|
| `ids` | the test-case id is one of these |
| `tags` / `anyTags` | the test carries all / any of these tags |
| `owner`, `priority`, `feature` | the `piwi:` annotation is one of these |
| `files` | the file path matches one of these globs (`**`, `*`, `?`): at most 100, each of up to 500 characters |
| `suitePath`, `text` | the describe chain / title (or file) contains this substring |
| `quarantined`, `flaky`, `neverRun` | the test is (or is not) in that state |
| `minPassRate` / `maxPassRate` | the [pass rate](/guide/concepts#pass-rate) is within bounds (0–1); a test with none matches neither |
| `minAvgDurationMs` / `maxAvgDurationMs` | average duration is within bounds |
| `lastStatus` | the latest execution's status is one of these |
| `failedInLastRuns` | the test failed within its last _N_ [runs](/guide/concepts#test-case) (N ≤ 25); a pass on a retry is no failure |

An unknown predicate is a validation error, so a typo never widens the set.

### Budgets and pins

`budget` turns a selection into a knapsack: tests are ranked (`failureLikelihood`, `recentFailure`, `priority`,
`slowest` or `fastest`) and taken until their summed average duration hits `maxTotalDurationMs`. "The best five minutes
of this suite" is an empty `include` plus a budget. `pins` force individual tests in (`add`) or out (`remove`) by test-
case id, on top of whatever the predicates matched. `limit` caps the count last.

## From a Playwright config

To run `PIWI_SELECTION=smoke playwright test` instead of `piwi run`, resolve the selection in an ESM config (it needs
top-level `await`):

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { wrapConfig, resolveSelection } from '@piwitests/reporter';

const selection = await resolveSelection(); // reads PIWI_SELECTION; undefined when unset
export default wrapConfig(defineConfig({ grep: selection?.grep ? new RegExp(selection.grep) : undefined }));
```

It stamps the run like `piwi run`, and returns `undefined` (so everything runs) when no selection is named or the
dashboard cannot be reached.

## Guard it in CI

`piwi gate --require-selection <key>` catches a smoke job that silently shrank: the dashboard re-resolves the
selection's current definition and fails the build if any test it now matches did not run, or ran and failed.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter run smoke                 # run the subset, stamping the run
npx @piwitests/reporter gate --require-selection smoke   # then assert it held
```

It composes with the other rules of the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-fails-it), which says what it
counts and leaves out.

## In the dashboard, and for agents

The project's **Selections** page lists the built-ins and your saved selections, with a builder that previews what a
definition resolves to (the matching tests, the estimated duration, any warnings and the exact command) before you save
it. Agents use the selection tools of the [MCP server](/reference/mcp-tools#workflow) and the `run-the-right-tests`
skill.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/test-selections.png" alt="The Selections page: built-in and saved selections with their commands, over the suggestions">
  <figcaption>A project's selections.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Health and drift

A selection resolves fresh every time, so the set it runs can change under you: a renamed file drops out of a `files`
glob, a test turns flaky and falls below a `minPassRate`, and the job stays green while covering less. The Selections
tab shows a **drifted** badge when what a selection resolves to now differs from what its last `piwi run` recorded
(the run stamped the hash and count it resolved then), and counts the quarantined tests it carries.

Above the list, a **coverage** line counts the tests that *no* stored selection matches: nothing routine runs them as
a named subset. Built-in selections don't count toward coverage (`quarantine-free` matches almost everything). Agents
get the same data from `analyze_selections`.

## Impact-from-diff

`piwi run impact --base <ref>` runs only the tests your change affects: the tests a changed file defines, the ones
that failed inside it, and the ones that executed it, down to those that ran the changed lines when tests record
coverage. How each file is mapped, and when a change widens the run to the full suite:
[Impact from a diff](/features/change-impact).

## Suggestions

Piwi can _propose_ selections and tags from the history it keeps, with the evidence attached, never applied. The
**Suggestions** panel on the Selections page (and the `suggest_selections` MCP tool) surface three kinds:

- **`@slow` tags**: tests whose average duration is above the suite's 95th percentile.
- **`@feature` tags**: the dominant route family a test hits (say `checkout`) when it carries no `feature` annotation.
- **A mined smoke suite**: a greedy set cover over _observed_ route coverage under a time budget, keeping the test
  that adds the most new routes until the budget is spent. Only stable tests qualify. "Save as selection"
  turns the picks into a selection pinned to exactly those tests.

Coverage here means the routes a test was _seen_ to hit on recent runs, not instrumented code coverage.

## What selections are not

- **Not static analysis.** Predicates read _observed_ history (durations, pass rates, statuses), and impact reads
  what tests were seen to run (frames, code reach, recorded coverage), never a build-time dependency graph.
- **Not a way to hide failures.** [Quarantine](/features/flaky-tests) decides a test's verdict; a selection only decides whether
  it runs. The full suite stays your reference; selections are for the fast loops in between.

## Related

- [Impact from a diff](/features/change-impact): the tests a change affects, down to the changed lines
- [Reuse forecast](/features/reuse-forecast): the test time that ran code identical to an earlier pass
- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli#select-run): every flag of `select` and `run`
- [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate): the gate in a CI job
- [Analytics](/features/analytics#test-filter): filter every number by a selection
- [Flaky tests & quarantine](/features/flaky-tests): what decides a test's verdict
