# Impact from a diff

`piwi run impact --base <ref>` runs only the tests your change affects. The reporter diffs the working tree against
`<ref>`, and the dashboard maps each changed file to tests through what they were seen to do, never a build-time
dependency graph:

- **Direct**: a changed file that _is_ a test file maps to the tests defined in it.
- **Reach**: a changed support file maps to the tests that failed inside it, per their source frames.
- **Code reach**: a changed application file maps to the tests that executed it
  ([code reach](/features/code-reach)), and a route handler to the tests that called its route.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter run impact --base origin/main
```

It fails safe, widening to the full suite with a warning, when a changed file maps to no test (a stylesheet too,
unless [CSS coverage](/features/css-coverage) maps it) or only through source frames, which miss passing tests. A
docs-only change runs nothing. `piwi select impact` prints the Playwright arguments instead of running them, for a job
that passes them to `playwright test`: nothing when the run widens, and `--pass-with-no-tests --grep-invert .` when no
test is impacted, under which Playwright runs none and passes.
[`piwi preflight --run`](/features/preflight) runs the same tests along with those of the locators the change breaks.

## Line level

When tests record coverage ([code reach](/features/code-reach) at `functions`,
[CSS coverage](/features/css-coverage), or [server coverage](/features/server-coverage)), a modified file selects
only the tests that ran the lines you changed, not every test that touched the file. The reporter sends each modified
file's changed lines with the git blob id of its version before the change, and the dashboard reads them against each
test's recorded coverage of that same version:

| A changed line… | selects the tests that… |
| --- | --- |
| is a statement, with server coverage at `lines` | ran that line |
| sits inside a function: any other line, an insertion, or coverage at `functions` | ran that function |
| sits inside a style sheet rule, with CSS coverage | matched that rule |
| sits outside every function (module code, a declaration, an attribute), or crosses from one function into the next | reach the file at all |

An added line counts by the lines around it, so it selects the tests that ran the code it was added to. A test whose
coverage cannot rule it out stays in: coverage of another version of the file, coverage with no line or function
ranges, or an incomplete capture, or coverage whose run was deleted. A test file, failure frames and route reach are
never narrowed. Added, deleted and
renamed files count as whole files.

A changed line inside a function no test ran selects nothing from that file: no test can catch a mistake there. The
answer names it as `notRun`, the line a new test should cover, numbered as in the file before the change: the version
the tests' coverage recorded.

The rule assumes a line a test did not run cannot change that test's path, as every coverage-based selection does,
and it reads each test's latest recorded coverage. Keep running the full suite on a schedule: it stays the reference.

## Read the answer

`piwi select impact --json` prints the resolution, and `impact.files` gives, for each changed file:

- `level`: `lines` when its tests were read against the changed lines, `file` when not, `none` when no test maps to it;
- `tests`, each with how it was selected: `test-file`, `lines`, `functions`, `frames`, `route`, or `file` (its
  coverage reaches the file and cannot rule it out), and the changed lines it ran;
- `ruledOut`, the tests that reach the file and ran none of its changed lines;
- `fileLevelLines` and `notRun`, as above.

## For agents

The `get_impacted_tests` [MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#workflow) takes a diff (`git diff --full-index <base>`) and
returns the same answer per file, the tests by name, and a command to run them. The `run-the-right-tests`
[agent skill](/features/agent-skills) calls it after every code change, and offers to write a test for the
`notRun` lines.

## Related

- [Test selections](/features/test-selection): saved subsets, shards and the CI guard
- [Code reach](/features/code-reach) and [server coverage](/features/server-coverage): what the tests record
- [Uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes): the changed lines no suite ran, on a pull request
- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli#select-run): every flag of `select` and `run`

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/run-variables -->

# Run variables

Run variables are a few environment variables, `NAME=value`, that a project sets on every run Piwi starts for its
tests and at the start of every command it gives to copy. They are for one app that serves several projects from one
folder: each tenant is a project of the instance, and its tests need `TENANT=acme` to build, start and test the right
one.

## Set them

A project admin sets them in **Project → Settings → Run variables**: up to 10 rows of a name and a value, checked as
you type.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/project-run-variables-settings.png" alt="Project Settings, Run variables: one row TENANT = acme, the Add a variable button, and the command it starts, TENANT=acme npx playwright test, under the Linux / macOS tab">
  <figcaption>A project of a multi-tenant app, its tenant set once for every run Piwi starts.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **A name** is capital letters, digits and `_`, not starting with a digit, 64 characters at most, each name once.
- **A value** is 1 to 500 letters, digits, spaces and `_ - . , : / @ + =`: a tenant, a region, a brand or an address
  (`https://acme.example.com:8443/app`). No `$`, backslash, quote or shell operator, no space at either end, and not
  starting with `//`.
- **Never a secret.** Every copied command and every confirmation shows the values. A secret stays in each machine's
  own `.env`.
- **Refused names**: a run variable never sets a variable that changes which code runs, which browser starts, which
  certificates are trusted, where results and requests go, or the CI a run reports. `PATH`, `HOME`, `PREFIX`,
  `NODE_OPTIONS`, `BASH_ENV`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `CI` and `COMSPEC` are refused, and so is every name starting with
  `PIWI_`, `PLAYWRIGHT_`, `NODE_`, `NPM_`, `GIT_`, `GITHUB_`, `LD_` or `DYLD_`, among others. Windows reads names
  whatever their case, so `Path` is `PATH`.

The settings save refuses a list with one refused variable whole, and each app that runs the tests checks the list
again before it runs anything: a variable refused there runs nothing, rather than run without it.

## Where they apply

- **Copied commands**: the retry commands of a run, a test and a selection, **Copy as command** in the desktop app,
  the verify command of a fix plan, a saved selection's commands, the Flake Lab commands, and the test step of the
  reproduce recipe and its bisect. In bash a command starts with the variables (`TENANT=acme npx playwright test …`);
  in PowerShell it sets them for the rest of the session first (`$env:TENANT='acme'; npx playwright test …`). A copy
  button copies the form of the shell you last picked in a command block, else your computer's. The Markdown of a fix
  plan, an issue and an auto-heal pull request show the bash form.
- **The desktop app's runs**: Re-run, **Run with options…**, Reproduce, Bisect, Flake Lab and a bug report's
  reproduction. The app reads the variables of its own project when it starts each run, never from the page, and the
  run's line in **Local runs** shows them. The install step of a checkout gets none.
- **[Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine)**: the confirmation lists them among its checks and starts the command with
  them. **Run** reads them again: when one changed since the window showed the command, it shows the new command
  instead of running. An app too old to apply them cannot take the request, which waits for one that can and says to
  update the app.
- **The editors' runs**: VS Code and JetBrains run a test, a file, a selection, a debug run and the runs an agent starts
  with the variables of the project their folder follows. The first run asks you, **Allow** or **Not now**, once per
  set of values while the editor runs; until you allow them, Piwi runs nothing for the project. A run you start in a
  terminal is yours: Piwi sets nothing there.

A re-run in CI passes arguments only: a CI action picks its tenant with its fixed inputs, per
[deployment environment](./ci-actions#what-an-action-has).

## Per environment

Each [environment](./environments) of the project (Local, Staging, Production) holds up to 10 run variables of its
own, with the same rules. A run Piwi starts for one gets the project's, then the environment's, the environment's
value winning for a name both set, at most 20 together, and `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT` set to its key. The runs above and
most copied commands offer the environment to pick ([where](./environments#choose-the-environment-of-a-run)); **None**,
a fix plan's verify command and the reproduce recipe apply the project's alone.

## Building and starting the app

Piwi runs no command of a project's settings before a run. Building and starting the app for a tenant belong in the
Playwright config, so CI, a terminal, the editors and every Piwi run take the same steps, reviewed with the code:

```ts
const tenant = process.env.TENANT ?? 'acme';
const port = { acme: 3001, globex: 3002 }[tenant] ?? 3000;

export default wrapConfig(
  defineConfig({
    use: { baseURL: `http://localhost:${port}` },
    webServer: {
      command: 'npm run build && npm start',
      env: { TENANT: tenant, PORT: String(port) },
      url: `http://localhost:${port}`,
      reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI,
    },
  }),
  { projectName: `shop-${tenant}` },
);
```

A port for each tenant keeps `reuseExistingServer` from reusing a server another tenant started. The project name the
config computes sends each run to its tenant's project.

## One folder, several projects

The desktop app links one folder to as many projects as you like. **Local folder** in a project's settings names the
other projects linked to its folder, and says when the config computes its project name rather than writing it out.
An editor follows one project per folder: the one with the lowest id.

## Limits

- The PowerShell form keeps the variables set in that window: a command copied later for another project, in the same
  window, runs with them too. Copied commands are written for bash, zsh and PowerShell.
- The commands the MCP tools return name no variable. The fix plan lists the project's run variables beside its verify
  command, and tells an agent to set them.
- Listing the tests of a config for the editors' test tree sets no variable.

- [Desktop app](./desktop)
- [Re-run in CI](./ci-rerun)
- [Test selections](./test-selection)

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/environments -->

# Environments

An environment is a deployment of the application a project's tests run against: Local, Integration, Staging,
Production. Each one is a record of the project, with a key, a name and its own [run variables](./run-variables). A
run's label files it under one, and a run Piwi starts, or a command it gives to copy, can be for one.

## What an environment holds

A project admin keeps the list in **Project → Settings → Environments**:

- **Key**: the label its runs report (`staging`), unique in the project ignoring case: 1 to 80 letters, digits,
  spaces and `_ - . , : / @ + =`. A changed key stays as an alias.
- **Name**, shown in the pickers and the project's filters (`Staging`), and a **description** for the team ("data
  reset every night at 02:00").
- **Aliases**: up to 20 other labels that name it (`stg`), or patterns where `*` matches any run of characters
  (`pr-*`).
- **Run variables**: up to 10, set over the project's on the runs Piwi starts for it.
- **Built from the checkout**, the **env file**, **protected** and its **required tags**: the sections below.
- **The order** every picker shows.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/project-environments-settings.png" alt="Project Settings, Environments: Local, Integration, Staging and a protected Production, each with its key, aliases, run variables and env file, then a discovered preview environment">
  <figcaption>Four declared environments and a discovered one.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Archive** takes an environment out of the pickers: its runs keep it, and no run Piwi starts can be for it.
**Delete** removes it: its runs keep their label and lose their environment, and the next run that reports the label
adds it back as a discovered one. Archive it to keep a label from coming back. Deleting one a URL pattern or CI action
names is refused.

## How a run's label resolves

A run's label is the reporter's `environment` option, else `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`
([Reporter options](/reference/reporter-options)). Piwi keeps it as it came, trimmed and cut at 200 characters, and
resolves it once, when it stores the run:

1. no label: no environment;
2. the environment whose key equals the label, ignoring case;
3. else the one with an alias equal to it, ignoring case;
4. else the first, in the list's order, with a `*` alias that matches it.

A label nothing takes adds a **discovered** environment, with the label as its key and name, so a project whose
settings nobody opened still gets a complete list. A project holds at most 50 discovered environments and 100 in all;
past that, a run keeps its label and has no environment. A discovered environment stays marked as such until a project
admin saves it.

Saving an environment resolves the project's runs again. Adding `stg` as an alias of Staging moves the runs that
reported `stg` to Staging, and removes the discovered `stg` that held them.

## Default environment

The project page's **Filters** and status filter offer its environments, the labels none takes, and **No environment**;
Staging keeps the runs resolving to it, `stg` included. With a **default environment**, set below the list, the project
page, its tabs, [Analytics](./analytics#environment-policy), [quarantine candidates](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out)
and pull-request feedback read only its runs, never one with no environment, until you pick another or **All
environments**, like the [default branch](./branches#filtering-by-branch). A copy carries it to a project with none.

## Choose the environment of a run

Each place Piwi starts a run offers the project's unarchived environments, and **None**. With **None**,
Piwi applies the project's run variables only and sets no label: the config decides, as in a terminal.

A run Piwi starts for an environment gets:

- **the run variables**: the project's, then the environment's, which wins for a name both set; at most 20, checked as
  one list by every app that runs the tests, which runs nothing when one is refused;
- **`PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`** set to the environment's key, which the reporter sends as the run's label. A config that sets
  the reporter's `environment` option reports that one instead;
- for a protected environment, the filter of its [required tags](#protected-environments).

Where you pick it:

- **Copied commands**: in **Copy retry command**'s options on a run, under **More** on an execution, and beside
  selection, locator and Flake Lab commands, starting on the environment of the run the page shows, unless protected
  or archived, else **None**.
- **[Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine)**: the request's window offers the same picker, and the app's
  confirmation names the environment and lists its variables.
- **[The desktop app](./desktop)**: its runs offer the environments of the project the folder is linked to. A folder
  also linked to a project of a team instance offers that project's environments too, read from that instance at
  each run, never kept on the machine.
- **[The editors](./editors)**: VS Code and JetBrains run with the environment picked for the workspace folder. The
  editors' **Allow** question covers each new set of values, an environment's included.

A command copied for Staging:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
TEST_ENV=staging BASE_URL=https://staging.example.com PIWI_ENVIRONMENT=staging npx playwright test tests/checkout.spec.ts
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:TEST_ENV='staging'; $env:BASE_URL='https://staging.example.com'; $env:PIWI_ENVIRONMENT='staging'; npx playwright test tests/checkout.spec.ts
```

:::

## The Playwright config

Piwi never reads or changes the config: the config reads the variables. The common pattern, with one `.env` file per
environment for its secrets:

```ts
import { config as loadEnv } from 'dotenv';
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import { wrapConfig } from '@piwitests/reporter';

const testEnv = process.env.TEST_ENV ?? 'local';
loadEnv({ path: `.env.${testEnv}` }); // this environment's secrets, never committed

export default wrapConfig(
  defineConfig({
    use: { baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? 'http://localhost:3000' },
    webServer:
      testEnv === 'local'
        ? { command: 'npm start', url: 'http://localhost:3000', reuseExistingServer: !process.env.CI }
        : undefined,
  }),
  { environment: testEnv },
);
```

With it, Piwi's Staging holds `TEST_ENV=staging` and the env file `.env.staging`, and its key is `staging`, the label
the config reports. CI sets `TEST_ENV` and the secrets itself. `dotenv` never overrides a variable already set, so the
values Piwi sets win over the file's.

## Built from the checkout, or deployed

An environment is **built from the checkout** when the application under test comes from the same commit as the tests:
a `webServer` in the config, a preview deployment of the pull request. Any other is
[deployed](./deployed-environments): Piwi reads the application's commit its runs tested.

## Secrets and the env file

An environment holds no secret: its values show in every copied command and confirmation. A secret stays in the
machine's own file, ignored by git, or in the CI's secret store. The **env file** names that file: `.env`, then parts
after a dot (`.env.staging`), never a folder. Piwi never reads it and never sends it:

- the desktop app's folder check says when the file is missing in the linked folder;
- Reproduce, Bisect and Flake Lab run in a worktree, which holds no untracked file: they copy the env file into it from
  the linked folder, and delete it with the worktree.

## Protected environments

A protected environment, Production as a rule, holds at least one required tag (`@smoke`). Every run Piwi starts
against it:

- **runs only the tests carrying one of its required tags**, and the setup and teardown projects they depend on, which
  Playwright runs whole: Piwi adds a `--grep-invert` that leaves out every other test, and keeps the run's own filter
  case-insensitive: Piwi refuses `-G /…/` without `i`. The command shown carries it. On Windows, PowerShell may break its quoting when `npx` resolves to
  `npx.cmd`: start these runs from the desktop app or Run on my machine;
- **is confirmed**, its name shown, in the desktop app, the app taking a Run on my machine request and the editors'
  question;
- **is started by a project admin only**: the instance gives a protected environment's run variables, and takes a
  request naming it, only to someone holding `project:manage`. For anyone else the pickers show it locked, and the
  list hides its variables;
- **is never picked by default**: a re-run of one of its runs, and a command on its run's page, start on **None**;
- **is never an agent's**: an agent's request naming it is refused.

These rules govern what Piwi starts. A command you type in a terminal stays yours.

## Copy from another project

**Copy from another project**, in **Project → Settings → Environments**, copies the declared environments of a project
you can read into one you manage: every field, at the end of its list. An environment whose key or one of its aliases
the project already names is left as it is, and listed. Nothing links a copy to its source: a value that differs per
project, such as a tenant's `BASE_URL`, is edited on each copy.

## The run page's warnings

The run page names the run's environment, and says when the run may not have tested it:

- **Started for Staging; the config reported production.** A run requested for one environment whose label resolved
  to another, or to none: the config's `environment` option wins over `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`, so a config that writes
  its own label reports it.
- **The tests opened http://localhost:3000, which no URL pattern of Staging matches.** The run's Playwright `baseURL`
  is outside every [URL pattern](./extension-connection#url-patterns) of its environment, which catches a config that
  ignores the variables. It shows only for an environment some URL pattern names.

## Limits

- Each project has its own environments: a Staging in two projects is two records, kept apart.
- A filter (notifications, issue automation, test management) keeps keys and `*` patterns, matched against a run's
  environment key and aliases.

## Related

- [Run variables](./run-variables)
- [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine)
- [Desktop app](./desktop)
- [Run environment](./run-environment): where a run executed
- [Environment incidents](./environment-incidents): runs that failed because the app was down
- [Glossary: environment](/guide/concepts#environment)

# Deployed environments

A deployed environment, such as Staging or Production, runs whatever version of the application was last deployed
there, whatever the commit of the tests that run against it. Piwi reads a run of one as two versions: the tests', the
run's commit, and the application's, its **deployed commit**. An environment, a discovered one included, is built
from the checkout until a project admin turns its **Built from the checkout** setting off
([Environments](./environments#built-from-the-checkout-or-deployed)): only then is it deployed. The setting also tells
an agent, through the MCP tool `list_environments`, whether a failure's commit holds the code that ran.

## The deployed commit

The first source that names one wins:

1. **The server under test** reports the commit it was built from (`appCommit`), through an
   [instrumentation package](/guide/backend-logs#server-environment).
2. **A deploy marker** of the environment carries the commit its pipeline deployed
   ([Recording deploys from CI](./timeline-markers#recording-deploys-from-ci)): a run takes the latest one before it
   started.

With neither, the deployed version is unknown, and every view below says it may differ from the run's commit.

The application is assumed to live in the project's repository, as in a monorepo: the commits between two deployed
commits are read there, with the project's [source control](/guide/source-control) credential. For an application
kept in another repository, only its deployed commits mean something: the range and the suspect lines look for them in
the project's repository.

## What changes for a run of a deployed environment

- **The run page** names the deployed commit in its facts line (`app a1b2c3d`), and **Details → Application** says
  where it comes from.
- **The Changes tab** adds a **Deployed to Staging** card beside the tests' commits: the deployed commit of both runs,
  the application's commits between them, and the environment's deploy markers between the two runs
  ([What changed in a run](./run-changes)).
- **[Suspect lines](./server-coverage#suspect-lines)** are read on the application's range, from the last green run's
  deployed commit to the failing run's, since the coverage is the deployed application's. With the run's deployed
  commit unknown, they are read on the tests' range, and say so.
- **[Uncovered changes](./uncovered-changes)**: what the run reached of the application is the deployed version's.
  When that is not the change's head, or is unknown, the answer and the pull request comment say so, and the reach
  counts as any run's.
- **The [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis)** gets an Environment Under Test section: the environment's name and
  description, whether it is built from the checkout, the deployed commits, the application's range and the deploy
  markers.
- **Bisect** walks the tests' commits, so against a deployed environment it can find a change of the tests, never one
  of the application. The Reproduce section and the [fix plan](./fix-plans) list the deploys between the last passing
  run and the failing one instead.

## The first failing deploy

A [failure cluster](./failure-clusters) first seen in a deployed environment names its **first failing deploy**: the
deploy marker between the last run of that environment where one of its tests passed and the run it first failed in.
When several fall there, the latest is the one the first failing run tested. When none does, the line says that no
deploy happened since the last pass: as far as the markers tell, the application did not change, so the tests, the
data or the infrastructure did.

The cluster's **What changed** line leads with it, the execution page's since line names it ("New regression after
Staging deploy 7 (a1b2c3d) on Staging"), and the AI diagnosis and the MCP tool `get_cluster` (`firstFailingDeploy`)
carry it with both runs' deployed commits.

## An environment's activity

In **Project → Settings → Environments**, each environment opens its activity: its last run, its last
[environment incident](./environment-incidents), its deploy markers with their commits, and for a deployed one the
commits and application versions its recent runs ran against, each with where the commit came from.

## Limits

- A deploy marker counts for the environment it names. A marker with no environment counts for none.
- A deployed commit from a deploy marker is the commit posted, not proof of what the servers run: a server that reports
  its own wins over the marker.
- Bisect never walks the history of an application kept in another repository.

- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters)
- [Backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs)

# Reuse forecast

The reuse forecast answers two questions from the coverage your runs already record: how much of the last month's test
time re-ran code that had already passed unchanged, and which tests failed even though the code they ran had not
changed. It lives on a project's **Selections** page and in the `get_reuse_forecast`
[MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#workflow).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/reuse-forecast.png" alt="Pass reuse forecast card: 15% of the test time ran code identical to an earlier pass, and one test that needed a retry with its code unchanged in two browsers">
  <figcaption>The pass reuse forecast: the test time a run could have skipped, and the tests that failed or retried anyway.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What counts as reusable

The forecast reads the 30 days before the project's latest run. A result is **reusable** when an earlier result of
the same test, in the same Playwright project, the same [environment](/features/environments) and another run, passed
on its first attempt, is at most 14 days older, and either:

- recorded file versions (runtime, path and git blob) that are all among the versions the result itself ran;
- or ran at the same commit, both runs on CI, which also counts a failure that stopped before reaching code the pass
  ran.

For a deployed environment, both runs also ran the same version of the application (below); a run of one whose version
nothing names is never reusable.

The code that pass ran had not changed, so a run could have skipped the result and kept the pass. The card gives the
share of test time that was reusable, split between the [default branch](/features/branches) and the other branches
when both have results: a branch's results may match a pass recorded on the default branch, since the comparison is
by content, not by branch.

## Failed with the code unchanged

A reusable result that failed, or passed only on a retry, ran code identical to an earlier pass. Its failure came
from the test, its data or its environment, not from a change to the application. The card lists those tests, each
with the failing execution and the pass it matched, which is strong evidence when you investigate a
[flaky test](/features/flaky-tests).

## What it needs, and its limits

- **Coverage with file versions**: [code reach](/features/code-reach) at `coverage.browser: 'functions'` or
  `'lines'`, or [server coverage](/features/server-coverage). With `'files'` a test records which files it ran but
  not their version. A pass stands in for a later result only when it recorded file versions; a result that recorded
  none is reusable only at the same CI commit as such a pass.
- **An upper bound.** The comparison sees the application files coverage records. A change to the test code itself,
  to the Playwright configuration or to a dependency is not part of it, and would make more tests run.
- **Runs that do not count**: Flake Lab, probe, bisect, reproduction, `piwi bug` and private runs, and runs flagged
  as an [environment incident](/features/environment-incidents).

## Skipping reusable tests

**Experimental.** With the pass reuse capability on, `piwi plan` and `piwi run --reuse` skip the tests the forecast
would count as reusable, with a stricter rule. A test's pass stands in for it only when that pass came from a clean
checkout of a commit, with the same Playwright version and environment, and every result of the test in that run passed
on its first attempt with coverage naming its file versions. The environment is the label the run reports (`--environment`,
else `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`; `piwi run` passes the flag to Playwright as the variable, which the reporter's `environment`
option overrides when the config sets one), resolved as a run's label is; a run
that names none reuses the passes of any environment. For a [deployed environment](/features/deployed-environments), the
pass ran against the application it runs now: the same commit, from its latest
[deploy marker](/features/timeline-markers#recording-deploys-from-ci) or its servers'
[`appCommit`](/guide/backend-logs#server-environment), else the same application versions its servers report. With
neither, every test runs. Mark an environment whose application the config's `webServer` builds as built from the
checkout: as a deployed one, its passes stand in only where a version is named. The working tree is diffed against that commit: the test runs when
[impact from that diff](/features/change-impact) selects it, when a changed file maps to no test, or when a file the
pass ran changed. A test that is quarantined, in an open failure cluster, failed or was retried in its last 20
executions, tagged `@no-reuse`, or in a spec file holding a serial group always runs. A run skips only the tests the plan names, in the Playwright projects
their pass ran them in, so a new or renamed test runs. The diff counts untracked files, and a commit a shallow clone
lacks is fetched. A plan is kept for 24 hours, and a job other than the one that made it uses it only when both
checkouts are clean at the same commit; a job that cannot use it (an unreachable dashboard, an expired plan, another
checkout) runs the whole suite, not a shard of it. With Playwright 1.62 or later in the project, the reporter skips the
plan's tests itself as Playwright builds the run, so every reporter shows each one as skipped with the run whose pass
stands in for it (`passed in run #41`), and the reporter sends the dashboard none of them; below 1.62, `piwi run` leaves
them out with Playwright's `--test-list-invert`. A reporter that cannot read the plan runs every test, the whole suite
in a shard. The run records the tests it skipped and did not execute as its
reused results: the run page's header counts them and lists them with the pass each one reuses, the pull-request
comment counts them, and the `get_run` MCP tool returns their count. The run's own status, pass rate, flaky scores,
durations and fix verification read executions only. The [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-fails-it) can limit reuse, and counts a reused test as passed in a run
that passed with no run error. A run that claimed a plan it was not made for (another commit, a dirty checkout,
another Playwright version or environment, another version of a deployed application, an expired plan) records no reuse, and fails the gate's reuse rules. A run whose shards' blob
reports are merged by `merge-reports` claims no plan, so its reuse is not recorded.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-reused-tests.png" alt="Reused tests of a run: each test with its file and Playwright project, and a link to the earlier pass at its commit">
  <figcaption>A run whose plan skipped every test: each reused test with the pass that stood in for it.</figcaption>
</figure>

Commands: [`plan`](/reference/cli#plan). Design record: [pass reuse](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/proposals/pass-reuse.md).

- [Impact from a diff](/features/change-impact): the tests a change affects, down to the changed lines

# Scenario gaps & the Test Map

The test catalog lists the tests you have. **Scenario gaps** describe the ones you don't: the route no test requests,
the page nothing visits, the test that is the only thing standing between a page and no test at all. Each gap is a
suggestion with its evidence and a next step, never a verdict. This page covers the Test Map, its gaps and the Coverage tab's
**Gaps** and **Map** views; the **Code** view is [Combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage).

Gaps come from the **[Test Map](/guide/concepts#test-map)**: one graph per project of what the application exposes
(routes, pages, controls, links, and the handlers and dependencies behind them) and which tests
[reach](/guide/concepts#reach) each of them. It is built from what the reporter and the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) already record: the requests
and page visits of every run.

> **Observed reach first.** A gap on a route, a page or a control says a test *observably reached* it, or that
> nothing did, measured from real runs. The detectors of code, such as *Code nobody executes*, read the coverage the
> runs or uploaded reports record. "No edge" means "no evidence", not "proof of absence".

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/test-map-graph.svg" alt="Tests reach pages and routes; routes lead to handlers and dependencies; nodes colored by gap class">
  <figcaption>Three rows of a Test Map: a route whose test missed a probe, a page only one test reaches, and surface no test reaches.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What a gap is

A **[detector](/guide/concepts#detector)** reads the Test Map and the default branch's last 30 runs and reports one
kind of gap: a route observed only with success statuses, a node exactly one test reaches, a new page no test reaches
yet, a declared route nothing requests. [Gap detectors & exposure](/reference/gap-detectors) lists every detector
with its evidence. Each gap names its detector and its **[class](/guide/concepts#gap-class)**:

| Class | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **blind-spot** | nothing reaches it: a node, or a path inside reached code such as an error status | `Observed 412 times over the last 30 runs, always 200` |
| **false-comfort** | the tests pass without checking it: a [probe](/features/probes) broke it, or the app logged an error, and they still passed | `Tests pass when POST /api/orders breaks` |
| **fragile** | what reaches it could stop at any time | `Only checkout › coupon reaches this` |

[Server probes](/features/probes#server-probes) add **findings** in two more classes, **unhandled** and **degraded**:
the application itself did not cope with the fault, whatever the tests saw.

Gaps are ranked by a score, the detector's confidence times **[exposure](/guide/concepts#exposure)**: how often the
code behind a node changes, whether it was in an earlier escaped failure and the priority of the tests reaching it, and, for a changed file,
how long it has been changing. The score and its factors show on every gap, and
[which gaps get which factors](/reference/gap-detectors#exposure) varies. Counts are per class, never a coverage percentage: a percentage over an observed
surface looks complete when that surface is sparse.

An [uncovered change](/features/uncovered-changes) is a gap too, raised at pull-request time, and so is a page with
open [bug reports](/features/bug-reports), and code no suite runs, error paths no suite runs, or code only one test runs.

## The Coverage tab

The project's **Coverage** tab has three views. **Gaps** lists gaps and findings by feature, ranked, each with its
class, score factors and evidence: the top 200 of the status picked, so a large map is read one status or one feature
at a time. A gap on a file, a handler or a route names the files behind it with the lines the suites ran. **Code** is
the [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage) of a commit.

**Map** opens on the **feature map**: one circle per feature (from the
[`piwi:feature` tag](/reference/test-metadata)), sized by the routes, pages and controls it groups, colored by its
worst open gap, and linked to the features it shares nodes with. A feature also groups what its tests miss nearby,
such as the controls on its pages, and a **hub** most tests reach links no features
([how features group](/reference/gap-detectors#features)).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/scenario-gaps-feature-map.png" alt="Feature map: four feature circles colored by worst gap, beside their counts">
  <figcaption>Four features of an admin console, each with what it groups, its tests and its worst gap.</figcaption>
</figure>

A feature, or a gap's node, opens in the **feature graph**: the node in the middle, what leads into it on the left,
what it leads to on the right, nodes colored by class and edges by kind. The **neighbors** list under it has every
neighbor; click a node to recenter on it. A file's coverage page opens it on the file's nodes, and a file or handler
links back to [its coverage](/guide/concepts#coverage-and-the-test-map). Agents walk the same graph with the
[`get_feature_graph`](/reference/mcp-tools#get_feature_graph) MCP tool.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/scenario-gaps-graph.png" alt="Feature graph centered on the page /settings/api and its neighbors">
  <figcaption>A page one test reaches: what leads to it on the left, what it contains, links to and loads on the right.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Triage

Every gap takes the same four verbs as an inbox item:

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/scenario-gaps-tab.png" alt="Five ranked gaps of the Users feature with evidence and triage verbs">
  <figcaption>The top gaps of one feature, ranked, each with its evidence and the inbox verbs.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **Accept** copies a draft test skeleton to your clipboard: a title from the gap, the `piwi:` annotations of the
  nearest test, the path from a reached page to the gap as steps, and a TODO where the assertion goes.
- **Snooze** for a day, a week, or until the node changes.
- **Dismiss** with a reason: *not worth testing*, *covered elsewhere* (which records the covering test as reaching the
  node), or *wrong*.
- **Covered by** names the test written for it and closes the gap. A gap closed this way stays closed when its
  detector raises it again, and the covering test is recorded as reaching the node.

Gaps persist, so triage survives recomputation, and a gap **closes itself** when its detector no longer finds it,
which is not always a test written ([when a gap closes](/reference/gap-detectors#when-a-gap-closes)). Home lists the
gaps still accepted a week after their acceptance: the tests not yet written.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/scenario-gaps-loop.svg" alt="Sources feed the Test Map, detectors, ranking and delivery; triage flows back">
</figure>

Every verdict is also a labeled example that counts
[for or against its detector](/reference/gap-detectors#precision). A detector below 60% precision on a project with twenty or more verdicts **mutes itself**
there ([what muting changes](/reference/gap-detectors#precision)).

The top new gaps of each project are the **Gaps digest**
[quality report](/features/quality-reports#what-a-report-contains); [schedule it](/features/quality-reports#report-schedules)
to your channels. Agents list, draft and triage gaps with the
[MCP tools](/reference/mcp-tools#list_scenario_gaps), and the
[write-the-missing-test](/features/agent-skills) skill drives the loop.

## What feeds the map

Every run adds the routes its tests requested on the application's own origin and the pages they ran locator calls
on or ended on. Three optional sources add the rest:

- **The [page inventory](/guide/concepts#page-inventory).** With `capturePageInventory` on (off by default), the
  reporter records the controls and links of the pages a passing run visits. Control and link nodes, and the
  detectors that read them, appear only then.
- **Server spans.** With the [backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs#server-spans) for Nitro, each route gains
  the handler that served it and the dependencies that handler called.
- **The declared surface**, below.

### Declared surface

Beyond what tests observe, the map can hold what the application *declares* it exposes, so a route or page nothing
reaches is named a **declared, never hit** blind spot instead of staying invisible. Three sources feed it:

- **The instrumentation's route manifest.** The [backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs#route-manifest) serves
  the application's routes at `/__piwi/manifest` in development and test, and the reporter uploads it with the run.
- **A committed manifest.** A `piwi.manifest.json` next to your Playwright config (`{ "routes": [...], "pages": [...] }`)
  is uploaded whenever present, whatever the backend.
- **An OpenAPI URL**, set per project under Project → Settings → Coverage → Scenario gaps. Piwi reads the document
  when the URL is saved, every night and on a recompute, declares each path under the path of the document's first
  server (or Swagger's `basePath`), and records each route's documented response codes, so a *success only* gap can
  name the error codes a route documents but never returned under test. A route a later read no longer finds stops
  being declared.

A declared pattern is reached by every request it serves, as in a router: `/blog/{slug}` by `/blog/hello`.

### Map health

Under the gap list, **map health** counts each input against what it could hold and names the detectors it wakes;
an input that is short shows the step that fills it, so a quiet tab is not mistaken for a covered application.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/scenario-gaps-map-health.png" alt="Map health: seven inputs of a Test Map, probes short of half the routes">
  <figcaption>Six inputs complete; probes reach under half the routes, with the step that adds the rest.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What this is not

- **Not a test generator.** A gap proposes a scenario; the assertion is yours.
- **Not a gate.** Uncovered changes can only warn; see [the gate flags](/features/uncovered-changes#the-gate-flags).

The Test Map and its server probes are optional: [decline](/operate/capabilities#declining-a-capability) either per
project or for the instance, and these surfaces disappear.

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › Gaps](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/5?tab=gaps): Ten tests against a whole admin console: routes never seen failing, pages linked and never visited, declared routes nothing requests, a save that passed while the backend logged an error, page-object methods no test calls, and the team’s verdicts on them. In the Map view, map health shows probes short at 7 of 16 routes.

- [Probes](/features/probes): whether a test that reaches a route would notice it breaking

# Uncovered changes in pull requests

A pull request that changes `server/api/orders/[id].patch.ts` while no test ever requests that route passes CI and
proves nothing about the change. When a run finishes, Piwi joins the files its change touched to the tests that
[observably reach](/guide/concepts#reach) them, and names the changed files nothing reaches: the **uncovered
changes**. Each one is a *changed, unreached* [scenario gap](/features/scenario-gaps). Its draft starts from the route or
page the file serves, or the nearest one a test reaches under the same path, with that test named. When the head commit has
[combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage), the same section counts the changed lines too, and names those no
suite ran, in every file.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/uncovered-changes.svg" alt="A pull-request run's changed files are joined to the tests that reach them; each is reached, an uncovered change (a gap), or not counted, with the reason; the result goes to the pull request">
</figure>

## One rule for every changed file

The comment, its commit status, the gate, the MCP tool and the *changed, unreached* detector read one rule. A changed
file is:

| Reach | When | Counted |
|---|---|---|
| **Reached** | a test of this run reached it, or a suite of the head commit's coverage ran one of its changed lines | yes |
| **Reached earlier** | no test of this run did, but a test of the project's last 30 runs did: a run narrowed by a [selection](/features/test-selection), not a missing test | yes |
| **Unreached** | Piwi can observe the file, and nothing above reached it: an **uncovered change**, and a *changed, unreached* gap | yes |
| **Not observable** | nothing maps the file to a test, so nothing can be said either way | no |
| **Out of scope** | the project's [coverage scope](/features/combined-coverage#the-coverage-scope) leaves it out: tests, build output and generated code by default | no |
| **Deleted** | the change removed it | no |

A test reaches a file when it:

- requested a route or visited a page the file serves, matched by the framework's file naming (`server/api/**`,
  `server/routes/**`, Nuxt `pages/**`);
- ran a step whose locator is written in the file (a page object, a helper);
- executed one of the file's functions, with [code reach](/features/code-reach) on.

Piwi can observe a file when one of these could happen to it, or when the head commit's coverage counts its changed
lines. A skipped test reaches nothing. A *changed, unreached* gap closes once its file no longer counts as uncovered
([when a gap closes](/reference/gap-detectors#when-a-gap-closes)).

Before the pull request, the [editor extensions](./editor-coverage#uncovered-changes) mark the lines of an uncovered
change of a page or a server route in the file itself, by a rule of their own: no coverage scope, no window of runs,
and a page counts as reached only when a test's locator acted on it.

The diff comes from the [source control](/guide/source-control) connection. A run of a pull request is compared
with the branch it merges into, so every push reports the whole pull request: the one its CI names, else the one
open on its branch, so a push-triggered workflow reads its pull request too. Any other run is compared with the
commit of the last passing run. A public repository is read without a token, so
its uncovered changes and their gaps appear in Piwi, though nothing is posted; a private one needs a
[SCM credential](/guide/source-control#set-the-credential). With no diff, nothing appears.

## On the pull request

With [pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback) turned on, the comment gains an **Uncovered changes** section.
The uncovered changes come first, grouped by ticket (read from the commit messages and the pull request):

```md
#### 🟣 Uncovered changes · 3 of 7 files · 2 tickets
Changed files no test reached, in this run or the last 30 runs. Observed reach, not instrumented coverage.

**PROJ-418**
- `server/api/orders/[id].patch.ts` · changed (+41 −3) · 0 tests in 30 runs
  → [open its gap](https://piwi.example.com/projects/4?tab=coverage&gap=31): **Accept** copies a draft test
```

When the head commit has [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage), the section also counts the change's lines
that can run (its patch coverage), and names the changed lines no suite ran in the files a test did reach: a test
visiting a file is not a test running the change.

```md
**Patch coverage 82.9%**: 34 of the 41 changed lines ran (unit 28, end to end 19), at `a1b2c3d`.

**Changed lines no suite ran**
- `api/Orders/OrderService.cs` · 7 of 12 ran · not run: 14 to 18, 40
```

The section ends with what it did not count: *Not counted: 2 files Piwi cannot observe, 1 file outside the coverage
scope.*
With **Only comment on failures** on, a run with no failure still gets the comment when its change left a file no
test reached.

Three more detectors read the whole pull request at each run: an error status a route's handler gains that no run
answered with, a control a page gains, and a title no test's words match ([the detectors](/reference/gap-detectors#detectors)).
Their gaps carry the pull request's number, close when a later run no longer raises them
([when a gap closes](/reference/gap-detectors#when-a-gap-closes)), and the section counts them
with a link to the pull request's gaps, where the change-coverage status leads too.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/uncovered-changes.png" alt="The Uncovered changes section of a pull-request comment">
  <figcaption>Patch coverage, the changed files no test reaches, and the changed lines no suite ran.</figcaption>
</figure>

A coverage report uploaded for the commit after the comment, or the run's own coverage arriving after it, posts the
comment again a few seconds later; a later push's comment is never overwritten by an earlier commit's.

When commit statuses are on too, a second status joins the run's own: `piwi/tests/change-coverage` with the default
status context, described as *3 of 7 changed files no test reached*, with the patch coverage when there is one. It is
always **success**, so it informs a reviewer without blocking the merge, and it leads to the pull request's gaps on the
Coverage tab.

The files no test reached are the Test Map's part: they are left out while the *changed, unreached* detector is
[muted](/features/scenario-gaps#triage) on the project, or where the Test Map is declined. The changed lines are
coverage's part and stay either way.

## From an agent

The [`get_change_coverage`](/reference/mcp-tools#get_change_coverage) MCP tool returns the same join for a run or for
an explicit base and head commit, grouped by ticket, without recording anything: each file's `reach`, its `lines`
when the coverage counts them, and the files not counted. The [write-the-missing-test](/features/agent-skills) skill
takes it from there. The REST endpoint is in the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api).

## The gate flags

Two warn-only flags of the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-only-warns) read the same rule, one per form:
`--max-uncovered-changes` the files, `--min-patch-coverage` the changed lines. They never change the verdict, because
the numbers inform rather than prove, and a stored evaluation keeps their warnings. Run the second after the unit-test
jobs uploaded their reports.

## Limits

- **Observed reach, then lines.** Without coverage, a reached file may still hide an untested branch; with it, the
  changed lines no suite ran name it. An unreached file may be dead code.
- **Naming conventions.** Files map to routes and pages through Nitro and Nuxt file naming; other frameworks rely on
  locators, code reach and coverage, so without those more of their files are *not observable* and not counted.
- **Ten files listed.** The comment names at most ten files per list and counts the rest.
- **A deployed environment.** A run against one reached the [deployed](/features/deployed-environments) application's
  lines: when its deployed commit is not the change's head, or is unknown, the section says so.

## Related

- [Scenario gaps & the Test Map](/features/scenario-gaps): the other gaps, and triage
- [Combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage): the coverage the changed lines are counted on
- [Pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback): the comment this section joins
- [Source control](/guide/source-control): the token that provides the diff
- [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate): the warn-only flags beside the gate's rules

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/code-reach -->

# Code reach

Code reach answers "which tests reach this file?" for application code: an opt-in capture records the source files
whose functions ran during each test in the browser, so a change to a component or a module maps to the tests that
execute it. An ASP.NET Core or Nitro backend built for coverage adds the code each test ran on the server:
[server coverage](./server-coverage). This page covers the browser's side, and for both sides what a test ran
([on the execution page](#on-the-execution-page)) and [which tests run a file](#which-tests-run-a-file).

## Turn it on

Set `captureCodeReach: true` in the reporter options, or `PIWI_CAPTURE_CODE_REACH=true`, with the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in place: it records files. `coverage.browser: 'functions'` or `'lines'`
records more ([the modes](/reference/coverage-cost#the-modes)). Coverage adds time to every test and reach changes slowly, so
turn it on in one scheduled job; a run without it keeps the reach the last one recorded.

```ts
// playwright.config.ts, in the nightly job
reporter: [['@piwitests/reporter', { captureCodeReach: !!process.env.NIGHTLY }]],
```

## What it records

The fixtures start Chromium's JavaScript coverage on each page the test opens, and on up to 16 pages already open as
it starts (a `beforeAll`'s, an earlier test's), and at teardown turn each script into source files:

- a module a dev server serves by path (Vite's `/src/components/Pay.vue`, `/@fs/…`) is the file itself;
- a bundle is read through its source map, inline or fetched once per worker (20 MB and 5 seconds at most).

A file counts when one of its functions ran. A module's top-level code runs as soon as it is imported, so it does not
count, or every eagerly loaded file would be reached by every test. Paths are relative to the repository root;
files under `node_modules` or outside the repository are dropped, and at most 2,000 files are kept per test. Only the
paths leave the machine, never code, counts or line numbers.

`coverage.browser: 'files'` is the same as `captureCodeReach: true`; `'functions'` adds each function's start and end
line, through the source map, and the file's git blob: line numbers then leave the machine. With `'functions'`, the
run also records every function the pages' scripts declare, run or not, so the run's coverage can say how many of a
file's functions ran. A function declared inside a function that never ran is not listed: V8 has not seen it.

`'lines'` adds the lines that ran, from V8's block coverage, which counts each branch and block apart. A file's
executable lines are the lines its source map maps code to, so a Vue component counts the lines its compiled module
maps back to, not the hot-reload code the dev server adds; a module with no map counts the lines holding code
inside its functions. A line ran when code mapped to it ran. A module's top-level lines count as run in the run's
coverage once it is imported, and in a test's only when one of its functions ran. Block coverage slows the page's
scripts more than function coverage does: [Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost) has the numbers.

Paths resolve against the Playwright config's directory, then the repository root. Set `codeReachRoots` to the dev
server's root when it is elsewhere; for Nuxt that is `app/`:

```ts
reporter: [['@piwitests/reporter', { captureCodeReach: true, codeReachRoots: ['app'] }]],
```

When the tests reach several dev servers that serve modules at the same paths (one per portal, each with its own
`/js/index.ts`), give `codeReachRoots` an object: each origin with its directories, `*` for every other origin. A
script resolves against its own origin's directories, else those of the page that loaded it, so the key can be the
address the tests open:

```ts
codeReachRoots: {
  'http://localhost:5001': 'portals/admin/src',
  'http://localhost:5002': 'portals/customer/src',
  '*': ['shared'],
},
```

Code a bundler or dev server adds (module wrappers, hot-reload hooks) counts for no file.

With an instrumented backend (the [Nitro or ASP.NET Core packages](/guide/backend-logs)), the handler file of each
route a test called counts as reached too. The ASP.NET Core package also names each handler's line, from the build the
tests called, so the [editors](./editors) put a lens above each handler tests called (`GET /api/orders/:id · 4 tests ·
1 failing`), which runs them.

## Supported builds

| Build                               | Source maps                             |
| ----------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Vite dev server, Nuxt dev included  | none needed: modules are served by path |
| Vite build                          | `build: { sourcemap: true }`            |
| Next.js dev, Turbopack or webpack   | on by default                           |
| Next.js build, Turbopack or webpack | `productionBrowserSourceMaps: true`     |
| webpack build                       | `devtool: 'source-map'`                 |

The map must be linked from the bundle: `sourcemap: 'hidden'` and webpack's `hidden-source-map` write the map but
not the comment that names it, so they record nothing.

Each was checked on a React app (Vite 8, webpack 5.111, Next.js 16.3) and Piwi's own Nuxt dev suite: every test
recorded exactly the files it ran.

## Cost

Code reach reads V8's function coverage, so its cost grows with the modules each document loads and the full page
loads a test makes: on a large application served by dev servers, its UI tests took 40 to 50% longer, by file or by
function alike, so turn it on in a scheduled run there. Every mode, its figures and how each was measured:
[Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost).

## On the execution page

An execution's **Source** tab lists what the test ran: server files by executed lines, then browser files. A file the
failure's [suspect lines](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines) name, or that changed since the last pass, is marked. A file
with line numbers unfolds to its source at the version the test ran, marking what it ran and, from the run's own
coverage, the executable lines it did not.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/execution-coverage.png" alt="The Coverage section of an execution's Source tab">
  <figcaption>What a failing test ran.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Which tests run a file

A file's **tests** link, on an execution, a cluster's suspect lines or the [Test Map](./scenario-gaps), opens its
coverage page: its source at the version most tests ran, each line with how many tests ran it, the executable lines
none runs marked. Select a line or a range for its tests and their latest outcome; on a line no test runs, the nearest
test to copy. The page also lists the file's nodes in the [Test Map](./scenario-gaps) with their open gaps, and opens
the Map view on one.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/coverage-file.png" alt="A file's coverage page">
  <figcaption>Which tests run each line.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Where it is used

- **[Impact-from-diff](./change-impact)** maps a changed file to the tests that executed it, and
  with function or line coverage to the tests that ran the changed lines ([line level](./change-impact#line-level));
  a changed file no test reached still widens the run to the whole suite, since code reach misses top-level code,
  server code without [server coverage](./server-coverage) and type-only modules.
- **[Uncovered changes](./uncovered-changes)** counts a changed file as reached when a test executed it.
- **[Locator preflight](./preflight)** calls a break _likely_ only when one of its tests reaches the changed file.
- **[Coverage in the editor](./editor-coverage)** marks the lines tests ran and the ones none runs, in VS Code and the
  JetBrains IDEs.
- **[Suspect lines](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines)**: the changed lines a failure's tests executed, on the failure
  pages' [What changed](./failure-clusters#the-cluster-page), in the [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis#scm-grounded-context)
  and the [fix plan](./fix-plans).

The [API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) (`/settings/api` on your instance) serves the tests reaching a file and a branch's map.

## Limits

- **Chromium only** in the browser: other browsers have no JavaScript coverage and record no browser files. Server
  coverage works with every browser.
- **Browser files are reached, not covered:** a reached file may hide an untested branch.
- A build with neither per-module URLs nor source maps yields nothing, and so does code rendered on the server only,
  React server components included.
- A module whose top-level code calls its own functions, a table built on import, counts for every test that loads it.
- A function a minifier inlines into another counts for the file it was inlined into.
- Chromium drops the coverage of a document the page leaves, so each document is read as it goes: the capture adds a
  `beforeunload` listener in an isolated world, out of the page's reach, and the debugger stops on it for that read. A
  document left without `beforeunload` (a crash) keeps only what an earlier read saw.
- On a page open before the test, what ran there before counts only if it runs again, and what a page runs on its own
  meanwhile (a timer, a poll) counts too.
- Reach is per branch: a branch's own runs replace its tests' reach, and the default branch's stands in for the rest.

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › Users table paginates 25 rows per page: the server lines this test ran](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-run-cases/711?evidence=source): The Source tab’s Coverage section lists the five files of the ASP.NET Core API the test ran, 20 lines, the users endpoints first with the suspect lines it ran, then the three browser files of the users page; open a server file to read its source with the lines the test ran marked, and the executable lines it did not run in a lighter mark.
- [Web Dashboard › UsersEndpoints.cs: which tests run each line](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/5/coverage?file=api/Users/UsersEndpoints.cs): The users endpoints of the ASP.NET Core API at the version its tests ran, each line marked with how many of the three users tests ran it and the executable lines none runs; select a line to list the tests that ran it, with their latest outcome.

- [Server coverage](./server-coverage): the code each test ran in an ASP.NET Core or Nitro backend

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/css-coverage -->

# CSS coverage

Each test records the rules of your style sheets its pages matched: a rule counts once an element on the page matched
its selector. A change to a style sheet then selects the tests that rendered the rules it touched, where a style
change used to run the whole suite. It sits beside [code reach](./code-reach), the scripts' side, and
[server coverage](./server-coverage).

## Turn it on

Set `coverage.css: 'rules'` in the reporter options, or `PIWI_COVERAGE_CSS=rules`, with the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in place. It is a choice of its own, independent of `coverage.browser`.

```ts
reporter: [['@piwitests/reporter', { coverage: { browser: 'functions', css: 'rules' } }]],
```

## What it records

The fixtures start Chromium's CSS rule usage on each page the test has, in the same capture as code reach, and read
it as each document is left and when the test ends. Each style sheet goes to its file:

- a sheet with a source map (Sass, Less, PostCSS, a `.vue` file's `<style>` with Vite's `css.devSourcemap`) counts in
  the map's sources;
- a `<style>` element a Vite dev server injected counts in the file its `data-vite-dev-id` names, at its lines there,
  a component's `<style>` block included;
- a sheet served as written (`/assets/app.css`) is the file at that path, found as
  [code reach](./code-reach#what-it-records) finds a module.

Without a source map, a sheet's lines are the file's only when each rule sits at the same line in the file: a
preprocessor's output served without its map (Sass, PostCSS, Tailwind, an inlined `@import`) counts at file level, so
a change to that file keeps every test that matched one of its rules.

A style rule counts from its selector to its closing brace, like a function. A grouping rule (`@media`, `@supports`,
`@layer`, `@container`) counts its first line once a rule inside it matched. Every rule of each sheet, matched or not,
goes with the run, for the file's ratio. The rules also count in the project's **Functions** ratio, beside the
scripts' functions.

## Where it is used

Wherever browser files are read: the execution page's coverage, a file's coverage page, the tests behind a line,
[test selection](./change-impact) (a changed rule selects the tests that matched it; a change outside every rule, at
file level, the tests that matched any), and [uncovered changes](./uncovered-changes).

On the sample application, a change to its stylesheet selected 24 of its 32 tests by file, and 12 by line for a change
to one rule, where it ran all 32 before.

## Cost

Its cost is Chromium's style recalculation, which grows with a page's rules and re-renders: turn it on where style
changes are frequent, or in a scheduled run. The figures: [Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost#css-rules).

## Limits

- **Chromium only**, like JavaScript coverage.
- **A state the tests never reach reads as unused:** a `:hover` never hovered, a breakpoint never rendered, a theme
  never set.
- **Utility CSS** (Tailwind) maps into the framework's own sheet under `node_modules`, which counts for nothing: the
  classes a test used are in the templates code reach already covers.
- **CSS-in-JS and constructed sheets** (`adoptedStyleSheets`) have no file.
- **Production builds:** Vite writes no source map for its CSS and minifies it to one line, so a built sheet maps to no
  source. Record CSS coverage against a dev server, or an application serving its CSS as written.
- A `<style>` in a page's HTML counts only when the page's address names its file (`/index.html`).
- A document replaced without `beforeunload` (`page.setContent`) loses the rules it matched: Chromium drops them with
  it.

## Related

- [Code reach](./code-reach): the scripts each test ran
- [Change impact](./change-impact): the tests a change selects
- [Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost): what each mode costs

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/server-coverage -->

# Server coverage

With an ASP.NET Core or a Nitro backend built for coverage, each test records the backend code it ran: its files, the
functions that ran in them and, at the finest granularity, the executed lines. Requests are told apart, so tests running in
parallel against one shared backend each keep their own. The browser side is [code reach](./code-reach); both feed
the [execution page](./code-reach#on-the-execution-page), the [file coverage page](./code-reach#which-tests-run-a-file),
the [editors](./editor-coverage) and the [coverage insights](./coverage-insights).

## Turn it on

1. Build the backend for coverage, in the test environment only:
   - **ASP.NET Core:** add the `PiwiTests.Instrumentation.Coverage` package to every project whose code you want
     covered, as its
     [README](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/integrations/aspnetcore/PiwiTests.Instrumentation.Coverage#readme)
     shows, serve it with `app.UsePiwiTestLogs()` ([backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs)), and build with
     `-p:PiwiCoverage=true`. It refuses to start in the Production environment, and `PiwiCoverageForbidden` makes a
     build fail when coverage reaches it
     ([README](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/integrations/aspnetcore/PiwiTests.Instrumentation.Coverage#enabling-it)).
   - **Nitro:** with the plugin and the module of `@piwitests/instrumentation-nitro` in place
     ([README](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/integrations/nitro#server-coverage)), set
     `PIWI_COVERAGE_BUILD=true` when the server is built (`nitro build`, or `nitro dev`). The module then instruments
     the server's own code. A coverage build refuses to start where `NODE_ENV` is `production`, which `nitro build`
     makes it, unless `PIWI_TEST_LOGS_DISABLED=false` serves it there; `PIWI_COVERAGE_FORBIDDEN=true` makes a coverage
     build fail.

   Never ship that build to production: its code runs slower, and its coverage endpoints expose source paths and line
   numbers.
2. Set the reporter's `coverage.server` option, or `PIWI_COVERAGE_SERVER`, with the
   [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in place.

```ts
reporter: [['@piwitests/reporter', { coverage: { server: 'lines' } }]],
```

Against a backend that is not a coverage build, no response names any coverage, so the reporter collects nothing and
the option costs nothing: it can stay on, and the build decides.

## What it records

| `coverage.server` | Records per test |
| --- | --- |
| `files` | the backend files that ran, paths only |
| `functions` | also the start and end line of each function that ran |
| `lines` | also the executed lines |

With `functions` and `lines`, each file names the git blob its line numbers refer to. At the end of the run the
reporter also sends each backend's run-level coverage, attributed to no test, with each file's executable lines at
`lines`: the lines no test runs, in every assembly or every Nitro server file built with coverage, including those
whose code never ran. A test
whose coverage the backend held only in part, or that could only partly be collected, is marked incomplete; one whose
collection failed outright records no backend coverage at all.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/server-coverage.png" alt="The backend files one test ran, recorded by line">
  <figcaption>One test's backend files, with the lines it ran.</figcaption>
</figure>

The backend names the checksum of the source each file was built from. When the file in the reporter's checkout
differs (the backend was built from another commit), the reporter keeps the file's path but drops its line numbers,
which would point at the wrong lines, and marks the test incomplete; the run-level coverage drops them the same way.

### Suspect lines

A failure's **suspect lines** are the lines changed since its last passing run that the failing tests executed, read
from their coverage, browser or server, and the diff of the source control range: each changed hunk they executed,
ranked by how many passing tests of the same run executed it too (the Ochiai score of spectrum-based fault
localization, 1 when only failing tests did). Line coverage names the executed lines, function coverage the changed
lines inside a function that ran, and file coverage the whole hunk. When the host names the file's version at the
head (GitHub, or a local clone in the desktop app), coverage of another version counts as file coverage. The failure
pages' **What changed** line names the first, the cluster's diff marks them, the
[AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis#scm-grounded-context) lists them and sends their files' patches first, and the
[fix plan](./fix-plans) carries the top five. For a run of a [deployed environment](./deployed-environments), the
range runs between the deployed commits of the last green run and the failing run.

## How it is collected

Each response names its request's coverage in an `X-Piwi-Coverage` header. Once the test ends, outside its time, the
reporter asks each backend origin for the coverage its pages and API calls named, several tests per call. The
run-level coverage is read as the run's last test ends, while a Playwright `webServer` is still up, and the lines and
functions the tests' coverage named are added to it. Every answer names the backend process: a random id, which also
starts each request id, and when the process started. The run-level coverage is whole only when the process that
answers it is the one that served the run's first requests.

## Limits

- **API calls** through Playwright's `request` fixture keep their last response's coverage only: a redirect's earlier
  responses, and a response `failOnStatusCode` turns into an error, name none.
- **One backend per request:** a call the backend makes to another counts there only if it forwards the
  `X-Piwi-Coverage` header.
- **A restart during the run:** the new process starts with no coverage. Each test's lines are kept, from its own
  coverage; what the earlier process ran outside a request (startup, background work) is lost, and a test whose
  requests it served but the reporter had not yet collected is marked incomplete. The reporter warns, the run's header
  reads *Coverage incomplete: the backend restarted during the run*, and the run's coverage in the
  [API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) names the origin and about when it restarted. A backend unreachable at the
  end of the run is flagged the same way, with only the tests' lines kept. The commit's
  [combined coverage](./combined-coverage) notes the run, and its `e2e` suite reads as incomplete unless a complete
  run of the commit counts beside it. A Nitro development server restarts on every rebuild.
- **The backend's whole life:** the run-level coverage holds everything the process ran since it started, so with a
  server Playwright reuses (`reuseExistingServer`), a shared staging backend, health checks or clicks by hand, code no
  test ran counts as run by the end-to-end suite. A backend started for the run reads true.
- **Run level only:** work outside a request (hosted services, timers started at startup), and work a request started
  that still runs once the reporter collected its coverage. On ASP.NET Core, lambdas created at startup too (inline
  minimal API handlers, inline middleware, DI factory lambdas); the methods they call count normally. On Nitro, a
  module's top-level code: it runs when the module loads, often inside the first request that reaches its route.

**ASP.NET Core:**

- **Exclusions:** the coverage build leaves out what coverlet does, read from the project's coverlet settings
  ([README](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/integrations/aspnetcore/PiwiTests.Instrumentation.Coverage#what-it-leaves-out)):
  an excluded member has no executable lines and no coverage.
- C# and Visual Basic only.

**Nitro:**

- **The server's own code only:** the files the build bundles, under the repository, outside `node_modules`. A
  dependency Nitro keeps external is not covered. A Nuxt application's `server/` code is; its pages and components
  rendered on the server are not.
- **Lines are the statements' first lines**, as Istanbul and Vitest count them: a statement spanning several lines
  counts its first one. A class field's initializer is not instrumented.
- **Callbacks that lose the request's async context**, such as those a library queues without `AsyncResource`, count
  at run level.
- Node only: the Bun, Deno and edge presets are not covered.

## Cost

The coverage build alone runs within 1% of a normal build, and per-test coverage stayed under 10% of the UI tests' time on a large
application, at every granularity alike: [Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost) has the figures for both backends
and how they were measured.

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › a run whose backend restarted](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-runs/63): The ASP.NET Core API restarted halfway through the run: its header says the coverage is incomplete, and the commit’s combined coverage notes that its e2e suite may read low.

- [Backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs): the middleware that serves the coverage
