<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/combined-coverage -->

# Combined coverage

The unit tests of the front end and the back end run your code too. `piwi coverage upload` sends their coverage
reports to the dashboard, keyed by the commit they ran on and a suite name you choose (`unit-front`, `unit-back`), to
sit beside the coverage Piwi records from [code reach](./code-reach) and [server coverage](./server-coverage) for the
same commit. This page covers the uploads, a commit's combined ratio and the Coverage tab's **Code** view; its
other views are [Scenario gaps](./scenario-gaps).

## Upload a report

Run the unit tests with coverage in Cobertura or LCOV, then upload the report from the same checkout:

```bash
npx vitest run --coverage --coverage.reporter=cobertura
npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml --suite unit-front
```

```bash
dotnet test --collect "XPlat Code Coverage"
npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload "**/TestResults/*/coverage.cobertura.xml" --suite unit-back
```

Each upload says what it sent:

```txt
Uploaded unit-front for a1b2c3d (main): 214 files from 1 report, 388 tracked files in scope.
12 files are outside the project's coverage scope.
```

The command reads the project, the dashboard URL and the API key (Uploader role) as the reporter does
(`PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `PIWI_API_KEY`), the commit from git and the branch from the CI or
`PIWI_BRANCH`. A path naming no file of the checkout is dropped and
counted (`--root` sets where paths start). Every flag is on the
[CLI reference](/reference/cli#coverage).

| Tool | Format | Command |
|---|---|---|
| Vitest (`@vitest/coverage-v8`) | Cobertura or LCOV | `vitest run --coverage --coverage.reporter=cobertura` |
| coverlet | Cobertura | `dotnet test --collect "XPlat Code Coverage"` |
| Microsoft code coverage | Cobertura | `dotnet test --collect "Code Coverage;Format=cobertura"` |
| Piwi's .NET recorder | Piwi | `PIWI_COVERAGE_OUTPUT=TestResults/piwi/ dotnet test -p:PiwiCoverage=true` |

On .NET, run the unit tests on the [server coverage](./server-coverage) build: each test host writes a report with
the span table's lines, at a fraction of coverlet's cost. Upload `"TestResults/piwi/*.json"` and set
`VSTEST_TESTHOST_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT=30000`: VSTest otherwise stops a host 100 ms after its tests.

Upload from the full unit-test run: Vitest lists the files nothing ran only when every test ran and `coverage.include`
names them.

## In CI

The unit tests and the Playwright suite usually run in separate jobs, tied by the commit: each uploads its own
report; a suite uploaded in parts (shards, portals) is merged.

::: code-group

```yaml [GitHub Actions]
- run: npx vitest run --coverage --coverage.reporter=cobertura
  working-directory: apps/web
- run: npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload apps/web/coverage/cobertura-coverage.xml --suite unit-front
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: https://piwi.example.com
    PIWI_PROJECT_NAME: shop
    PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
```

```yaml [Bitbucket Pipelines]
- step:
    name: Unit tests
    script:
      - dotnet test --collect "XPlat Code Coverage"
      - npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload "**/TestResults/*/coverage.cobertura.xml" --suite unit-back
```

```yaml [Azure DevOps]
- script: dotnet test --collect "Code Coverage;Format=cobertura" --results-directory $(Agent.TempDirectory)/coverage
- script: npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload "$(Agent.TempDirectory)/coverage/**/*.cobertura.xml" --suite unit-back
  env:
    PIWI_API_KEY: $(PIWI_API_KEY)
```

:::

On Bitbucket and Azure DevOps, set the `PIWI_` variables as pipeline variables. The first
Playwright run creates the project.

## One ratio per commit

For each commit, the dashboard counts every suite that ran the code: the reports uploaded for it, and `e2e`, the run
coverage of the commit's complete Playwright runs (never a partial, probe or flake-lab run; a run narrowed only by
`--project`, or cut short by `--max-failures`, still counts as complete). The totals are recomputed seconds after each upload or run; read them with the
[API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) or the MCP `get_coverage_summary` tool.

- **One set of executable lines per file version.** Tools disagree on which lines can run, so every suite counts on
  the same lines: the span table's, from [server coverage](./server-coverage) or
  [browser lines](./code-reach#what-it-records), when a run recorded them for that version of the file; otherwise the
  reports' own. A line a tool marks outside them is ignored.
- **Undetermined lines.** At `coverage.browser: 'functions'`, the browser suite records functions, not lines: an unrun
  line whose innermost function it ran is undetermined, shown beside the ratio, never counted as run.
- **Functions** count across suites by start line: one ran when any suite ran a function starting there.
- **Classes of lines.** Each executable line is unit only, end to end only (what the Playwright suite alone
  protects), both, none, or undetermined.
- **Files without coverage data** are tracked files in scope no suite names, counted apart from the percentage. They
  come from an upload's inventory, so a commit with no upload has none, and they count every file in scope, a README
  or an image included: narrow the scope to the code.
- **Carried forward.** A suite the commit lacks comes from the newest commit whose coverage arrived before it, on
  the commit's branch then on the default branch, file by file where the file's version is unchanged.
- **A run whose backend restarted** still joins `e2e`, adding only lines that ran; alone, it marks `e2e` incomplete.

The **Code** view of the project's **Coverage** tab shows the commit whose coverage arrived last, and a run's header
links its commit's.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/combined-coverage.png" alt="A project's combined coverage in the Code view">
  <figcaption>Three suites of one commit, counted on the same lines.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What the numbers leave out

On a branch, each suite keeps only the report of the commit whose coverage arrived last; an earlier push keeps only
its totals, never recounted ("totals only" on its run). The default branch keeps its newest commit and each day's last
for 90 days, and totals for a year. Notes above the numbers say when a commit has only totals, a suite is
carried, a report was cut, a known suite is missing, no inventory was sent, a run's backend restarted, the scope changed since, or runs did
not count.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/coverage-notes.png" alt="A note above a branch's coverage">
  <figcaption>A suite carried from the push before.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Find what is not covered

Every bar in the Code view splits lines by class, as a file's marks do. **Files** is a foldable tree, each
folder and file with its bar and its open [scenario gaps](./scenario-gaps), sortable by lines not run; beside it, the selected folder's suites and least-covered
files. A file opens on its source, through the
[source control](/guide/source-control) connection, each line marked by the suites that ran it; **Next range** jumps to
the next lines no suite ran. **In the Test Map** lists its routes and pages with their [scenario gaps](./scenario-gaps), each with its
**Accept**, **Snooze**, **Covered by** and **Dismiss**. Code no suite runs, or only one test runs, raises gaps of its own
([the detectors](/reference/gap-detectors#detectors)). The view reads the branch the project's filters pick, or the
default branch when they pick none or several.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/combined-coverage-file.png" alt="A file's lines marked by suite">
  <figcaption>Line 40 ran in e2e and unit-back.</figcaption>
</figure>

## In pull requests

The pull-request comment's [Uncovered changes](./uncovered-changes#on-the-pull-request) section counts the change's
patch coverage over the same scope, and the [CI merge gate](./merge-gate#what-only-warns) can warn under a minimum.

## Over time

The **Coverage trend** [Analytics widget](./analytics) charts the combined line coverage per day over the projects in
scope, each suite dashed, with the change against the comparison period; the
[quality report](./quality-reports) gives it as one line. Each project counts
once a day, at its last commit with coverage, on the default branch or the scope's first branch with one.
Kept per day, it outlives the reports; a day without coverage names the day it carries, and
one counting an incomplete `e2e` says so.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/combined-coverage-trend.png" alt="The Coverage trend widget">
  <figcaption>A month of coverage, each suite dashed.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Export

The Code view's card menu downloads the commit's combined coverage as LCOV or Cobertura, for Sonar, Codecov or an
IDE (`coverage-export?format=` in the API). A line any suite ran has 1 hit, else 0, an undetermined line included:
Piwi keeps no hit counts and no branches.

## The coverage scope

A project's coverage scope decides which files count: include and exclude patterns over repository-relative paths, in
the syntax CODEOWNERS uses. With no include pattern every file counts; an exclude wins. The defaults leave out tests,
build output (`bin/`, `obj/`, `dist/`, `.next/`, `.nuxt/`, `.output/`, `.svelte-kit/`) and generated sources; a folder
pattern matches at any depth. Set it in **Project → Settings → Coverage**, or with the
[API](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) (`coverageScope`). The upload sends only the files in scope, and the commit's
inventory: its tracked files in scope and their blob ids.

## Areas

Name the parts of the code in the same settings (`coverageAreas` in the API): `front: apps/web/`, `back: src/Api/`. A
file belongs to the first area whose patterns match it, and every suite splits the same way: the Code view gives
each area its totals and each suite's share, the coverage trend a line per area, and the pull-request comment the
changed lines per area. A change recounts the commits that keep their reports; a removed area
leaves the trend.

## What is sent

Paths, line numbers and blob ids: for each file, its executable lines, the lines and functions that ran, and every
function the tool knows. No source code, no test names, no hit counts.

## Limits

- **Formats:** Cobertura, LCOV and Piwi's own. Istanbul JSON, OpenCover and JaCoCo are not read.
- **coverlet can skip an assembly** whose dependencies it cannot resolve, saying so only in its diagnostic log.
- **Exclusions.** A .NET file counts the span table's lines, so code only a unit tool excludes still counts: the
  coverage build reads coverlet's exclusions from the project or its `RunSettingsFilePath`
  ([details](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/tree/main/integrations/aspnetcore/PiwiTests.Instrumentation.Coverage#what-it-leaves-out)),
  never Microsoft code coverage's. Exclude a whole file in the scope too.
- **EF Core migrations count**, in both tools: add `**/Migrations/` to the scope. `Program.cs` counts too, its inline
  minimal API handlers at run level only.
- **One commit, one checkout:** upload from the checkout the tests ran in.
- **Functions match by start line.** coverlet starts a method at its opening brace, the compiler's span table at its
  declaration, so a .NET function both report can count twice.

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › every suite’s coverage of one commit](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/5/coverage): The back end’s and the front end’s unit tests and the Playwright run of one commit, counted on the span table’s lines: the share each suite ran, a folder’s files, and the two tracked files no suite names.
- [Web Dashboard › a branch’s coverage, carried and superseded](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/5/coverage?branch=develop): The newest push of develop uploaded the front end’s unit tests only: the notes above its numbers say the back end’s suite is carried from the push before, and link to it, whose file detail went when this push arrived: it keeps only its totals.

# Coverage insights

Once tests record [coverage](/guide/concepts#coverage), Piwi compares it in four ways: a failing execution against
the test's last passing one, a test's recent runs against each other, a set of tests against every other test, and a
test against the lines it was written to reach. Each answer is in the dashboard, the API, an MCP tool for coding
agents and, for a failure, the AI diagnosis.

## Turn it on

The insights read the coverage your runs already record, from the browser ([code reach](./code-reach)), the
backend ([server coverage](./server-coverage), `coverage: { server: 'lines' }`), or both: either side is enough. Line answers need the
`lines` granularity (`coverage.browser: 'lines'` in the browser); `functions`, on the server or in the browser (`coverage.browser: 'functions'`), gives function
answers, and `files` gives file answers. A run without coverage changes nothing, so a nightly job with coverage on is
enough for the comparisons across runs.

Two rules hold in every answer:

- **Line numbers are compared only within one version of a file**, the git blob each covered file names. A file whose
  version differs between the sides is named as changed, never compared line by line;
  [suspect lines](/guide/concepts#suspect-lines) cover changes.
- **An incomplete capture never says that something did not run.** When the backend no longer held part of a test's
  coverage, or its collection failed, the claims that would need it are left out, and the answer says which side was
  incomplete.

## A failure's path against its last pass

For a failed or timed-out execution, Piwi takes the test's latest passing execution with coverage that started
before it: in the same Playwright project on the same branch first, then the same project on the default branch, then
another project on the same branch, then on the default branch, and among the newest three of that choice, a complete
capture first. The answer names that baseline (execution, run, start, branch, commit, project) and lists, per runtime
and file:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `only-here` | Only the failing execution ran the file |
| `diverged` | Both ran the same version, not the same lines or functions: the lines and functions only each side ran |
| `only-baseline` | Only the passing execution ran the file |
| `changed` | They ran different versions of the file, not compared |

The failing side comes first: "the code this run took that the last passing run did not" is where an error path, a
fallback or a retry branch shows. A failed execution's **Source** tab shows it in its Coverage section, under
*Compared with the last passing run*; a file both ran at one version opens on the lines each ran. The
[AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis) carries it as its **Code paths vs last pass** section, at most twelve files each way.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/coverage-divergence.png" alt="A failed execution compared with its last passing run">
  <figcaption>The lines only the failure ran, and only the pass.</figcaption>
</figure>

## A path that depends on the tests before it

For a test, Piwi reads its last 30 executions with coverage outside lab runs, in the Playwright project that has most
of its recent executions, leaves out the incomplete ones, and compares them on the files every execution that ran
them ran at the same version. The code that ran in some executions only is grouped by the executions that ran it,
the most evenly split first, with how many ran it and how many of those failed.

It then looks for a test whose having run before predicts that split. The backend is shared by every worker, so the
first relation is **earlier in the run**: the other test finished before the execution started, in the same run. The
second is **earlier on the worker**, the same on the execution's worker and shard, reported when it predicts the split
better. A test is named only when:

- the group and the test each split the compared executions with at least **3 executions on each side**;
- it predicts at least **90%** of the executions that have a start time, either way: the code runs after it, or only
  when it has not run.

When at least two executions failed and 90% of them fall on one side of a group, the answer says the failures follow
that code. When they follow the code the earlier test predicts, the test is marked **order-dependent**: it depends on
state another test leaves behind, and the [flaky root-cause classification](./flaky-tests#root-cause-classification)
names it `order`, ahead of every other category. That check runs only for a test with at least two recent failures
that recorded coverage. A test's page shows the answer in its **Path variation** card.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/path-variation.png" alt="The Path variation card of an order-dependent test">
  <figcaption>The earlier test that predicts the path, and the failures that follow it.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What quarantining or deleting tests leaves uncovered

For up to 50 tests of a project, Piwi reads their latest coverage on the default branch and every other test's, and
lists per file and version the lines and functions no other **trusted** test runs. Trusted means not quarantined; the
tests asked about are left out of the others.

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `only-these` | No other trusted test runs the file |
| `only-flaky` | The only other trusted tests running it are flaky: they carry a flaky root cause |
| `partial` | Other tests run the file, not every line: the lines no other trusted test runs, and the lines only flaky ones run |
| `uncertain` | The other tests recorded the file only at another version, or without lines, so no line is claimed |

Where the project records coverage, the dashboard's quarantine actions preview it: beside the Quarantine and Release
buttons, in the More menus and in the confirmations. The MCP tools that quarantine or release tests add the same
summary to their answer.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/quarantine-coverage-loss.png" alt="A Quarantine button with the code quarantining the test leaves uncovered">
  <figcaption>What quarantining a flaky test leaves to no other trusted test.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Did a new test reach its target lines

Given a test, a file and target lines, Piwi reads the test's latest execution with coverage, or the execution you
name, and splits the target lines into those that **ran**, those that **did not run** (from a complete capture
only) and those it **cannot tell** (file granularity, or an incomplete capture). At function granularity a line ran
when the innermost function around it ran: a callback nested in a function that ran, and never called, did not. When
a run recorded the file's executable lines for that version, target lines that cannot run (blank lines, comments) are
set apart.

When a target line did not run, the answer names the **nearest test**: the one running most of the function around
the first target line at that version, else of the target lines, else, at another version, of the file. It is the
test to copy. The `write-the-missing-test` [agent skill](./agent-skills) runs a new test with server coverage on and
checks its target lines this way until they run.

## For agents

Three read-only MCP tools, listed with the rest on [MCP tools](/reference/mcp-tools), carry these answers. They
belong to the `core` module and depend on the **Coverage** capability: declining it for the instance in **Settings → Capabilities**
drops them.
For a project with no coverage, each answers one sentence saying how to turn it on.

- `get_coverage`: a file's executed ranges grouped by the tests that ran them and its executable lines, with the
  nearest test for target lines; or an execution's files, one file's ranges, or which target lines a test ran. A test
  can be named by its spec file and title.
- `compare_coverage`: a failure against its last pass, or a test's recent runs against each other and the earlier test
  that explains them.
- `get_coverage_loss`: what quarantining, skipping or deleting tests would leave uncovered.

The same answers are in the dashboard's API; see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) (`/settings/api` on your
instance).

## Limits

- **As fresh as the last run with coverage.** A test's latest coverage can be a nightly job old; every answer names
  the executions it read.
- **Executed is not checked.** A line that ran may still be wrong with every test green.
- **Order needs times and variety.** An execution without a start time from the reporter takes no part in finding the
  earlier test, and a suite whose order never changes gives no split to explain.
- **Coverage loss reads each test's latest coverage as stored**: another test whose own capture was incomplete can
  make a line look run by these tests only.
- **What the capture cannot see** stays unseen: see the limits of [code reach](./code-reach#limits).

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › toggles dark mode: a failed attempt against its last pass](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-run-cases/830?evidence=source): The Source tab compares the failed first attempt with the test’s last passing run: in the preferences endpoints, only the failure ran the conflict handler that keeps the stored theme, and only the pass published the change; open the file to see both marked.
- [Web Dashboard › toggles dark mode: a path that depends on the tests before it](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-cases/53): Its Path variation card: in the 3 executions that started before updates the organization name finished, it ran the conflict handler, and only those failed, so its flaky root cause is order.

## Related

- [Code reach](./code-reach) and [server coverage](./server-coverage): recording coverage, browser and server
- [Flaky tests & quarantine](./flaky-tests): root causes and the quarantine these answers inform
- [AI diagnosis](./ai-diagnosis): the evidence a diagnosis reads
- [MCP server](./mcp): connecting an agent

# Probes

[Reach](/guide/concepts#reach) says a test touched a route, not that it would fail if the route returned garbage, and
many passing tests would not. A **[probe](/guide/concepts#probe)** replays a passing test with one fault injected
behind one request and records whether the test noticed. A route that stays green under a fault becomes a
**not noticed** gap: the most dangerous class, because the suite says everything is fine.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/probes-two-levels.svg" alt="Client probes rewrite a response in the browser; server probes sign a fault the backend instrumentation applies inside the server; both record whether the test noticed">
</figure>

## Client probes

`piwi probe` runs the probe plan the dashboard computes for a project:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter probe --project my-project
```

It fetches the plan, runs `playwright test` on the tests in it with the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures)
in probe mode, and posts each outcome back. The fixtures apply the fault at the Playwright boundary, on the matching
response after the page's first navigation:

| Fault | What the test receives |
|---|---|
| `status-500` | a 500 in place of the response |
| `empty-body` | the right status with an empty body |
| `drop-field` | the JSON body with its first field removed (from each element of an array) |
| `stale-value` | an earlier response to the same request in place of the current one |
| `slow` | the response five seconds late |

The plan pairs each passing test with a route it reaches: pairs never probed come first, then pairs whose test
changed since its last probe, and each test gets one fault per run, up to a budget (50 pairs by default,
`--budget` to change it). The plan rotates through `status-500`, `empty-body` and `drop-field`, the faults that break
what a test checks: `slow` reads a test's timeout rather than its assertions, and `stale-value` needs an earlier
response. [Quarantined tests](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) and tests whose last run failed are left out. A fault that did not change the response
(a body with no field to drop), a test skipped and a run interrupted record the pair as *inconclusive*, and a pair no
probe has decided returns to the plan a week after its last probe.

A test counts as changed when the source lines its steps run from differ from those of its passing runs before the
probe: an added assertion, an edited helper or a moved line. A new tag or owner does not count, and neither does a
change to the route's handler alone.

A probe run is stamped as one, with retries off and no failure limit, whatever the config and its projects set.
Every project of the config runs each planned test; pass Playwright's own flags after `--` to narrow it
(`-- --project=chromium`). A probed test that notices its fault fails, so a non-zero Playwright exit is expected. The
[CLI reference](/reference/cli#probe) lists every flag.

### What a probe run never counts

A probe run injects its failures on purpose, so it never counts as a real run: no failure clusters, no regression
signals, no notification ([`run.interrupted`](/reference/notification-events) included), no pull-request feedback, no
issue tracker write ([which runs send nothing](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin)), no metric or analytics, no
quarantine streak, no branch status, never the baseline another run is compared with, never an
[environment incident](/features/environment-incidents), and nothing in the Test Map but the probe outcomes. It never
moves a pass rate, a duration or the `failed` selection either, and leaves a test's tags, owner, locks and locator
snapshots as they are.

## What an outcome records

Each outcome is recorded, and a decisive one (noticed or not noticed) is the *checks* edge in the
[Test Map](/features/scenario-gaps) between the test and the route. An inconclusive outcome, or one of a fault that
only delays a response (`slow`, and the server's `delay` and `slow-first`), never replaces it. When several
Playwright projects probe one pair, the outcome that says most is kept: a pass under the fault, then a failure. The *not noticed* detector reads the edges: a route with at least one probe that no test noticed,
and none that did, is a **false-comfort** gap:

```
Tests pass when POST /api/orders breaks
A probe (status-500) on POST /api/orders did not make checkout › pay fail. Assert the effect the request should have.
```

The next step is an assertion on what the request is for: the order appears, the total changes, the error shows.
Once a probe on that route is noticed, the gap [closes itself](/reference/gap-detectors#when-a-gap-closes).

## Server probes

**Experimental.** Server probes are off by default. The rule for when to turn them on (client probes reporting
*not noticed* on one probed pair in ten) has not been measured yet. The design is in the
[scenario gaps design record](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/adr/scenario-gaps.md#level-two--server-probes-m3-on-an-entry-condition).

A client probe rewrites the response in the browser, so the server never runs its error path. A server probe signs a
fault onto one request (`X-Piwi-Probe`, an HMAC signature made with `PIWI_PROBE_SECRET`), and the
[backend instrumentation](/guide/backend-logs#server-probes) applies it inside the server: a thrown error, a status,
a delay, a mutated response or a failed dependency call. The instrumentation reports the fault it applied, so a probe
it did not honor records as *inconclusive*, never as a pass.

Two signals come back: whether the test noticed, as with a client probe, and whether the application coped. An
uncaught page error once the fault applied, or a blank page (no accessible content when the test ends) after a backend
error, makes an **unhandled** finding. A console error, a dialog, a blank page alone, or a backend error the fault did
not inject itself makes a **degraded** one: the 500 of a `throw` or `status` fault is the fault, and the browser's
*Failed to load resource* line only repeats a status, so neither counts. A fault the server never applied makes no
finding, nor does a probe whose test was skipped or interrupted. Findings rank by severity and reach, and the *unprobed dependency* detector names the dependencies no probe
has decided yet.

It needs:

- the Nitro plugin or the ASP.NET Core package in the application under test, with `PIWI_PROBE_SECRET` set and
  `PIWI_SERVER_PROBES=true`. Both apply faults only in development and test environments by default. The ASP.NET Core package applies throw,
  status, delay and extreme-value faults; its data and dependency probes record as *inconclusive*;
- the same `PIWI_PROBE_SECRET` where `piwi probe` runs;
- **Server probes** turned on under **Scenario gaps** in **Project → Settings → Coverage**,
  where the fault classes and routes are allow-listed. A test gets the first class in the list that its route allows,
  `dependency` aside, so list first the class that matters most; a dependency fault goes to a test the other classes
  left, on a route whose handler calls a dependency. Dependency faults on state-changing routes (`POST`, `PUT`,
  `PATCH`, `DELETE`) stay off unless you allow them.

With server probes on, half of the budget is kept for server faults, for the tests the run's client faults did not
take, once a run of the project has recorded a request the backend instrumentation answered. A pair a probe decided,
at either level, is not planned again until its test changes.

## Try it in the demo

- [Web Dashboard › Gaps](https://piwitests.dev/demo/projects/5?tab=gaps): Client probes the tests did not notice (an empty revenue response, a failed invitation, a stale organization name), an invite form that degraded when sendgrid failed, and a revenue page that threw when clickhouse failed.

- [Piwi CLI: probe](/reference/cli#probe): every flag
- [Gap detectors & exposure](/reference/gap-detectors): the *not noticed*, *unprobed dependency* and *not handled*
  detectors

# Analytics

The **Analytics** page (`/analytics`) steps back from single runs and tests: it aggregates every
project over a period you choose, to show where the suite as a whole is drifting. This page covers what
every analytics view shares: the scope, where the numbers come from, drilling down, chart export and
targets. Arranging widgets into an analytics dashboard of your own is on [Dashboards](./dashboards), and
sending one as a document on [Quality reports](./quality-reports).

## Scope

The **Filters** block at the top sets what every widget counts, with *Reset* in its header. On a phone
it folds to a one-line summary.

- **Period**, with the comparison and the buckets (below). The line under it states the resolved dates,
  the comparison and any note (a project without the chosen selection, a deleted marker).
- **Runs**: the projects (intersected with the ones you can see), environments and branches (optional
  multi-select, see [Environment](/guide/concepts#environment)), the environment and branch policies (below)
  and *Full runs only*, which excludes partial runs. All but the projects are the
  **Filters** block a project page opens with, so a drill-down lands on the same runs.
- **Tests**: optional; a selection, test tags or browsers (below).

Probe runs (the fault-injected replays `piwi probe` produces) are never counted, whatever the filters.
Two widgets read past the period: **Flakiest tests** ranks each project's last 50 runs whatever the
period or *Full runs only*, and applies an environment or branch only when exactly one is picked; **Failure
clusters** lists every open cluster, using the period only for its resolved count.

### Periods

- **Rolling**: the last 7 days to 12 months, in whole UTC days, today included.
- **Calendar**: this or last week, month, quarter or year. Boundaries follow your time zone (the one set
  under Settings → Localization, else your browser's); a week starts on your locale's first day.
- **Custom range**: two dates, both included.
- **Since a marker**: from a [timeline marker](./timeline-markers) to now.
- **Release cycle**: between two consecutive `release` markers, the current one or the previous one.
- **Sprint**: a start date and a length, this sprint or the last.
- **All time**: everything still stored.

### Comparison and buckets

Every change on the page is measured against the **comparison**: the previous period of the same length
(the default), the previous calendar unit, release cycle or sprint, the same period a year earlier, or
nothing.

**Buckets** decide how the trends and the heatmap cut the period: automatic (about 31 buckets), daily,
weekly or monthly. Buckets start at UTC midnight, so a heatmap cell is one UTC day.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/analytics-scope-bar.png" alt="The Analytics page's Filters block with the period picker open: rolling, calendar and release periods, a custom range, since a marker, a sprint, then the comparison and the buckets">
  <figcaption>The scope of the Analytics page, its period picker open.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Branch policy

By default only runs on each project's **default branch** count, so a broken feature branch does not
move the trends. A run whose branch is unknown (a trace import, a run outside git) counts only in a
project that never reported a branch. The default branch is the project's setting, else
the one its latest run reported, else `main`. *All branches* counts every run; branches picked in the
Filters block override both.

### Environment policy

With no environment picked, a project with a [default environment](./environments#default-environment) counts only
its runs, and a project without one counts every environment. *All environments* counts every run; environments
picked in the Filters block override both. **Environment comparison** compares every environment unless you pick some.

### Test filter

The *Tests* filter narrows every number to some tests:

- a **selection**, by key: `smoke` resolves in each project to that project's
  [selection](/features/test-selection) with that key, so a convention shared across projects works on the
  cross-project page; a project without it is left out and named;
- **test tags**: tests carrying all of them;
- **browsers**: the Playwright projects the executions ran on.

It means the tests that match **today**, with their whole history. The widgets then count from the
stored executions, final attempt per test, browser and `--repeat-each` repetition, so they reach back only
as far as retention keeps runs. A widget that cannot narrow (the failure clusters) says so above its card.

With one project in scope, *Save as selection* stores the tags as a selection you can run with
`piwi run <key>`.

### Sharing a view

The address carries the scope (`?period=last-month&sel=smoke`), so a copied link opens on what its
sender saw; without it, the page opens on the scope you used last in this browser. To keep your own
view, save an [analytics dashboard](./dashboards).

### Where the numbers come from

The [pass rates](/guide/concepts#pass-rate), run counts, durations, CI time, [wasted time](./slow-tests#wasted-time) and regression counts are read from
**daily rollups**, one precomputed row per project, UTC day, environment, branch and run kind, kept at
ingest and checked nightly against the stored runs. When [retention](/operate/storage#data-retention)
deletes old runs, their numbers stay in the rollups, so a one-year pass-rate line survives a 30-day
retention window. Lists of tests and clusters, and anything under a test filter, read the stored runs.
The rollups also [export](/operate/metrics) to a BI tool or a Prometheus scraper. The coverage trend reads the
[combined coverage](./combined-coverage) kept per project and day, which outlives the reports it came from.

## Widgets and metrics

The page opens on the built-in **Overview** [analytics dashboard](./dashboards), in four bands, unless you or an
administrator [made another the default](./dashboards#your-default-dashboard). [Analytics widgets](/reference/analytics-widgets)
lists every widget an [analytics dashboard](./dashboards) can place, and [Metrics](/reference/metrics) defines every
number they show, with its unit and which direction is better.

## Hand-back outcomes

The **Hand-back outcomes** section, in the *Where the pain is* band, says what became of what Piwi handed back over
the period, one line per kind:

- **Locator heals**: call sites whose code now uses the recommended locator, whoever changed it, and the
  [auto-heal](./auto-heal) pull requests merged or closed.
- **AI diagnoses**: those written, rated helpful, and confirmed by a fix that changed the files they named.
- **[CI gate](./merge-gate)**: failed [gate verdicts](./pr-feedback#the-gate-verdict), and pull requests merged anyway, with any
  failure that came back.
- **Flaky tests**: fixes a [Flake Lab](./flake-lab) verify run proved, and those that flaked again.
- **Fix attempts**: fixes a person or an agent reported, and what the runs made of them.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/analytics-handbacks.png" alt="Hand-back outcomes: locator heals, AI diagnoses, the CI gate and a verified flaky test">
  <figcaption>Hand-back outcomes: what became of each fix Piwi handed back.</figcaption>
</figure>

A rate needs 10 ratings, pull requests or fixes; below that the line says the sample is too small. The counts
survive retention, and are kept per project and day, so branch and environment filters do not narrow them. A
project that declined a kind's capability is left out of it. Each number is also a [metric](/reference/metrics).

## From a number to its rows

A number links to the list behind it, opened with the same period and filters. In the portfolio, a
project's runs, flaky tests and open failure clusters open that project's lists; each heatmap cell opens
the project's runs of that day. With one project in scope, the headline tiles and every bucket of a chart
do the same. The project page says the list came from Analytics and offers **Show every run**.

## Exporting a chart

Every chart carries a menu in its header. **Copy as PNG** puts the chart, with its title, on the clipboard
as an image, ready to paste into a slide; a browser that cannot copy images downloads the PNG instead.
**Download Excel** saves the numbers behind the chart as an .xlsx workbook, one row per bucket or group:
numbers and dates are real cells, and a test title is never run as a formula. To send a whole
analytics dashboard, export it as a [quality report](./quality-reports) instead.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/chart-export-menu.png" alt="A chart's export menu open on the Analytics page: copy the chart as an image, or download its data as Excel">
  <figcaption>A chart's export menu.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Targets

A project can carry **targets**, set in the **Targets** section of its **Settings** tab: a test pass rate to reach, and
limits on flaky tests, wasted CI minutes per week, the age of the oldest open failure cluster and the median time to fix.
Each one is optional. Over the period an analytics dashboard shows, a target is **met** or **missed**:

- the headline tiles mark each number that has a target, met or missed, with one project in scope;
- the portfolio's **Targets** column counts the targets each project meets;
- the insights feed says which target a project missed, and by how much;
- a quality report lists every target, met or missed, and its risks name the missed ones.

A weekly target (wasted CI minutes) is scaled to the length of the period, so a 30-day period is checked
against about four weeks of it.

## Related

- [Dashboards](./dashboards): analytics dashboards of your own
- [Quality reports](./quality-reports): this page as a document, with **Quality report**
- [Flaky tests](./flaky-tests): the per-project analysis these widgets aggregate
- [Timeline markers](./timeline-markers): annotate the trends with real-world events
- [Cut costly flakiness](/recipes/flaky-cleanup): from the flaky leaderboard to an afternoon of fixes
- [Cut the time it costs](/recipes/faster-suite): where the CI minutes go, and how to get them back

# Dashboards

An **analytics dashboard** is a named arrangement of [analytics](./analytics) widgets in bands, with a default
[scope](./analytics#scope): its projects, filters and period. This page covers the analytics dashboards
themselves: the built-in ones, saving and editing your own, sharing them and showing them on a wall screen.
The scope and what the numbers mean are on [Analytics](./analytics); sending one as a document is on
[Quality reports](./quality-reports). On this page, "dashboard" means an analytics dashboard.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/saved-dashboard.png" alt="A shared dashboard: the checkout smoke tests over the current sprint, with a list, the period's releases and a note">
  <figcaption>A shared dashboard over the current sprint.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Built-in and saved dashboards

The header's switcher lists every dashboard you can open, with a search:

- **Built-in**: Overview (four bands and sixteen widgets, where `/analytics` opens unless a
  [default](#your-default-dashboard) is set), and the report dashboards
  Executive, Engineering and Gaps digest (only where the [Test Map](./scenario-gaps) is not declined), whose
  contents [Quality reports](./quality-reports#what-a-report-contains) describes. The Team dashboard is a quality
  report only, offered when the report's tests have an owner. A built-in dashboard cannot be changed, only duplicated.
- **Shared**: saved dashboards someone shared with every signed-in user.
- **Personal**: your private dashboards.
- **Unused**: shared dashboards nobody opened for 90 days, where their owner or an administrator can
  delete them.

`/analytics/d/<id>` opens one dashboard; *Manage dashboards* (`/analytics/dashboards`) lists them all,
with *New dashboard* (empty, or a copy of any dashboard you can open), *Rename…*, *Duplicate* and *Delete*.
*Rename…*, also in a dashboard's **⋯** menu, changes the name and the description of a saved dashboard you
can edit; duplicate a built-in one first.

## Your default dashboard

`/analytics` opens, in this order: the dashboard you picked with *Make it my default* (kept in this
browser), the dashboard an administrator set for everyone under *Manage dashboards* (a built-in or a
shared one), else Overview. Overview keeps the scope you used last in this browser; another dashboard
opens on its own saved scope. Either way the address carries the scope, so a copied link shows what you
saw.

## Editing a dashboard

*Edit* (or *Duplicate*, on a dashboard you cannot change) turns the page into the editor:

- Each band gets a title, a description, *Add widget* and a menu to move or remove it; *Add band* is at
  the bottom.
- Each widget gets a menu: *Configure*, *Half width* or *Full width*, *Move up*, *Move down*, *Move to
  band*, *Duplicate*, *Remove*. Moves are buttons, so the editor works on a phone and from a keyboard.
  Below the `xl` breakpoint every widget is full width.
- The **Filters** block, titled *Default filters*, sets the scope the dashboard opens with.
- Widgets preview from your unsaved changes. *Save* writes them; *Save as…* writes a new dashboard.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/dashboard-editor.png" alt="The dashboard editor: band title and description, Add widget, and a widget's menu">
  <figcaption>The dashboard editor: a band, Add widget, and a widget's menu.</figcaption>
</figure>

If someone saved the dashboard while you were editing it, *Save* says so and offers to reload their
version or save yours as a copy; nothing is overwritten.

### Widgets

*Add widget* lists every widget, grouped by the band it usually belongs to, with a search: the fifteen of
Overview, the report widgets (verdict, what is being done, risks, scenario gaps), the engineering
widgets (ownership, environment comparison, movers; see [Analytics widgets](/reference/analytics-widgets)), and:

- **Metric**: one number of the metric catalog, drawn as a number, a line, bars, a table or a heatmap
  (below).
- **List**: the latest runs of the period, the open failure clusters with the most occurrences, the
  flakiest tests, or the highest-scored open scenario gaps, top 5 to 25, each linking to its page.
- **Timeline markers**: the [timeline markers](./timeline-markers) of the period, optionally of some categories.
- **Note**: text in Markdown. Raw HTML is shown as text, so a shared dashboard cannot carry a script.
- **One project**: spec health, slowest tests, performance trend, timeout opportunities and selection
  health, the analyses of the project page. They need a scope with exactly one project and say so
  otherwise.

A widget a later release removed shows "This widget is no longer available" instead of breaking the
dashboard.

### The metric widget

Pick a metric, a display and, optionally, a **breakdown**: "wasted CI minutes by browser", "pass rate by
project tag", "open failure clusters by assignee". The breakdowns a metric offers depend on what it
counts:

| Metric counts | Breakdowns |
|---|---|
| Runs and tests (pass rates, durations, wasted and CI minutes, regressions) | project, project tag, environment, branch, run kind; browser, test tag, owner, priority, feature, spec directory |
| Failure clusters | project, project tag, error type, status, assignee |
| [Quarantined tests](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) | project, project tag, owner, test tag |

With a breakdown, *Bars* and *Table* show one row per group for the period, *Line* one line per group
(the first eight), *Heatmap* one row of buckets per group. Groups are sorted worst first; the top 5 to 25
are shown, the rest grouped as *Other*. Breakdowns by project, environment, branch or run kind
read the daily rollups, so they reach as far back as the rollups do; breakdowns by test or browser read
the stored executions, as far back as retention keeps them.

### Periods and filters per widget

*Configure* also sets a widget's own scope: a period that replaces the dashboard's (a *Last 7 days*
number on a quarterly dashboard), and filters that **narrow** the dashboard's (only some projects, a
selection, test tags, browsers). A widget never widens the dashboard's filters, so what a dashboard
covers can be read off its **Filters** block.

## Sharing and access

- A dashboard is **private** (its owner) or **shared** (listed for every signed-in user). Anyone signed in
  keeps private dashboards; sharing needs the Maintainer role or above on at least one project, or an administrator.
- A shared dashboard is changed by its owner or an administrator; everyone else duplicates it.
- With authentication off, every dashboard is shared.
- **A dashboard grants no access.** Every widget is computed for the projects you can open, and the line
  under the dashboard's name says how many projects of the dashboard's scope are hidden from you
  ("1 project hidden (no access)").
- A private dashboard whose owner is deleted goes with the nightly orphan sweep; a shared one stays,
  editable by administrators.

## Live refresh and TV mode

An open dashboard refreshes a widget when a run of one of its projects finishes, at most once every 30
seconds per widget. Widget answers are cached on the server for 60 seconds. The tests a test filter
matches are kept for 30 seconds, so the widgets of one page resolve the filter once; a finished or deleted run, or a
change to a selection or a quarantine, in one of its projects resolves it again.

**TV mode** (*TV mode* in the menu, or `?tv=1`) is for a wall screen: no navigation, larger type, and a full refresh every five minutes on top of the live one. Add `?cycle=12,15&every=60`
to rotate through several dashboards, one every 60 seconds (15 at least). TV mode needs a signed-in
session; a wall screen with nobody signed in opens a [live dashboard link](./share-links#live-dashboard-links)
instead.

## Scheduling and exporting a dashboard

*Quality report* renders the dashboard on screen as a [quality report](./quality-reports) (the saved dashboard
is offered first), and *Schedule…* creates a [report schedule](./quality-reports#report-schedules) on
it. Deleting a dashboard that schedules render names them first; they stop, shown as inactive with the
reason on the Quality reports page, until their owner picks another dashboard.

## From an agent

The [MCP server](./mcp) has `list_dashboards` and `get_dashboard`, which returns every widget's data,
the JSON the page renders, over the dashboard's scope; each key you pass replaces the dashboard's.

## Related
- [Analytics](./analytics): the scope, the periods and the widgets of Overview
- [Quality reports](./quality-reports): a dashboard as a document, on a schedule

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/quality-reports -->

# Quality reports

A **quality report** is a document about the state of one or several projects over a period, written
for a reader who may never open the dashboard: a manager, a release owner, a client. It is not the
Playwright HTML report a run carries (the **run report**); it is the [Analytics](./analytics) page turned
into something you can send. This page covers the report: what it contains, exporting it, report schedules
and snapshots. The analytics dashboards a report renders are on [Dashboards](./dashboards).

## What a report contains

A report renders an [analytics dashboard](./dashboards) over a **scope**: the projects, branches,
environments, test filter and period of the analytics **Filters** block. Any saved analytics dashboard can be
exported and scheduled; four built-in ones are written for reports:

- **Executive**, for stakeholders, in plain words with no locators and no stack traces: a verdict,
  six headline numbers, the [pass rate](/guide/concepts#pass-rate) over time with the comparison period and your
  [timeline markers](./timeline-markers), what changed, what is being done (failure clusters fixed, assigned or
  ticketed, tests released from [quarantine](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out)) and the risks (metrics moving the wrong way, projects
  failing run after run, the oldest open failure clusters).
- **Engineering**, for the team that owns the suite: the executive report, then the flakiest tests,
  the failure clusters, wasted CI time, regressions, CI time, the [combined coverage](./combined-coverage) trend
  (left out when no project in scope has coverage), the browser matrix and slow endpoints.
- **Team**, the engineering report for the tests one owner holds (`piwi:owner` or CODEOWNERS), offered
  when a test in scope has an owner.
- **Gaps digest**, the [Test Map](./scenario-gaps)'s weekly digest: the top five new gaps of each
  project, then open gaps by class and feature. A project that declined the Test Map is left out.

The engineering report ends with the same gap counts. **Overview**, the analytics page itself, can be
exported too.

Every report ends with a footer stating the scope, the branch and environment policies, the period and its
comparison, each metric's definition, and its limits: lists of tests reach back only as far as
[retention](/operate/storage#data-retention) keeps runs, and days are UTC.

### The verdict is built by rules

The opening sentence ("The pass rate on main fell 2.1 points to 95.8%, and 3 failure clusters were
fixed.") comes from fixed rules over the numbers, never from a model. Its tone is **good** at a pass rate
of 90% or more that did not drop by more than a point, **bad** under 50% or after a drop of 5 points or
more, **mixed** otherwise.

## Exporting a report

Click **Quality report** on the Analytics page (the current scope) or on a project page (that project, last 30
days). The dialog previews the report; pick another dashboard or the language, then **Download**:

| Format | What you get |
|---|---|
| PDF | Vector text and charts, one band per page so pages drop into a slide deck; each page names the report and is numbered |
| HTML | One self-contained file: inline charts, no script, no remote resource |
| Markdown | Tables, and a text sparkline (`▁▂▃▅▇`) under each series; pastes into Confluence, Jira or a pull request |
| Excel | An .xlsx workbook, a sheet per table named after its widget; numbers and dates are real cells, text never runs as a formula. Each section's **Excel** button downloads just that section |
| JSON | The report bundle itself, for scripts and BI tools |

Scripts can ask the API for `format=csv`, formula-guarded with a leading `'`.

A report grants no access: it covers only the projects its reader can open.

## Report schedules

A **report schedule** sends a quality report on its own. **Schedule…** on the Analytics page or in a
project page's menu opens the form with the filters on screen; **New schedule** on the **Quality
reports** page starts an empty one. A Contributor or above on the project, or an administrator, creates schedules.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/report-schedules.png" alt="The Quality reports page: report snapshots and schedules">
  <figcaption>The Quality reports page: snapshots and schedules.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **When**: daily, weekly, every other week or monthly, at a time in the instance time zone (UTC when
  that setting follows each browser).
- **Which period**: the whole days since the previous report, so a weekly Monday schedule reports on
  Monday to Sunday; the first one covers the days since you created it. A period with no run is still
  sent, because a stopped pipeline is news.
- **Where**: [notification channels](./notifications). Email carries the verdict, the numbers and the
  trend as an image; Slack and Microsoft Teams the same as a message; a webhook the whole bundle as signed JSON; a browser
  channel a notification. With **Share link** on, each report carries a
  [share link](./share-links#report-share-links) that opens it without an account.
  **AI narrative** adds the [narrative](/reference/analytics-widgets#where-things-stand) the AI model writes.
- **Who receives it**: **Send to** lists each channel with its recipient (an address, the Slack or Teams
  channel its webhook posts to, a webhook's host, dashboard tabs) and whose it is: yours, global, or
  another person's. The schedules on the **Quality reports** page show the same, with each schedule's owner.

**Run now** sends the last complete period straight away; **Preview**, in the form, shows that report
before you save, as its email and as the full report, and sends nothing. **Mute** keeps the snapshots
and sends nothing; **Pause** stops the schedule. Each firing uses its owner's current roles, and a report to someone's
own channel is dropped once they can no longer open every project it covers. A **global**
schedule covers every project, goes to global channels and needs an administrator.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/report-schedule-preview.png" alt="The schedule form's preview: the email the Weekly executive report schedule would send now">
  <figcaption>Preview in the schedule form: the email the schedule would send now.</figcaption>
</figure>

The server checks schedules every five minutes; a firing missed while it was down happens at the next
check, for its own period. The [desktop app](./desktop) fires them while it runs; the demo
has no scheduler.


### Report snapshots

Every report sent is kept as a **report snapshot** with its numbers as they were: a report received in
March reads the same in June, whatever [retention](/operate/storage#data-retention) deleted since. The
**Quality reports** page lists them with how each was delivered, to read, download or
[share](./share-links#report-share-links). You see a snapshot
when you can open every project it covers. Snapshots go after `PIWI_RETENTION_REPORT_DAYS` days (365; 0
keeps them).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/report-snapshot.png" alt="A stored report snapshot: when it was generated and delivered, then the report: the verdict, the headline numbers, the pass rate over time, what changed, what is being done and the risks">
  <figcaption>A report snapshot: the report as it was generated.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Language

Reports come in English and French: by default the project's
[ticket language](./issue-tracking#language) over one project, else the instance locale. Test titles
and error messages stay as recorded.

## Cost of a CI minute

An administrator can give a CI minute a price in **Settings → Performance**: an amount and an ISO 4217
currency, such as 0.008 USD. `PIWI_CI_MINUTE_COST` (`"0.008 USD"`) pins it and makes the setting
read-only. Once set, every wasted-time number is followed by its cost, on the analytics page and in the
quality report; unset, only minutes show. The cost is one instance-wide value.

## From CI, an agent or a script

- The [`piwi report`](/reference/cli#report) command prints a report with an API key, so a scheduled CI
  job can post the Markdown every Monday:
  `npx @piwitests/reporter report --project checkout --period 7d --format md`.
  `--fail-on bad` makes it exit 1 on a bad verdict.
- The [MCP server](./mcp) offers `get_quality_report` (the bundle), `get_metric_trend` (one metric over
  time) and `compare_periods` (the headline numbers over two periods).
- The REST API renders a report for a dashboard, format, language and analytics scope, keeps one as a snapshot,
  manages schedules and reads snapshots. See the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api), or `/settings/api` on your
  instance.

## Turning reports off

Quality reports are an optional [capability](/operate/capabilities#declining-a-capability). Declining it in **Settings → Capabilities** hides
the *Quality report* and *Schedule…* actions and the *Quality reports* page, and drops `get_quality_report` from
the MCP tools; the analytics page and the metric tools stay, since analytics is core. A schedule or a
snapshot counts as use, so the capability stays on while one exists: delete them first.

## Related

- [Analytics](./analytics): the same metrics, explored on the page
- [Dashboards](./dashboards): a page of widgets kept for a team or a screen
- [Notifications](./notifications): the channels a scheduled report is sent through
- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli#report): a report from CI or a script

# Timeline markers

Timeline markers let you record **dated events** against a project — a deploy, a config change, an infrastructure migration, a dependency bump, an incident — and see them overlaid as vertical lines on the analytics trend charts. When a pass-rate drop or a performance regression lines up with a marker, you have your prime suspect: "the slowdown started the day we switched CI runners".

## What a marker is

Each marker belongs to one project and carries:

- **Label** — a short title (e.g. _Migrated CI to ARM runners_).
- **Date & time** — when the event happened; this is where the line is drawn.
- **Category** — one of `deploy`, `config`, `infra`, `incident`, `release`, or a generic `event`. The category sets the marker's icon and color.
- **Environment** _(optional)_ — one of the project's [environments](./environments), picked from its list. Leave it
  empty to apply to all environments. Through the API, `environment` names one by its key, an alias or a run's label,
  resolved as a run's label is.
- **Commit** _(optional, `deploy` markers)_ — the application's commit the deploy put in place, 7 to 40 hexadecimal
  characters. A run of a [deployed environment](./environments) that started after the marker ran against that commit,
  unless its server reported its own.
- **Description** _(optional)_ — free-text detail.
- **Run** _(optional, API only)_ — the id of one of the project's runs the event belongs to.

## Where markers show up

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/run-trend-marker-tooltip.png" alt="A project's Run trend with markers drawn as dashed vertical lines, one hovered: a Release marker named v2.3.0 with its date, environments and description">
  <figcaption>Markers on the Run trend; hovering one shows its details.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **Project charts** — the **Run trend** and **Performance trend** charts render each marker as a dashed vertical line with a colored flag handle. Hover the line or its flag for the marker's details (category, label, date, environment, a deploy's short commit, linked run, description); click it to open the marker in the **Markers** panel, in its edit form when you can edit markers.
- **Markers panel** — a **Markers** button beside the **Run trend** chart (on the project's Runs tab) opens a panel listing the project's markers, newest first. **Add marker** and each marker's edit button open the form in the panel itself; **Delete** is on each marker and in the edit form.
- **Test-case history** — a single test's duration history chart shows the same markers, so you can tell whether an event affected that specific test. Clicking one opens it in the project's **Markers** panel.
- **Analytics charts** — the trend charts of the [analytics page](./analytics) draw the markers too, with the same details on hover: every marker with one project in scope; across projects only `release`, `infra` and `incident` markers, each labeled with its project. The **Timeline markers** widget lists a period's markers, and the analytics periods *Since a marker* and *Release cycle* start from them.
- **Run detail** — a run shows an **"After: …"** chip for the nearest preceding marker of its environment, or of all environments, so a single run tells you which event it followed.

## Environment scoping

Markers tie into the project's existing **environment filter**. When you filter the project view to one or more environments, the charts show only markers of the selected environment(s) plus any global (no-environment) markers. This keeps a staging-only event from cluttering your production view. The analytics charts follow each project's environments the same way: with none picked, a project with a [default environment](./environments#default-environment) shows that environment's markers and the global ones, unless **All environments** is on. A marker belongs to an environment as a run does: a marker written for `stg`, an alias of Staging, shows under Staging, and so does the analytics period's count of markers.

A marker keeps the label it was written with and the environment that label resolved to. Deleting the environment leaves the marker its label, matched as text.

## Who can edit markers

Reading markers is available to anyone who can read the project. Creating, editing, and deleting them requires the **Contributor** role or above on the project, or an administrator ([roles](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do)). (When authentication is disabled, everyone can edit.)

## Automatic markers

Piwi can create markers for you when a run's tooling changes. On each finished run it compares the run against the previous run **in the same environment** (the environment its label resolved to, so `stg` and `staging` runs of Staging are one lineage) and, when the **Playwright version** or **reporter version** changed, adds an `auto` marker (category `config`) at that run's time — for example _Playwright 1.49.0 → 1.50.0_. Auto markers are labeled with a small sparkle icon and can be edited or deleted like any other.

When a run's [environment](./run-environment) differs from the previous run on the same branch and in the same
environment, it gets one `auto` marker per kind of change, labeled with the fields that changed: its runner or a
browser (category `infra`), or a server under test (category `config`). A kind either run did not record counts as no
change. A project that declines the Timeline markers [capability](/operate/capabilities) gets none of these.

A run flagged as an [environment incident](./environment-incidents) gets an `auto` marker in the `incident`
category, linked to the run.

This is enabled by default. Set `PIWI_AUTO_MARKERS=false` to turn all three off. See the [configuration reference](/reference/configuration).

## Release markers keep their run

A `release` marker linked to a run keeps that run forever: [data retention](/operate/storage#keeping-runs-forever) never deletes it, and the marker's label becomes the reason shown on the run. Deleting the marker, or changing its category to anything but `release`, releases the run again — unless someone kept it by hand or the reporter kept it at ingest, in which case the keep stays.

From CI, create the marker after the test step with the run id the reporter writes to its outputs (`piwi_run_id` on GitHub Actions, see [CI → Getting the run URL back out](/guide/ci#getting-the-run-url-back-out-of-ci)):

```bash
curl -X POST "$PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL/api/projects/<projectId>/markers" -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIWI_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"label":"v2.3.1","category":"release","occurredAt":"2026-09-24T12:00:00Z","runId":1234}'
```

## Recording deploys from CI

A deploy pipeline records each deploy as a `deploy` marker that names the environment by its key and the commit it
deployed. A run of that [deployed environment](./environments) that starts after
it reads its application at that commit, unless its server reports its own through an
[instrumentation package](/guide/backend-logs#server-environment). Instrumentation is off in production by default, so
production relies on these markers. The step runs after the deploy, with the project's id and an API key whose owner
can add markers on the project (Contributor and above, `marker:write`), kept as a CI secret.

On GitHub Actions, after the deploy step:

```yaml
- name: Record the deploy in Piwi
  env:
    PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL: ${{ vars.PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL }}
    PIWI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.PIWI_API_KEY }}
  shell: bash
  run: >-
    curl --fail --show-error -X POST "$PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL/api/projects/12/markers"
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIWI_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json"
    -d "{\"label\":\"Deploy to staging\",\"category\":\"deploy\",\"environment\":\"staging\",\"commit\":\"$GITHUB_SHA\",\"occurredAt\":\"$(date -u +%FT%TZ)\"}"
```

On GitLab CI, in the deploy job, with `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and `PIWI_API_KEY` as masked CI/CD variables:

```yaml
deploy-staging:
  stage: deploy
  script:
    - ./deploy.sh staging
    - >-
      curl --fail --show-error -X POST "$PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL/api/projects/12/markers"
      -H "Authorization: Bearer $PIWI_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json"
      -d "{\"label\":\"Deploy to staging\",\"category\":\"deploy\",\"environment\":\"staging\",\"commit\":\"$CI_COMMIT_SHA\",\"occurredAt\":\"$(date -u +%FT%TZ)\"}"
```

The commit is the pipeline's own, since the application lives in the tests' repository. A commit that is not 7 to 40
hexadecimal characters is refused. [Pass reuse](./reuse-forecast#skipping-reusable-tests) reads these markers too: a
deployed environment's passes stand in only for runs against the commit deployed now.

## API

Markers can also be managed through the REST API. See the interactive [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) for request and response shapes.

## Related

- [Regression or flake?](/recipes/regression-or-flaky): correlating a failure with a deploy
- [Analytics](./analytics): the trend charts the markers annotate

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/notifications -->

# Notifications & alerts

Piwi pushes run events to a **browser** tab, **email**, **Slack**, **Microsoft Teams** or an **HTTP webhook**, so your
team hears about failures, new failure clusters, flakiness spikes and performance regressions without watching the
dashboard.

## What it does

1. A **channel** is a destination: a browser tab, an email address, a Slack channel, a Teams webhook, or your own URL.
2. A **subscription** links a channel to the events you care about, for every project or one, with filters and a
   delivery mode.
3. When an event fires, Piwi matches the active subscriptions and writes each delivery to an outbox, which a scheduled
   task sends with retries. It drops a delivery whose subscription was muted or turned off since, or whose recipient
   can no longer open its project. A browser channel is delivered at once to every open dashboard tab.

## Where it is

**Settings → Notifications** manages channels and subscriptions, and the **bell** on a project page subscribes to that
project. The new-channel form shows where to get each destination, offers the right type for a URL pasted under another, and can **send a test** before saving; a test that goes
through saves the channel as verified. Email goes only to a verified address: an email channel once a test reached it, the account email
once its owner verified it. With authentication off, the instance is single-tenant and every channel and subscription is
**global**. With `PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED=true` ([authentication](/operate/authentication)), each user keeps
their own, and administrators can add global ones.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/notifications.png" alt="Settings, Notifications: the SMTP status with the environment variables to set, a Slack channel, and its subscription to project 1's failed runs and new clusters">
  <figcaption><strong>Settings → Notifications</strong>: email delivery, the channels, and what each one is subscribed to.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Events

Run events fire when a run finishes or fails, cluster events when a failure cluster appears, is fixed or regresses,
and others on a flakiness spike, a performance regression, a [stuck test](./stuck-tests), a finished AI diagnosis and
an auto-heal pull request.
When each event fires, and its payload, are in
[Notification events & webhooks](/reference/notification-events). A
[report schedule](./quality-reports#report-schedules) sends its report to the channels it names, with no subscription.
A run from an editor, a bisect step, a reproduction, or a partial run from a developer's machine or the desktop app
fires no run event and no new-cluster, fixed, regressed, flakiness or performance event
([run origin](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin)).

## Channels

### Browser

Sends native OS notifications to any open Piwi tab, even in the background, through the [Notifications API](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Notifications_API); grant permission when prompted.

- **With authentication**: create a channel of type `browser` in **Settings → Notifications** and subscribe it to events; the stream then delivers exactly the events and projects your subscriptions cover.
- **Without authentication**: no channel is needed; the **bell** on each project page stores per-browser preferences (a cookie) for which events raise notifications.
- **In the [desktop app](./desktop)**: on with no setup for failed runs and environment incidents; a project's bell changes them. On Windows and Linux, a click on one opens what it is about (on Windows, while the toast shows).

Diagnosis-completion notifications can be switched off per browser in **Settings → AI → Diagnosis
notifications**.

### Email

Requires SMTP (see below). Sends to a destination address; [what each email shows](/reference/notification-events#emails). With authentication on, each user with an account email also gets an automatic **Account email** channel.

### Slack

Under **Send with**, pick an incoming webhook or a bot token; both post the same message.

**Incoming webhook.** Paste an [incoming webhook](https://docs.slack.dev/messaging/sending-messages-using-incoming-webhooks) URL
(`https://hooks.slack.com/services/…`). Without one, the form's **Create a Slack app for Piwi** link opens Slack with an
app already filled in, asking only for the `incoming-webhook` permission: create it, choose **Install to Workspace** and
the channel, then copy the URL from **Incoming Webhooks**. A Slack-compatible server (Mattermost, Rocket.Chat) works too.

**Bot token.** Piwi posts with the Web API's
[`chat.postMessage`](https://docs.slack.dev/reference/methods/chat.postMessage). The same link asks for `chat:write`
and `chat:write.public` instead: install the app, copy the **Bot User OAuth Token** (`xoxb-…`) and the channel's
**Channel ID**, and invite the app to a private channel first. The token is encrypted (`PIWI_SECRET_KEY`) and never
returned; a global channel's is a [credential](/operate/credentials#connections-and-slack-channels). A refusal names Slack's error code (`not_in_channel`, `invalid_auth`) with what to do.

Through either, a delivery Slack rate-limits retries after its `Retry-After`, up to an hour.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/channel-form-slack.png" alt="The new channel form for Slack: incoming webhook or bot token, the three steps to create the Slack app, a pasted webhook URL recognized as a Slack incoming webhook, Send test and Save channel">
  <figcaption>Adding a Slack channel: the URL is recognized before you save it.</figcaption>
</figure>

### Microsoft Teams

In the Teams channel's **⋯** menu, open **Workflows**, pick the template *Send webhook alerts to a channel*, choose the
team and channel, and paste the URL the workflow shows. A legacy Microsoft 365 connector webhook still works while
Microsoft keeps it, and the form flags it. Each event, digest and
[quality report](./quality-reports#report-schedules) arrives as an Adaptive Card.

### Webhook

Piwi `POST`s a JSON body to your URL. When the channel has a secret, which the form can generate (storing it needs
`PIWI_SECRET_KEY`), each request is signed with an HMAC-SHA256 `X-Piwi-Signature` header. Private and loopback
addresses are refused.
The body, its fields and how to verify the signature are in
[Notification events & webhooks](/reference/notification-events#webhook-body).

### Reaching the person who fixed it

`cluster.fixed` and `cluster.regressed` resolve the fixing commit's author through the SCM provider, which for a private repository needs an [SCM credential](/guide/source-control) (for a regression, the author of the fix that did not hold). On top of the normal subscription routing, the event is then delivered to that person directly, when the commit's email belongs to a registered Piwi user who can open the project:

- **Email**, through the same outbox, when SMTP is configured. The mail goes to that user's account email, never to the raw commit address, so a fix by an outside contributor never becomes a mail to a stranger.
- **A browser notification** for that user, delivered even when they have no matching subscription.

When the lookup fails (a private repository without a token, a host that exposes no email), subscriptions alone apply.

### Global channels & subscriptions

Admins can mark a channel **global** so it is available to all users, and mark a subscription **instance-wide** (from the project bell) so it delivers whoever is signed in: the way to route every failure to one team Slack channel. Global subscriptions must target a global channel. Other users see where a global webhook points, never its full URL.

## Subscriptions

A subscription controls *what* is delivered and *how*. The project **bell** creates one for that project — a channel, one or more of the events above and, optionally, the branches and environments it covers, delivered in real time. **Settings → Notifications** lists them with their filters, and mutes one for 7 days or removes it.

### Branches and environments

The bell offers the branches the project's runs reported, its [environments](./environments), and takes a typed name
too: `*` matches any characters, so `release/*` covers every release branch. A subscription delivers only events from
runs on one of its branches **and** in one of its environments (by key or alias); a run that reported no branch (or
environment) matches none, and an empty list matches every run. The filters apply to every event that comes from a run: the `run.*` events,
`flakiness.spike`, `perf.regression`, the `cluster.*` events, `bug.looks_fixed` and `test.stuck`. `diagnosis.completed` and
`auto_heal.pr_opened` are not filtered.

### Through the API

The subscriptions REST API (see the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api)) adds:

- **Scope**: all projects (`projectId: null`, for a user who can access every project), or a single project.
- **Filters**: `branches` and `environments` as above; for run events, status; **owner**, which applies to the
  `run.*` events, `flakiness.spike`, `perf.regression`, `cluster.new` and `test.stuck` and delivers them only when a
  test behind the event belongs to that team (see [Tags & ownership](/guide/concepts#tags-ownership)); `flakinessThreshold`
  (a 0–1 rate) and `perfRegressionPct`. Lists hold up to 100 values of at most 256 characters; branch and environment
  patterns, up to 200 characters and 10 `*` each, 2,000 together.
- **Mode**: `realtime`, sent as events happen, or `digest` with `digestAt` (`HH:MM`, UTC, from `00:00` to `23:59`),
  held until then and sent as **one combined message** per email, Slack or Teams channel.
- **Mute**: `mutedUntil`, any time, without deleting the subscription.

## SMTP configuration

Email channels and the account flows (verification, password reset, invites) need SMTP. Slack, webhook and browser channels work without it. SMTP is set via environment variables only and shown read-only in **Settings → Notifications**; `PIWI_SMTP_HOST` and `PIWI_SMTP_FROM` are enough for a relay that accepts unauthenticated mail:

```bash
PIWI_SMTP_HOST=smtp.example.com
PIWI_SMTP_PORT=587            # default 587
PIWI_SMTP_FROM=noreply@example.com
PIWI_SMTP_FROM_NAME=Piwi Dashboard   # optional display name
PIWI_SMTP_USER=apikey         # only when the server requires authentication
PIWI_SMTP_PASS=••••••••        # only when the server requires authentication; never returned by the API
PIWI_SMTP_SECURE=false        # implicit TLS, default on for 465
PIWI_SITE_URL=https://piwi.example.com   # base URL used in email links
```

Send a test email from **Settings → Notifications** to confirm delivery.

## Limits

- **Digests group email, Slack and Teams only.** Webhook and browser deliveries are always one per event.
- **A browser channel needs an open tab.** Nothing reaches a closed browser; the
  [desktop app](./desktop) shows OS notifications while its window is in the background.
- **Email needs SMTP**, set through environment variables only.

- [Authentication](/operate/authentication): per-user channels and subscriptions
- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration): every environment variable
- [Notification events & webhooks](/reference/notification-events): every event and the webhook body

- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters): what triggers the cluster events
