# Write, run and fix a test

This page takes a new test from an empty spec to a passing run, and names the tool for each step. Each step has a page
of its own; this one is the map. The editor does most of it, in VS Code or a JetBrains IDE; Piwi Picker, the browser
extension, does the same steps from the browser, and the desktop app runs them on your machine without an editor.

## Before the first test

- **The capture fixtures** in your specs: a test that imports `test` from `@playwright/test` runs, but never stops at a
  breakpoint, and the run says so ([Capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures)).
- **The editor extension**, connected to your instance or to the desktop app ([Editor extensions](./editors),
  [Editor connection](./editor-connection)).
- **Optional:** [Piwi Picker](./extension), paired with the editor, to pick and record in your everyday browser and
  follow runs in its [Runs window](./runs-window).

## The steps

| Step | In the editor | Outside the editor | Read on |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write the test | **Record a new test file…**, or **Record here…** at the cursor | Piwi Picker's **Record**, then **Send to editor** | [Record tests from the editor](./editor-recording), [Recorded code](./recorded-code) |
| Run it | **Run with Piwi** from the gutter, the Testing view or the test at the cursor; **Verify ×3** | the desktop app's **Re-run** of tests | [Runs from the editor](./editor-runs), [Desktop app runs](./desktop-runs) |
| Watch it | the status bar, and the run's page on the instance | the Runs window, and the page itself once you **Watch** at a stop | [Follow a run](./watch-a-run), [Watch a local test](./watch-running-test) |
| Stop it | a breakpoint, **Pause**, **Step**, **Run to the cursor** | the pause bar in the test's page | [Breakpoints in the browser](./editor-breakpoints), [Pause and step from the editor](./editor-run-control) |
| Fix it at the stop | **Pick a locator**, **Record**, **Assert**, **Mock a request** | **Pick a locator** and **Record** from the pause bar; all four from the Runs window | [Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code) |
| Debug a failure | **Debug in my editor**, from the failure's page | the failure page's Locator fix | [Debug in my editor](./debug-in-editor), [Locator healing](./locator-healing) |

## Write it

**Record a new test file…** offers the spec beside the one you are in, else in the config's `testDir`, and writes what
you do in the browser as a test, with locators verified on the page and the page objects of your suite where they
match. **Record here** writes steps at the cursor, in a test, a page object or a helper. A flow recorded in Piwi Picker
lands at the cursor the same way through **Send to editor**: at the top level of a spec, as a new test.

## Run and watch it

A run Piwi starts reports to the instance like any other, with the run's origin. In a project that runs in CI, a
failure seen only in developers' own runs stays out of the team's inbox until someone shows it; one that fingerprints
like a failure CI saw joins that cluster ([Failure clusters](./failure-clusters)). A run you start in a
terminal is followed too, when the editor is open: [Runs started outside Piwi](./terminal-runs).

## Stop it and write the fix there

Set a breakpoint on the line you are working on and debug the test (**Debug the test at the cursor**). It stops before that line's call, in a headed
browser with Piwi's pause bar, or, headless, with the page shown in the editor. **Pick a locator**, **Record** and
**Assert** (in the headed browser) and **Mock a request** write their code where the stopped statement stands now, after the edits you made
since the run started ([Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code)); **End the test** skips the rest of it
([End the test](./end-the-test)).

## When it fails

While its run's [Hold failures](./watch-a-run#hold-failures) is on (from the start of a run with breakpoints), a
failing test holds its page and the editor shows the failure as a stop, with the same actions. Otherwise its page on the
instance explains it: the clues rank the likely cause, and the Locator fix panel offers the replacement locator.
**Debug in my editor** on that page runs the failing test again from the editor and stops at the line it failed on.

## Related

- [Editor extensions](./editors): what the editor shows from your suite.
- [Failure clusters](./failure-clusters): where failures land once they reach the team's runs.
- [Run control for agents](./agent-run-control): the same stops, steered by an agent.

# Watch a local test

**Watch** in your own tools shows a test's page in your editor, Piwi Picker's Runs window or the
desktop app, in a run on your machine or a remote container, read-only in a CI run of your branch. On the
team instance, it is the [live view](./live-view); a run's progress and stops: [Follow a run](./watch-a-run). The page
shows up to ten images a second, through the test's next tests and stops, and the worker Playwright starts in its
place after a failure. It needs
`@piwitests/reporter` after 0.67.0 and the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures). Nothing leaves your
machine: [what is sent](#what-is-sent-and-kept).

## Where to watch

| Where          | Open it                                                                                                                                                                 | At a stop                                                                                                                               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| VS Code        | **Piwi: Watch a worker's test**, the eye on a worker's row of the Piwi panel's **Runs** view, or the status bar's menu during a run: `Piwi: worker 2` beside the editor | While it watches in sight, a headless stop shows there, not on the paused page, with its controls, **Interact** and the pick on a click |
| JetBrains IDEs | **Tools → Piwi → Run control → Watch a worker's test**, or a worker's row's right-click in the Piwi tool window's **Runs** tab: its **Worker 2** tab                                  | While it watches in sight, a headless stop shows there, not on the **Worker 2** page tab, with its controls and **Interact**            |
| Piwi Picker    | **Watch** on a worker's row of the [Runs window](./runs-window#watch-live)                                                                                              | Its controls above the view; the stopped worker scrolls into view                                                                       |
| Desktop app    | **Watch** on a running row of its own runs opens the [Local runs](./desktop-runs#watch) tray on it                                                                      | The tray shows the stopped worker, behind its tab in a run of several                                                                   |

**Pause and watch**, which also stops the test before its next call, is **Piwi: Pause and watch a worker's test**
(**Tools → Piwi → Run control → …**), and a button beside **Watch** in the Runs window and the desktop app. With several workers, the editor asks which.

While a run is in progress, VS Code's **Runs** view and the JetBrains **Runs** tab list each run with how far it is,
each worker by its lane with its test and whether it stands stopped, and the run's page on the dashboard. A row opens
the stopped line or the test, and its buttons (VS Code) or its right-click (JetBrains) offer **Watch**, **Pause and
watch** on a test that can pause, **Resume**, **Step** except at a failure, and, for a run the editor started, **Stop
the run**. A run that can hold its failures says when it does (`Hold failures on`) and turns it over from its row.

## A CI run of your branch

A CI run of your branch shows beside your runs, read-only, and **Watch** opens its lanes from the team instance:
[CI runs in your editor](./editor-ci-runs).

## What you see

Each view names the worker by its lane (`Worker 2`) and says what it does: its running test, the call a Pause waits
in, its stop, between tests, or starting. Across a **Step**, a **Resume** or between two tests, the last image
stays until the next one comes, dimmed in VS Code, the Runs window and the desktop app, the last two marking it
**Running…**. A still page sends none. Watching pauses while the view is out of sight (another tab in front,
a minimized Runs window) and starts again as it shows. It ends when you turn it off or close the view, or as the run
ends.

## Beside the image

Under the image, the editor's view, a CI run's lane included, the Runs window and the desktop app's tray show what the
pixels cannot: why the test waits, the page's events, its text and a filmstrip of its calls
([in your own tools](./live-view-layers#in-your-own-tools)). While an editor watches a worker of your run, the page's
events go to VS Code's `Piwi: Page` output, its console and uncaught errors to the JetBrains Piwi tool window's **Page**
tab, each test named as it begins.

## The running line

While your run goes, the editor marks the line of the call each running test is in until the test ends or stops,
naming the worker and the call: VS Code dims the line (`Worker 2 · Click getByRole('button')`), a JetBrains IDE adds an
inlay. Workers on one line share its mark (`Worker 2, Worker 4 · Click`). The watched worker's line follows its call
log; each other worker's comes from its reporter, four times a second at most, with a reporter newer than 0.71.0 (an
older one's is marked only while watched). `piwi.runningLines` marks every running test's line, the watched worker's
alone, or none ([settings](/reference/editor-settings#in-the-editor)).

## Open the trace so far

**Open the trace so far** opens Playwright's trace viewer on the running test's trace up to now, on the machine the
run runs on, with a reporter newer than 0.68.0, while the worker runs a test: beside **Watch** in the VS Code panel
(**Piwi: Open the trace so far**), in the JetBrains **Worker** tab, and in a watched page's head in the Runs window
and the tray. The editor service or the desktop app's server asks the worker where its trace grows,
checks that file, and starts the viewer with your project's own Playwright; the path never leaves it, and each tool
hears why when the viewer does not start. Playwright 1.59 to 1.65 shows the trace as it stood when it opened: close
it and choose the button again for what came since.

It shows only where it can open: the machine has a display (on Linux, `DISPLAY` or `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` set), the tool
knows the run's folder, and a Runs window reaches the hub without a forwarded port. The attempt must be traced, from
its first browser context: `trace: 'on'` or `'retain-on-failure'` (`wrapConfig`'s default) traces every attempt,
`'on-first-retry'` and `'on-all-retries'` a retry alone.

## Interact

At a stop, **Interact**, beside **Watch** once the view is on, sends your clicks, the wheel and your
[keys](/reference/keyboard-shortcuts#piwi-picker-s-runs-window) on the view to the page as a person's would, the
picker and the recorder included. The first takes the stop, so an agent waits until you give it back, and the view
names who drives and watches it ([driving a stop](/guide/concepts#presence-driving-a-stop)). It stays on across the
worker's next stops, where your first input takes the stop again. **Give back**, `Esc` on the view, watching off or
refused, another lane's stop, a stop that takes no input, the view hidden or closed, or the run's end turns it off and
gives the stop back, once the input sent before has reached the page; what you hold down is let go before the test
goes on. While a pick or a check runs on the page, `Esc` skips the pick or closes the check instead; in a recording it
gives the stop back.

## What is sent and kept

The frames go from the test's worker only to that worker's views (an editor's, the desktop app's window, Piwi
Picker's Runs window through the extension's background worker), on your machine or through the port your IDE
forwards from a [remote window](/guide/remote-development), and to the team instance while the run is
[shared live](./share-live). The worker takes images only while a view watches it, and paints over password fields
and the fields of one-time codes and card numbers first. The editor service or the desktop app's server passes each
on, one view of the page serving every viewer. Nothing stores them.

The images follow the test's own screencast: when the test records its own (a video, a trace with screenshots), the
view takes its size and quality; when none can start, it is an image of the page twice a second. A frame over 384 KB
gives way to a lighter image, twice a second; when even that is too heavy, the view says so.

## Limits

- **One worker per editor.** The panel or tab watches one worker, a CI run's lane included: watching another moves it
  there.
- **The test's `page`.** A popup or a second page is not shown. A download a click on the view starts and a dialog
  the page opens go to the test as its own would: Playwright deletes the download with the test's context, and
  dismisses the dialog unless the test handles it.
- **An older reporter** shows a stopped test alone: the Runs window's row and the desktop app's tray hold their
  **Watch**, saying to update it, and the editors offer no Watch for its workers.

## Related

- [Pause and step from the editor](./editor-run-control)
- [Live view of a run](./live-view)
- [CI runs in your editor](./editor-ci-runs)

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/end-the-test -->

# End the test

At a stop, **End the test** ends the test there, as if it had called `test.skip()` at that line: the locator call it
stopped before never runs (Playwright 1.62 or later), nor the rest of the test, and Playwright reports it as skipped,
its `skip` annotation reading `Ended from Piwi`. Its result reads **Ended at a stop**, never a plain skip, on the run's
page, the test's pages, Piwi Picker's Runs window, the desktop app's Local runs tray and both editors. The run goes on with its next test. Use it once you have seen what you stopped for, or recorded the
steps you were missing, and the rest of the test has nothing to show you.

## Where it is

It is offered at any stop but a failure, with a reporter newer than 0.62.0:

- **VS Code**: **End the test** in the stopped line's hover, the status bar beside **Finish**, and **Piwi: End the test** in the palette. It has no key: bind one in **Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts**
  (search `piwi`).
- **A JetBrains IDE**: **End the test** in the stopped line's inlay and the arrow's menu, **Tools → Piwi
  → Run control → End the test** and the status bar item's menu. Give it a key in **Settings → Keymap**.
- **The [pause
  bar](./editor-breakpoints#pause-a-run)**: **End the test**.
- **Piwi Picker's [Runs window](./runs-window)** and the
  desktop app's [Local runs tray](./desktop-runs): **End the test**, beside **Finish**.
- **An
  [agent](./agent-run-control)**: `run_control` with `end`, answered as the test ends.

## While a Pause waits for a call

**Pause** stops a test before its next call, so a test inside a long one (a click that waits for a button, a
`waitForTimeout`) stops only once it returns. Meanwhile, with a reporter newer than 0.67.0, the Runs window and the
desktop app's tray say the call it waits in and, for a locator call, how long it has run, and offer **End the test**
there. The Piwi item reads `Piwi: pausing… · waits in` the call and how long it has waited, in both editors, the call's line
says the worker waits there with **End the test** after it (in its hover in VS Code), and **End the test** in the item's
menu (**Tools → Piwi → Run control → End the test** in a JetBrains IDE) ends it too:

- **A locator call or an assertion**, with Playwright 1.62 or later, is given up at once, and the test is skipped.
- **Another call** (a `waitForTimeout`, a navigation) finishes first, and the test is skipped at its next locator
  call, or as its function ends.

## What runs, and what does not

- **At a locator call or an assertion** (`click`, `fill`, `expect(locator).toBeVisible()`), the call is given up
  before it runs, with Playwright 1.62 or later; an older one runs it first, and the editor says so. At a
  `page.pause()`, nothing after it runs.
- **At another call** (a navigation, a key press on the page, `page.evaluate`), the call runs first: Piwi does not
  hold it. The test is skipped at its next locator call, or as its function ends, and the editor says so.
- **At a failure**, it is not offered: **Resume** lets the test end as it failed, and the failure is kept.
- **In a `beforeEach` hook**, it skips the test. **In an `afterEach` hook or a fixture's teardown**, the test's
  function already ended: it goes on as **Resume** does, keeping the test's result, and says so. Piwi never stops in a
  `beforeAll` or `afterAll` hook.
- **After it**, the test's `afterEach` hooks and its fixtures' teardown run as after any skip, so its page closes as
  usual, with nothing of Piwi left in it.
- **A retry** is an attempt of its own. Playwright does not retry a skipped test; a failure you let end runs the next
  attempt, which stops at your breakpoints as the first did.

## How the result reads

The test keeps Playwright's status, skipped: it counts among the skipped tests, and its run passes or fails on its
other tests. What changes is the mark each tool puts on it:

- **The dashboard**: the test's row on the run page, its execution's status chip and its line in the test's recent
  executions read **Ended at a stop** instead of Skipped, and the run page's header marks the run beside its status
  (**Ended at a stop**, or `3 ended at a stop` for more than one). Copy run summary names them among the skipped:
  `4 skipped (1 ended at a stop)`.
- **Piwi Picker's Runs window**: the run's progress line counts them, `9 of 9 tests · 1 ended at a stop`, in the
  window's language; the desktop app's Local runs tray reads `Passed · 1 ended at a stop` once the run ended.
- **The editors**: the status bar's run progress counts them (`1 ended at a stop`), and the notification of a run the
  editor started names them beside the skipped, `3 passed, 0 failed, 1 skipped (1 ended at a stop)`.

The count reaches the editors, Piwi Picker and the desktop app from a reporter newer than 0.68.0; with an older one
they count the test as skipped. The dashboard reads the `skip` annotation, so it marks results already stored too.

## Limits

- **Playwright's calls alone.** The test's own code between two calls, a loop or a helper, runs until its next call.
- **One test.** It ends the stopped worker's test; the run's other tests run. To end the run, **Stop** it (one Piwi
  started, from the editor, the desktop app or the [Runs window](./runs-window)) or end it in its terminal.

## Try it in the demo

- [E2E Checkout › a cart test ended at its breakpoint](https://piwitests.dev/demo/test-run-cases/834): A run started from the editor stopped the test at its breakpoint and ended it there with End the test: Playwright skipped it, and its execution reads Ended at a stop.

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/ai-steps -->

# AI steps

AI steps let you locate elements and drive flows in **plain English**, without giving up the determinism of hand-written Playwright:

```typescript
// Find one element by description
await page.piwiLocator('the email address field').fill('ada@example.com')

// Run a whole flow, with type-safe parameters
await page.piwiRun('sign in as {email}', { email: 'ada@example.com' })
```

The guiding principle is **the LLM is a compiler, not a runtime**. The first time a prompt is seen, an agent resolves it **once** into a committed, deterministic JSON artifact. Every run after that *replays* that artifact with ordinary Playwright calls — **zero LLM calls and zero network** in the default `replay` mode. Your CI stays fast, offline, and reproducible; the model is only ever involved while authoring.

::: tip This composes with the capture fixtures
AI steps are a separate opt-in from the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures), and compose with them. Replayed actions flow through the instrumented page, so they feed traces, reports, and [locator healing](/features/locator-healing) exactly like hand-written code.
:::

## Setup

Extend your test with `extendPiwiAi`. Compose it over `extendPiwiFixtures` to get the capture fixtures too:

```typescript
// tests/fixtures.ts
import { test as base } from '@playwright/test'
import { extendPiwiFixtures, extendPiwiAi } from '@piwitests/reporter'

// AI steps + capture fixtures
export const test = extendPiwiAi(extendPiwiFixtures(base))
export { expect } from '@playwright/test'
```

`page` now carries two extra methods:

| Method | Returns | Use for |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `page.piwiLocator(template)` | a real, synchronous `Locator` | locating one element by description |
| `page.piwiRun(template)` | `Promise<void>` | replaying a compiled multi-step flow |

While a missing entry is being authored (`resolve` mode), `piwiLocator` returns a stand-in that supports direct actions such as `.fill()` and `.click()`, but not chaining (`.first()`) or `expect(...)`; those work once the entry is committed.

Placeholders are type-checked at compile time: a template with `{param}` **requires** a matching params object, and a misspelled or missing name is a TypeScript error.

```typescript
await page.piwiRun('add {qty} of {sku} to the cart', { qty: '2', sku: 'PIWI-1' })
```

## The lifecycle: author once, replay forever

An AI step moves through three modes, set with the `ai.mode` option or `PIWI_AI`. An `ai.mode` set in `wrapConfig` overrides `PIWI_AI`, including the one `piwi ai resolve` sets:

| Mode | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `replay` *(default)* | Executes the committed artifact read-only. **Never** calls the model. Fails closed on a missing entry. |
| `resolve` | Authors any missing entry by driving the model, verifies it against the live page, and writes it to disk. |
| `heal` | Behaves exactly like `resolve`: committed entries are replayed as they are, and missing ones are authored. |

The intended workflow:

1. **Write** the test with `piwiLocator` / `piwiRun` prompts.
2. **Author** locally in `resolve` mode (see below). The agent produces a JSON artifact next to your spec under `__piwi__/`.
3. **Commit** that artifact to git alongside the test.
4. **Replay** everywhere else — locally and in CI — with zero model calls.

### Authoring (resolve mode)

Authoring needs a running Piwi dashboard with an AI provider configured (**Settings → AI**, or the `PIWI_AI_PROVIDER` [environment variables](/reference/configuration#ai-diagnosis)). The reporter sends each iteration to the server; the server calls the model and returns one decision, which the reporter compiles deterministically. **API keys stay on the server.**

Point the reporter at that server and run the suite in resolve mode:

```bash
export PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL="https://piwi.example.com"   # the authoring server
export PIWI_API_KEY="…"                                # a key with upload rights
export PIWI_AI=resolve

npx playwright test           # or: npx piwi ai resolve --grep "sign in"
```

`piwi ai resolve` runs the suite in resolve mode for you (forcing `--workers=1` so authoring is serial). Once it finishes, review and **commit** the generated files.

::: warning Authoring drives the real page
In `resolve` mode each step is executed against the live page with your real parameter values so the flow can advance. Author against a disposable environment, not production.
:::

### Replay and CI

In `replay` mode a missing entry is a hard, actionable failure — the run does not silently pass and does not reach for a model:

```
piwi AI: no committed entry for "sign in as {email}" in test "checkout".
  expected file: tests/__piwi__/checkout.spec.ts/checkout.sign-in-as-email.a1b2c3d4.json
  run:  piwi ai resolve --grep "checkout"
```

That means an environment with no model access (a locked-down CI runner, an air-gapped box) can never accidentally author — it either replays a committed artifact or fails. If you would rather a missing entry mark the test **fixme** (yellow) instead of failing red, set `ai.onMiss: 'fixme'` (`PIWI_AI_ON_MISS=fixme`).

Replay is plain Playwright: commit the artifacts and your existing CI job replays them.

## What's inside an artifact — and why it's safe

An entry is **data, never code**: an allowlisted locator program plus, for a flow, an ordered list of steps and a postcondition oracle. Determinism and safety come from several guarantees:

- **Deterministic bytes.** The model only *names* an element (its ARIA role, accessible name and snapshot `ref`); the [`@piwitests/core`](/guide/concepts#locator-snapshot) scorer turns that into the committed locator, or Playwright's own locator for the `ref` when two elements share the name. Sampling never changes the file; a no-op re-resolution leaves the tree clean.
- **No evaluation.** Every locator method and action is checked against an allowlist before it touches the page. A tampered or malformed artifact can never become arbitrary execution.
- **Drift guard.** Each step records the element's role/name at author time. On replay, if the page positively shows that element has drifted (a rename), the flow **stops before acting** rather than clicking the wrong thing.
- **Postcondition oracle.** Every flow ends with an assertion the agent chose (an element became visible/hidden, or the URL changed). Replay verifies it, so a subtly wrong flow fails loudly instead of passing.
- **Ajax waiting, race-proof.** A step can wait for a network response it triggers (an XHR/fetch the agent observed while authoring). The wait is armed *before* the action fires, so a fast reply can never slip through the gap.

## Intent in the dashboard

Each test's replayed AI steps are reported to the dashboard as a small usage manifest: the committed artifacts it exercised (powering the project's **AI steps** liveness tab) plus **intent mappings** — each compiled locator paired with the prompt it came from. Two places use them:

- **Locator healing**: when the failing locator was compiled from a prompt, the **Locator fix** panel shows it — *"Compiled from prompt: 'the email address field'"* — so you fix the intent, not just the selector.
- **AI diagnosis**: the diagnosis context includes an *AI Steps* section listing the prompts behind the test's locators, so a root cause can be phrased in intent terms ("the element the test calls *the email address field* was renamed"). Capped by `PIWI_AI_MAX_STEP_INTENTS` (default 20, `0` disables).

Intent mappings keep `{param}` placeholders and `{{param}}` markers: parameter values never appear.

## Privacy

Parameter values are **masked out of everything sent to the model**, with one exception: the opt-in `screenshotFallback` image is sent as-is. The page snapshot the agent sees has your `{param}` values replaced with markers, and placeholders survive compilation as markers that are substituted locally at replay. With `screenshotFallback` off (the default), secrets in parameters never leave your machine. See [Privacy & data flow](/guide/privacy) for the full picture.

## Keep the artifacts healthy

`piwi ai check` is offline and fits a CI lint step: it exits `1` on an entry whose prompt was deleted or renamed, or a
file that isn't in canonical form, and reports two prompts that collide as a warning that does not fail it.
`piwi ai prune` deletes nothing and exits `2`: delete an orphaned entry's file by hand, and re-author a
non-canonical one with `piwi ai resolve --update-ai`. Every subcommand and flag is in the
[CLI reference](/reference/cli#ai).

## Configuration

Set these under the `ai` key of `wrapConfig`'s second argument, which copies them into the `PIWI_AI*` variables the
test workers read; an `ai` key on a plain `['@piwitests/reporter', { … }]` entry is ignored, so without `wrapConfig`
use the environment variables. Every option has an environment-variable equivalent, and all
of them are in the [AI steps section of Reporter options](/reference/reporter-options#ai-steps). Authoring also reads
`PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and `PIWI_API_KEY` (the server that runs the model), and `PIWI_AI_UPDATE=true` (or
`--update-ai`) forces re-authoring of entries that already exist.

On the **server** side, two limits bound each authoring iteration (see the
[AI steps section](/reference/configuration#ai-steps) of the configuration reference):

- `PIWI_AI_STEP_MAX_SNAPSHOT_CHARS`: snapshot characters the model receives.
- `PIWI_AI_STEP_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS`: output tokens the model may return. **Reasoning models** spend tokens on hidden
  chain-of-thought, so raise this (up to `8192`) when authoring with one, or the JSON decision can be truncated.

A key makes at most 300 authoring calls in five minutes (a 20-step flow takes about 40), then gets a 429.

# Editor extensions

The Piwi extension for VS Code (and Cursor, VSCodium) and the Piwi plugin for the JetBrains IDEs with the LSP API
(WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate, Rider, from 2024.1) bring what the dashboard knows about your suite to the line you
are editing. Both run the same editor service; the [JetBrains plugin](./jetbrains) page lists what the plugin needs
and draws differently.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/vscode-heal.png" alt="VS Code: a CI failure at its line, the heal offered as a quick fix">
  <figcaption>The latest run's failure at its line, and the heal as a quick fix.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Install and connect

**You need a Piwi instance:** the [desktop app](/features/desktop), `npx @piwitests/server` or the Docker image.
Recording, running a test by its line, and pausing and stepping through it need none. Piwi reads Playwright Test
suites in JavaScript and TypeScript.

Install **Piwi** from the
**[Visual Studio Marketplace ↗](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=PiwiTests.piwi)** (`piwitests.piwi`
in the extensions view) or the **[JetBrains Marketplace ↗](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/34674-piwi)**
(**Settings → Plugins**). It starts on a trusted workspace holding a Playwright config, and reads the connection
the reporter already uses: the `PIWI_*` variables in the environment or the workspace `.env`, or the
[desktop app](/features/desktop). Otherwise, run **Piwi: Connect…** (**Settings → Tools → Piwi** in a JetBrains IDE)
and sign in with the browser: [Editor connection](./editor-connection) has the steps.

The first workspace with a Playwright config opens the first steps: VS Code's **Get started with Piwi** walkthrough
once per machine (unless `workbench.welcomePage.walkthroughs.openOnInstall` is off), a JetBrains IDE's **Get started**
tab once per installation ([JetBrains plugin](./jetbrains#install-and-start)). **Piwi: Get started** opens them
again. The desktop app and MCP offers follow one at a time: one per window in VS Code, per IDE session in a JetBrains
IDE. VS Code 1.101 and later lists the MCP server itself.

In VS Code, the extension also opens a path clicked in the dashboard:
[Open in editor](./ide-integration#vs-code-the-piwi-extension).

Self-hosted, zero telemetry. No file of your workspace is sent to the instance: the project's
[locator index](/guide/concepts#locator-index), [code reach](/features/code-reach) and latest run are compared with
your files locally.

## CI failures in the Problems panel

The failures of the latest complete [CI run](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin) on the checked-out branch, else the
default branch, are in the Problems panel at the line that failed, with your local runs laid over them, and each
failing line follows your edits until a run covers its test again. The heal, the trace, a rerun and the fix plan are
quick fixes on the failure, and the failures view lists them as a tree: [Failures in the editor](./editor-failures).

## The tests behind each line

Lines above the code (CodeLens):

| File | What it shows | Click |
|---|---|---|
| A spec | the tests Piwi knows in it; beside each `test(…)`, its latest result in the gutter, a failing test's body tinted, and on hover that result's run, the pass rate, [flaky](/features/flaky-tests) score and root cause, quarantine and selections | runs those tests |
| A page object or spec | above each locator line (in a spec, unless its only test is the one around it), the tests using it, their actions, and how many fail or flake | runs those tests |
| An application file | the tests that reach it, from [code reach](/features/code-reach); with [coverage](./editor-coverage), each function's too | runs those tests |
| A page file (Nuxt `pages/**`) | the tests acting on that page, its locators and how many are brittle | runs those tests |

Above a flaky test: Flake Lab's **flaky N%** and [top suspect](./flake-lab#from-the-editor-and-the-failure-pages), then
**Reproduce this flake** and, once reproduced, **Verify the flake fix**, which run `piwi flake`; beside a team instance,
**Reproduce this flake in the desktop app**.

## Timeouts

A test whose `test.slow()` is no longer needed, or whose timeout is far above its p95, gets a note and a quick fix:
remove `test.slow()`, or set `test.setTimeout` to the suggested value.

## Completion

- After a page and a `.` in a spec or a page object: the locator chains your suite already uses on the pages this
  file's tests visit, most used first and brittle ones last. The page is `page`, `this.page`, or any page the code at
  the cursor can use, the same ones [a recording](/features/editor-recording#start-a-recording) offers: another page
  fixture of the test (`adminPage.`), a page object's page field (`this.root.`), a page the test opens
  (`newPage()`, a popup).
- Right after `expect(`: the same chains on the page in use there, such as
  `page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Pay' })`, so an assertion's locator is written in one step.
- At the start of a statement: the [functions](/features/test-functions) of your catalog whose URL pattern matches
  those pages, as a call with a placeholder per parameter.
- In a `piwi:` annotation: the types (`piwi:owner`, `piwi:priority`, `piwi:feature`, `piwi:link`), then the owners,
  priorities or features they take; in `tag: ['@…']`, the tags your tests already use.

## Brittle locators

A locator the [stability rules](/reference/locator-stability) rate brittle is a warning on its line; one worth a
look is a hint. When the capture fixtures stored a stable alternative for that call site on its last passing run, the
quick fix replaces the chain with it.

## The locators a change breaks

In an application file, the unsaved buffer is compared with `HEAD` as you type, as
[`piwi preflight`](/features/preflight) compares a diff. A changed line whose string a locator finds its element by is
a warning, with the chains it breaks on hover, and one quick fix that rewrites every call site.

## Piwi's MCP server for the agent

In VS Code 1.101 and later, the extension provides Piwi's [MCP server](/features/mcp) to the editor's agent with the
connection it already has. Elsewhere, **Piwi: Copy the MCP server configuration** puts an entry on the clipboard: VS Code's
`mcp.json` or Cursor's `mcpServers`, as you choose; in a JetBrains IDE, an `mcpServers` entry running `mcp-remote`,
for your agent's MCP settings (the AI Assistant's, when it is installed and enabled). It holds your API key: keep it out of the repository.

The key carries your whole role, write tools included. For a token of the agent's own, set `piwi.mcpAuthorization`
to `sign-in` (**Settings → Tools → Piwi → Agents (MCP)** in a JetBrains IDE): the server comes without a key, and the
agent [signs in](/features/mcp#authentication) in your browser when it first connects. You revoke that token with
your API keys. The desktop app keeps its own token. For the runs the editor starts:
[Run control for agents](./agent-run-control).

## Colors and hidden messages

VS Code's theme colors, set in `workbench.colorCustomizations`: `piwi.failingTestBackground` and
`piwi.failingLineBackground` tint a failing test and the line it failed at, `piwi.failingTestOverviewRuler` and
`piwi.failingLineOverviewRuler` mark them in the scrollbar; `piwi.flakyForeground` colors the word flaky after a flaky
test's line in the Testing view; `piwi.recordingBlockBackground` and `piwi.recordingBlockOverviewRuler` mark the block
a recording writes; `piwi.executionPointBackground` and `piwi.executionPointOverviewRuler` the line a test is stopped
at, `piwi.failurePointBackground` and `piwi.failurePointOverviewRuler` the line it holds a failure at. The coverage
marks have [their own](./editor-coverage#the-marks). A JetBrains IDE has the failing test, its line, the lines being
recorded and the stopped line under **Settings → Editor → Color Scheme → Piwi**.

**Don't Show Again** on a message that may come again adds its kind to VS Code's `piwi.hiddenMessages`
([Editor settings](/reference/editor-settings#advanced) lists the kinds); remove a kind to see its message again.

VS Code's Piwi settings come in five groups, Connection, Runs, In the editor, Agents (MCP) and Advanced, as JetBrains'
settings page does: [Editor settings](/reference/editor-settings) lists each one, what the editor shows among them.
Your own choices (how runs start and notify, breakpoints, the status bar's alert, the agent's sign-in) hold in
every workspace: a repository's `.vscode/settings.json` sets only the instance and the project, the failure severity,
serving runs to agents and Piwi's tests in the Testing view. A JetBrains IDE keeps the same choices in its own
settings, for every project, and the failure severity and serving runs to agents for each project.

## Commands

Each extension's commands, under **Piwi:** in VS Code's command palette and **Tools → Piwi** in a JetBrains IDE, are
listed with what they do on [Editor commands](/reference/editor-commands). Both editors bind `Ctrl+Shift+Alt+K` to
run the test at the cursor, `Ctrl+Shift+Alt+F` to re-run the failing tests, `Ctrl+Shift+Alt+R` to record at the cursor
and stop the recording, and `Ctrl+Shift+Alt+B` to open the failures, in a JavaScript or TypeScript file or Piwi's
views; `Cmd` for `Ctrl` on macOS. Some JetBrains keymaps, macOS's among them, take other letters:
[Keys](/reference/editor-commands#keys). **Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts** changes them in VS Code (search `piwi`),
**Settings → Keymap** in a JetBrains IDE (search `Piwi`).

## JetBrains IDEs

The plugin runs with the project's Node.js interpreter, 20 or later, and shows the failures in the Piwi tool window,
the lines above the code with Code Vision, and its actions under **Tools → Piwi**: [JetBrains plugin](./jetbrains).

# Editor connection

The [editor extensions](./editors) read everything from your Piwi instance. They find it in this order, and the first
that names an instance wins:

1. the [desktop app](/features/desktop), while it runs, when you chose it with **Piwi: Connect…** on this machine;
2. `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `PIWI_API_KEY` and `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME` in the environment the editor was started with;
3. the same variables in the `.env` next to the Playwright config, then at the repository root (a URL there takes only
   its own key);
4. the instance saved with **Piwi: Connect…**;
5. the desktop app, while it runs.

A project set up for the reporter needs nothing more. An editor started from the Dock or the Start menu may not see
the variables your shell exports: the `.env` or Connect work either way.

## With the desktop app

The desktop app needs no pairing with the editor: while it runs, it publishes its address and a local token in
`~/.piwi/desktop.json`, which the editor reads, as the reporter does. The editor notices within seconds when the app
starts or quits. With nothing else naming an instance, the editor uses the app as soon as it runs.

The editor sends the app's token only to a server that proves it holds that token: before its first request that
carries the token, the editor asks the address in `desktop.json` for the app's proof. A server that gives none, or the
wrong one, gets no token, and the editor says the app's token was not sent. An app that does not answer is asked
again on the next request, and so is an app after a request with the token failed to connect or was refused, or after
the app restarts (a new process in `desktop.json`). The MCP server entries the editor offers for AI assistants (**Copy the MCP server
configuration…** and the VS Code agent's server list) include the app's token only after the same proof; the
assistant that receives the entry sends the token to the address itself.

The app is looked for on the machine the extension runs on: in a remote window of VS Code (Remote SSH, WSL, Dev
Containers), that is the remote machine, and `localhost` in `piwi.serverUrl` names it too.

### Beside a shared instance

When the environment, a `.env` or Connect names your team's instance, the desktop app sits beside it rather than
replacing it. In VS Code, **Piwi: Connect…** lists the desktop app, the instance the workspace names, and **Another
instance**, and marks the one in use; in a JetBrains IDE, Connect reads the project from **The Piwi desktop app,
while it runs** or **An instance**. Choose the desktop app, and the editor reads it first while it runs, then the
shared instance again when the app quits. Choosing the instance switches back; its address, project and key stay saved
throughout.

The choice is kept on your machine only (VS Code's workspace state, `.idea/workspace.xml` in a JetBrains IDE), never
in a file the team shares. In a JetBrains IDE, **Settings → Tools → Piwi** shows it too, under **Read this project
from**. When the app starts while the editor reads another instance, the editor offers the
switch once per workspace.

### The project

With the app chosen, the project is the one picked with Connect, else the one whose **linked folder** holds the
workspace's Playwright config (link the folder on the project's page in the desktop app), else `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`.
When the app is used because nothing else names an instance, `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME` comes first, since the reporter
sends its runs there under that name too. Several Playwright configs of one repository reading the same project share
what the editor reads from it: the instance answers each read once.

## Connect

Run **Piwi: Connect…** from the command palette, or click `Piwi: connect` in the status bar.

1. When the desktop app runs, Connect lists it first, with the instance the workspace already names: choose
   **The Piwi desktop app**, and pick the project if none is linked to the folder, or choose the instance to switch
   back to it. Otherwise, or with **Another instance**, give the instance's address, such as
   `https://piwi.example.com`.
2. When the instance has a login, choose **Sign in with the browser**, or paste a key you created yourself. An
   instance without a login needs no key.
3. Pick the project.

In a JetBrains IDE, Connect is one dialog holding the Connection panel of **Settings → Tools → Piwi**
([JetBrains plugin](./jetbrains#install-and-start)).

The browser sign-in opens the instance's page with a code: check that the editor shows the same code, then click
**Allow**. While it waits, the editor keeps the code and the page's link at hand, with **Copy code**, **Copy link**
and **Open browser again**, for a browser that opened elsewhere. The editor receives an [API key](/operate/api-keys)
created for you and named after it, such as "Piwi in WebStorm on macOS", which you revoke under **Settings →
Account → [Connected apps](/features/run-on-my-machine#connected-apps)**.

When the environment or a `.env` names another instance, Connect saves your choice and says which source comes first.
In a JetBrains IDE, an instance on your machine is reached at `localhost`, `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`, whichever it
listens on: Test connection and the project list try all three and keep the one that answered.

## What is saved where

| | VS Code | JetBrains IDEs |
|---|---|---|
| Address and project | `piwi.serverUrl` and `piwi.project` in the workspace settings | `.idea/piwi.xml` |
| The desktop app chosen, and its project | The workspace state, on this machine only | `.idea/workspace.xml`, on this machine only |
| API key | The editor's secret storage | The IDE's password safe |

The address and the project can be shared with the team. The key never goes to a file, and is saved for its instance
only: a repository whose settings name another instance never receives it. **Piwi: Disconnect** (the **Disconnect**
button in a JetBrains IDE) forgets the address, the project, that instance's key and the choice of the desktop app.

## Which connection is in use

The status bar's tooltip names the instance and where it came from, and says when the desktop app runs while another
instance is in use, or was chosen and is not running. In a JetBrains IDE, **Settings → Tools → Piwi** and the **Piwi**
tool window say the same, or why the editor is not connected. The plugin starts its service when you
open a file of a project that holds a Playwright config; until then, both say so, and Connect still finds the desktop
app.

## Behind a proxy

In VS Code, the editor service reaches the instance through the editor's own proxy settings: `http.proxy`, with
`http.proxyAuthorization` when it is a `Basic` credential, `http.noProxy`, and `http.proxyStrictSSL`, which turned
off leaves every certificate unverified. An instance on your machine (`localhost`, `127.0.0.1`), and the desktop
app, are reached directly. With `http.proxy` empty, the `HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY`
variables of the environment VS Code was started with apply, as they do to the editor. A change of these settings
starts the service again. An instance whose certificate a private certificate authority signed needs that authority
in `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` in the environment VS Code was started with: the extension passes the environment through
to the service.

In a JetBrains IDE, the service gets the HTTP proxy of **Settings → Appearance & Behavior → System Settings → HTTP
Proxy** for the instance the project names, and reaches this machine's addresses directly. A private certificate
authority goes in `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` in the environment the IDE was started with.

## An unreachable instance

When the instance does not answer, or answers with an error, the status bar reads `Piwi: unreachable` instead of
`Piwi: connect`: the connection is kept, and the editor reads the instance again on its own, 15 seconds later, then
twice as long each time, up to every five minutes. A click on the item, or **Read the instance and the configs again**,
reads it now. A key the instance refuses still reads `Piwi: connect`, since only signing in again helps.

When the desktop app answers but cannot prove it holds its token, which happens with a desktop app older than the
editor or with another program on its port, the item reads `Piwi: restart the desktop app`: the editor does not
send the app's token there. Restart or update the desktop app; the editor reads it again once the app starts.

The **Piwi** failures view says the same in both editors, naming the instance and why it does not answer, with
**Retry**. When the editor service itself stops, VS Code's status bar reads `Piwi: not running` and its view offers
**Piwi: Restart the editor service**, as does an unanswered **Read the instance and the configs again**.

**Piwi: Open settings** in VS Code opens the extension's settings.

## Related

- [API keys](/operate/api-keys): the key the editor signs in with, and how to revoke it
- [Desktop app](/features/desktop): the local instance the editor finds by itself

# JetBrains plugin

The Piwi plugin brings the [editor extensions](./editors) to the JetBrains IDEs with the LSP API: WebStorm, IntelliJ
IDEA Ultimate, Rider and the others, from 2024.1. It runs the same editor service as the VS Code extension, so the
editor pages describe it too, with the JetBrains names of each action. This page lists what the plugin needs, and
where it shows what VS Code shows differently.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/jetbrains-failures.png" alt="WebStorm: the failing tests tinted in the spec, the Piwi tool window below with the run's failures">
  <figcaption>WebStorm: the latest run's failures in the Piwi tool window, a local run laid over them, the failing tests tinted above.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Install and start

Install **Piwi** from **Settings → Plugins** or the
**[JetBrains Marketplace ↗](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/34674-piwi)**. IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition and
Android Studio lack the LSP API the plugin needs.

The plugin starts the editor service with the project's Node.js interpreter, 20 or later (**Settings → Languages &
Frameworks → Node.js**, which the status bar opens when it is missing or older), once it finds a Playwright config
within four folders of the project's (in Rider, the solution's) or of its Git root and you open a file, and looks again
on **Tools → Piwi → Read the instance and the configs again**. It reads the connection the reporter already uses;
otherwise, **Settings → Tools → Piwi** signs you in with the browser: [Editor connection](./editor-connection).

The first trusted project with a Playwright config opens a **Get started** tab in the Piwi tool window, once per
installation: the steps of VS Code's walkthrough, each with its button and a check mark once done. **Help → Get
started** opens it again.

In a project opened in safe mode, Piwi runs nothing and says it waits for your trust; trusting the project starts it.

**Settings → Tools → Piwi** opens on the connection in use, with **Reconnect**, then where the project reads from: the
desktop app, with its projects, or an instance, with its address and **Test connection**, its key with **Sign in…**,
**Paste key…** and **Remove**, and the project, picked from the instance's list. **Connect…**, under **Tools → Piwi**
and in the tool window's gear menu, is the same panel as one dialog. Nothing is saved before **Apply** or **Connect**, but **Disconnect**, which asks first.
When the environment or the workspace `.env` names another instance, the page says so, and an empty **Server URL**
shows its address. While the service cannot start, the page and the **Piwi** tool
window offer **Node.js settings…**, and the service starts again once you close the settings.

When the service stops, the **Piwi** tool window says so and offers **Restart the editor service** and **Open the log**, as
does a balloon that says it is not running; both are also under **Tools → Piwi** and in the tool window's gear. The
**Log** tab holds the service's starts and stops, why it could not start, its errors and the requests that failed.

Piwi reads Playwright Test suites in JavaScript and TypeScript. A Rider solution whose Playwright tests are written in
C# (a `.csproj` referencing `Microsoft.Playwright`) and that holds no Playwright config gets no tool window or status
item: a notification says so, once per project.


## Where things are

The IDE's LSP client shows warnings, quick fixes (Alt+Enter) and hover in open files.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/jetbrains-heal.png" alt="WebStorm: a broken locator's failure at its line, and Alt+Enter offering the heal that replaces it">
  <figcaption>The heal of a broken locator, offered with Alt+Enter.</figcaption>
</figure>

The rest is native, and every action that is not about a selected item is under **Tools → Piwi**, **Go to the stopped
line** on the debugger's Show Execution Point key:

- **The Piwi tool window** names the connection and holds the [failures view](./editor-failures#the-failures-view),
  since the IDE highlights open files only, and a **Tests** tab: the tree of
  [VS Code's Testing view](./editor-runs#the-testing-view-vs-code), with a filter, each node run from its right-click.
- **Code Vision** shows the lines above files, locators and failing lines, a line's entries side by side (a failing
  line's reason and **Run with Piwi**), up to the number the IDE's Code Vision settings show
  per line (five by default), in a group named Piwi under **Settings → Editor → Inlay Hints → Code Vision**, where they
  can be moved or hidden; each test's result is in the gutter, and either click on its icon opens the test's actions:
  **Run with Piwi** and **Verify ×3 with Piwi**, which report to the instance as Piwi's own runs do, **Record steps in
  this test…**, a failure's trace and screenshot, **Open in dashboard**, **Copy context for agent** and the test's Flake Lab commands.
- **[The status bar](./editor-status-bar)** item has an icon for the run's state, and the error color for a new
  failure a run you started produced. It counts a run you started (`3 of 9 · 1 failed`) as
  the run itself reports it, with no instance too; with one, the run's node in the Piwi tool window counts it the same
  way. While a run is [shared live](./share-live), its menu opens the run's page,
  copies its link, and has **Stop sharing the run**, which asks first.
- **The editor's and the project view's context menus** have a **Piwi** submenu, in the VS Code extension's order:
  run, then record. **Tools → Piwi** has six sections: run, record, run control (a submenu), dashboard,
  agents, connection. Each menu leaves out what does not apply.
- **[Recording](./editor-recording)** starts from **Record here…**, Alt+Enter or Alt+Insert, and **New → Playwright test
  (recorded)…** on a folder of a Playwright config; its controls are in a banner above the editor.
- **[A paused run](./editor-run-control)**: the line a run is stopped at, Piwi's or [one the IDE's own **Run**
  started](./terminal-runs), has an arrow in the gutter and an inlay above it with **Resume**, **Step**, **Finish** and **Write code…**, the
  other controls in its context menu; they are also in the status bar item's menu, after each stop to go to, and
  under **Tools → Piwi → Run control**, with **Pause the run** and **Stop the run**. A headless test's page shows in its worker's tab of
  the Piwi tool window (**Worker 1**), with the same controls, where a click on the image picks the locator of the
  element under it (Playwright 1.60 or later). On a JetBrains
  Gateway backend, forward the ports **Copy the pairing address for Piwi Picker** names:
  [Remote development](/guide/remote-development#jetbrains-gateway).
- **[A running test](./watch-running-test)**: while the **Worker** tab watches one, an inlay after the line of
  the call it runs names it, and the **Page** tab lists its page's console and uncaught errors, each test named first
  (closed, it stays closed until the next run).
- **[Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code)**: the inlay, the arrow's menu, the status bar item's menu and **Tools →
  Piwi** also offer **Pick a locator**, **Record**, **Assert**, **Assert a region** and **Mock a request** (the
  inlay names them shorter), whose code goes above the stopped line in one undoable edit; the end of the caret's line
  says how many elements its locator matches on the stopped page, and a failure held there reads `Held at its failure · …`.
- **The settings**: **Settings → Tools → Piwi** holds the options in the groups of
  [Editor settings](/reference/editor-settings), the IDE's Playwright runner among them, each group linking its
  section there.
- **[Run control for agents](./agent-run-control)**: **Tools → Piwi → Copy the runs' MCP server configuration for
  agents** gives an agent that starts commands (the AI Assistant among them) the test runs the project starts, to follow, stop and act on, and
  **…for Claude Code or Cursor** the HTTP entry they read; **Reset the runs' MCP server token** gives it a new token;
  **Settings → Tools → Piwi → Agents (MCP)** turns it off. A stop's menu and **Tools → Piwi** offer **Share the
  stopped test's browser with Playwright tools**, after a warning.
- **[Open in editor](./ide-integration#jetbrains-ides-the-piwi-plugin)**: a path clicked in the dashboard or the desktop
  app opens at its line, with nothing to set up.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/jetbrains-tests.png" alt="WebStorm: the Piwi tool window's Tests tab, a spec's tests with their results, a test's two Playwright projects, a loop's two tests and the Not in this checkout group">
  <figcaption>The Tests tab: each test's latest result, a node per Playwright project, a loop's tests one by one.</figcaption>
</figure>

The shortcuts are those of VS Code ([Commands](./editors#commands)), but in a keymap that gives one to another action
([Keys](/reference/editor-commands#keys)) and for a run's controls, which use the debugger's shortcuts of your keymap
while they apply and the debugger does not take them ([the controls](./editor-run-control#the-controls)): in the
default keymap `F9` resumes, `F8` steps, `Alt+F9` runs to the caret (`Alt+Shift+9` in the Linux default keymaps) and
`Shift+F8` finishes, and Pause has none; in the Visual Studio keymaps `F5`, `F10`, `Ctrl+F10` and `Shift+F11`, and
Pause the debugger's `Ctrl+Alt+Break`. **Settings → Keymap** changes them (search `Piwi`).

Each Piwi balloon is titled Piwi and filed by kind in **Settings → Appearance & Behavior → Notifications**: Piwi
(results), Piwi requests (Debug in my editor, a run shared live: they stay until answered), Piwi suggestions, Piwi
problems and Piwi confirmations (Copied., Connected to …), so muting one kind keeps the others.

# Remote development

In remote development the editor's window is on your computer, while the code, the
[editor service](/features/editors) and the test runs are on another machine: a server over SSH, WSL, a dev container
or a codespace. What the editor shows from the service works there as it does on your computer: failures, runs,
[pausing and stepping](/features/editor-run-control), a headless stop's live preview and Pick on it,
[code from a pause](/features/editor-stop-code). [Piwi Picker](/features/extension) is the part that needs a word: it
runs in the browser on your computer and reaches the editor through a pairing address on the loopback interface,
which in remote development is the local end of a forwarded port.

The editor's **Watch** and **Interact** controls use its existing connection. They need no Piwi Picker pairing or
extra port forwarding. The steps below are for using Piwi Picker's separate Runs window and Send to editor.

## VS Code

In a remote window (Remote SSH, WSL, Dev Containers, or a codespace opened in VS Code desktop):

1. Run **Piwi: Copy the pairing address for Piwi Picker** in that window. VS Code forwards the window's Send to
   editor port to your computer, on the same number when it is free there, and copies the local end on `127.0.0.1`,
   whatever name VS Code gives it: `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/piwi/send#<token>`.
2. In Piwi Picker's settings, under **Editor**, open Piwi Picker's **Pair with an address**, paste it and click
   Piwi Picker's **Use this address**.

Piwi Picker's **Pair**, which finds the editors on your computer and asks one for a code, does not look at a forwarded
port.

Piwi Picker then sends locators and recordings to the remote window, and its
[Runs window](/features/runs-window) lists the runs that window starts, and shows a headless test's page live: when
Piwi Picker asks for them, VS Code forwards the port of the window's run hub too, and the hub accepts a connection on that local port once
the window has named it, which Piwi Picker reaches on `127.0.0.1` too. Both forwarded ports show in the **Ports** view. The pairing's token, the proof that the
editor holds it, and the browser extension's origin are checked as on your own computer.

One pairing reaches the runs of one window when it is remote, and of every local window when it is local: pair from
the window whose runs you follow. After the window reloads, VS Code forwards the pairing's port again; when it lands
on another local port, pair again.

### Codespaces in the browser

A codespace opened in a browser tab forwards ports to an `https://…app.github.dev` address behind GitHub's sign-in,
not to your computer's loopback interface. Piwi Picker pairs with a loopback address only, so neither Send to editor
nor the Runs window reaches a codespace in the browser: open it in VS Code desktop instead.

## JetBrains Gateway

A JetBrains Gateway backend runs the IDE, its built-in server and the editor service on the remote machine. The
platform offers plugins no supported way to forward a port to your computer, so you forward the ports yourself:

1. Run **Tools → Piwi → Copy the pairing address for Piwi Picker** in the remote IDE. Besides copying the pairing
   address, its notification names the IDE's port (63342 by default) and the ports of the open projects' runs.
2. In the JetBrains Client, forward each of them under **Ports**, with the local port the same as the host port.
3. Paste the pairing address in Piwi Picker's settings under Piwi Picker's **Pair with an address**.

The numbers must match: Piwi Picker checks the IDE's proof for the port it asked on, and a run's hub accepts its own
port alone. A project's run port changes when its editor service starts again (the IDE restarted, the project was
reopened): copy the address again, and forward the port the notification names.

  editor.

# Record tests from the editor

**Piwi: Record here…** opens a browser through your project's own Playwright and writes what you do there at the cursor,
as you do it: steps inside a test, a page object's method or a helper function, a new test anywhere else in a spec. It
works in VS Code (and Cursor, VSCodium) and in the JetBrains IDEs with the
[Piwi plugin](./jetbrains), and needs no instance, no desktop app and no browser extension.

<figure>
  <video src="/videos/editor-recording-loop.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline controls aria-label="VS Code beside the browser the project's Playwright opened: Piwi: Record here at a blank line of a test, then a coupon typed and applied and the total checked in the browser, each step written in the test as it is made, the coupon's two steps becoming a call to the page object's applyCoupon, and Stop ending the recording with Run and Verify ×3 offered"></video>
  <figcaption>Record here: the steps written as you go, folded into your page object's method.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Start a recording

| Editor | Record at the cursor | Record a new test file |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code | **Piwi: Record here…**, from the command palette, the editor's context menu (**Piwi** submenu) or a spec's editor title (unless a stop's controls hold it), or **Ctrl+.** (**Cmd+.** on macOS); any editor's title shows **Stop recording** while one runs | **Piwi: Record a new test file…**, also in the explorer's **Piwi** submenu while the editor is connected to an instance |
| JetBrains IDE | **Tools → Piwi → Record here…**, **Alt+Enter** or **Alt+Insert** (Generate), or the editor's context menu (**Piwi** submenu) | **New → Playwright test (recorded)…** on a folder of a Playwright config, or the project view's **Piwi** submenu |

**Record steps in this test…**, among a test's actions (its result icon in a JetBrains IDE, **Piwi: Show the test's
actions…** in VS Code), records into that test after the last line of its body, wherever the cursor is.

Before the browser opens, the editor asks for:

1. **The start page**: a path on the project's `baseURL`, or an address; left empty, the browser opens the `baseURL`.
2. **The page the steps run on**, when the code around the cursor offers several: `page`, a fixture such as
   `adminPage`, or `this.page` in a page object. A fixture named like a page object (`todoPage`) comes after `page`
   until the test calls a page method on it. Any other expression can be typed.
3. **The Playwright project**, when the config has several. The browser gets its `use` options: `baseURL`,
   `storageState`, the viewport and device, the locale, the extra headers and `testIdAttribute`.

The editor offers your last answers. A new spec goes beside the one at hand, else in `testDir`, and receives the whole
recording.

## While it records

- **The block** the recording writes is tinted and marked in the gutter, and written again as each step arrives: a run of steps becomes one call
  to your own page object or helper once its last step is recorded. Started on a line inside a call that spans several
  lines, the block goes after that statement.
- **The controls**: the step count, **Stop** and **Pause** (**Resume** while paused), above the block in VS Code and in
  a banner above the editor in a JetBrains IDE, and **Pause**, **Stop** and the checks in the browser's recording bar. The status
  bar shows the recording too. While paused, from the editor or the browser, what you do in the browser is not
  recorded: use it to reach a page or set up data without writing those steps; **Resume** continues from there.
- **Checks**: **Check an element** in the browser's recording bar lets you pick an element and check its text, its
  value, its accessible name or its state, starting from what it shows now; **Check the address** checks the page's
  address. Each is written as an `await expect(…)` where you added it.
- **Typing in the block** pauses the recording. **Resume** writes the block again from the recorded steps, over your
  edits; **Keep my edits** stops the recording and keeps the code as you changed it.
- **Warnings** (a [brittle locator](/reference/locator-stability), a password read from the environment, a file to upload) are on their lines. They stay
  after the recording, each until its line is edited.

What the code holds, from locators to imports, and the options in the Playwright config that shape it:
[Recorded code](./recorded-code).

## Stop and undo

**Stop** in the editor or in the browser's recording bar, or closing the browser, ends the recording, and the code stays.
Closing the file ends it too. One **Undo** then removes the whole recording, imports included. In VS Code, a save or an
edit of the file during the recording starts a new undo step, so your own changes stay undoable on their own; in a
JetBrains IDE, that Undo also takes back the edits you made in the file meanwhile, and Redo brings everything back.

### Run it, or verify it three times

Once the recording stopped, a notification says what it wrote, `Recorded 6 steps into checkout.spec.ts.`, with two
actions for the test that holds the block, the new test or the test you recorded steps into:

- **Run** runs that test, with your breakpoints, as **Piwi: Run the test at the cursor** does.
- **Verify ×3** runs it as a [verification](./editor-runs#when-your-run-ends), as **Piwi: Verify the test at the
  cursor ×3** does.

Both save the file, then run the test by the line of its `test(…)` call
(`npx playwright test "^/repo/tests/checkout.spec.ts:42"`, by its whole path), so neither needs an instance. A verification that reached none is
told by its exit code, which cannot tell a pass from a skip: `None of 3 runs failed: tests/checkout.spec.ts:42`, or
`Failed at least 1 of 3: tests/checkout.spec.ts:42 (exit code 1)`. Steps recorded into a
page object or a helper offer neither action: no test holds them.

### Choose another locator

The recorder keeps up to five locators for each element it acts on, each verified to find that element alone on the
page, and writes the best one. Once the recording stopped, a warning on a step that has other locators offers each of
them as a quick fix, best first: **Piwi: use getByTestId('pay')** in the light bulb menu in VS Code, with **Alt+Enter** in a
JetBrains IDE. It puts that locator in place of the one written on the line, as one edit that **Undo** takes back, and
the line's warning goes. While the recording runs, none is offered: each step writes the block again.

The quick fix replaces the locator only where the line holds it once, as it was written: a line that calls your own
page object or helper has none of its own, and offers none.

## Send from Piwi Picker

A locator picked with the [Piwi Picker](./extension) browser extension in your everyday browser, or a flow it
recorded, lands at the editor's cursor too, once Piwi Picker is [paired with the editor](./editor-pairing). A picked
locator's row, the top locator of the [Elements sidebar](./devtools#the-elements-sidebar), the
[Locators console](./devtools#the-piwi-panel) in DevTools and a recording's finish panel then show **Send to editor**. A
locator is inserted in the copy form you chose; a recording is rendered as the body of a test, like
[`piwi codegen --body`](/reference/cli#codegen), or as a new test outside one. With no editor open, a JetBrains IDE
puts it in a new scratch file. A locator picked at a stop of a run Piwi starts reaches the editor the same way.

## Limits

- The browser is the one your tests use, installed by Playwright (`npx playwright install chromium`).
- Your project's Playwright runs with the first `node` on the editor's `PATH` in VS Code (when it is Node 22 or later,
  else with the editor's own runtime), and with the project's Node.js interpreter in a JetBrains IDE.
- The recording does not start your `webServer`: start the application first.
- It records the top-level page: clicks inside an iframe, and steps in a popup or a new tab, are not recorded yet. The
  editor says so when the application opens a tab or a popup.
- A file takes one recording at a time.
- A recording starts on a fresh page. To record where a test already is (signed in, halfway through a flow), pause the
  test there and [record from the pause](./editor-breakpoints#record-from-a-pause).

- [Piwi Picker](./extension): records in your everyday browser, for a test or a bug report with its evidence.

# Recorded code

A [recording from the editor](./editor-recording), and a flow [sent from Piwi Picker](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker),
are written as the code your suite would hold: locators verified on the page, calls to your own page objects and
helpers, no password in the file. The Playwright config sets how that code looks for everyone who records in the
repository.

## What a recording writes

- **Locators** come from the same converter as Piwi Picker's recordings and [`piwi codegen`](/reference/cli#codegen):
  each is verified to find the element alone on the page, the stable ones first and those your tests already use
  preferred. A check of the element's text takes a locator that does not find it by that text, when one is not
  [brittle](/reference/locator-stability). A `getByTestId` uses the attribute your config sets.
- **Pages**: an address on the project's `baseURL` is written as a path, and the step that leads to another page is
  followed by a wait for it, except next to a call to your own code, which waits for its pages itself.
- **Imports**: a call to your own code, and `expect` when a step checks something, are imported at the top of the file
  when it lacks them: `expect` from `@playwright/test`, or from your fixtures module when the file or a spec beside it
  imports `expect` from there. A new test in a file that imports no `test` imports it as the specs beside it do. A spec
  that loads `test` with `require` gets `require` lines after its last one.
- **Titles**: a new test is titled `recorded flow`, numbered (`recorded flow 2`) when the file has one already.
- **Your own code**: when the editor is connected to an instance or the [desktop app](./desktop), steps that match one
  of your [test functions](./test-functions) become a call to it, as soon as the last of those steps is recorded.
- **Passwords** are never recorded: the code reads them from an environment variable named after the field, such as
  `process.env.E2E_PASSWORD`, including in a call to a page object.

## Code options in the Playwright config

How the recorded code looks is set for the whole repository in `playwright.config.ts`, under the `'@piwi'` key at the
top level, next to `testDir` and `use`. Everyone who records in the repository from the editor gets the same code,
with or without an instance; [`piwi codegen`](/reference/cli#codegen) reads its own flags instead:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test';
import type {} from '@piwitests/reporter'; // declares '@piwi' on the config; already there with wrapConfig

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: './tests',
  '@piwi': {
    codegen: {
      testSteps: 'page',
      tags: ['@recorded'],
      annotations: [{ type: 'piwi:owner', description: '@shop-team' }],
    },
  },
});
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `pageWaits` | `true` | `false` leaves out the wait for the next page after a step that leads to it |
| `values` | `'literal'` | `'env'` reads every typed value from an environment variable named after its field, not only passwords |
| `envPrefix` | `'E2E_'` | What those variables start with, as in `E2E_PASSWORD`: upper-case letters, digits and underscores |
| `testSteps` | `'none'` | `'page'` wraps the steps of each page in `await test.step('/cart', …)`, so the report reads like the scenario; in a test only, not in a page object or a helper |
| `tags` | none | Tags a new test gets |
| `annotations` | none | Annotations a new test gets, `{ type, description? }` |

The editor reads the section through your project's own Playwright, so it applies to the recordings started after the
config is saved, and to what Piwi Picker sends to the editor. An unknown option or a value of the wrong kind is left
out, and the recording says so when it starts.

- [Test functions](./test-functions): the page objects and helpers a recording calls.
