# CI runs in your editor

While CI runs your branch, the [editor extensions](./editors) show that run beside your own: its progress, its tests
as they end, the line each running test is at, and, when its project has the [live view](./live-view) on, its pages.
It is watched only, but for the controls offered to the people who may control the run: **Let it go** on a test the
project [holds at its failure](./hold-ci-failure), and **Pause**, **Resume** and **End the test** when the project lets
them [pause a CI test](./pause-ci-test). Nothing else steps, holds or shares a CI run from the editor.

## Which runs

A CI run of the branch your workspace reads or has checked out, or a teammate's on it or on the branch your results
are [compared with](./editor-status-bar#compare-with-another-run), shows while it runs. The editor finds it as the
instance announces it, or as it reads the latest run of the branch in progress. It follows the two newest runs of a
branch at most, and stops following a run as it ends, as a newer run takes its place, or when the workspace reads
another instance, project or branch.

VS Code's status bar says `CI run #125` or `run #126`, and its Testing view `Piwi: CI run #125 on main`, with results
as they end; your own run keeps the status bar. A test line Piwi marks keeps its own latest result, and its hover
names the CI run running it.

## The CI run's tests

- **The CI Runs view** of VS Code's Piwi panel, and the **CI run** tab of the JetBrains Piwi tool window, show while a
  CI run runs. Each lists `CI run #78`, its branch and progress, **Open run #78** and its tests: those running, then
  the latest that ended, failures first. A running test opens the call it is at, else its spec (a double click in
  JetBrains).
- **The line each running test is at** ends with a plain mark in the CodeLens or inlay color, `CI run #78 · worker 2:
  Click getByRole('button')`: a [CI position](/guide/concepts#ci-position), never a stop, on the line of the run's
  commit. It shows in a file of your workspace only, placed from the run's own steps: never one in `node_modules` or
  outside the workspace.
- **Piwi Picker's Runs window** lists them too: [CI runs](./runs-window#open-it).

## Watch a CI lane

**Watch**, under a running test whose project has the [live view](./live-view) on, opens its lane read-only, named
`CI run #78 · worker 2`, in the VS Code worker panel, the JetBrains **Worker** tab or the Runs window: no
**Interact**, no pick. It follows the lane through its next tests, and ends with the run, as you hide or close the
view, or as the instance closes it, saying why. Its images come from the
[team instance](./live-view#what-is-sent-to-whom-and-what-is-kept), read with the editor's connection; under the
image, the same layers as a local lane ([Beside the image](./watch-running-test#beside-the-image)).

**Watch on the dashboard** opens the lane on the run's page, offered where the editor cannot show it (an older
instance, a refused **Watch**).

### A failure held for you

When the project [holds a failing CI test](./hold-ci-failure) for its controllers and your editor's connection may
control the project's runs (its key is a Maintainer's or a Project admin's), your watch of a lane counts: a test that
fails in it waits at its failure, as it would for the run page. The worker panel or the **Worker** tab then says
**Failed, held at its line · Held for Ana · until 12:05**, the error, its place (which opens the failing line), and
that the CI job's own timeout still runs; the CI Runs list marks the test **Failed, held at its line**. **Let it go**
ends the wait, once: the test tears down as it would have, its result unchanged.

**Let it go** goes on your watch of that lane, so it shows only while you watch it, and only once the instance has
said your connection may control the run. The Runs window does the same with its own connection
([Where it shows](./hold-ci-failure#where-it-shows)). Anyone else watching sees the hold without it. A refusal is said in the
instance's words, under the caption.

### A test paused for you

When the project also lets its controllers [pause a CI test](./pause-ci-test), the same watch offers **Pause** while
the lane's test runs. Until the test stops before its next call, the panel or tab says **Pause asked by Ana**, and
**Resume** takes the Pause back; one the worker dropped says why. Paused, it says **Paused by Ana · until 12:05**, the
call it stopped before and its place, and the job's timeout note, with **Resume** and **End the test**; the CI Runs
list marks it **Paused**. Each button is asked once in each state of the lane, its refusal in the instance's words.

## Limits

- **Watched only, but Pause, Resume, End the test and Let it go, for those who may control it.** No other
  control, share or hold reaches a CI run, and its position is never a stop.
- **One worker per editor.** The worker panel or tab watches one lane, a local worker's or a CI run's: watching another
  moves it there.
- **A run's steps.** The positions come from the steps the CI run's reporter streams, so a run whose reporter streams
  none lists its tests without them.

## Related

- [Watch a local test](./watch-running-test): a test running on your machine.
- [Live view of a run](./live-view): the team instance's view of a run, which a CI lane comes from.
- [Failures in the editor](./editor-failures): the CI run's failures once it ended.

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/ide-integration -->

# Open in editor

Every source path the dashboard shows is clickable: the failing call stack ("Failed here"), a run's test-case list, a
test case's file, flaky lists, cluster evidence, the AI suggested fix. Hover a path and a small **open in editor** control
appears: click it to open that file, at its line, in your local editor, or open the chooser to pick a method.

The dashboard runs in your browser while the source lives on your machine, so the mapping from a repo-relative path
(`tests/checkout.spec.ts`) to a real file is set **per browser** and stored there.

## JetBrains IDEs: the Piwi plugin

With the [Piwi plugin](./jetbrains) installed in Rider, WebStorm, IntelliJ IDEA Ultimate or another JetBrains IDE,
clicking a path opens it there with **nothing to set up** once the project is connected to the instance the dashboard
belongs to:

- The dashboard asks every JetBrains IDE running, on its built-in server (ports 63342 to 63361). The IDE whose open
  project holds the file opens it at its line and brings its window to the front.
- The dashboard then shows **Opened in Rider** (or the IDE's name), or, when no open project holds the file, says so
  and lists the projects the IDE has open.
- The path, relative to the folder the tests ran in, is looked up under each Playwright config's folder in the
  project, the project folder and its content roots, so a Rider solution in a subfolder, or a monorepo, needs no
  workspace root and no project name. A workspace root, when set, is tried first; the file must still be in the
  project.
- When several IDEs hold the file, the one matching the **JetBrains product** you set wins; when several projects do,
  the one connected to the same Piwi project wins.

The IDE answers only a page of the Piwi instance one of its open projects is connected to (**Settings → Tools →
Piwi**, or `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` in the environment or the workspace `.env`), or of the [desktop app](./desktop.md) on
the same machine, and finds files only in the projects connected to that instance. A page from any other address,
another page on your machine included, gets no answer whatever the IDE's built-in server settings allow, and the first
address refused in an IDE session is named in a notification. When the dashboard you use is the project's instance
under another address, connect the project to that address.

## VS Code: the Piwi extension

With the [Piwi extension](./editors#install-and-connect) installed in VS Code, Cursor or VSCodium, a path opens there
with **no workspace root**: the dashboard hands the editor a `vscode://piwitests.piwi/open` link with the path as the
run reported it, and the extension looks for it under the folder of each Playwright config in the window, then the
workspace folders. It opens the file at its line and column, and never a file outside the workspace folders.

- The editor hands the link to its window **focused last**. When that window holds no such file, a warning there says
  so: focus the window of the project and click the path again.
- Like any URL scheme, the link reports nothing back: the dashboard shows **Asked the Piwi extension in VS Code**, and
  if nothing opens, the extension is not installed in the flavor you chose.
- With a workspace root, or a project's linked folder in the desktop app, the absolute path opens instead, through
  `vscode://file` or the desktop app's launcher (below).

## Set it up

1. Hover any source path and click the **⌄** caret, then **Configure…**, or open it from the user menu (bottom-left)
   → **Open in editor…**.
2. For VS Code without the Piwi extension, or a JetBrains IDE without the Piwi plugin, set your **workspace root**: the
   absolute path of the folder the tests run from, such as `/home/me/my-repo` (or `C:\Users\me\my-repo` on Windows).
   Repo-relative paths are joined onto it. With the Piwi extension, leave it empty and tick **The Piwi extension is
   installed in VS Code**, or click **Use the Piwi extension** on the toast that asks for a workspace root.
3. Pick a **method**, or leave it on **Auto**. The **Test** row's **Open package.json** and **Open &lt;your Playwright
   config&gt;** open a known file with your current settings. In the desktop app, the config's file name is read from the linked folder; elsewhere it is `playwright.config.ts`.

## Methods

| Method | How it opens | Needs |
|--------|--------------|-------|
| **VS Code** | `vscode://file/<abs-path>:<line>` URL scheme with a workspace root; without one, the Piwi extension's `vscode://piwitests.piwi/open` link | A workspace root (for the absolute path), or the [Piwi extension](./editors#install-and-connect) in the editor. Flavors: VS Code, Insiders, VSCodium, Cursor. |
| **JetBrains: Piwi plugin, else URL** | `jetbrains://<product>/navigate/reference?project=<name>&path=<rel>:<line>` | Without the plugin: [JetBrains Toolbox](https://www.jetbrains.com/toolbox-app/), the IDE product tag (e.g. `idea`, `rider`) and the open project name (in Rider, the solution's name). |
| **JetBrains: Piwi plugin, else local server** | `http://localhost:63342/api/file/<path>:<line>` | Without the plugin: the IDE running with the **[IDE Remote Control](https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/19991-ide-remote-control)** plugin and **Settings → Build → Debugger → "Allow unsigned requests"** enabled, which lets any page reach the IDE's local server. |
| **Auto** | The Piwi plugin, then the other methods in turn (see below) | Whatever the method that answers needs. |

### Desktop app: direct launch

In the [desktop app](./desktop.md), whatever method you pick, clicking a path runs your IDE's **command-line
launcher** before any URL (a JetBrains method or Auto asks the Piwi plugin first):

- VS Code family: `code --goto <file>:<line>:<column>` (or `cursor`, `codium`, `code-insiders`, matching the flavor
  you chose);
- JetBrains: `<product> --line <line> --column <column> <file>`, where `<product>` is the product tag you set
  (`rider`, `idea`, `webstorm`, …).

Unlike a URL scheme, it reports whether the launcher started, and flags a missing file. It needs a workspace root or
the project's [linked folder](./desktop.md). The app finds the launcher on your
`PATH`, then where the IDEs install it (an app started from the Dock or the Start menu misses your shell's `PATH`):

- **Windows:** the Toolbox scripts folder, then the IDE's `bin` folder under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs` or
  `C:\Program Files\JetBrains`, newest version first; VS Code's `bin` folder.
- **macOS:** the Toolbox scripts folder, `/usr/local/bin`, `/opt/homebrew/bin`, then the app bundles in
  `/Applications` and `~/Applications`.
- **Linux:** the Toolbox scripts folder, `~/.local/bin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/bin`, `/snap/bin`, then
  `/opt/<IDE>/bin`.

When no launcher is found, the app falls back to the URL scheme of the chosen method.

### Auto: the first method that works

Only the **Piwi plugin** can confirm the file opened. The IDE Remote Control server cannot, and the URL schemes are
handed to the operating system with **no success signal** but the browser's own "Open &lt;app&gt;?" prompt. **Auto**
tries, in order:

1. The Piwi plugin in any JetBrains IDE running. If an IDE answers that none of its open projects holds the file,
   Auto says so rather than launch another editor.
2. In the desktop app, the command-line launchers: JetBrains first when a JetBrains IDE is running, VS Code first
   otherwise.
3. The IDE Remote Control local server, reported as **Sent to JetBrains**, not as opened.
4. A single URL scheme: VS Code when a workspace root is set, otherwise `jetbrains://` when a JetBrains project name
   is set, otherwise the Piwi extension in VS Code while **The Piwi extension is installed in VS Code** is ticked,
   reported as "opening…" or "asked".

If you only use one editor, set the method explicitly to skip the other steps.

::: warning HTTPS and the IDE on localhost
The Piwi plugin and the local server are reached on `http://127.0.0.1` or `http://localhost`. When the dashboard is
served over **HTTPS** from another address, some browsers block that request as mixed content, and recent Chrome
versions ask once for permission to reach apps on your device. These two methods work best with the dashboard on
**http / localhost**, or in the desktop app; over HTTPS, Auto still falls back to the URL schemes.
:::

## Per-project overrides

If you view several projects that live in different local checkouts (or a monorepo), open **Configure…** from a path
inside that project: the dialog then offers a **workspace root override** and a **JetBrains project name** for that
project alone. Everything else falls back to your global settings. The Piwi plugin needs neither.

## Privacy

The method, workspace roots, editor flavor and JetBrains product and port live in your browser's `localStorage` under
`piwi-ide-prefs`. Nothing about your local filesystem is sent to the Piwi server. The Piwi plugin is asked from your
browser directly, on your own machine, with the file path, the workspace root and the Piwi project's name; the Piwi
extension's link carries the file path and line to VS Code through your operating system. Neither goes anywhere else.

## Related

- [Editor extensions](./editors): Piwi's answers inside VS Code and the JetBrains IDEs.
- [JetBrains plugin](./jetbrains): what the plugin needs, and where it shows what.
- [Debug in my editor](./debug-in-editor): both Piwi links, to run a failed test to its failing line.

# Browser extension

Piwi Picker is a Chrome, Edge and Firefox extension that picks ranked, stable Playwright locators from the page you
are looking at, scored by the same engine the dashboard uses, and records a multi-page flow into a runnable TypeScript
spec, or into a failing test and a bug report once you mark what the page gets wrong. It works standalone and sends
nothing by default; connecting it to a Piwi instance adds what needs your project's history. This page lists the
tools, where they are, the permissions they use and their limits; each tool has its own page.

## What it does

Every tool below runs on the live page, from the toolbar popup. The last three need a
[connection to a Piwi instance](#connecting-to-a-piwi-instance); the others work without one, and some do more with it:
a pick names the tests that reach the element, a recording sends its report, Developer tools lists your projects'
viewports.

| Tool | Key | For |
|---|---|---|
| [Pick an element](./pick-an-element) | `2` | a ranked locator for one element, re-checked against the page |
| [Multi-pick](./pick-an-element#multi-pick) | `3` | the shared pattern of a list's rows or cards |
| [Lint overlay](./lint-overlay) | `5` | the elements that would make bad locator targets |
| [Assertions](./pick-an-element#assertion-suggester) | `4` | `expect(...)` lines for an element |
| [Agent context](./pick-an-element#copy-context-for-agent) | `7` | one block about an element for a coding agent |
| [Record](./record-actions) | `1` | a runnable test from clicks, fills and checks across pages, with the evidence |
| [Record a bug report](./report-a-bug) | | a failing test and a report, once a recording marks what the page gets wrong |
| [Replay](./replay-a-bug-report) | `R` | a recording's steps played again in a tab, to see whether each still holds or the bug shows there |
| [Developer tools](./devtools) | | in DevTools: the selected element's locators, the locator console, the session, mocks, viewports |
| [Runs window](./runs-window) | `U` | pause, step and resume the tests your editor runs, and watch a headless one live |
| [Matching functions](./record-actions#matching-functions) | | a recording that calls your own functions |
| [Test functions](./test-functions#using-the-catalog) | `6` | which of your functions work on this page |
| [Tested elements](./tested-elements) | `T` | which elements of this page your tests reach |

## Where it is

Install Piwi Picker from the
**[Chrome Web Store ↗](https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/piwi-picker/pakhnokpjboejcghgcmkjlpnogfjihhe)** for
Chrome or Edge 118 or later (in Edge, click **Allow** on the *Allow extensions from other stores* banner once, then
**Get**), or from **[Firefox Add-ons ↗](https://addons.mozilla.org/firefox/addon/piwi-picker/)** for Firefox 140 or
later.

Every tool in the popup has a tile with a line under its name saying what it is for, and the key in the table above,
pressed with the popup open. **Record** and **Pick an element** come first, then the **Pick** section, with
Multi-pick, Assertions, Lint overlay, Test functions and Agent context, and the **Tests** section, with Replay, Runs
and Tested elements. One tool runs at a time and **Esc** cancels it; a recording runs until its own **Finish**, and
while it runs, **Take a screenshot** (`S`) takes Replay's place. The tools that need no pick on the page are in the
browser's DevTools: [Developer tools](./devtools).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-popup.png" alt="The Piwi Picker popup over a shop page, one tile per tool">
  <figcaption>The popup: one tile per tool, with its key.</figcaption>
</figure>

Picking also has a shortcut, `Ctrl+Shift+E` by default (`Cmd+Shift+E` on macOS); the popup footer shows the key
bound.

## Test functions against this page

The popup's **Test functions** checklist, with a connection: see
[Using the catalog](./test-functions#using-the-catalog).

## Tested elements

With a connection, the popup's **Tested elements** outlines what your tests reach on the page: see
[Tested elements](./tested-elements).

## Runs from the editor

With Piwi Picker [paired with VS Code or a JetBrains IDE](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker), the popup's
**Runs** tile, under **Tests**, opens the [Runs window](./runs-window).

## Languages

Piwi Picker speaks English, French, German, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese, following the browser unless
**Language**, in the settings, picks another. German, Spanish and Portuguese are unreviewed drafts:
[suggest a correction](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/issues/new?template=translation.yml). A bug report is
written in the extension's language; locators, test ids and specs never are.

## Permissions, explained

| Permission | Why |
|---|---|
| `activeTab` | acts on the tab you are looking at, only when you click the toolbar icon or press the shortcut |
| `debugger` (Chrome and Edge) | trusted input for a replay, a recording's evidence, DevTools' request conditions and the viewport it sets in the tab, attached only while one of them runs: see [The debugging bar](#the-debugging-bar) |
| `scripting` | injects Pick an element, the recorder or another tool into that tab on demand, and marks your instance's pages once [connected](./extension-connection#what-is-sent); nothing else runs unasked |
| `storage` | keeps your copy format and, only if you connect, the instance URL, URL patterns, cached catalogs and the last three [locator indexes](./tested-elements), on your machine. The API key and the desktop app's and editor's tokens live in the extension's own database, out of reach of web pages; the session and a running recording use `chrome.storage.session`, cleared when the browser closes |
| `cookies` (optional, not granted in advance) | [Save login for tests](./devtools#save-login-for-tests) asks for it, for the one site whose login you save |
| `optional_host_permissions` (none granted in advance) | recording asks for the one site you are on, to follow you across its pages; a connection asks for your instance's origin; [pairing](./editor-pairing) asks for the editors' ports of `127.0.0.1`. Never `<all_urls>`. The settings list every site allowed under **Sites Piwi Picker may run on**, each with **Revoke** |

### The debugging bar

In Chrome and Edge, the features below use the browser's debugging protocol on the tab they act on, and Chrome
shows its bar saying Piwi Picker started debugging the browser while one runs. Each attaches when it starts and lets
go when it ends; the session is detached once none holds it. Nothing read through it leaves your machine unless you
send it. Firefox has no `debugger` permission, and **Cancel** on the bar ends the session: each feature then goes on
without it, and says so.

| Feature | With the protocol | Without it |
|---|---|---|
| [Replay](./replay-a-bug-report#trusted-input) | Trusted input, as Playwright sends it, at the viewport size each step was recorded at | The page's own events, the panel saying which, step by step |
| [Record](./report-a-bug#how-the-evidence-is-collected) | The console, every failed request, the screenshots and a screenshot of each step, in the tab the recording started in, from the page's first script | A script in the page sees `fetch` and XHR calls only; a screenshot needs the `activeTab` grant |
| [Request conditions](./mock-requests#slow-down-or-fail-a-request) | Any request, and the Network and CPU throttling | The page's `fetch` and XHR calls only, no throttling |
| [Viewport in this tab](./devtools#open-this-page-at-a-viewport) | The tab itself at a project's viewport | A new window of that size |

### Sites Piwi Picker may run on

Recording, replaying, Save login and the DevTools pane each ask for the site you are on the first time they need it,
and the access stays until you take it back. Settings → **Sites Piwi Picker may run on** lists every site allowed
with a **Revoke** button; Piwi Picker then runs there only when you click its icon. A site a recording or a replay runs
on keeps its access until it ends, and your instance's address, the desktop app's and the editor's are given back by
**Disconnect** and **Unpair**.

## Connecting to a Piwi instance

Optional and off by default: **Connect** in the settings, the URL patterns that say which project a page belongs
to, and [what a connection sends](./extension-connection#what-is-sent), never a recording, are on
[Extension connection](./extension-connection).

## Limits

- **One frame at a time.** Pick an element, the recorder and Replay see the top-level document, not iframes.
- **Open shadow roots only.** Pick an element reaches inside open shadow roots; a closed one is out of reach, and a pick
  there picks its host element. The recorder records the fields of open shadow roots, and from a closed one only the
  keys of a password field (Enter, Escape, the arrows).
- **Recording covers one origin.** On another site it stops capturing: finish, or start again there.
- **No ARIA snapshot from a plain pick.** `toMatchAriaSnapshot()` code comes from **Assert a region**, at a stopped
  test in the [Runs window](./runs-window).

## Related

- [Fix a broken locator](/recipes/broken-locator): from a failing locator to the one to use instead
- [Extension connection](./extension-connection): connecting in one step, and the URL patterns kept on the instance
- [Tested elements](./tested-elements): the elements your tests reach, drawn on the page
- [Runs window](./runs-window): the editor's runs, steered and watched from the browser
- [Write, run and fix a test](./write-run-fix): a test from an empty spec to a passing run, with the tool for each step
- [Test functions catalog](./test-functions): the functions a recording can call
- [Locator healing](./locator-healing): the replacement Piwi proposes after a failure

# Extension connection

[Piwi Picker](./extension) works on its own. Connected to your Piwi instance, it also matches a recording against
your project's [test functions](./test-functions) and shows [Tested elements](./tested-elements). Connecting takes
one click, and the URL patterns that say which project a page belongs to live on the instance, so a team sets them
once. Pairing with the desktop app, and what each connection sends, are here too.

## Connect in one step

1. In Piwi Picker's settings (the gear button in its popup), type your instance's address.
2. Click **Connect**. The browser asks to let Piwi Picker reach that one address; allow it.
3. A tab opens on your instance. Sign in if asked, with a password or your usual sign-in provider: you come back to
   the same page. It names the connecting browser ("Piwi Picker in Chrome on Windows") and shows a code.
4. Check that the settings page shows the same code, tick **My Piwi Picker shows this same code**, then click
   **Allow**. The link carries the code, so anyone could send you one: if you did not just click **Connect**, deny.

The tab closes, the settings say **Connected as** your name, and the instance's URL patterns show under **From your
Piwi instance**.

Allowing creates an API key for your account, named after the browser, with your instance role and project roles. It is
listed under **Settings → Account → [Connected apps](/features/run-on-my-machine#connected-apps)**, where you revoke
it; the browser is then disconnected at its next request. **Deny**, or ten minutes without an answer, creates nothing.

With [authentication](/operate/authentication) off, **Allow** only confirms the connection: there is no account to
own a key, and none is needed.

### Is the connection working?

The popup says how the last request to your instance went, under **Active project** ("Connected to
piwi.example.com, checked 5 minutes ago"), or since when nothing answers, the key is refused or the instance answers
with errors, with a link to the settings, which show the same beside the address. A revoked key thus shows at the
next request, before a tool fails: click **Connect** again.

### Use an API key instead

Under **Use an API key instead**, paste a key created in your account's [API key settings](/operate/api-keys) and
click **Save and test**. An instance older than the one-step connection needs this.

### The desktop app as your instance

Once the [desktop app](./desktop) is [paired](#pair-with-the-desktop-app) and no instance is connected, **Use the
desktop app as your instance** fills in the app's address and token as the API key, checks them and connects: the
app's instance answers only requests carrying that token. If the app, installed again, refuses it, paste the one from
its **Pair with Piwi Picker** card, or pair again. Typed by hand, the address must use
`127.0.0.1`, since `localhost` may reach another program.

## Pair with the desktop app

Pairing lets Piwi Picker [run a report with Playwright](./replay-a-bug-report#running-it-with-playwright) in the app,
follow its runs in the [Runs window](./runs-window) and use it as its instance. Under **Desktop app** in the settings,
click **Pair**, then **Allow** in the app's window, which shows the same code. **Pair by hand** takes the address and
token shown in the app's **Settings → Desktop app**, under **Pair with Piwi Picker** (`http://127.0.0.1:3000` by
default). While an instance is connected and no app is paired, the settings point here.

The token goes out only after the program at that address proves it holds it, before every request: another program
on the app's port receives nothing, after **Unpair** too. **Disconnect** leaves the shared address granted to the app,
and **Unpair** to the instance or the editor.

## URL patterns

A URL pattern is a glob over a page's whole address: `*` matches within one part of the path, `**` across parts. So
`https://staging.shop.example/**` covers every page of that site, and `https://shop.example/admin/*` the pages one
level under `/admin`. A pattern starts with `http://`, `https://` or a wildcard.

Each project keeps its own list in the **Browser extension** section of its **Settings** tab. A pattern can name:

- an [environment](./environments) of the project, shown by name in Piwi Picker;
- a **branch**, the one deployed at those addresses, whose tests [Tested elements](./tested-elements) shows;
- a **path prefix**, the part of the path your site serves its pages under and the tests did not: `/app` when the site
  serves `/app/checkout` and the tests ran at `/checkout`. Piwi Picker removes it before comparing the page with the
  [pages the tests ran on](./tested-elements#this-page), whole parts only (`/application` keeps its path), and a bug
  report sent from the site keys its page without it. It is a plain path of at most four parts, with no query, hash or
  wildcard;
- a **tests' path prefix**, the reverse: the part of the path the tests ran the pages under and the site does not,
  `/app` when the tests ran `/app/checkout` and the site serves `/checkout`. Piwi Picker puts it in front of the page's
  path; the site's root becomes `/app`. With both set, the one replaces the other (`/app` on the site, `/v2` in the
  tests), and a page outside the path prefix is left as it is.

The editor suggests one pattern per site your suite already visited, grouped by the environment each run's label
resolves to (the [reporter](/guide/reporter)'s `environment` option or `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`), from the newest few runs
of every environment, so a nightly production suite shows beside a staging one. A run's site
is its `baseURL`; for a run with none, the full addresses its tests opened with `page.goto` and the pages it loaded
(its `document` requests), then the [Test Map](./scenario-gaps)'s pages and the absolute pages its locators ran on. A
run merged from blob reports (`npx playwright merge-reports`, or a blob report imported in the dashboard) has no
`baseURL`, which Playwright leaves out of them, so its sites come from the page loads the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) record for every test, or the trace of a failed test. **Add** puts a
suggestion in the list with its environment, **Add all** every suggestion of that environment; **Save patterns** stores
them. When there is nothing to suggest, the editor says why: every site already
has a pattern, or no recent run recorded a `baseURL`, opened a full address or kept the network requests of a page it
loaded. Editing the list takes the Project admin role.

### Which project applies

Piwi Picker reads the patterns of every project you can see when it connects and each time its settings open, and
keeps a copy, so a page's project is known with the instance out of reach. For a page it decides in this order:

1. the project chosen in the popup's **Active project** on that site, for the rest of the browser session or until you
   disconnect;
2. the patterns under **This browser only**, the first that matches;
3. the instance's patterns, by project, in each project's order, the first that matches.

A pattern kept in the browser is an override for that browser alone, and the settings mark where each comes from. **Disconnect** sets the patterns of this browser aside: connecting to the same instance
again brings them back, and connecting to another drops them, since they name the first one's projects. A connection
left unfinished leaves them aside for the next one.

### Add a site

When the tab matches no pattern, the popup offers **Add this site**, which opens the settings with
`https://<site>/**` filled in: choose a project and click **Add to Piwi**, or **Keep in this browser only**. Adding to
the instance takes a role that edits the project; without one, the settings say so and keep the second choice.

## What is sent

Connecting, and pairing with the desktop app, send the browser's and operating system's names, nothing else about
the machine. It then downloads the projects, the URL patterns, each mapped project's function catalog,
locator index and bug reports, and the runs in progress. It sends the instance nothing else but these, each on your
click: a site's pattern (**Add this site**), a bug report after the **Send to Piwi…** preview
([sending one](./bug-reports#sending-a-report)), and a replay's answer (**Share result…**). A recording goes only to a
paired editor (**Send to editor**), and steps only to the paired desktop app (**Run with Playwright…**). Only the settings
page and the background worker make requests, never a page's script.

While connected, Piwi Picker also marks your instance's pages in this browser: a script sets `data-piwi-picker`, with
the extension's version, on each page. The dashboard then stops suggesting Piwi Picker, as it does once you click
**Don't show again** on its hint. The script reads nothing from the page and sends nothing, and **Disconnect** stops it.

## Related

- [Browser extension](./extension): everything Piwi Picker does, with or without a connection
- [API keys](/operate/api-keys): create, list and revoke keys; Piwi Picker's is under Connected apps
- [Tested elements](./tested-elements): what a connection shows on the page
- [Access, roles and groups](/operate/project-access): which projects, and so which patterns, a user sees

# Piwi Picker and your editor

[Send to editor](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker) and the [Runs window](./runs-window) reach your editor
through one pairing. The desktop app has a pairing of its own, which the Runs window follows beside it
([the desktop app's runs](./runs-window#the-desktop-app-s-runs)).

## Pair

1. In Piwi Picker's settings, under **Editor**, click Piwi Picker's **Pair**. It asks the ports the editors of this
   computer listen on which editor answers there, VS Code on 7247 to 7251 and a JetBrains IDE's built-in server on
   63342 to 63361, and lists them when it finds more than one. The browser asks once for access to `127.0.0.1`;
   Piwi Picker gives back the ports it did not pair with.
2. Piwi Picker shows a code, and the editor shows the request: Piwi Picker in your browser asks to pair. Click **Type
   the code…** in the editor's notification or in its pairing panel and type the code Piwi Picker shows; deny a
   request you did not make. The editor hands over the pairing's token with a proof of the code typed, and Piwi
   Picker keeps it only when the proof is of its own code: a program that answers on an editor's port never sees the
   code, so it cannot pair itself.

**Piwi: Pair with Piwi Picker** (**Tools → Piwi → Pair with Piwi Picker** in a JetBrains IDE, also in the status bar
item's menu) opens the pairing panel. A request nobody answers expires after five minutes; a new Pair takes the place
of the one before, an extension denied waits a minute before it asks again, and an editor holds three at once at
most. VS Code windows listen where Piwi Picker looks once Piwi starts; a second window of the same editor leaves the
port to the first.

Without a code, the editor's **Piwi: Copy the pairing address for Piwi Picker** copies `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/…#<token>`,
which Piwi Picker's **Pair with an address** takes. That is the way for a remote window, which Piwi Picker does not
find on its own: [Remote development](/guide/remote-development).

Every test run Piwi starts gets the pairing address and token as `PIWI_EDITOR_SEND`, so a locator picked at one of its
stops reaches the editor: such a run starts the listener and creates the token if there is none. The capture fixtures
hide it from the processes a test starts; the Playwright runner and its `webServer` still have it, and programs
running as your user are not kept out.

## The pairing panel

The editor shows the pairing in a panel of its own: the **Piwi Picker** view of the Piwi panel in VS Code, the
**Piwi Picker** tab of the Piwi tool window in a JetBrains IDE. It lists a request that waits, with **Type the
code…** and **Deny**; once paired, the browser it is paired with and since when, when Piwi Picker was last heard from (it asks for
the runs while its Runs window is open), and the port it reaches the editor on. Not paired, it says how to pair.

**Unpair** there (**Piwi: Unpair Piwi Picker**) gives the editor a new token, after asking: Piwi Picker, and any run
started before, reach it again only once paired again. Each JetBrains IDE keeps a token of its own, so Unpair in one
leaves the others paired. The connections to the runs Piwi Picker holds already last
until the editor service restarts. In VS Code, a window that kept the port of an earlier pairing
outside 7247 to 7251 moves to one of them.

## What the pairing reaches

The editor listens on the loopback interface only, answers only a request addressed to `127.0.0.1` or `localhost` at
its port, and accepts one only with the token. Before Piwi Picker sends the token, the editor proves it holds it, so
another program that took the port is sent nothing; the settings ask for that proof as they open and after
**Pair**. With several VS Code windows open, the one holding the paired port receives; when it closes, another open
window takes the port within seconds, unless every other one already listens on a port of its own for a run it
started meanwhile.

Piwi Picker's background worker reaches the editor's services on `127.0.0.1` only once the paired port proves it holds
the pairing's token ([how the pieces connect](./editor-run-control#how-it-works)), as the desktop app proves it holds
its own. The Runs window talks to that worker alone, and makes no network call of its own. An older editor extension
gives the image and the controls alone.

## Windows that open and close

An editor window you open later shows in the Runs window within seconds: each window's service names the others,
without their tokens, and the worker asks the paired editor for them. While the Runs window is open, it also asks
every minute. A run whose window stops answering stays listed, grayed and as last heard, until that window answers
again, ten minutes at most, and a stop's **Watch** starts again then.

## When the editor does not answer

A line under the Runs window's title says how each paired tool stands, a broken pairing included, with **Look again**
or **Open the settings** where its sentence needs them. When the paired port answers without proving it holds the
token, the worker asks a few times more, then once a minute while the Runs window is open: click Piwi Picker's
**Pair** again if the editor moved to another port. One that answers with no proof and no such page is not
your editor's Piwi extension. While no window of a paired tool answers, the popup's **Runs** tile stays, muted, and
the Runs window says why.

## Related

- [Runs window](./runs-window): the runs it follows, and their controls.
- [Record tests from the editor](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker): what Send to editor inserts.
- [Remote development](/guide/remote-development): the pairing address of a remote window.
- [Browser extension](./extension): Piwi Picker's other tools, and its permissions.

# Pick an element

**Pick an element**, in the [Piwi Picker](./extension) popup or with its shortcut, ranks the Playwright locators of one
element of the page you are looking at, checks each against the page, and writes what a test needs around it. This
page is where the pick itself, the narrowing of a locator that finds several elements and the copy forms are
explained; the [DevTools sidebar](./devtools#the-elements-sidebar), the [lint overlay](./lint-overlay) and the
[Tested elements](./tested-elements) replacements reuse them.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-pick.png" alt="The ranked locators of a Checkout button, the unique one first">
  <figcaption>Pick an element: the locator that finds exactly one element comes first.</figcaption>
</figure>

## How a pick works

Hover highlights, a click picks. The pick snaps to the nearest actionable ancestor (the text inside a button picks
the button), and ↑/↓ walk the DOM tree, showing the locator each step would produce. When a locator that is not
brittle already finds the element alone, the results open at once, and **Scope to a parent…** in them opens the
**anchors** step: stable parents to scope the locator to, each listed with its strongest hook (a test id, an `id`, a
labeled landmark, a role), with a live match count, after which the results show again
with the scoped locators. When none finds it alone, the anchors step comes first.

<figure>
  <video src="/videos/picker-pick-loop.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline controls aria-label="Picking on a shop page: the outline and the locator follow the pointer, the arrow keys walk up to the parents and back, and a click on Checkout opens its ranked locators"></video>
  <figcaption>Hover, walk the tree with ↑ and ↓, click: the ranked locators open.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Enter** picks too: the highlighted element when the pointer is on one, otherwise the element that has the keyboard
focus, so a control reached with Tab is picked without the mouse. **Esc** cancels the pick.

Elements inside a web component's open shadow root are picked like any other: ↑ walks out of the shadow root through
its host element, and the anchors step lists the host and its parents and counts the matches inside open shadow roots,
as Playwright's locators do.

Every candidate uses the names Playwright computes (a tab with a count badge is `{ name: 'Regressions 5' }`), is
scored as the dashboard scores locators, and run against the page. Those that find only the picked element come
first; a narrowed one ranks just under the candidate it was built from.

## Narrowing a locator that finds several

A candidate that finds the picked element among others is narrowed, trying in this order and keeping the first that
finds the element alone:

1. **Exact**: the name or text matched exactly (`exact: true`).
2. **The element's own text**: `.filter({ hasText })` with its text, when that text is short. Controls that share a
   name often still say different things.
3. **A parent with a test id unique on the page**, the author's own hook.
4. **The repeated row, list item or card** the element sits in: the nearest ancestor whose copies hold the other
   elements the candidate finds. The copies are recognized by a shared test id, else a shared tag and role, else a
   shared readable class. The container is picked by its own accessible name when its author gave it one
   (`aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`), else by a short text it shows and no other copy contains: a heading first, then
   a text that names rather than counts (a name before a price or a quantity), the shorter first, and a visible text
   before a hidden one:
   `getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: 'Blue mug' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })`.
5. **The nearest landmark**, or a named dialog, region, form, row, list item or other named group around it.

Only when none of these finds it alone is it offered with `.first()` or `.nth()`, and a warning, which the
[stability rules](/reference/locator-stability) mark as a position.

## The results

While the results are open, the picked element stays outlined on the page, and the results move to the other side of
the page when they would cover it. **Pick another** closes them and starts picking the next element, without going
back to the popup or the shortcut.

Each locator leads with a word: `stable`, `watch` or `brittle` for one that finds the element alone, by what the
[stability rules](/reference/locator-stability#levels) say of it, and `unique by position`, `3 matches` or
`not checked` otherwise, the words the DevTools sidebar uses. Its **Details** give the reasons
(`unique · brittle: CSS class`) and the stability score.

## Copy as a locator, an action or an assertion

Every locator Piwi Picker offers, here, in the DevTools sidebar and in the Locators console, copies three ways, and
each button names what it writes, such as **Action (fill)** or **Assertion (toHaveText)**:

- **Locator**: `page.` and the locator.
- **Action**: the call the element calls for, `fill` with what a field holds (`'value'` for an empty field or a
  password), `check` for a checkbox or a radio, `selectOption` for a select (an array for several options), `click` for
  anything else.
- **Assertion**: the element's first [suggestion](#assertion-suggester) (`not.toBeChecked` for an unchecked box), and
  `toHaveCount` for a locator that finds several elements.

Where the element is not known, the action is a `click` and the assertion `toBeVisible`. **Copy all** copies every
ranked locator, one per line, for a project's [Locators page](./locator-usage#the-locators-page). **Add to session**
names a locator for the session that the DevTools Piwi panel's Session tab lists and copies as a page object, as the
Elements sidebar does (see [Developer tools](./devtools)).

## Multi-pick

Pick two or three similar items (rows, cards) to get the pattern they share, such as
`getByRole('row').filter({ hasText: … })`. Pick the same button in two rows or cards (Delete, Add to cart) and the
pattern is the button inside the repeated row or card, with how many elements it finds on the page:
`getByTestId('product-card').getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })`, then each pick as its card filtered by a
text only that card shows, such as its heading. It warns when only `.nth()` could tell them apart.

## Assertion suggester

With the popup's **Assertions** tile, pick an element to get the `expect(...)` candidates that apply to it, most telling first (`toHaveValue`,
`toBeChecked`, `toContainText` with the start of a long text, `toHaveText`, `toHaveAccessibleName`, `toBeVisible`),
built on its top-ranked locator. `toHaveAccessibleName` is offered only for an
element that has a name, as Playwright computes it: a paragraph takes none from its text, a field takes its label's.

## Copy context for agent

With the popup's **Agent context** tile, pick an element to copy one block for a coding agent: the page URL, the element and every ranked locator.

## Related

- [Browser extension](./extension): the other tools, the permissions and the limits
- [Developer tools](./devtools): the same ranking for the element selected in DevTools
- [Lint overlay](./lint-overlay): the elements no stable locator finds alone
- [Locator stability](/reference/locator-stability): the rules behind the words
- [Fix a broken locator](/recipes/broken-locator): from a failing locator to the one to use instead

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/record-actions -->

# Record a test

**Record**, the first tile of Piwi Picker's popup (`1`), captures what you do on a site, across its pages, and turns it
into a runnable Playwright test. The same recording becomes a [bug report](./report-a-bug) once you mark something
the page gets wrong; this page covers the recording itself and a test that passes.

<figure>
  <video src="/videos/picker-record-loop.mp4" autoplay loop muted playsinline controls aria-label="Recording on a shop page: a search typed, a mug added to the cart, a coupon applied, each counted on the recording bar as a step, then Finish opens the finish panel with the steps and the test to copy"></video>
  <figcaption>Each action becomes a step on the bar; Finish opens the finish panel.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Starting a recording

The first time on a site, Record asks the browser for access to it, so the recorder can follow you from page to page.
The popup closes once the browser's prompt shows, and the recording starts when you allow it. If you refuse, nothing is
recorded, and the next time you open the popup on that tab and site it says the recording did not start because Piwi
Picker was not allowed there. While the recording runs, a red border marks the tab and the popup's first tile reads **Finish (3)**, with
the number of steps so far.

The recorder captures clicks, double clicks, fills, checks, choices, drags, the names of chosen files (never their
content), the keys that submit, close or move through a list, a click on what a hover shows, and the browser's
**Back**, **Forward** and reload as a step to the page they reach. Each element is recorded with up to five locators
that find it alone, ranked, so a replay has others to try when one no longer holds. Passwords are never captured, nor
a card number, its security code or a one-time code in a field whose `autocomplete` names it: the test reads them from
`process.env`.

## The recording bar

A bar in a corner of the page lists the last steps and holds the recording's tools:

- **Check an element**: pick an element, then choose what to check: its text, its value, its name as screen readers
  announce it, or its state (visible or hidden, usable or grayed out). The dialog starts from what the page shows, on
  its **The page shows** line; keeping it records an `expect(…)` that passes.
- **Check the address**: an `expect(page).toHaveURL(…)` of the page you are on, starting from its path.
- **Something is missing**: an element that should be on the page and is not.
- **Screenshot**: the page as it is now, while the debugging protocol takes the screenshots (below).
- **Pause** stops capturing without ending the recording, on every page and tab of it, so signing in or closing a
  banner stays out of the test, until **Resume**.
- **Finish** ends the recording and opens the finish panel.

Changing what a check expects, or naming something missing, marks the page as wrong and makes the recording a bug
report: [Record a bug report](./report-a-bug). When the bar covers something you need to click, its four-arrow button
(**Move this bar to another corner**) moves it to the next corner, where it stays on every page. Under its buttons, the
bar lists the [test functions](#matching-functions) the steps look like, with a connection, then the evidence collected
so far.

## Evidence

Every recording keeps the evidence a bug report needs, whether or not you mark anything wrong: the console errors, the
failed requests, screenshots, a screenshot of each step, and the window's size, which the test sets with
`page.setViewportSize`. In Chrome and Edge it reads them through the browser's
[debugging protocol](./extension#the-debugging-bar), so Chrome shows its bar saying Piwi Picker started debugging the
browser for as long as the recording runs; the recording bar says why, and Chrome's bar goes when you finish. In
Firefox, or once that bar is cancelled, a script in the page reads the console and the requests instead, and the
popup's **Take a screenshot** (`S`), which takes Replay's place while a recording runs, takes the screenshots. What is
kept, and how: [Evidence](./report-a-bug#evidence). Nothing leaves the browser unless you send it.

## The finish panel

**Finish**, on the bar or in the popup, opens the finish panel: a **Title**, filled with the first page's own title (or,
left empty, the first step in words), which names the test; the steps, each step a test function covers marked with its
name; a line summing up the evidence; and a checkbox to keep or leave out the screenshot of each step. Then two rows of
actions:

- **Copy test** copies a runnable Playwright test that opens the addresses as recorded and waits for each page it
  opens. With steps that match your test functions, it calls them, and **Without your functions** copies the same test
  with locators only.
- [**Send to editor**](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker), with an editor paired, inserts it at the editor's
  cursor.
- [**Replay**](./replay-a-bug-report) plays the steps again in the tab, to see that each still finds its element.
- **Copy report** copies the recording as Markdown, **Download .piwibug** saves its steps, its test and its evidence as
  one [file](/reference/bug-report-file). Once a step is [marked wrong](./report-a-bug), **Send to Piwi…**, with a
  connection, sends it to your instance as a bug report after a [preview](./bug-reports#sending-a-report).
- **Discard** drops the recording.

Until you discard it, the popup's first tile reads **Review (7)** and opens the finish panel again. Once a step is marked
wrong, the panel is a bug report's and **Copy test** becomes **Copy failing test**:
[The report](./report-a-bug#the-report).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-record.png" alt="The finish panel after a recording: its title, seven steps and Copy test">
  <figcaption>The finish panel: every step, the test one click away.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Matching functions

With a connection, the recorder loads the [function catalog](./test-functions) of the project mapped to the page and
ranks, while you record, the functions the steps look like, under **Matching test functions** on the bar. In the copied
test, a complete match becomes a call to your function. No AI: it scores your registered functions' DOM patterns.

## Limits

- It follows one site, in the top-level document only: see the [extension's limits](./extension#limits).
- [Recording from the editor](./editor-recording) uses the same bar with the checks only: it marks nothing wrong,
  keeps no evidence and writes the code in the editor instead of a finish panel.

## Related

- [Record a bug report](./report-a-bug): the same recording, with what the page should show and the evidence
- [Replay a recording](./replay-a-bug-report): play recorded steps again in a tab
- [Bug report file](/reference/bug-report-file): what **Download .piwibug** saves, `steps.json` included
- [Send to editor](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker): the test inserted in VS Code or a JetBrains IDE
- [Browser extension](./extension): the other tools, the permissions and the limits

# Lint overlay

The **Lint overlay**, under **Pick** in the [Piwi Picker](./extension) popup, checks every button, link and
field of the page with the ranking [Pick an element](./pick-an-element) uses.

One click outlines every interactive element no stable locator finds alone and says what to add, with a **Copy**
button for each and **Copy as a Markdown checklist** for all of them:

- **A test id named after the element**: its accessible name, label or placeholder, else the nearest heading with the
  role (`data-testid="submit-order"` for a button named "Submit order", `shipping-address-button`), else the role. A
  value the page already uses, or another suggestion took, gets `-2`, `-3`.
- **A test id on the repeated container** when the element sits in a row, a card or a list item whose copies hold the
  same element: named after the text that tells this copy apart (`data-testid="blue-mug"`), with the locator a test
  then uses, `getByTestId('blue-mug').getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })`. The container and the text are
  chosen as [Pick an element narrows a locator](./pick-an-element#narrowing-a-locator-that-finds-several), and the
  overlay also counts copies that share only their tag, which no locator tells apart until they get a test id. The
  container is outlined in amber.
- **A scope** when those copies already share a test id: no attribute to add, the locator filters by the copy's text,
  `getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: 'Blue mug' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })`.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-lint.png" alt="Four unnamed wishlist icon buttons outlined in their product cards, each with a test id named after its card's heading">
  <figcaption>Lint overlay: four icon buttons without a name; each gets a test id named after its card's heading. The Add
  to cart buttons beside them are not listed: the ranking finds each one through its card.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Related

- [Pick an element](./pick-an-element): the ranked locators of one element
- [Locator stability](/reference/locator-stability): what makes a locator stable
- [Browser extension](./extension): the other tools and the permissions

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/tested-elements -->

# Tested elements

Open a page of your application, and see which of its elements your tests reach, through which
tests, and which buttons, links and fields no test reaches. **Tested elements** is a tool of the
[Piwi Picker extension](./extension), connected to your Piwi instance: open it from the toolbar
popup, or press `T` with the popup open.

It reads the project's [locator index](./locator-usage), the locator chains your tests used in
their steps, and evaluates each chain on the page the way Playwright would: roles and accessible
names, text and label matching, test ids (with the project's `testIdAttribute`), CSS and XPath,
`filter()`, `and()`/`or()`, `nth()`, open shadow roots and same-origin frames. Nothing about the
page is sent to your instance: the index comes down, the matching happens in the tab.

## Reading the overlay

- **Green boxes** are elements tests act on: click, fill, check, select, press.
- **Blue boxes** are elements tests only assert on (`toBeVisible`, `toHaveText`, …).
- **Dashed amber boxes** are visible buttons, links and fields that no test reaches.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/tested-elements-overlay.png" alt="A shop page under the Tested elements overlay: green and blue boxes with test counts on the search field, filters and Add to cart buttons, dashed amber boxes on the favorite buttons, the newsletter form and the footer links, and the side panel counting 14 tested and 20 untested elements">
  <figcaption>Fourteen elements reached by eight tests, twenty reached by none: the newsletter form, the favorite buttons, the footer links.</figcaption>
</figure>

Each box carries the number of tests that reach it; **Heat map** shades the boxes by that number
instead. A dotted border means every locator reaching the element matches several elements on
this page: the test may use it on another page, or in a state where only one of them exists.

Hovering a box shows the locators and tests behind it, clicking pins that card, and each test
links to its page in the dashboard. **Find these locators in Piwi ↗** opens the project's
[Locators page](./locator-usage#the-locators-page) with the element's locators already checked.

The side panel sums up the page: how many of its interactive elements a test reaches, how many
none does, and how many tests have locators resolving here. Its tabs list the matched
elements, the tests, the elements no test reaches (**Not tested**), each with a filter, and the brittle locators
([**At risk**](#brittle-locators)). A row of **Not tested**
copies a ranked locator for that element, to start writing its test. The page is re-checked as it
changes, so opening a menu or a dialog adds what the tests reach inside it.

## One element at a time

**Limit to an element**, in the panel, narrows the view to one part of the page: point at it
and click, with `↑` to widen the outline to its container and `↓` to narrow it back. The click
that chooses never reaches the page, so a link or a button is chosen without being followed or
pressed. The boxes, the summary and the tabs then count only the element and what is
inside it: a form, a card, a menu.

**Around it** lists the tested elements that contain it: a test checking that the product card
is visible reaches the card, not the button inside it, which is a weaker answer. Clicking one
moves the view to that container, **Container ↑** does the same one level up, and **Whole page**
or **Esc** drops the limit.

Picking an element with the extension, while connected, gives the same answer without opening
the overlay: under its ranked locators, the tests that reach the element itself, those that
reach only something inside it, and those that reach only a container around it, each with
the actions they run. **Show tested elements inside it** opens the overlay limited to that
element. [**Copy all**](./pick-an-element#copy-as-a-locator-an-action-or-an-assertion) copies every ranked
locator for the [Locators page](./locator-usage#the-locators-page) of the dashboard.

## This page

When the index knows the [page each locator ran on](./locator-usage#pages), which the capture fixtures record, the
panel opens on **This page**: what tests do on the page you are on, `/checkout` or `/orders/:id`, plus the uses whose
page no run recorded. A **Save** button a test clicks on `/settings` does not light up a lookalike on `/profile`; its
row under **Not tested** says which locator matches it and where tests use it. **All pages** counts every locator that
matches here, as without the fixtures.
A site served under a path the tests never saw (`/app/checkout` for `/checkout`) needs the
[path prefix](./extension-connection#url-patterns) on its URL pattern, and a suite that ran under a path the site does
not use needs the tests' path prefix; the panel's subtitle then names the prefix removed or added.

**At risk** then adds two lists above the brittle locators:

- **Missing here**: locators tests use on this page, to act on an element or to assert it is there, that find nothing
  now. Those used as the page loads come first: a test will fail on them. The others ran after the test acted on the
  page, so the menu or dialog they belong to may just be closed. The collapsed pill counts the first kind.
- **Several match here**: locators tests click or fill on this page that find several elements. Playwright's strict
  mode refuses that action.

Open a preview deployment of a branch with the default branch selected: **Missing here** lists what the default
branch's tests will not find, before the branch's suite runs. The lists follow the page as it changes.

## Brittle locators

The overlay marks an element a [brittle locator](/reference/locator-stability#levels) finds with an orange corner;
**Brittle**, in the panel, hides the marks. A locator at the *Watch* level reads **Watch** on the element's card, followed by the rules that flag it.

The **At risk** tab lists the brittle locators finding something on the page, those used by a failing or flaky test
first, then those shared by the most tests, with their tests and call sites. For one that finds a single element, it
offers a replacement, or says to give the element a test id, as
[Replacements](/reference/locator-stability#replacements) explains. **Copy the change** copies each call site with the
old and the new locator. The element's card says the same next to the locator, and picking the element with the
extension names the brittle locators finding it.

## Setting it up

1. Connect the extension to your instance and map the application's URLs to its project: see
   [Extension connection](./extension-connection). A mapping can
   name the branch deployed at those URLs, a staging site on `develop` for instance: the
   overlay then shows what that branch's tests reach, as the [Locators page](./locator-usage#branches)
   reads a branch. The branch select in the panel changes it for the rest of the browser session.
2. Let a few runs arrive. The index fills in from the steps the reporter already sends: see the
   [requirements](./locator-usage#requirements-and-limits). With the
   [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures), it also records the page of each use.
3. For projects that set `testIdAttribute` in their Playwright config, the reporter records it
   with each run, and `getByTestId` reads that attribute on the page.

The extension keeps a copy of the index for a minute, then downloads it again in the background;
the panel's **Refresh** downloads it now.

## What it does not tell you

- **Where the test used the locator, without the capture fixtures.** A chain is then matched on
  whatever page you're on: `getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' })` used on the settings page also
  outlines a **Save** button on the profile page. The card lists the call sites, so you can check.
- **States the page is not in.** Only what is in the DOM now is matched: a closed menu, another
  step of a wizard, or content behind a login shows once the page shows it.
- **Locators the index skips**: chains cut short, `locator.describe()`, and locators used only
  through getters such as `textContent()`, as listed in the
  [index limits](./locator-usage#requirements-and-limits).
- **Cross-origin frames**, which an extension's page script cannot read, and a few selectors that
  depend on layout (`:left-of()`, `:near()`, …), listed under the panel's **Notes**.
- **While a modal dialog is open**, the browser keeps the rest of the page inert: the boxes stay
  visible, and the panel works again once the dialog closes.

A green box says a test reached the element, not that the test checks what matters about it. Use
it to find what nothing reaches, and to see which tests to read before changing an element.

## Related

- [Who uses a locator](./locator-usage): the same index, read from a locator rather than a page
- [Browser extension](./extension): install Piwi Picker and connect it
- [Locator stability rules](/reference/locator-stability): what makes a locator brittle, and how its replacement is
  chosen

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/devtools -->

# Developer tools

The [Piwi Picker extension](./extension) answers one question beside the browser's own DevTools: what will a test see
on this page, and how does the test get there? Its developer tools live here rather than in the toolbar popup, which
keeps the tools that act on the page. In Chrome and Edge, the
[request conditions](./mock-requests#slow-down-or-fail-a-request) and a viewport set in the tab itself go through the
browser's debugging protocol, under Chrome's [debugging bar](./extension#the-debugging-bar).

## The Elements sidebar

Open DevTools, go to **Elements**, and choose the **Piwi** tab beside Styles and Computed. Select a node and the pane
lists its locators, ranked and checked against the page as it is, the same list [Pick an element](./pick-an-element)
shows:

```
getByTestId('cart-button')                        ✓ unique · stable
getByRole('button', { name: 'Cart, 2 items' })    ✓ unique · watch: number in text
getByText('🛒 2')                                 ✓ unique · stable
```

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/picker-devtools.png" alt="The Piwi pane in the Elements sidebar: the selected button's three locators, ranked, the test id first">
  <figcaption>The pane for a selected button: each locator checked against the page, copied as a locator, an action or an assertion.</figcaption>
</figure>

A locator that finds the node among others says how many it finds. Under each one, **Locator**, **Action** and
**Assertion** copy it [as Pick an element does](./pick-an-element#copy-as-a-locator-an-action-or-an-assertion). **Add to session** puts it
in the session under a name (the panel's Session tab, below). With an editor
[paired](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker), **Send to editor** under the top locator inserts it at the
editor's cursor, in the copy form you chose last. The pane ranks again when the selection changes and after
the page navigates; **Refresh** ranks the same node on the page as it is now. DevTools' own element picker
(`Ctrl+Shift+C`, `Cmd+Shift+C` on macOS) selects what the pointer is on.

The first time on a site, the pane asks for access to it with **Allow on this site**, as recording does. It is not
needed on a tab where you have just used the toolbar popup.

Elements inside an iframe are not ranked: their locator would need the frame's prefix, and
[Pick an element](./extension#limits) sees the top-level document only too. The **Locators** console below finds
elements in same-origin frames.

## The Piwi panel

DevTools also gets a **Piwi** panel of its own, with the tabs below. It shows what runs on the page and stays up while the
page navigates; the recording and replay panels on the page stay too, for when DevTools is closed.

- **Record** lists a recording's steps as they are captured, each with the locator it was recorded with. A recording
  is finished from its bar on the page or from the popup, which collect the last evidence; once it is, **Copy test**
  copies its test, the failing one when a step is marked wrong, and **Discard** drops it, as the
  [finish panel](./record-actions#the-finish-panel) does.
- **Replay** lists a replay's steps with their results and the verdict once it ends. **Pause**, **Continue**, **Next
  step** and **Stop** act on the replay running in the page.
- **Network** lists the page's `fetch` and XHR requests, from DevTools' own log while it is open; **Other sites too**
  adds the requests to other origins. Select one to mock it, slow it down or make it fail: [Mock and slow down requests](./mock-requests).
- **Locators** is the locator console: type a locator and the elements it finds are listed, as Playwright finds
  them, with the strict-mode verdict. It reads the expression, never runs it: every `getBy*`, `locator()`, chains,
  `filter()`, `and()`/`or()`, `.nth()` and same-origin frames. Hovering one outlines it on the page, and **Reveal**
  selects it in the Elements panel. **Enter** tries the locator at once and keeps it in a history that the up and down
  arrows go through, as in a shell; the history lasts until the browser closes, so the panel opened again shows the
  last locator. Under the field, **Copy as** writes it
  [as a locator, an action or an assertion](./pick-an-element#copy-as-a-locator-an-action-or-an-assertion), for the
  first match. **Add to session** names it for the Session tab. With an editor paired,
  [**Send to editor**](./editor-recording#send-from-piwi-picker) inserts it at the editor's cursor in the copy form
  chosen last. A `page.` typed in front is left out of what is copied or sent.
- **Session** lists the elements named with **Add to session**, and copies them as a page object, a Markdown table or
  JSON.

The toolbar starts the popup's tools on the inspected page without leaving DevTools:
[**Pick an element**](./pick-an-element), the [**Lint overlay**](./lint-overlay), and **Tested elements**, which shows
what your tests reach once Piwi Picker is connected to your instance and the site is mapped to a project (the button
says what is missing until then). In a narrow panel the tools show their icons alone, named by their tooltips. The
first time on a site, the click asks for access to it, as recording does. Then **Viewport**, **Playwright view** and **Save login for tests** set the page up for a test (below).

## Save login for tests

**Save login for tests**, in the Piwi panel's toolbar, saves the site's login as the
file Playwright's `storageState` reads: the site's cookies, `httpOnly` ones included, which a page's scripts cannot
read, and its `localStorage`. IndexedDB is left out. **Save login file** asks, the first time, for permission to read
that one site's cookies, on any of its ports and on its parent domains, where a login cookie is often set, then
downloads `user.json`:

```ts
test.use({ storageState: 'playwright/.auth/user.json' });
```

The file logs anyone in as you until the session expires: save it with a test account, as
`playwright/.auth/user.json`, and add `playwright/.auth` to `.gitignore`. The page offers both lines, and a setup test
that refreshes the file.

## Open this page at a viewport

**Viewport**, in the Piwi panel's toolbar, shows a bar that opens the inspected page in a new window whose viewport,
not its outer frame, has the size of one of your Playwright projects: **Mobile Safari (390×664)**. With a connection, the sizes come from the `use.viewport`
the [reporter](/guide/reporter) sends with each run, per project; without one, or for another size, choose **Size typed
by hand**. In Chrome and Edge, **In this tab** gives the tab itself that viewport instead, as DevTools' device toolbar
does, until **Back to the window's size**. Either way it sizes the viewport only, without touch, device pixel ratio or
user agent.

## Playwright view

**Playwright view**, in the Piwi panel's toolbar, labels the page as a test sees it: each button, link, field, heading and
landmark with the role and name `getByRole` finds it by, such as `button · Apply coupon` or `link · Cart (2)`, and its
test id beside it when it has one. Two marks point at the elements a test will struggle with:

- **Red**: no stable locator reaches it. A `<div>` with a click handler, a `tabindex` or a pointer cursor but no role,
  or a button or link with no name, and no test id either.
- **Amber**: its `getByRole` finds other elements too, two buttons both named "Show popup", or "Save" beside "Save
  draft". A test needs `exact: true`, a scope or `.nth()`.

The labels follow scrolling and come back after the page changes. Labels of elements side by side never cover one
another: each sits above its element, or a row or a few lower or higher when that place is taken. Where elements crowd
too closely for that, the labels left over are not drawn and the panel says how many. The panel in the corner counts
each kind, and **Role** shows the labels of one role only. Hidden elements get no label, as `getByRole` does not find them. Press
**Esc** to turn it off. The [lint overlay](./lint-overlay) stays for suggesting the test ids to
add.

## Related

- [Browser extension](./extension): install Piwi Picker and connect it
- [Pick an element](./pick-an-element): the ranked locators of any element on the page
- [Mock and slow down requests](./mock-requests): answer, slow down or fail the page's requests
- [Lint overlay](./lint-overlay): the elements a test would struggle to find

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/mock-requests -->

# Mock and slow down requests

The **Network** tab of the Piwi panel in [Developer tools](./devtools) lists the page's `fetch` and XHR requests. Select
one to write it as a mock for a test, or to try the page under a slow or failing request.

## Mock this response

Select a request in the Network tab and the panel writes it as a route for a test:

```ts
await page.route('**/api/cart?_=*', (route) =>
  route.fulfill({
    json: { items: [{ sku: 'SPRING-TEE', qty: 1 }], total: 40 },
  }),
);
```

The URL pattern drops the origin and turns the query values that change on every request (a timestamp, a cache
buster) into `*`; edit it before copying. A status other than 200 is kept, and a method other than GET is checked.
**Answer with** switches to a server error (500) or a network failure (`route.abort()`), for testing the page's
error state. A body over 100 kB goes to a file the route reads, such as `mocks/cart.json`, downloaded beside the code.

Until you tick **Show hidden values**, credentials are written as `<hidden>`:

- **By name**: the whole value of a JSON field, a form field or a query parameter named like a password, a token, a
  key, a signature, a session or a cookie, whatever it holds.
- **By shape**, anywhere in the body, a JSON text inside a JSON string included: a JWT, a `Bearer` or `Basic`
  credential, a private key, a cookie a `Set-Cookie:` line sets, a key with a service's prefix (AWS, Google, Stripe,
  GitHub, GitLab, Slack, OpenAI, npm, Twilio), and a random token of 40 characters or more.
- **Kept**: ids, hashes and slugs (a UUID, a number, a git SHA, a file id shorter than 40 characters) and base64 that
  encodes text, such as a pagination cursor.

The URL pattern keeps the host, matches a hidden query value with `**` and a path segment shaped like a credential
with `*`. Headers, cookies included, are never written. A body that is neither JSON nor a form is written as the
server sent it but for those values: read it before you commit it. Nothing is sent anywhere: the code reaches your
clipboard when you copy it.

## Slow down or fail a request

Under a selected request, the Network tab also offers **Slow down** by the seconds you type, **Fail with 500** and
**Fail (network error)**: the flaky conditions a test has to survive, tried by hand in your own tab. The first time,
Piwi Picker asks for access to the site. From then on the tab's requests to that URL wait, answer 500 or fail, on every
page of the site in that tab, until you remove the condition, click **Turn all off and reload**, or close the tab. A
banner on the page says which conditions are on, with **Turn off**; other tabs are not affected.

In Chrome and Edge, a condition reaches any request, documents, scripts and images included (tick **Every kind** to
list them), and the toolbar's **Network** and **CPU** throttle the whole page as DevTools does: fast or slow 3G,
offline, or a CPU 4, 6 or 20 times slower. They go through the [debugging protocol](./extension#the-debugging-bar):
Chrome shows its debugging bar until you turn them all off, and **Cancel** on it ends the throttling, leaving the
requests' conditions to the page's `fetch` and XHR calls. Firefox has only those: documents, scripts, images and a
service worker's requests go past, and a page that replaces `fetch` itself may behave differently.

A replay started while a condition is on runs under it, and its panel says which conditions were on, beside the
verdict.

- [Developer tools](./devtools): the Piwi panel and its other tabs
- [Browser extension](./extension): the permissions these use
- [Replay a recording](./replay-a-bug-report): a replay under the conditions on
