# Local runs tray

The **Local runs** tray of the [desktop app](./desktop) lists every run the app starts: a **Re-run**, a reproduction, a
bisect, a [Flake Lab](./flake-lab) run, a bug report's run, a run an agent started. It is docked at the bottom of the
window, under the page, and opens as a run starts and at each stop. Drag its top edge to resize it, or **Maximize**
it; the window remembers its height. While it is open, the run page's **On your machine** card points to it.
**Local runs**, at the foot of the sidebar, opens and closes it, and so do `g` then `t`. Closing it stops nothing.
This page is about the runs the tray lists: how far each is, **Stop**, **Run again**, the code their stops make, their
output, a reload and a restart. Each
run's workers, their stops and their page: [Desktop app runs](./desktop-runs).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/desktop-runs-tray.png" alt="The desktop app's window, the Local runs tray docked under the run page: on its left three runs, the newest counted 5 of 12 tests, 1 failed, and waiting at a stop; on its right that run's worker stopped at its page.pause() with Resume, Step and Finish and its page">
  <figcaption>A run that goes on, counted as its own process counts its tests.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Each run

A run says how far it is as its own process counts its tests: **5 of 12 tests · 1 failed**, a test held at its
failure among the failed, then the flaky ones and those [ended at a stop](./end-the-test). Its run button on the page
and the sidebar's entry, **1 local run** while it goes on, count the same. Before its first test, and with a reporter that does not count,
the run counts the results Playwright prints.

Once it reported to the app, a run links **Open run #N**, and **Compare with run #N** when its tests come from another
run. A failed one leads to its failure: **Open the failure**, on the run and in the message at its end, opens the
page of its first failed test, the one its process named first; the run's page when the run names none. A run of
several Playwright projects reports one run for each: the failure is the first one of the first project that failed,
in that project's run. **Run again**
starts an ended run as it ran, with its options and its [**Hold failures**](./watch-a-run#hold-failures).

**Stop** ends a run as `Ctrl+C` would in a terminal: Playwright stops its workers and the reporter still sends the
run's end. While it winds down, the button gives way to **Force stop**, which kills the process at once, beside
**Ends within 10 s**, after which the app kills it anyway. Force stop takes no click for a moment, so a double-click
only stops. [Piwi Runner](./piwi-runner) stops a run the same way.

An ended run lists the tests it failed on above its output, failed then flaky, each with its project, the first lines
of its error and its file, to open in your editor. They come from its runs on the dashboard, else from its output.
Each has **Open**; a test of a run of tests also has **Run again**, for that test alone, and **Run again with Hold
failures** when the run can hold.

An ended run's **More actions** menu holds **Copy the command**, for a run of tests: the command that runs them in
your terminal, as the run button's **Copy as command** writes it, and **Remove from the list**; **Clear finished
runs** removes all of them. While the tray is
closed, a run that ends marks the sidebar's **Local runs** with a dot, red when it failed, until you open the tray.

**Open the run in a separate window**, the run's window button, shows the whole run in a window of its own:
its **Stop** or **Run again**, **Hold failures**, links, workers, failures and output. **Run again** there runs in
that window; a link opens in the app's window. **Show in the tray**, closing the window, or that button, now **Show
the run here**, brings it back. The window stays open whatever page the app shows and through a reload, and closes as
its run leaves the tray and with the app; one the reloaded tray shows no run in closes.

A reproduction, a bisect step or a Flake Lab run that went to the editor open on the project's linked folder
([A reproduction in your editor](./desktop-runs#a-reproduction-in-your-editor)) says where its tests wait,
**In Visual Studio Code**, read only, with no **Hold failures**: the editor holds them. Its line is marked while one
waits, **Stop** still ends it, and it ends with its own verdict.

## Stops while you look elsewhere

The tray opens at each stop, where a headless test waits for you. With the window in the background, the system tells
you of a failure or a `page.pause()`, never of a step or a pause you asked for. The window listens on every page, again
as soon as it reloads while a run of the app goes on. On a page without the tray (an analytics dashboard in TV mode,
an error page), the system tells you of every stop, whatever the window shows, and no failure is held; a
`page.pause()`, a step or a breakpoint waits until the tray shows it again, or [Piwi Picker's Runs
window](./runs-window) or [an agent](./desktop-runs#for-agents) answers it. With no run of the app going on, the window
stops listening, and a stop goes on at once.

## The runs list

On its left (a select in a narrow window), the tray lists **Running now**, **Started in another window**, then
**Finished**. A line of its own says how its run stands and how long it ran; any line is marked while a test waits
at a stop. A click shows the run on the right: its command, actions, links, workers, failures and output. A run that
starts or stops is shown, unless you are working in the run shown.

## Code from the runs

The app holds no editor, so the code a stop of its runs makes comes to the tray, under **Code from the runs**:

- **Assert a region** picks a region of the page, once you watch a headless stop live: its ARIA snapshot becomes a
  `toMatchAriaSnapshot` check.
- **Mock a request** lists the page's fetch and XHR responses, credentials hidden: the one you choose becomes a
  `page.route`, with what to review in it.
- **A locator picked**, on the image or with the pause bar's **Pick a locator**, shows with the line it was picked
  for.
- **An agent's code** (`code_write`) comes here too ([for agents](./desktop-runs#for-agents)).

Each code shows the line it goes above and, apart, its import lines, each with **Copy**, made from the file as it is
on disk in the folder linked to the project.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/desktop-run-live-code.png" alt="Code from the runs in the desktop app's tray: a mocked request, the page.route call to write above tests/checkout.spec.ts:18, with Copy">
  <figcaption>A mocked request, as code to copy above the stopped line.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Its output

Each run shows its output under its workers, in Playwright's terminal colors, following its newest line until you
scroll up; **Go to the latest line** follows it again. Above it, a field keeps only the lines holding what you type,
case and accents ignored; **Go to the first error** scrolls to the first failure Playwright printed; a toggle wraps
long lines; and **Copy output** copies every line the tray keeps, without the colors. Its corner drags it taller.

## A reload

A reload of the window keeps the tray's runs. A run still going is followed again: its output goes on, with its
**Hold failures**, its separate window, and how far each of its ended projects came, as you left them. A run whose
step ended during the reload ends with that step's exit code, and goes on to its next step if it has one; a
reproduction, a bisect or a Flake Lab job that ended meanwhile still records its verdict, once. A run of tests that
was starting, its first Playwright project or its next, goes on with the one the app started. Any other run that was
starting as the window reloaded ends, saying so: run it again. What the run printed while the window reloaded is lost, and the tray
keeps the last 300 lines of each run's output through a reload.

The last 15 runs that ended outlive a restart of the app, with their last 300 lines of output, **Run again** and their
links. Each shows how long it took instead of its counts.

## Limits

- **One window's runs.** Another window of the app lists its own; this tray lists them under **Started in another
  window**, their workers shown as you choose one or a test of theirs stops.
- **A run that reports to the team instance** (a run it asked for) has no **Open run #N**, **Compare with run #N** or **Open the
  failure** here: under its workers, **Run #78 · Open** opens its page on the instance in your browser.

## Related

- [Desktop app runs](./desktop-runs): each worker, its stops, its page and the code a stop makes.
- [Desktop app](./desktop): what it runs, and how it links a project to its folder.
- [Share a local run live](./share-live): let a teammate watch a run of the tray.

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/run-on-my-machine -->

# Run on my machine

Run on my machine lets a signed-in person ask the desktop app or [Piwi Runner](./piwi-runner) on their own machine to
run tests they found on the dashboard; either one is enough. The instance carries the request; the app asks them before every run, in its own window, and runs the tests
in their own folder. The run it starts reports back to the instance as a **requested run**: theirs alone, and kept
out of everything the team sees.

## Experimental

**Experimental.** Run on my machine is off by default. The design is in the
[Run on my machine design record](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/proposals/run-on-my-machine.md).

## Turn it on

An administrator turns it on in **Settings → Capabilities → Off until turned on → Run on my machine → Turn on**, and
off the same way. It needs [sign-in](/operate/authentication) turned on: a request belongs to the person who made it,
so an instance without accounts refuses it. A project admin declines it for one project in **Project → Settings →
Capabilities**, which lists it while the instance has it on.

Turned off or declined, the instance refuses every request for that project, and a connected app receives none.

## Who may ask

- **Contributors and up** may ask (`run:request`), on the projects where they hold the role. A Contributor cannot
  submit a run with an API key, and need not: the app reports a requested run with a key for that one run.
- **Only a signed-in session** creates a request: never an API key, a CI job or an MCP client.
- **A request goes only to the person's own apps**, which take it only on projects where they may run tests.

## Connect the desktop app

In Piwi Desktop, open **Settings → Team instance**, enter the instance's address and click
**Connect**. The app opens the instance's page, which asks you to allow **Piwi Desktop** with the code the app shows.
Once allowed, the app keeps its key in the operating system's keychain (Keychain on macOS, Credential Manager on
Windows, the Secret Service on Linux), never in a file, and holds its connection to the instance open while it runs.
An app connects to one instance at a time. **Disconnect** removes the key from the keychain; the app stays listed in
the instance's Connected apps until you revoke it there. A key the instance revoked leaves the keychain too.

Each project's folder is linked on this machine, per instance, when its first request asks, or beforehand on
**Settings → Team instance**, which lists them with **Unlink**. **Find it for me** looks where your runs came from, for the repository's clones and
in your code folders; a picked folder without the tests gets a better one offered.

## Ask for a run

The run button of a run (its failed tests, or all of them), an execution or a test (that test) lists your apps under
**Where** where the capability is on and you may ask: **Run on my machine**, or **Run on my machine or CI** with
[CI actions](./ci-actions). With an app picked, the dialog offers the run options of **Copy retry command**: headed,
trace, repeat each, workers and, when the tests ran in more than one, the Playwright project. A request holds at most
200 tests; a test with no recorded line is left out, and the dialog says how many.

## In the app

The request opens the desktop app's window, in front: the instance that asked, the project, the tests, the checks of
the linked folder, and the exact command. Nothing runs until you click **Run**:

- **The folder**: linked, with a Playwright config and `@playwright/test` installed, and every spec of the request
  inside it.
- **The commit**: the run's branch and commit against the folder's. On another commit, or with uncommitted changes, the
  tests are picked by their titles (`--grep`) rather than by their lines, which may have moved.
- **One run per folder**: while another run goes on in the folder, the request waits, and is checked again once it
  ends. A command takes at most 24,000 characters.
- **The [environment](./environments)** the request names, which an older app cannot apply, and the
  [run variables](./run-variables) of the project and the environment: listed among the checks; the command starts
  with them.

**Not now** declines it, or refuses it with the checks that failed, and the page says which. A request nobody answers
in the app within 10 minutes ends.

The app takes the command and a key for this one run from its own server, never from the page or the window. That key
starts one run within 30 minutes and nothing else. The run shows in the app's Local runs while it goes on.

## Follow and stop

Once sent, the dialog follows the request: waiting for your app, shown in the app, running, ended with its outcome,
and a link to its run. Until it ends, a row above the project's [runs](./ci-rerun#waiting-rows) shows it to you
alone. **Stop** ends it from the page: the app stops the run, or drops a request it has not run. **Run
again** sends the same tests with the same options. **Settings → Account → Your runs on my machine** lists your last 20
requests and their project, with **Stop** for one still going on. Quitting the app stops its requested runs. A run
that ends while the app's server restarts keeps its outcome. After a crash, the app ends the requests it lost:
unanswered ones are refused, runs end as errors.

## What leaves your machine

The run's results, as any run reports them: the tests, their steps, errors, attachments, traces and reports, sent to
the instance that asked and seen by you alone. For a requested run, the reporter sends no coverage, test manifest,
code reach or environment details, AI steps only replay, and the run stays out of the desktop app's own dashboard.

The app starts the run with `PIWI_REQUEST_INSTANCE`, the instance that asked, and `PIWI_REQUEST_TOKEN_FILE`, a file
only you can read that holds the key of that one run. The reporter and its workers send the run there with that key,
whatever server and credentials the config names. A file that is missing or holds no key turns the reporter off for
the run, and it says why; on macOS and Linux, so does a file others can read.

## Connected apps

**Settings → Account → Connected apps** lists the apps you connected from their own window: Piwi Picker, an editor, the
desktop app. Each shows when it connected and, for an app that runs tests, **Online now** while its connection is open
and it called the instance within the last two minutes, or else when it was last seen. **Revoke** disconnects one: the
instance closes the connection of an app that runs tests at once, and refuses its next call. An administrator sees the
same list for any user in **Settings → Users → API keys**. The keys these apps hold are not listed under API keys.

The instance sends a connected app each request as it is made, with the time it stops waiting, and the requests still
waiting each time the app connects again. When a waiting request is stopped, or another of your apps takes it, the
instance tells the others to drop it. An app can also ask for its requests instead, where a proxy cuts long connections.

## A requested run is yours alone

A requested run shows to the person who asked for it, and to nobody else:

- **Its own page** opens for you, and reads as not found for anyone else, as do its executions, attachments,
  traces and reports.
- **The test's recent executions** list it for you, marked **On your machine**. The test's pass rate, flaky score and
  history leave it out.
- **No list a project's members read** shows it: the project's runs, search, analytics, the MCP tools.
- **With sign-in turned off, or once its requester is deleted**, nobody sees it.

Run on a branch and a machine the team did not choose, it stays out of everything the team sees: no
failure clusters, flakiness, analytics or baselines; no notifications, pull-request comments or tracker writes; no
coverage, and it never sets the project's default branch. It is never kept forever: retention removes it, and you can
delete it yourself from its page.
Someone who holds `run:delete` on the project can delete it through the API without seeing it.

A [share link](./share-links) you make for one of its executions opens for whoever has the link, as any share link
does, so you can show a teammate what happened on your machine. It appears in the project's list of share links.

## Related

- [Desktop app](./desktop): the app that takes requests
- [Desktop app runs](./desktop-runs): the runs the desktop app starts and how you follow them
- [Share links](./share-links): showing one execution to someone without an account

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/features/compare-with-team -->

# Compare with team instance

A test fails in the desktop app, on your machine. Compare with team instance answers the first question you ask: is it
this machine, or does the CI see it too? The desktop app asks the team instance it is connected to how the same test
does in that project's CI, and shows the answer on the failure's page, with the facts behind it. Nothing runs, and
your run's results, its error and your machine's environment stay on your machine.

## What it shows

On a failing execution, the situation block gets a **Team CI** line:

- **One sentence of conclusion**, from the rules below, with a link to what it read on the team instance: the cluster
  of the same error, or the CI execution.
- **The test's results on the team instance**, one strip per environment its CI ran it in (`mco`, `integration`), the
  environment of your run first, and one strip for your teammates' own runs reported there, each with its pass rate.
  A busy environment never hides the others: each keeps its latest results.
- **Open on the team instance**, which opens the test's page there in your browser.
- **The environment differences from the closest CI pass**, in a side panel.

The test's own page shows the same strips in a **Team CI** card, without the conclusion. Neither shows while the app
is connected to no team instance. Connected, a project whose folder is linked to no team project says so, with a link
to **Settings → Team instance**, where you pick it; a project with no folder on this machine says to link one first,
under **Project → Settings → Local folder**.

The results are the team's CI runs. Your teammates' runs show apart and never count in the conclusion: their machines
are not the reference. A run someone asked for with [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine) is theirs alone and never
shows, nor do Flake Lab and bisect runs.

## The conclusion

The sentence comes from the first rule that applies. When your run has an [environment](./environments), the rules
read that environment's CI results alone, since two deployed environments do not run the same application; the team
instance reads your run's label as it reads a run's, so an alias names its environment. A CI run marked as an
[environment incident](/guide/concepts#environment-incident) never counts.

1. **Same error in CI**: the team instance holds the same error in a [failure cluster](./failure-clusters), seen in CI
   in the last 30 days, in your run's environment. The failure is not specific to your machine. A CI failure a retry
   passed counts too.
2. **Passes in CI on this commit**: the latest CI result on the commit you ran passed, so the failure is likely
   specific to your machine. When your checkout had uncommitted changes, the sentence says so instead.
3. **Fails in CI too**: the latest CI result on your commit, else the latest one, failed. When the fingerprints could
   be compared, the sentence adds that the error is another one than yours.
4. **Passes in CI on another commit**: the latest CI result passed, on a commit that differs from yours or that one of
   the two runs did not record, so there is no conclusion to draw yet.
5. **No CI result to compare with**.

The same error is found by the failure's fingerprint, which both servers compute the same way. When the desktop app and
the team instance run Piwi versions that compute it differently, the sentence never claims the error is new: rule 1 is
left out.

## What differs from the closest CI pass

The [closest CI pass](/guide/concepts#closest-ci-pass) is the passing CI execution your run is compared with. The side
panel lists what differs between the two, as the [environment diff](./evidence) of a failure does against the last
pass: the time zone and locale of the machine and the browser, headless or not, the Playwright, Node and browser
versions, the viewport, the operating system, the CI image. The keys that always differ between a machine and the CI
(the branch, the CI provider, the reporter's version) show apart, as varying naturally. A difference is a fact to
check, never the verdict: the side panel says which run it compared with, and opens it on the team instance.

## Setting it up

- **Connect the desktop app to the team instance**: **Settings → Team instance → Connect**, then allow **Piwi
  Desktop** on the instance's page. The instance needs sign-in turned on, since the connection's key belongs to you.
  The same connection takes [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine) requests where an administrator turned it on; the
  comparison works either way.
- **Link each project's folder to its team project**: on the same page, **Projects and team projects** lists the
  projects of the app that have a folder on this machine; pick the team project of each. The comparison reads the CI
  of the team project the folder is linked to. A Run on my machine request links the folder of its project too. A team
  project has one folder: picking it for another project moves its link there.
- A connection made before the comparison existed cannot compare: the page says so, and connecting again replaces it.

It is on for every project. An administrator declines it for the instance on **Settings → Capabilities**, and a
project in its own settings, where a project can also turn it back on for itself: the team instance then refuses or
serves each comparison by those decisions.

## What leaves your machine

The desktop app sends the team instance the test's name and file, its Playwright project, your run's environment
label, branch and commit, and the fingerprint of the failure. It never sends the error's text, your machine's
environment or your code: it compares the environments itself. It reads only what you could read on the team
instance in a browser, with the key of its connection, and keeps each answer in memory for two minutes.

# Piwi Runner

Piwi Runner takes [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine) requests from one team instance, without the dashboard:
one window for the connection, the confirmation of each request and the runs it started. It is for a machine that only
runs what the instance asks, where the [desktop app](./desktop) and its local dashboard are more than needed. It
keeps no database and serves no dashboard.

## Where it is

- Piwi Runner: Runs the tests a team instance asks for, without the dashboard. Not needed beside the desktop app, which takes the same requests. On the [latest release](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/releases/latest): Windows x64, per user (.exe): `Piwi-Runner_x64-setup.exe`; Windows x64, per machine (.msi): `Piwi-Runner_x64.msi`; macOS, Apple silicon (.dmg): `Piwi-Runner_aarch64.dmg`; Linux x86-64, any distribution (.AppImage): `Piwi-Runner_amd64.AppImage`; Debian, Ubuntu, x86-64 (.deb): `Piwi-Runner_amd64.deb`; Fedora, RHEL, x86-64 (.rpm): `Piwi-Runner_x86_64.rpm`.

Its installers are of the same kinds as the desktop app's, for the same systems, with the same needs and the same
unsigned first start: [the desktop app's installers](./desktop#where-it-is).

## Updates

Piwi Runner checks the latest release when it starts, and a notification says when a newer version is out. **Check for
updates…** in the system tray menu checks again; when one is found, **Install and restart** downloads it, checks its
signature, installs it the way it was installed (`.exe`, `.msi`, `.dmg`, `.AppImage`, `.deb` or `.rpm`) and starts
the new version, after asking to stop the runs still going. Your connection and linked folders stay. **Settings → About**
in its window shows the version installed and where the tray's update and log items are, with links to this page, the
release notes and the page to report a problem. A new release's Piwi Runner files can reach the release a few minutes after the desktop app's; until then the check finds nothing new
or fails, and the next one finds them. On a desktop that shows no tray icon, install a new version from the latest release over
the old one.

## Piwi Runner or the desktop app

You need one of the two, not both. The desktop app takes the same requests, with the same confirmation and checks,
and adds the dashboard on your machine; a requested run can be paused, stepped and watched from either window.
Piwi Runner is for a machine that only runs what the instance asks.

Installed together, they live side by side, and neither installer replaces the other: each has its own name, install
folder, Linux package, settings, linked folders and keychain entry. Connected to the same instance, both are listed in
**Connected apps**, and a request goes to the one you pick on the page.

## Connect it

Until it is connected, its window opens on the instance's address, with the three steps from a test there to its run
here. It connects the way the desktop app does: enter the instance's address and click **Connect**, then allow **Piwi
Runner** on the instance's page with the code the window shows. Its key stays in the operating system's keychain.
Each project's folder is linked on the first request for it. The rest, from the confirmation to **Stop**, is described
in [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine#in-the-app).

Once connected, the top of the window says which instance it takes requests from, with a dot of its state: green while
connected, amber while it connects or the instance does not answer, when a line above the runs also says that its
requests reach the machine again once it answers. A click on it opens the connection's settings.

**Settings** shows a section at a time: **Connection** (the instance, a button that opens it in the browser, and
**Disconnect**, which asks first: connecting again means allowing Piwi Runner on the instance again), **Folders** (the
folder linked to each project, with **Unlink**: the next request for that project asks for its folder again),
**General** (the two background settings and the language) and **About**.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/runner-settings.png" alt="Piwi Runner's Settings on its Connection section: the instance it is connected to, Open piwi.example.com, Disconnect, and the list of sections: Connection, Folders, General and About">
  <figcaption>Settings, on the Connection section; the header says which instance Piwi Runner takes requests from.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Pause and watch a run

Each run Piwi Runner starts shows in its window live, as the desktop app's runs show in its
[Local runs tray](./desktop-runs): each worker's test and where it stands, **Pause**, **Step**, **Resume** and
**Finish**, **Pause all** and **Resume all**, and the stopped test's page, live with **Watch**. A `page.pause()`,
a step or a breakpoint waits in the window until you answer it, and the window comes to the front, on its runs. [**Hold failures**](./watch-a-run#hold-failures),
a switch on each running run you attend, off until you turn it on, keeps a failing test at its line too, until you
resume it. Once the run reported to the instance, it shows **Run #78 · Open**, which opens its page there, and keeps
it after the run ended. A run that goes on while the window reloads shows again, with **Stop**, or **Force stop**
while it winds down.
**Assert a region** and **Mock a request** make their code in the window, to copy: Piwi Runner has no editor and
writes no file. A requested run cannot be [shared live](./share-live): the instance gives it no [live view](./live-view) key, since it
[shows to you alone](./run-on-my-machine#a-requested-run-is-yours-alone). **Inspect** of a watched worker, which reads the test's pages from its trace, is the desktop app's alone.

The runs show as the desktop app's [Local runs](./local-runs-tray) do: the list on the left, the run you pick on the
right, and a select that names it in a narrow window. **Running now** lists the runs going on and **Finished** those
that ended, the last to end first, each line saying how its run stands, whether a test of it waits at a stop, and how
long it ran. A run you confirm shows at once, and a test that stops shows its run, unless you are working in the run
shown. The run shown has its project, when it started and how long it has run, **Stop**, which gives way to
**Force stop** while the run winds down, whether you or the instance stopped it, as in the
[desktop app](./local-runs-tray#each-run), its workers live, the tests the request asked for and its output.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/runner-runs.png" alt="Piwi Runner's runs: on the left, one run under Running now and two under Finished, one failed and one passed; on the right, the run going on, its worker running, with Pause, Watch, Hold failures and Stop">
  <figcaption>The run going on, shown beside the list, its worker live.</figcaption>
</figure>

Once a run ended, its tests say how each came out, as its output tells it, a failed one with the first lines of its
error, and it shows **Run #78 · Open** once it reported to the instance. The output keeps Playwright's colors and its
last 2,000 lines, with a filter, **Go to the first error** and **Copy output**, as the
[desktop app's](./local-runs-tray#its-output) does. **Clear finished** empties the Finished list; the window keeps the
last 15 runs that ended in any case, never dropping one the moment it ends.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/runner-run-results.png" alt="Piwi Runner's runs with the run that failed shown: its two tests, one passed and one failed with its error, and its output in Playwright's colors">
  <figcaption>The run that failed: how each test came out, and its output.</figcaption>
</figure>

Piwi Runner is the hub of its own runs only: Piwi Picker, the editors and an agent reach the runs the desktop app or an
editor starts, not Piwi Runner's.

## In the tray

Closing the window leaves Piwi Runner in the system tray, still connected, so the instance can reach it; a request brings the
window forward. The tray menu has, with the [desktop app](./desktop)'s glyphs and in its order:

- **Open Piwi Runner** (on Windows and macOS, a click on the icon does the same);
- **Run in background**, on by default: turned off, closing the window quits the app, once you agree to stop the runs
  still going;
- **Start on login**, which launches it in the tray when you sign in;
- **Check for updates…** and **Show logs**;
- **Quit Piwi Runner**, which stops its runs, after asking.

The **General** section of the window's **Settings** has the same two settings, for a desktop that shows no tray icon (GNOME without an
AppIndicator extension): turn **Run in background** off there, and closing the window quits.

Its icon is the Piwi mark on a teal tile with a play sign, so it reads apart from the desktop app's in the tray and the
taskbar.

## Languages

Piwi Runner speaks English, French, German, Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese, in its window, its tray menu and its
questions: your system's language, or the one you choose in the **General** section of its window's **Settings**. German, Spanish and
Portuguese are drafts no native reader has reviewed yet: while one is on screen, a line says so and links to a form for
a correction. Test titles, files, commands and a run's output stay as they are, the reason a run could not start
included, and so do two answers of the runs' hub, where a locator picked on the image and a code made at a stop wait
to be copied. The start screen keeps the
language Runner started in until it starts again. The [desktop app](./desktop) stays in English.

## Related

- [Run on my machine](./run-on-my-machine): who may ask, how an administrator turns it on, and what a request holds
- [Desktop app](./desktop): the other app that takes requests, with a local dashboard

# MCP server

The dashboard serves a **Model Context Protocol (MCP) server** at `/mcp` from its own process, with nothing to
install. Any MCP client (Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, Claude Desktop, Gemini CLI) can query your test
results, failure clusters and AI diagnoses, and triage them. **Settings → MCP server** in the dashboard has a live setup
guide for this instance.

## What it provides

The server exposes tools, mostly read-only, from listing projects to one failure's full evidence and a cluster's
fix plan; [MCP tools](/reference/mcp-tools) lists every one, and the dashboard's **MCP server** page opens each
tool on its whole description and its parameters. Two answer questions about Piwi itself:
`describe_piwi` reads the documentation bundled with the server, and `get_release_notes` the changelog up to the
running version. Three read the [coverage](/features/coverage-insights) tests record: `get_coverage` (a file's lines
and the tests behind them, or which target lines a test ran), `compare_coverage` (a failure against its last pass, or a
test's runs against each other) and `get_coverage_loss` (what [quarantining](./flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out) or deleting tests leaves uncovered).
`get_impacted_tests` takes your working diff and returns the tests it impacts, narrowed to the tests that ran the
changed lines where coverage was recorded ([line level](/features/change-impact#line-level)), with a command to run
them. They return compact JSON, list tools page with `{ items, nextCursor }` (`get_project_test_catalog`
with `offset`/`nextOffset`), and a tool that fails returns a normal result with `isError: true` and a readable
message (one whose SCM or AI provider is not configured returns `{ error }`).

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/mcp-tool-details.png" alt="The MCP server page with the get_fix_plan tool opened: its description and its parameters">
  <figcaption>One tool on the MCP server page, opened: what it does and the parameters it takes.</figcaption>
</figure>

**Modules.** Every tool belongs to one module, `core`, `workflow`, `healing` or `agents`, the groups **Settings → Capabilities**
asks about. Declining a capability drops the tools that depend on it. Append `?modules=core` (comma-separated) to the
MCP URL to narrow the list further; narrowing never re-enables a declined tool.

**Access.** The server follows the REST API's [roles](/operate/project-access): with authentication on, a Member's key
reads only the projects its owner holds a role on, and cross-project tools (`list_recent_activity`,
`list_open_clusters`, `search`) are filtered to them. The write tools (triaging clusters and gaps, deciding a merge
suggestion, dismissing a quarantine proposal, setting a bug report's status or a run's incident flag, re-running a
cluster in CI, linking or filing an issue, setting a cluster's baseline commit, running, recording or rating a
diagnosis, reporting a fix attempt, registering a test function) need the same
[permission](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do) as the same action in the dashboard and the REST API, on
the project they act on, and `get_instance_stats` needs an administrator.

**The write log.** Every call of a write tool is logged with the API key that made it, the tool, what it acted on and
the result; read tools never are. A cluster's **Activity** section shows the calls on it, the log is pruned after
`PIWI_RETENTION_NOTIFICATION_DAYS`, and declining the **Agent write log** capability in **Settings → Capabilities** keeps none.

**Transport.** Streamable HTTP: JSON-RPC 2.0 over `POST /mcp`, with no session, for clients of protocol `2026-07-28`
and those that open with `initialize` (`2025-11-25` down to `2024-11-05`). Any other gets a `400`.


## Authentication

With authentication on, a client signs in through OAuth, as the
[MCP authorization specification](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic/authorization)
describes: you give the client the MCP URL only, and the first time it connects it opens this instance in your
browser. Sign in if asked, check the client's name and where the answer goes, and click **Allow**. The client then
holds an access token of one hour, which it renews on its own for 30 days after its last use. The tokens act with your
role and project access, on the MCP server only: the REST API refuses them. Each connection is listed, named after
the client, with your API keys in **Settings → Account → API keys**; revoking it there disconnects the client.

Claude Code (`/mcp`, then **Authenticate**), Cursor, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Opencode and Claude Desktop through
`mcp-remote` sign in this way. The instance is its own authorization server; PKCE is required. A client registers on
its own, or, once [`PIWI_MCP_CLIENT_METADATA_DOCUMENTS`](/reference/configuration#authentication) turns it on, names
its metadata document's HTTPS address as its client ID. The API reference
(`/settings/api` in your instance) lists the endpoints under **MCP OAuth**.

A client that cannot sign in sends an API key instead, the same `pd_` keys as the REST API, created in **Settings →
Account → API keys** (administrators manage anyone's keys from **Settings → Users**), as a Bearer token on every
request:

```
Authorization: Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY
```

When `PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED` is not set, every request is accepted without a key and there is nothing to sign in to,
except in the desktop app, which requires its local access token as the Bearer value.

## Client setup

Replace `<your-piwi-url>` with your dashboard base URL (for example `http://localhost:3000`). A client that signs in
through OAuth leaves out the `headers` entry (`--header` on a command line); any other replaces `pd_YOUR_API_KEY`
with a real API key. The dashboard's **MCP server** page shows both forms. In the
[desktop app](#in-the-desktop-app), the MCP server page detects the installed clients and writes their entry in one
click instead.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/mcp-client-setup.png" alt="The MCP server page's client setup card: the agents listed on the left, Claude Desktop picked, its config entry on the right">
  <figcaption>The <strong>MCP server</strong> page writes the setup for each client with this dashboard's URL already filled in.</figcaption>
</figure>

### In the desktop app

In the [desktop app](/features/desktop#connecting-ai-assistants), **Settings → MCP server** detects Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Cursor, Opencode, VS Code, Windsurf and Gemini CLI and
connects each in one click, writing a `piwi-desktop` entry that runs the app's built-in bridge
(`piwi-desktop mcp-stdio`). No address or token is copied; the bridge finds the app at start, so the app must run, and sends the token only
to a server that proves it holds it. The bridge handles one call at a time, for every client it serves: a `run_follow` or a
`run_control` that waits holds the next call, 40 seconds at most (a 30-second wait, then the stopped page's snapshot). It writes only its own entry and keeps the first backup beside
the config. A disk image (DMG), a translocated copy or a dev build writes nothing, for Connect, Disconnect and the
startup repair alike; each client shows **Manual setup** with the reason. After a move, startup points that entry at the app again,
as it does for an earlier version's address-and-token entry. One you edited shows **Needs update**; **Update** replaces it. Restart the client afterwards. The page also installs the [agent skills](/features/agent-skills) into a linked folder.

### Claude Desktop

Add to `claude_desktop_config.json`, then restart Claude Desktop. On macOS it is in
`~/Library/Application Support/Claude/`, on Linux (beta) in `~/.config/Claude/`. On Windows, recent versions keep it in
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Claude-Data\claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\`. An older install keeps it in one of these folders; a
`.user-data-left.*` file there means it moved to `Claude-Data`:

- `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\Claude_pzs8sxrjxfjjc\LocalCache\Roaming\Claude\`, an MSIX install (Microsoft Store, WinGet)
- `%APPDATA%\Claude\`, the classic installer

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "piwi": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": [
        "-y",
        "mcp-remote@0.14.3",
        "<your-piwi-url>/mcp",
        "--transport",
        "http-only",
        "--header",
        "Authorization:${AUTH_HEADER}"
      ],
      "env": {
        "AUTH_HEADER": "Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Claude Desktop only starts local commands from this file and ignores an entry with a `url`, so
[`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote), a small Node bridge, carries the HTTP connection; `npx`
needs Node on your PATH. Keep its version in the entry: `npx` without one runs whatever release npm serves that day,
with your key in its environment, and a release before 0.1.16 runs a command a hostile server hides in its sign-in
address ([CVE-2025-6514](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-6514)). The header goes through `env` because Claude Desktop mishandles arguments with spaces. Plans
that offer **Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector** take the `/mcp` URL directly.

### Claude Code (CLI)

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http --scope user piwi <your-piwi-url>/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
```

`--scope user` makes the server available in every folder, not only the one the command ran in. Restart Claude Code, then check with `/mcp` that **piwi** is listed.

### Cursor

Add to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` (global) or `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project root:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "piwi": {
      "url": "<your-piwi-url>/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### VS Code (GitHub Copilot, agent mode)

With the [Piwi extension](/features/editors) installed and connected, VS Code 1.101 and later list Piwi's server
without any configuration, with the extension's key, or signed in through OAuth when `piwi.mcpAuthorization` is
`sign-in`. Otherwise:

Add to `.vscode/mcp.json` in your workspace (VS Code 1.99+):

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "piwi": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "<your-piwi-url>/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

### Gemini CLI

```bash
gemini mcp add --transport http piwi <your-piwi-url>/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
```

### Windsurf / Continue

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "piwi": {
      "serverUrl": "<your-piwi-url>/mcp",
      "headers": {
        "Authorization": "Bearer pd_YOUR_API_KEY"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Windsurf reads `~/.codeium/windsurf/mcp_config.json`; Continue reads `~/.continue/config.json`, under `mcpServers`.

## Prompts

The server also exposes MCP **prompts**, which a client offers as slash commands, with nothing to install.
`setup_piwi` sets up a Playwright project that does not report here yet, with this instance's URL, whether it
requires a key and its existing projects, then walks the agent through `npx @piwitests/reporter init`, the API key and
a first run; an optional `projectName` names the project. Each workflow [agent skill](/features/agent-skills) is a prompt too (`investigate_failure`,
`apply_locator_healing`, `stabilize_flaky_tests`, `run_the_right_tests`, `write_the_missing_test`,
`fix_a_reported_bug`), in the version this server ships, with an optional `focus` (a run, a cluster, a test, a gap or a
bug report, as an id or a URL). Prompts need the MCP connection; installed skills work
offline.

# Agent skills

The [MCP server](/features/mcp) gives an agent tools over your results, mostly read-only; **skills** tell it what to *do* with them.
A skill is a single `SKILL.md` file, the portable open format (front matter plus Markdown instructions) that Claude
Code and other coding agents read from a project's skills directory. Piwi ships seven, and the reporter's CLI installs
them into your test project.

## What each skill does

| Skill | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| `setup-piwi` | Wire a Playwright project up to a dashboard: the same work `npx @piwitests/reporter init` does, driven by an agent. |
| `investigate-failure` | Investigate a failed run and propose a fix grounded in Piwi's evidence: error, steps, console, network, and the diff since the [last green run](/features/run-changes#the-baseline). |
| `apply-locator-healing` | Replace a [brittle locator](/reference/locator-stability) with Piwi's ranked [healed locator](/features/locator-healing) at its call site, then re-run to confirm. |
| `stabilize-flaky-tests` | Reproduce the highest-impact [flaky tests](/features/flaky-tests) with the [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab), fix what the reproducing condition points at (never by adding retries), then prove it with `piwi flake verify`. |
| `run-the-right-tests` | After a UI change, fix the locators it breaks with [preflight](/features/preflight); run the tests a change [impacts](/features/change-impact), down to those that ran the changed lines; or pick and run the right [selection](/features/test-selection) for the task (smoke, recently broken, a time budget) instead of the whole suite. |
| `write-the-missing-test` | Take the top [scenario gap](/features/scenario-gaps) in scope, draft it from the graph, finish the assertion and add it in the same change. |
| `fix-a-reported-bug` | Take a [bug report](/features/bug-reports), write its failing test with `piwi bug <id> --write`, reproduce, fix, then remove `test.fail()` and run the spec and the tests that visit the page. |

Each skill but `setup-piwi`, which uses no MCP tool, prefers a connected Piwi [MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools). When
MCP is not connected it falls back to the dashboard UI (`run-the-right-tests` and `fix-a-reported-bug` to the
reporter's CLI), so a skill works before the MCP server is set up, only more slowly.

## What agents report back

These workflow skills end by telling Piwi what the agent did, so the next diagnosis, the fix verification and the gap
detectors learn from it:

| Skill | Reports back with |
|------|--------------|
| `investigate-failure` | `record_diagnosis` (its own diagnosis, shown as written by an agent), `submit_diagnosis_feedback` (a rating of Piwi's) and `report_fix_attempt` (the change, its commit and the diagnosis it followed) |
| `apply-locator-healing` | `report_fix_attempt` with the locator edit |
| `write-the-missing-test` | `triage_gap` (accepted, covered by a test, or dismissed with a reason) |

The fix's commit carries a `Piwi-Cluster: <id>` trailer, the line `get_fix_plan` suggests. When the cluster's tests
pass on a later commit, Piwi records the attempt **verified**, tied by its commit, the trailer or its branch; a later
failure records it **regressed**. The cluster page's **Activity** section lists every attempt and every write an agent
made to the cluster over MCP, with the API key it used.

## Where it is

The skills ship inside the reporter package. `npx @piwitests/reporter init` installs the six workflow skills as part
of setup (everything but `setup-piwi`, which an agent runs before the reporter exists). **Settings → MCP server** in the
dashboard lists them next to the tools.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/mcp-agent-skills.png" alt="The agent skills section of the MCP server page, with the command that installs the skills">
  <figcaption>The agent skills on the MCP server page, with the command that installs them.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Use it

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter skills add          # install all seven into .claude/skills/
npx @piwitests/reporter skills list         # see what each one does
npx @piwitests/reporter skills add investigate-failure --dir .cursor/skills   # one skill, elsewhere
```

Invoke the CLI through the package name so npx resolves this package; a plain `npx piwi …` works once the reporter
is a project dependency. `init` takes `--skills <list>` (or `all`, `none`), `--skills-dir` and `--no-skills` to
change what setup installs. The [CLI reference](/reference/cli#skills) lists every flag.

The skills are agent-agnostic Markdown: only the destination is tool-specific, so `--dir` points the install wherever
your agent reads skills from. Each installed file carries `piwi-version` and `piwi-hash` in its front matter. A later
`skills add` replaces a skill you never touched that an older release installed, reporting it **outdated**, and keeps
one you **edited** unless you pass `--force`.

On the [desktop app](/features/desktop), the MCP server page also installs the workflow skills into a project's
linked folder, with the same rules.

Once installed, ask in plain words: "why did the last CI run fail", "fix the flaky checkout test", "write the test
we're missing for this change". The agent picks the skill whose description matches.

## Prompts, the no-install alternative

The MCP server also serves every workflow skill as a **prompt**, a slash command with nothing to install, in the
server's own version, plus a `setup_piwi` prompt that knows this instance; installed skills work offline. See
[Prompts](/features/mcp#prompts).

## Limits

- **Instructions, not code.** A skill tells an agent which evidence to read and in which order; the agent still
  writes the fix, and you review it.
- **Updated with the reporter.** A newer reporter ships newer skills; `skills add` updates the copies you never
  edited, and `--force` replaces the edited ones too.
- **Reporting back needs write access.** The write-back tools need a key whose owner holds the matching
  [project role](/operate/project-access#what-each-role-can-do) (Maintainer covers all of them); with a Viewer's key
  the agent reports what it did to you instead.

# Run control for agents

A coding agent on your machine (Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, the JetBrains AI Assistant) can work with a test run
the way you do with [Pause and step from the editor](./editor-run-control) and the [Runs window](./runs-window): follow
the run, stop it, look at the stopped page, act on it, and have the code written at the stopped line. The editor
service serves the runs of its window (in a JetBrains IDE, its project) as an MCP server of its own, apart from Piwi's
[MCP server](./mcp), which reads your suite's history on an instance; the [desktop app](#in-the-desktop-app) serves
its own.

## Connect your agent

**One entry for every repository.** `npx @piwitests/reporter mcp` serves the runs of every editor with Piwi and of
the desktop app as one MCP server, over stdio: add it once, at user scope, for any agent that starts a command.

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
claude mcp add --scope user piwi-runs -- npx -y @piwitests/reporter@latest mcp
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
claude mcp add --scope user piwi-runs -- cmd /c npx -y @piwitests/reporter@latest mcp
```

:::

How it routes each call: [`mcp`](/reference/cli#mcp). VS Code's own agent (1.101 and later) needs nothing: the extension lists its window's server as **Piwi runs**,
beside **Piwi**, which then leaves the desktop app's run tools of the same names out.

Each editor's server listens on `127.0.0.1` once the extension starts, at a port and behind a token the extension
keeps for this workspace (in a JetBrains IDE, this project). If another program holds that port, the server moves,
with a new token, and says so. To give an agent one window's runs alone, copy its entry: **Piwi: Copy the runs' MCP
server configuration for agents** in VS Code, **Tools → Piwi → Copy the runs' MCP server configuration for Claude Code
or Cursor** (an `http` entry, the token as a bearer header) or **…for Agents** (one that runs
`npx -y mcp-remote@0.14.3 <url> --transport http-only`, for the JetBrains AI Assistant) in a JetBrains IDE.

**The configuration holds the token.** Keep it in your user settings, never in a file of the repository such as a
project's `.mcp.json`: whoever reads it can drive your runs while the editor is open. **Reset the token** (**Piwi:
Reset the runs' MCP server token**; **Tools → Piwi → Reset the runs' MCP server token**) gives the server a new one:
an agent with the old one is refused until you copy the configuration again. `piwi.serveRunsToAgents` in VS Code, and
**Settings → Tools → Piwi** in a JetBrains IDE, turn the server off.

## The tools

| Tool            | What it does                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `run_start`     | Start a run of a spec, or of the test holding a line, built and checked as yours are and run where you see it, labeled with the agent's name, three at once at most; a failed test waits at its line by default while the agent follows the run                                                                          |
| `run_list`      | The runs of the window, what started each (the editor, a terminal or a test runner), their page, progress, [Hold failures](./watch-a-run#hold-failures) and who has them open, their workers, the test each one runs and where it stands stopped                                                                                                           |
| `run_follow`    | The run's events since a cursor: each test's start and end, each call with its place in your code and its result, the stops, and the page's navigations, console errors, uncaught errors and failed requests. It waits up to 25 seconds, and answers at once while the run is stopped or ended                                |
| `run_control`   | Pause, Step, Run to a line, Resume, Finish or [End the test](./end-the-test), answered when the run stops again, with the page's snapshot, when the test it ended ends, or when the run ends                                                                                                                                  |
| `page_snapshot` | The stopped page's ARIA snapshot in AI mode, a ref per element (`[ref=e5]`), to a depth you choose, with an image of the page when asked                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `page_act`      | Click, fill, press a key, check, uncheck or select an option on an element by its ref, answered with the page's change                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| `page_locator`  | Piwi's locators for an element by its ref, ranked as [Pick a locator](./pick-an-element) ranks them, each checked to find it alone                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `code_write`    | The steps `page_act` took, the element's locator in place of the stopped line's, or an assertion on it, written by the editor                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

An agent reads the page as text: the first snapshot whole (or to a depth), then what each stop and action changed. An
image costs more, and comes only when asked.

**The steps the agent takes** are kept as yours are when you record: each with the element's best locator, the
project's test id attribute first and the suite's own locators preferred. `code_write` renders them with Piwi's
generator, as [Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code) does, and the editor writes them above the stopped line as one
edit: one undo removes it. The test goes on with the code it started with: the new lines run next time.

An agent follows a run until two minutes after its last call on it: the run's calls and page events are told until
then; an action the page answers late may still take effect, kept as a step, and `run_follow` says so.

**An assertion on an element's text** checks the whole text, as the page shows it now (`toHaveText`); for a text
longer than 1,000 characters, it checks that the element contains its first words (`toContainText`, up to 200
characters). Piwi refuses to write a secret field's value, and a text or a value that holds a credential.

## What keeps it safe

- **Only this machine, only this window.** The server answers a request to its own address on `127.0.0.1` with the
  token, and refuses any other name for the machine and any request a browser sends (it carries an `Origin`). It serves
  the runs this window started, and those [started outside Piwi](./terminal-runs) that follow it, and nothing of an
  instance.
- **Only a stopped page, only the actions named.** An action needs the stop it answers, and goes nowhere once the test
  went on. The tools take a closed set of arguments. `run_start` runs a spec of your workspace as you would, with the
  command Piwi builds; no other tool evaluates code, reads a file or runs a command. Code reaches your files only
  through the editor, as an edit you see.
- **The page is untrusted.** A page can hold text written to steer a model. Everything that comes from it (its
  snapshot, its address and title, an element's name, text and value, the locators built from them, its console, its
  errors, its requests, and what the test says when a read of it fails) comes back apart from Piwi's own answer,
  between two markers that share a random value the page cannot know, and every tool's description tells the agent to
  read it as data, never as instructions. An image comes after a line that says it is the page's too.
- **Secrets stay hidden.** The value of a password field, a one-time code and a card's number or security code is
  never sent: its line in the snapshot reads `<hidden>`, in every frame, the image paints over the field (a page zoomed
  in gets no image), and no assertion writes it. Tokens and credentials in the page's text, its addresses and the locators `page_locator` shows are
  hidden, as on Piwi's other surfaces.
- **You watch it happen.** The agent's stops show in the editor and the Runs window as yours do, the editor's as
  `Paused by the agent · …`; its first action at a stop says so in a notification; the code it has written names it
  (`Piwi wrote the steps the agent took above checkout.spec.ts:30.`). You can take over at any stop
  ([driving a stop](/guide/concepts#presence-driving-a-stop)): the agent is refused there and told so.

## In the desktop app

The [desktop app](./desktop-runs#for-agents)'s MCP server serves the same tools for the runs it starts; there,
`code_write` writes no file and a run nobody attends is not served. `run_start` takes a spec of a linked folder,
which the app's window starts as you would from its Local runs tray, titled `Started by <agent>`, while a window is
open. It runs each test once, outside UI mode, and counts among the three runs agents start at once until its process
ends; a line in no test, or a spec whose name starts with `-`, is refused. `npx @piwitests/reporter mcp` sends the
app a spec no editor's workspace holds.

## Limits

- **A remote window** (SSH, a dev container, Gateway) runs the server on the remote machine: an agent there reaches it.
- An action needs a `@piwitests/reporter` at least as recent as the editor extension; at an older one's stops, the
  tools say what it cannot do.

## Related

- [Pause and step from the editor](./editor-run-control)
- [Code from a pause](./editor-stop-code)
- [MCP server](./mcp)
- [Runs window](./runs-window)
- [Share a stop with Playwright tools](./editor-run-control#share-with-playwright-tools)

# Test functions catalog

The test functions catalog is a **per-project registry of your own page-object methods and helpers**, each stored with the DOM pattern its steps produce. It lets recordings and agents refer to *your* code instead of raw locators: the [browser extension](./extension) collapses matched steps in a recording into a call to your function, and an MCP agent can register the functions it writes. The catalog lives in the dashboard: the extension reads from it, and MCP agents add to it.

## Where it lives

A project's **Test functions** page in the dashboard (**Project → More actions → Test functions**). Every entry is scoped to that project, and the [browser extension](./extension-connection) caches a mapped project's catalog locally so it can match against it while you record.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/test-functions.png" alt="The test function catalog: page-object methods and helpers, each with its module, the steps it performs and the URL it applies to">
  <figcaption>A project's <strong>Test functions</strong> page: each function with the steps it performs and the pages it applies to.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Registering a function

Four ways in, all producing the same kind of entry. The paste paths stop at a review form; the MCP tool saves directly, and its entries show an `ai-extracted` badge by default.

- **By hand** — **Add function** and fill in the name, kind (page-object method, helper function or fixture), module (its import specifier), parameters and DOM pattern yourself — plus the receiver and class for a page-object method, and an optional URL-pattern glob limiting which pages it applies to.
- **Paste the source, let AI propose it** — paste a page-object method or helper's source and a model proposes the name, parameters, and DOM pattern into a **review form you edit before saving**; the module and URL pattern are never inferred, so you fill those in. With [AI](/features/ai-diagnosis) configured on the instance, an **Extract** button calls it directly.
- **Bring your own AI** — no instance AI, or you'd rather not use it? **Copy prompt for your own AI** copies the full extraction prompt (the rules, the JSON schema, and your pasted code) to paste into any AI chat (ChatGPT, Claude.ai, an IDE assistant). Paste the reply back and it is validated against the exact same schema — no Piwi AI credits spent either way.
- **From a coding agent (MCP)** — an MCP-connected agent (Claude Code, Cursor, …) calls the `create_test_function` [MCP tool](/reference/mcp-tools#create_test_function) directly, reading the source with its own model. No AI call happens on the server side; the tool only validates and persists.

Registered entries are edited in place from the same page — the pencil button reopens the form with everything filled in. Registering, editing, deleting and both paste paths need the **Maintainer** role or above on the project, or an administrator; anyone who can read the project can view the catalog.

## Object parameters

A parameter can be typed **object**, for the options-bag argument most helpers take — `selectOption(page, { label }, { value })`. You list the bag's keys, and a parameter source then targets one key by name, so a generated call passes `{ label: 'Country' }` rather than a bare string.

## What extraction won't do

Extraction is deliberately conservative. A function that branches on its arguments, loops, or calls other helpers whose source isn't visible can't be captured as one fixed pattern — so it comes back with **low confidence and a note** saying what was left out, rather than a confident-looking guess you'd have to catch later.

## Using the catalog

- **While recording**, the extension live-ranks which catalog function the steps so far look like, and in the test the finish panel copies (**Copy test**, or **Copy failing test** for a bug report) matched steps collapse into a call to your function; anything unmatched stays as plain locators. The matcher only ever *selects among* the functions you registered — it never invents one. See the [browser extension](./extension#what-it-does).
- **While recording from your editor**, each run of steps a function performs is written as a call to it as soon as its last step is recorded, a page object taken from the test's fixtures when the file's tests take it there. See [Record tests from the editor](./editor-recording).
- **Against the current page**, the [extension](./extension) popup's **Test functions** checklist scores every function in the active project's catalog: **Ready to use here** (every step finds one element), **Partly found here**, or **Not on this page**.
- **In the Test Map**, a method or helper on a page the suite reaches that no test runs is a *catalog method, no test calls* [scenario gap](./scenario-gaps): the cheapest test to add, since its steps exist. A step whose target comes from a parameter names no element, so a function whose every target does gets no verdict. See [Gap detectors](/reference/gap-detectors).

## Related

- [Browser extension](./extension) — records against the catalog and consumes it
- [MCP server](./mcp) — the `create_test_function` tool
- [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) — **Extract** uses the research model when one is configured, otherwise the diagnosis model

# Command line

The `@piwitests/reporter` package installs a command, `piwi`, for what happens around a test run. Run it through the
package name, `npx @piwitests/reporter <command>`, or as `npx piwi <command>` once the reporter is a dependency of the
project. This page says which command serves which moment; every flag, and how a command finds the dashboard and its
API key, is on the [Piwi CLI reference](/reference/cli).

## Setting up

- **[`init`](/reference/cli#init)** wires a Playwright project up to a dashboard: the reporter, the
  [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures), a `.env` and the [agent skills](./agent-skills).
- **[`skills`](/reference/cli#skills)** installs or updates the agent skills in a project `init` did not set up.
- **[`mcp`](/reference/cli#mcp)** serves the runs of this machine's editors and desktop app to a coding agent
  ([Run control for agents](./agent-run-control)).

## In CI

- **[`gate`](/reference/cli#gate)** fails a job on the dashboard's analysis of the run: the
  [CI merge gate](./merge-gate).
- **[`rerun`](/reference/cli#rerun)** runs the tests a [re-run in CI](./ci-rerun) asked for, in a GitLab, Bitbucket
  or Jenkins job.
- **[`report`](/reference/cli#report)** prints a [quality report](./quality-reports), for a scheduler to post.
- **[`coverage`](/reference/cli#coverage)** uploads another tool's coverage of a commit, for
  [combined coverage](./combined-coverage).

## Choosing the tests

- **[`select` and `run`](/reference/cli#select-run)** resolve a saved [test selection](./test-selection), or the
  tests a diff reaches ([Impact from a diff](./change-impact)), and print or run them.
- **[`plan`](/reference/cli#plan)** plans a run that reuses the passes whose code has not changed
  ([Reuse forecast](./reuse-forecast)), an experimental capability.
- **[`probe`](/reference/cli#probe)** runs the dashboard's [probe plan](./probes).

## Chasing a flaky test

- **[`flake`](/reference/cli#flake)** makes a flaky test fail on demand under its suspects' conditions, then verifies
  the fix ([Flake Lab](./flake-lab)).

## Writing and fixing a test

- **[`codegen`](/reference/cli#codegen)** turns a Piwi Picker recording into a spec ([Record a test](./record-actions)).
- **[`bug`](/reference/cli#bug)** writes a [bug report](./bug-reports)'s failing test into the project and runs it.
- **[`preflight`](/reference/cli#preflight)** lists the test locators your change breaks, and fixes them
  ([Locator preflight](./preflight)).
- **[`ai`](/reference/cli#ai)** manages the committed artifacts of [AI steps](./ai-steps).

## Related

- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli): every command and flag
- [Write, run and fix a test](./write-run-fix): the loop the editor, Piwi Picker and the desktop app share
- [Reporter](/guide/reporter): the package the command ships in
