# Deployment

Piwi is one Node.js server with its data in one directory. Run it as a Docker container (recommended), with Docker Compose, on Kubernetes or with `npx`, then put an HTTPS proxy in front of it.

<figure>
  <img src="/diagrams/production-topology.svg" alt="CI runners, your team and coding agents reach one Piwi container through an HTTPS reverse proxy; its data sits on the /app/.data volume, or in PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible bucket; outbound calls go only to the services you configure">
  <figcaption>One replica behind a TLS proxy, with persistent data.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Docker (recommended)

### Quick start

::: code-group

```sh [Linux / macOS]
docker pull phenx/piwitests-server:latest
mkdir -p .data && sudo chown -R 1001:1001 .data # the container runs as non-root UID 1001
# Reachable from this machine only: with authentication off, anyone who reaches the port is an administrator.
# Publish it on every interface (-p 3000:3000) only once authentication is on.
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 -v $(pwd)/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

```ps1 [Windows (PowerShell)]
docker pull phenx/piwitests-server:latest
# Reachable from this machine only: with authentication off, anyone who reaches the port is an administrator.
# Publish it on every interface (-p 3000:3000) only once authentication is on.
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 -v ${PWD}/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

:::

The dashboard will be available at `http://localhost:3000`.

> **Linux hosts:** without the `chown`, Docker auto-creates `.data` owned by `root` and the container (non-root UID 1001) can't write to it. Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS handles this automatically. See [Permission issues with volumes](#permission-issues-with-volumes) if you hit a permission error.

### Registries

The same multi-arch image is published to two registries; use whichever your organization prefers:

::: code-group

```bash [Docker Hub]
docker pull phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

```bash [GHCR]
docker pull ghcr.io/piwitests/platform:latest
```

:::

GHCR additionally carries an **`edge`** tag rebuilt from every push to `main`. It's useful for trying a
fix before its release; don't run it in production: it has had no release testing and can change under you.

### Available tags

| Tag | Description | Docker Hub | GHCR |
|-----|-------------|:---:|:---:|
| `latest` | Latest stable release | ✅ | ✅ |
| `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` | One exact release (e.g. `0.26.1`) | ✅ | ✅ |
| `MAJOR.MINOR` | Latest patch of that minor (e.g. `0.25`) | ✅ | ✅ |
| `MAJOR` | Latest release of that major (e.g. `0`) | ✅ | ✅ |
| `edge` | Built from every push to `main` | — | ✅ |

Pin a specific version in production, and read [Upgrading](./upgrading) before you bump it, because
migrations are forward-only. Browse the published tags on
[Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/r/phenx/piwitests-server/tags) or
[GHCR](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/pkgs/container/platform).

### Image details

| Property | Value |
|----------|-------|
| Base image | `node:24-alpine`, pinned by digest |
| Image size | ~400 MB |
| Platforms | `linux/amd64`, `linux/arm64` |

### Volumes

Everything the server keeps lives under `/app/.data`, the volume the quick start mounts: the SQLite database
(`piwi.db`) and file storage (`storage/`, HTML reports and traces). Mount it on persistent storage, or point the
[database](./database) and [storage](./storage) elsewhere.

### Environment variables

The server reads three process-level variables directly:

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| `NODE_ENV` | `production` | Set automatically |
| `HOST` | `0.0.0.0` | Listen on all interfaces. The Docker image sets `NITRO_HOST=0.0.0.0`, which takes precedence — override the bind address there with `NITRO_HOST`. `npx @piwitests/server` defaults to `127.0.0.1` |
| `PORT` | `3000` | Application port |

Everything else is a `PIWI_*` variable, listed with its default and the Settings page that names it in the generated [configuration reference](/reference/configuration). The [configuration generator](/reference/configuration/generator) turns your choices into a ready-to-paste block from the same registry.

## One-click deploy

No server to run Docker on? Templates for Railway, Render, Fly.io, Koyeb and Coolify / Dokploy stand up the same
single container with authentication on and a persistent volume, which on Koyeb you attach yourself. [One-click deploy](./one-click-deploy) covers each
provider and what to check before you rely on it.

## Docker Compose

The repository ships a ready-to-use [`docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/docker-compose.yml) with commented options (secret key, auth, PostgreSQL). Minimal version:

```yaml
services:
  piwi:
    image: phenx/piwitests-server:latest
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000" # "3000:3000" once authentication is on
    volumes:
      - ./.data:/app/.data
    restart: unless-stopped
```

Run with:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

With authentication off, a reporter in another container that sends to `http://piwi:3000` needs
`PIWI_ALLOWED_HOSTS=piwi` in the dashboard's `environment`
([the host allowlist](./authentication#disabling-authentication)).

### Docker Compose with PostgreSQL

For production deployments requiring a robust relational database:

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:17-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: piwi
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: change-me
      POSTGRES_DB: piwi
    volumes:
      - pg-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    restart: unless-stopped

  piwi:
    image: phenx/piwitests-server:latest
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:3000:3000" # "3000:3000" once authentication is on
    volumes:
      - ./.data:/app/.data   # still used for report/trace file storage
    environment:
      - PIWI_DATABASE_URL=postgresql://piwi:change-me@postgres:5432/piwi
    depends_on:
      - postgres
    restart: unless-stopped

volumes:
  pg-data:
```

Run with:

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

## Kubernetes

Example deployment manifest. It reads its variables from the `piwi-config` ConfigMap and the `piwi-secrets` Secret
that the [configuration generator](/reference/configuration/generator)'s Kubernetes output creates: apply that first.

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: piwi-dashboard
spec:
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate   # never two pods at once, not even during a rollout
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: piwi-dashboard
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: piwi-dashboard
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 1001   # the image's non-root user, so it can write the volume
      containers:
      - name: piwi-dashboard
        image: phenx/piwitests-server:0.78.0 # x-release-please-version
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: piwi-config
        - secretRef:
            name: piwi-secrets
            optional: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /api/health
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /api/health
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 20
          periodSeconds: 30
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /app/.data
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: piwi-dashboard-data
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: piwi-dashboard-data
spec:
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: piwi-dashboard
spec:
  selector:
    app: piwi-dashboard
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
  type: ClusterIP
```

The Service stays inside the cluster: publish it through your Ingress with TLS, rather than as a plain-HTTP
`LoadBalancer`, with the proxy settings of [Reverse proxy (HTTPS)](#reverse-proxy-https). With authentication off, a
pod that calls the Service by name needs that name in [`PIWI_ALLOWED_HOSTS`](./authentication#disabling-authentication)
(`piwi-dashboard`, or the full `piwi-dashboard.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`); the probes call the pod's IP address
and need nothing.

## npm / npx (quick local run)

For a quick local run without Docker, the server is published to npm as
[`@piwitests/server`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@piwitests/server). It bundles the
prebuilt server and needs only **Node.js 22+**:

```bash
npx @piwitests/server
```

The dashboard will be available at `http://localhost:3000`.

The server creates the same `.data/` layout **in the current working directory**, so run the command from the
same directory each time to keep your data. It reads the same environment variables as the Docker image; for
example, to change the port:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
PORT=8080 npx @piwitests/server
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$env:PORT='8080'; npx @piwitests/server
```

:::

It listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so other machines cannot reach it: with authentication off, the default, anyone who
reaches the port is an administrator. To serve other machines, turn [authentication](./authentication) on, set
`HOST=0.0.0.0` and put [HTTPS](#reverse-proxy-https) in front: the session cookie is `Secure`, so sign-in over plain
`http://` works only on `localhost`.

Docker remains the recommended path for production: it ships a pinned Node runtime, runs as a non-root user and
isolates the environment.

## Health checks

`GET /api/health` verifies database connectivity and returns `200 {"status":"ok","database":"ok"}` when healthy, `503 {"status":"error","database":"unreachable"}` otherwise — use it for load-balancer targets, uptime monitors, and container orchestration. The Docker image ships a built-in `HEALTHCHECK` against it, so `docker ps` shows `healthy`/`unhealthy` out of the box. The version endpoint additionally reports the running version and database backend ([Upgrading](./upgrading#verifying-the-upgrade-landed)).

## Reverse proxy (HTTPS)

Always put a TLS-terminating reverse proxy in front of the dashboard for anything beyond localhost: with authentication on, browser sign-in needs HTTPS, since the session cookie is `Secure` and plain `http://` works only on `localhost`. A proxy gets two things wrong by default, which the nginx examples below set:

- **Upload size.** Trace and report uploads reach hundreds of MB: one upload (a report, or one test's files) is accepted up to [`PIWI_IMPORT_MAX_BYTES`](/reference/configuration#ingest-limits), 500 MB by default, and a run's results sent as one JSON document up to `PIWI_SUBMIT_MAX_BYTES`, 256 MB by default. Raise the proxy's body limit to match (`client_max_body_size` in nginx), or lower those limits to the proxy's.
- **Stream buffering.** Live runs, browser notifications and the [live view](/features/live-view) hold long-lived responses open, the CI workers' included: the proxy must pass them through unbuffered and keep them open (`proxy_buffering off` and a long `proxy_read_timeout` in nginx). Behind a buffering proxy the run page stops updating, and the live view's **Watch** shows no image.

**Caddy** (automatic HTTPS):

```text
piwi.example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:3000
}
```

**nginx:**

```nginx
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;    # nginx 1.25.1 or later; before it, `listen 443 ssl http2;`
    server_name piwi.example.com;

    # ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/piwi.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    # ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/piwi.example.com/privkey.pem;

    client_max_body_size 500m;   # trace + report uploads

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

        # Live runs, notifications and the live view are long-lived streams:
        proxy_buffering off;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
    }
}
```

Each stream also carries `X-Accel-Buffering: no`, which nginx obeys even with `proxy_buffering on` and keeps from the browser. With two proxies in a row (a front nginx before ingress-nginx, say) the inner one keeps it from the outer one, which buffers: turn `proxy_buffering off` on the outer one too. A proxy not built on nginx ignores the header.

**ingress-nginx** leaves responses unbuffered unless its ConfigMap turns `proxy-buffering` on; the same settings as annotations on the Ingress:

```yaml
metadata:
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-body-size: "500m"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-buffering: "off"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/proxy-read-timeout: "3600"
```

Serve the dashboard over HTTP/2 when people keep several tabs open. Over HTTP/1.1, plain HTTP or HTTPS without HTTP/2, a browser opens at most six connections to one address, and each Piwi page that follows a running run holds one: a run page that finds none left says **Live updates stalled**. Caddy speaks HTTP/2 by default; nginx needs `http2 on`, as above.

Set `PIWI_SITE_URL` to the public HTTPS URL, so email links and OAuth callbacks point at the right origin, and `PIWI_TRUST_PROXY=true` (step 4 of the [production checklist](./production-checklist#before-you-expose-it)). Have the proxy forward the browser's `Host` header, as the examples do: with authentication off, the [host allowlist](./authentication#disabling-authentication) reads it.

## Resource requirements

Piwi is a single Node.js process and runs comfortably on small machines:

| Deployment | Guideline |
|---|---|
| RAM | ~300 MB idle; 1 GB is comfortable headroom for large uploads and AI diagnosis |
| CPU | 1 vCPU is enough for a team; ingest is I/O-bound |
| Disk | The real variable — traces and HTML reports dominate. Budget by retention: e.g. ~50–200 MB per run with traces enabled. Prune old runs from **Settings → Storage** |
| Scaling | Run a single replica. SQLite requires it; with PostgreSQL the SSE event bus is still in-process, and so is whether a [Run on my machine](/features/run-on-my-machine) app is online and the [live view](/features/live-view)'s relay (sticky sessions do not help: a run's setup, its CI workers and its viewers are separate clients), so keep one instance |

## Security

Before you put an instance on a shared address, work down the [production checklist](./production-checklist).

## Troubleshooting

### Permission issues with volumes

On **Linux hosts**, the bind-mounted directory must be writable by the container's UID 1001:

```bash
mkdir -p .data
sudo chown -R 1001:1001 .data   # match the container's non-root UID 1001
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 -v $(pwd)/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

> On Windows and macOS, Docker Desktop manages volume permissions automatically — no `chown` is needed. Just run the container with `-v ${PWD}/.data:/app/.data` (PowerShell).

### Database locked

SQLite doesn't support concurrent writes well. For high-concurrency deployments, run a single instance or switch to PostgreSQL by setting `PIWI_DATABASE_URL`.

### Port already in use

Map to a different host port:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:3000 -v $(pwd)/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8080:3000 -v ${PWD}/.data:/app/.data phenx/piwitests-server:latest
```

:::

The dashboard will be available at `http://localhost:8080`.

# One-click deploy

If you don't have a server to run Docker on, these templates stand up an instance on a hosting provider
instead. They provision the same thing: **one container, one persistent volume mounted at
`/app/.data`, and authentication on**; on Koyeb you attach the volume yourself. Railway, Render and Coolify also generate `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`,
`PIWI_AUTH_SECRET` and `PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN`; on Fly.io and Koyeb you set them yourself. Beyond that, the difference is the provider's
own volume and pricing model.

The manifests are generated from the same variable registry as the
[configuration reference](/reference/configuration), so they can't drift from what the app actually reads.
The [configuration generator](/reference/configuration/generator) writes the same manifests for your own
choices of variables.

| Provider | How | Persistent volume | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Railway](#railway) | A service from the image | Yes | Managed PostgreSQL available alongside |
| [Render](#render) | Button | Yes, on a paid instance | Repo-driven; only `PIWI_SITE_URL` is set by hand |
| [Fly.io](#fly-io) | `fly launch` | Yes | One command rather than a button; cheapest always-on option |
| [Koyeb](#koyeb) | Button | Volume attached afterwards | Starts once you set its secrets; see the warning below |
| [Coolify / Dokploy](#coolify-dokploy) | Paste a Compose file | Yes | Onto a server you already own |

Not supported as one-click: **Vercel, Netlify and DigitalOcean App Platform** have no persistent disk, so
Piwi would need PostgreSQL *and* a bring-your-own [S3 bucket](./storage#s3-compatible-storage), at which
point it isn't one click. [Deploy it](./deployment) to a machine with Docker instead.

## Railway

Railway publishes templates from its own console rather than from a file in this repository, so the
template's exact contents live in
[`deploy/railway/template.md`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/deploy/railway/template.md)
and the repo ships a [`railway.json`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/railway.json) pinning
the health check to `/api/health` and the replica count to 1.

> **No button.** Railway lists no published Piwi template: create a service from the
> `phenx/piwitests-server:latest` image, add a volume mounted at `/app/.data`, and copy the variables from
> `deploy/railway/template.md`.

Railway injects `PORT`, which the image honors.

## Render

Render reads [`render.yaml`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/render.yaml) straight from the
repository, so the button is genuinely one click:

[![Deploy to Render](https://render.com/images/deploy-to-render-button.svg)](https://render.com/deploy?repo=https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi)

The blueprint asks for a **paid instance type**, deliberately: Render's free web services have no disk, and
without one the database and every stored trace are discarded on each redeploy. It also sets
`autoDeploy: false` so pushes to this repository don't redeploy your instance.

Set `PIWI_SITE_URL` to the service's public URL after the first deploy, so email links and OAuth callbacks
point at the right origin.

## Fly.io

Fly has no browser button, but [`fly.toml`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/fly.toml) makes
it one command plus the secrets:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
fly launch --no-deploy   # accepts the committed fly.toml
fly secrets set PIWI_SECRET_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 32) PIWI_AUTH_SECRET=$(openssl rand -hex 32) PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 32)
fly deploy
fly ssh console -C "printenv PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN"   # the first-admin form asks for it
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
fly launch --no-deploy   # accepts the committed fly.toml
$key = node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"
$auth = node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"
$setup = node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"
fly secrets set PIWI_SECRET_KEY=$key PIWI_AUTH_SECRET=$auth PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN=$setup
fly deploy
$setup   # the first-admin form asks for it
```

:::

`PIWI_SITE_URL` follows the app name `fly launch` picks (`https://<app>.fly.dev`); set it for a custom
domain. Autoscaling is deliberately off (`auto_stop_machines = false`, `min_machines_running = 1`): the
notification and retention sweeps run in-process, so a suspended machine silently stops doing scheduled work.

## Koyeb

Koyeb carries the whole service definition in the URL, so nothing needs to be in the repository:

[![Deploy to Koyeb](https://www.koyeb.com/static/images/deploy/button.svg)](https://app.koyeb.com/deploy?type=docker&image=docker.io/phenx/piwitests-server:latest&name=piwi&instance_type=small&regions=fra&ports=3000;http;/&env[PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED]=true)

> **The button alone gives you an ephemeral disk.** Koyeb volumes can't be attached from a deploy URL, so
> until you attach one, the database and every stored trace are lost on redeploy. Volumes are region-scoped
> and only standard (not free or eco) instances can mount them:
>
> ```bash
> koyeb volumes create piwi-data --region fra --size 10
> koyeb service update piwi/piwi --volumes piwi-data:/app/.data
> koyeb service update piwi/piwi --checks 3000:http:/api/health
> ```

Set `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`, `PIWI_AUTH_SECRET`, `PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN` and `PIWI_SITE_URL` in the Koyeb console after the first deploy,
because the URL can't generate secrets. With authentication on, the service refuses to start until
`PIWI_AUTH_SECRET` is set. The full command list is kept in
[`deploy/koyeb-deploy-url.txt`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/deploy/koyeb-deploy-url.txt).

## Coolify / Dokploy

Both consume a Compose file, so one stack covers them. In Coolify: **Add a new resource → Service →**
paste [`deploy/coolify/docker-compose.yml`](https://github.com/PiwiTests/piwi/blob/main/deploy/coolify/docker-compose.yml).
It uses Coolify's magic variables, so the domain and the secrets are generated for you and Traefik routing
and TLS are wired up automatically.

## Before you rely on any of them

- **One instance, always.** Don't scale the service past a single replica. SQLite requires it, and even on
  PostgreSQL the SSE event bus and the cron sweeps are in-process.
- **Budget disk by retention.** Traces and HTML reports dominate: roughly 50–200 MB per run with traces
  enabled. The templates ask for 10 GB; raise it, or set `PIWI_RETENTION_DAYS`, before you fill it.
- **Check the platform's request body limit and response buffering.** Trace and report uploads reach
  hundreds of MB, and live runs use long-lived `text/event-stream` responses; see
  [Reverse proxy (HTTPS)](./deployment#reverse-proxy-https) for what a proxy must allow.
- **Finish the auth setup.** These templates set `PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED=true`, so the first visit shows a
  **Create the first admin account** form. It asks for `PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN`, which the templates generate (read it in
  the platform's environment settings; on Fly.io and Koyeb you set it yourself), so nobody else can create the
  administrator. Complete it before sharing the URL, or provision the admin from a script as
  [Authentication → Initial setup](./authentication#initial-setup) shows.
- **Work down the [production checklist](./production-checklist).** The templates already turn
  authentication on (and, except on Fly.io and Koyeb, generate the secrets); pinning a version and backups
  are still yours to do.

## Related

- [Deployment](./deployment): Docker, Compose, Kubernetes and npx on a machine you run
- [Production checklist](./production-checklist): what to set before anyone else can reach the instance
- [Configuration generator](/reference/configuration/generator): the same manifests, with your own variables
- [Upgrading](./upgrading): pinning a tag and moving to a new one

# Production checklist

A fresh Piwi instance starts as an **open dashboard with authentication off** — right for localhost, wrong for a network. This is the one page that lists what to set before anyone else can reach it; [Authentication](./authentication) covers what turning sign-in on needs. Work down it before you put an instance on a shared address; the detail links go to the pages that explain each step.

## Before you expose it

1. **Turn authentication on.** Set `PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED=true` and a strong `PIWI_AUTH_SECRET` (session-cookie signing key). The server refuses to start with auth enabled and no secret, or one shorter than 32 characters, so this can't half-apply. Set `PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN` to a random value too: the first-administrator form asks for it, so whoever reaches the URL before you cannot make themselves administrator. Then create that account before you share the URL. See [Authentication](./authentication#initial-setup).
2. **Set the encryption key.** Set `PIWI_SECRET_KEY` so the credentials you store in the dashboard ([which ones](/guide/privacy#secrets-at-rest)) are encrypted with **your** key. Unset, the dashboard refuses to save them. Generate either secret with:

   ```bash
   node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"
   ```

3. **Terminate TLS.** Put the dashboard behind an HTTPS reverse proxy: browser sign-in needs HTTPS, and a proxy's defaults get the **upload size** and **event-stream buffering** wrong. See [Deployment → Reverse proxy (HTTPS)](./deployment#reverse-proxy-https).
4. **Tell Piwi its address and that it is behind a proxy.** Set `PIWI_SITE_URL` to the public HTTPS address: the links in emails, notifications and pull-request comments, and the OAuth callbacks, are built from it. Unset, emails and notifications link to `http://localhost:3000`, no pull-request comment is posted, and OAuth callbacks follow the request's host. Set `PIWI_TRUST_PROXY=true` so the per-client rate limits on the auth endpoints key on the real client address from `X-Forwarded-For` instead of pooling every request into the proxy's one address; while it is unset, the server logs a warning the first time a request carries that header. Leave it off when clients connect directly — see the [configuration reference](/reference/configuration#authentication).
5. **Persist and back up the data.** Mount `/app/.data` (or your configured database and storage paths) on a persistent volume, and set up a backup before you accumulate history you care about. See [Backup & restore](./backup-restore).
6. **Pin a version.** Running `latest` lets an unattended `docker pull` move you across a breaking change. Pin an exact tag and bump it deliberately — migrations are forward-only, so the rollback path is *restore a backup*, not "pull the old tag." See [Upgrading](./upgrading).

Never leave the built-in development secrets in place on a real deployment.

## What Piwi already does for you

The defaults are conservative, so the checklist above is short. Without any extra work:

- The container runs as a **non-root** user (`nodejs`, UID 1001).
- Passwords are hashed with **scrypt** and per-password salts, two at a time (up to 32 more wait, and one client address holds at most 4 of those places, an IPv6 address counted by its /64 network; past either limit the server answers `503` with `Retry-After` at once, and the refused request counts toward no rate limit). A stored hash that declares a higher scrypt cost than Piwi writes is refused as a wrong password is, and the server logs the account's id. Login, initial-setup and password-reset endpoints are **rate-limited** per client address, returning `429` with `Retry-After`. Failed logins are also limited per account in 15 minutes, its username and its email counted together: 5 from one address and 50 from all addresses together, so wrong passwords sent from other addresses do not stop the owner signing in until they pass 50. A password change allows 5 wrong current passwords per account and 20 per address in 15 minutes.
- No other site can frame the dashboard: every response carries `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN` and
  `frame-ancestors 'self'`. Status badges and report charts are images, so a README or a wiki still shows them.
- Stored credentials are encrypted with **AES-256-GCM**, API keys kept only as hashes, and secrets set by environment variable never written to the database: [Secrets at rest](/guide/privacy#secrets-at-rest).
- Database **migrations are forward-only** and run on startup, before any request reaches the database; if one fails, every database call fails and `/api/health` returns `503` rather than serving a half-migrated schema.

## Optional, and worth a thought

- **Public share links** are off by default (`PIWI_SHARE_LINKS_ENABLED`). If you turn them on, know that anyone with the link sees the execution, cluster, report snapshot or dashboard it opens without signing in — see [Share links](/features/share-links).
- **Retention.** Automatic pruning is opt-in; set `PIWI_RETENTION_DAYS` to cap how much run history you keep. See [Storage → Data retention](./storage#data-retention).
- **Observability.** Both are off by default. `PIWI_METRICS_ENABLED=true` serves the metric catalog to a Prometheus you run, and naming an OpenTelemetry collector sends it a trace of each request with the SQL statements it ran, their parameters as placeholders. See [Metrics and rollup export](./metrics) and [Tracing with OpenTelemetry](./tracing).

# Authentication

This page covers sign-in, instance roles, OAuth and user accounts; project roles are on [Access, roles and groups](./project-access), keys on [API keys](./api-keys). Sign-in is **off by default**: every request then acts as one administrator. Turn it on before anyone else can reach the instance; the [production checklist](./production-checklist) lists the rest.

## Roles

Every account holds one **instance role**:

| Instance role | What it can do |
|------|-------------|
| **Administrator** | Everything, on every project: users, groups, instance settings, AI providers, Jira connections, storage, tags, creating and deleting projects (a first upload [can create one too](./project-access#all-projects-or-one-project)). Never restricted by project roles. |
| **Member** | Signs in and manages their own profile, API keys, dashboards, notification channels and subscriptions. Everything else comes from their project roles. |

A Member's rights inside a project come from the **project roles** granted to them or their groups ([Access, roles and groups](./project-access)). The Administrator role is granted to a user, never to a group.

## Enabling authentication

1. Set these variables wherever you configure the server (the container's environment, `.env`, or your host's
   dashboard):

   ```bash
   PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED=true
   PIWI_AUTH_SECRET=your-auth-secret-here  # signs session cookies
   PIWI_SECRET_KEY=your-secret-key-here    # encrypts stored secrets (AI keys, credentials)
   ```

   Generate a strong random value for each secret (run it twice):

   ```bash
   node -e "console.log(require('node:crypto').randomBytes(32).toString('hex'))"
   ```

2. Restart the server. It refuses to start with authentication on and no `PIWI_AUTH_SECRET`, or one shorter than 32
   characters.

## Initial setup

While authentication is on and no administrator exists (even after members signed in through OAuth), the login page
shows a **Create the first admin account** form instead of the sign-in form, which signs you in as the administrator.
A script can make the same call:

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/setup -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"username": "admin", "password": "your-secure-password", "name": "Administrator"}'
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
$body = @{ username = 'admin'; password = 'your-secure-password'; name = 'Administrator' } | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri http://localhost:3000/api/auth/setup `
  -ContentType 'application/json' -Body $body
```

:::

The endpoint is rate-limited per client address. On an instance reachable from the internet, set `PIWI_SETUP_TOKEN` to
a random value: the form asks for it, and the API call carries it as `"setupToken"`, so a stranger cannot become the
administrator first. The Railway, Render and Coolify [one-click deploy templates](./one-click-deploy) generate it.

## Logging in

Sign in at `/login` with your username or your email address (letter case ignored, verified or not). A username wins
over another account's email, such as the old address a provider-created account kept as its username.

A session is an encrypted cookie, `__Host-piwi_session`, lasting 7 days, that neighboring subdomains cannot set. It is marked `Secure`, so browser sign-in needs HTTPS, except on `localhost`. Signing out ends the account's sessions in every browser.

## OAuth (Google, GitHub)

Users can also sign in with Google or GitHub; there is no other provider, nor generic OpenID Connect or SAML.

### Configuring OAuth

1. **Register an OAuth application** with each provider you want to use:

   - **Google**: in the [Google Cloud Console](https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/credentials), create an OAuth 2.0 Client ID with the Google callback URL below as an authorized redirect URI.
   - **GitHub**: under **Settings → Developer settings → OAuth Apps** on GitHub, create an OAuth app with the GitHub callback URL below.

   ```text
   https://your-domain.com/api/auth/oauth/google/callback
   https://your-domain.com/api/auth/oauth/github/callback
   ```

2. **Set the credentials** alongside the other variables:

   ```bash
   PIWI_OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=your-google-client-id
   PIWI_OAUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET=your-google-client-secret
   PIWI_OAUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=your-github-client-id
   PIWI_OAUTH_GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-github-client-secret
   ```

3. **Restart the server.** The login page shows a **Sign in with …** button for each provider whose `CLIENT_ID` and `CLIENT_SECRET` are both set.

> **Behind a reverse proxy:** set `PIWI_SITE_URL` to your public URL (e.g. `https://piwi.example.com`): the OAuth `redirect_uri` is built from it, else from the request's host, which a proxy may rewrite.

### Restricting who can sign in (allowlists)

By default any account at a configured provider can sign in. To restrict it:

- **`PIWI_OAUTH_ALLOWED_DOMAINS`** — comma-separated email domains (e.g. `example.com,acme.org`). Only **verified** provider emails in these domains may sign in. Applies to all providers.
- **`PIWI_OAUTH_GITHUB_ALLOWED_ORGS`** — comma-separated GitHub org logins. The user must belong to at least one; it requests the `read:org` scope to check membership, private included.

A rejected sign-in returns to the login page, saying why.

### Account linking

A first provider sign-in links an existing account or creates one. Email addresses are compared ignoring case, so `Bob@corp.com` and `bob@corp.com` are the same address, and an address belongs to at most one account.

- If a user with the same **verified** email exists (and isn't linked to a *different* provider), that account is linked. Linking needs proof on both sides: the provider asserts the email is verified, **and** the local account verified it too (a verification link, an accepted invite, or an earlier provider sign-in), so an address someone typed into their own profile cannot capture another person's sign-in.
- If the matching account has **not** verified the address, the sign-in is refused, saying why. The account's owner signs in with its password (or accepts their invite first) and connects the provider from **Settings → Account**.
- If the matching account is **linked to a different provider**, the sign-in is refused: one provider per account.
- Otherwise, a new user is created as a **Member** with no project role and no password, so it always signs in through its provider and sees nothing until it is [granted a role](./project-access#default-is-no-access). An email the provider has not verified never links an account, so GitHub accounts with no verified primary email always get a new account.

The new account stores the provider's email, unverified unless the provider verified it, or **no email** when another account uses it. Its username is its email, else the GitHub login, else `<provider>-<id>`; a taken one gets a number appended (`octocat-2`).

Each later sign-in updates the name, avatar and email from the provider, keeping the email when the provider sends none or one another account uses.

Piwi keeps no provider token: the access token serves the sign-in, then is discarded. The demo has no OAuth.

### Connecting / disconnecting a provider

Signed-in users link a provider from **Settings → Account → Connected accounts**:

- **Connect** attaches the provider identity to the current account; one already linked to another account is refused. An account without an email address takes the provider's, unless another account uses it.
- **Disconnect** removes the link, only when the account has a password, so a provider-only user cannot lock themselves out.

## User management

Administrators manage accounts under **Settings → Users** (`/settings/users`). **Add user** creates one with a
username, an instance role, an optional display name and email, and a password. Without one, the row's **Send invite email**
button mails the user a link to set their own. Each row shows the user's instance role and
[groups](./project-access#groups).

**Settings → Account** takes a profile picture (PNG, JPEG or WebP, under 1 MB, at most 1000×1000 pixels) that
replaces the provider's and that administrators can remove. Only its owner sees it; others see the initials.

An email address belongs to one account, ignoring letter case: creating or editing an account with an address another
account already uses is refused, and **Forgot password?** finds the account whatever the case typed. An upgrade that
finds such duplicates stops until an administrator fixes them: see
[What happens when a new version starts](./upgrading#what-happens-when-a-new-version-starts).

A link Piwi emails, to verify an address, accept an invite or reset a password, works only while the account holds
the address it was sent to; once the address changes, whoever changed it, resend to the new one.

### Email and account recovery

Invitations, address verification and **Forgot password?** need [SMTP](/features/notifications#smtp-configuration).
Without it, invites and verification links are refused, and **Forgot password?** says a link was sent but sends
nothing. Invite and reset emails name the sign-in username.

No administrator can set another account's password: a locked-out account recovers through **Forgot password?**, which
needs SMTP and an email address on the account. Give every administrator an email address, or keep two, so one can
set the other's address to one that receives mail.

### Changing a role

Each row's **Role** column sets the instance role, **Administrator** or **Member**, at once, revoking the user's sessions: the only way to make an account, [OAuth](#oauth-google-github) ones included, an administrator. The **last remaining administrator cannot be demoted**.

## Disabling authentication

Set `PIWI_AUTH_ENABLED=false`, or remove the variable, and restart the server.

With authentication off, the dashboard answers only requests whose `Host` header names an IP address, `localhost`, a
name under `.localhost`, the host of [`PIWI_SITE_URL`](/reference/configuration#general) or a name `PIWI_ALLOWED_HOSTS`
lists (the service name a container or pod calls it by, such as `piwi`, `host.docker.internal`, or `.example.lan` for a whole domain); any other gets
a `403` that lists those addresses. A request with no `Host` comes from no browser and is answered. Over plain HTTP, a
write must also come from the requested host, `PIWI_SITE_URL`'s or a listed one. The entry `*` of `PIWI_ALLOWED_HOSTS`
turns the first check off, and with it the protection against DNS rebinding.

Behind a [reverse proxy](./deployment#reverse-proxy-https), set `PIWI_SITE_URL` and have the proxy
forward the browser's `Host` header (Apache: `ProxyPreserveHost On`): the check reads `Host` alone, never
`X-Forwarded-Host`, so a proxy that sends its own local address instead lets every request through.

- [Access, roles and groups](./project-access): project roles, groups and the permission grid
- [API keys](./api-keys): authenticating the reporter, CI and scripts
- [Production checklist](./production-checklist): the secrets, TLS and proxy settings to go with it
- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration#authentication): every authentication and OAuth variable

# Access, roles and groups

This page covers **project roles**, the groups that hold them and who grants them; the instance roles, Administrator
and Member, are on [Authentication](./authentication#roles). With authentication on, a signed-in user's rights inside a
project come from the project roles they hold there. An Administrator can do everything on every project. A Member can do only what their project
roles allow, granted to them directly or to one of their groups; a Member with no role sees an empty dashboard.

## Project roles

A project role is a fixed set of rights inside a project, granted to a user or a group, on one project or on all
projects. The first four build on each other, each including everything the one before it can do. Uploader stands
apart.

| Role | Typical holder | What it is for |
|---|---|---|
| **Viewer** | stakeholder | Reads everything in the project. |
| **Contributor** | product owner, manager | Files issues, pins links, edits bug reports, schedules reports, adds markers. |
| **Maintainer** | QA engineer, developer | Triages failures, [quarantines tests](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out), runs AI diagnosis, uploads runs, creates share links. |
| **Project admin** | QA lead, tech lead | Edits the project settings and members, deletes runs. |
| **Uploader** | CI account | For CI: reads the project and uploads runs, nothing else. |

## What each role can do

Each row is one permission. The **Permission** column is how the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api) name
each endpoint's requirement (`x-required-permission`), so a script author can tell which role a call needs. In the app,
**Settings → Roles** shows the same table to every signed-in user.

| What you can do | Permission | Viewer | Contributor | Maintainer | Project admin | Uploader |
|---|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Read runs, executions, clusters, analytics | `project:read` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| File a Jira issue | `issue:create` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Pin, edit and remove links | `link:write` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Edit a bug report | `bug-report:write` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Save and schedule reports | `report:write` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Add and edit timeline markers | `marker:write` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Run tests on my machine from the dashboard | `run:request` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Connect an app that runs my requests | `run:receive` | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Create share links, share a dashboard | `share:create` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Triage clusters and gaps | `triage:write` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Quarantine and release tests | `quarantine:write` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Run AI diagnosis (spends tokens) | `ai:run` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Re-run in CI, bisect, Flake Lab, fix attempts, let a held CI test go, pause a CI test | `run:control` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Edit selections and test functions | `test-assets:write` | | | ✓ | ✓ | |
| Upload runs | `run:submit` | | | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Edit project settings and Jira binding | `project:manage` | | | | ✓ | |
| Manage the project's members | `project:members` | | | | ✓ | |
| Delete runs, release kept runs | `run:delete` | | | | ✓ | |

Only an Administrator holds the **instance permissions**: `users:manage`, `groups:manage`, `settings:manage`,
`connections:manage`, `credentials:manage`, `storage:manage`, `tags:manage`, `project:create` and
`project:delete`. An endpoint any signed-in user may call (their profile, API keys, dashboards, channels,
subscriptions) declares `signed-in`.

## All projects or one project

A role is granted on one project, or on **All projects**, which also covers projects created later. A user's rights on
a project are the **union** of every role they hold there, on that project and on All projects, directly and through
each of their groups. Maintainer on All projects plus Project admin on `web-app` means Project admin on `web-app` and
Maintainer everywhere else.

An administrator creates a project in the dashboard; results sent under a new project name create one too, from an
account that can upload on All projects.

## Groups

A group is a named set of users, such as *QA*, *Product owners* or *CI*. It receives project roles the way a user
does, so a new hire gets their access by joining groups. Administrators create, rename and delete groups and edit
their members in **Settings → Groups**.

- **Rights add up.** A user in *Product owners* (Contributor on All projects) and *QA* (Maintainer on All projects)
  can do what a Maintainer does everywhere.
- **No deny rules.** To take a right away, remove the role that grants it.
- **No nested groups.** A group holds users, never other groups.
- **A group never makes anyone an Administrator.** That instance role is granted to a user, on their own row in
  **Settings → Users**.

## Who manages access

**Administrators** manage everything: users, groups, and roles on every project and on All projects. A **Project
admin** manages the members of their own projects and may grant any project role there, Project admin included, but
cannot change roles on other projects or on All projects.

Roles are granted from four places, which all edit the same grants:

- **Settings → Permissions**, the [permission grid](#permission-grid): every group and user against every project.
- **Settings → Users → Project roles**, the action next to a user: their role on All projects and on each project,
  with the groups that add to them.
- **Project → Settings → Members**: the users and groups with a role on that project. Project admins see it for
  their own projects. Their picker lists the users who share a project with them; anyone else, such as a new account,
  is found by their whole username.
- **Settings → Groups** for who belongs to each group; its roles are set on the grid or in a project's Members.

Scripts read and change the same grants, called role bindings, through the API; see the
[API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api).

## Permission grid

**Settings → Permissions** lays every group and user against every project on one grid. Groups come first, above the
users; columns are projects, after an **All projects** column. Each cell is a role selector: pick a role to grant it
there, or none to remove it.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/permission-grid.png" alt="Settings → Permissions: groups above users down the side, projects across the top, and a role selector in each cell">
  <figcaption>The permissions grid: a role in each cell, for a group or a user on a project.</figcaption>
</figure>

- **Every change saves at once.** A change the server refuses is rolled back and reported.
- **Inherited roles show faint.** A role a user holds only through a group or All projects appears faint, and its
  tooltip names its source.
- **All projects** also covers projects created later. Removing a role there leaves the per-project roles as they were.
- **Administrators** can do everything everywhere, so their row is locked.
- **Hovering or focusing a cell highlights its row and column.** Tab enters the grid as one stop, the arrow keys move
  between cells, and Space or Enter opens the role selector.
- **Filter users** and **Filter projects** narrow the grid on a large instance.

## Default is no access

A new Member, added in **Settings → Users** or created by an [OAuth](./authentication#oauth-google-github) sign-in,
holds no role and sees an empty dashboard until you grant one, as does an account whose last role you remove. A
project the user has no role on is left out of the project list, sidebar, home dashboard, recent runs and search, and
its runs, test cases and clusters return **403**. A link to one of its pages opens a _No access_ page, answered with the
same 403, that says an administrator or a Project admin of that project can grant a role.

## CI accounts

Run the reporter in CI as a dedicated Member with the **Uploader** role, through its own
[API key](./api-keys#using-the-api-key-in-the-reporter): a leaked CI key can then read and upload, never triage, delete
or change anything. Grant it on All projects when CI should create
projects from a new project name, else on the projects it reports to. A CI account that the upgrade to project
roles made a Maintainer narrows the same way.

> **Try it in the demo:** the [live demo](https://piwitests.dev/demo/) ships with seeded identities, from an
> administrator to a viewer. Switch between them with the **Acting as** picker in the demo banner and watch the
> projects and actions change. See [UI overview → Live demo](/features/ui-overview#live-demo).

- [API keys](./api-keys): a key acts with its owner's instance role and project roles
- [Production checklist](./production-checklist): what to set before anyone else can reach the instance

# API keys

An API key is a long-lived token tied to one user account, and the recommended way to authenticate CI pipelines, the
Playwright reporter and scripts once [authentication](./authentication) is on. A key carries its owner's access: their
[instance role](./authentication#roles) and the [project roles](./project-access) they hold, directly or through
their groups. A key for a Member with the Uploader role on one project can read that project and upload to it, and
nothing else. The key a connected run target receives (the desktop app, Piwi Runner) is the one exception: it holds
`run:receive` and, for the desktop app, `project:read`, and serves only that app's routes.

For CI, give the key to a dedicated account that can only upload: [CI accounts](./project-access#ci-accounts) says
which role and where.

With authentication on, every endpoint needs a session cookie or an API key whose owner holds the permission the
endpoint declares (listed per endpoint in the [API docs](https://piwitests.dev/demo/settings/api)). The exceptions are the
health and version endpoints, the sign-in flows themselves, and live-run streaming, which uses per-run stream tokens.

## Security properties

- Keys are generated with 256 bits of cryptographic entropy (`pd_` prefix + 64-character hex string).
- Only a SHA-256 hash of the key is stored in the database: the plaintext is shown **once** at creation time and is
  never retrievable again.
- Each key displays a short prefix (`pd_xxxxxxxx…`) in the UI for identification without revealing the secret, with
  its creation date and when it was last used.
- Keys are sent as `Authorization: Bearer <key>` or `X-API-Key: <key>` headers.
- Keys can be given an optional expiry date.

## What a key cannot do

A key acts for its owner everywhere except on the account's own credentials. These take a signed-in session, and a
request with a key gets a 403:

- creating an API key, for any account;
- allowing a [browser extension](/features/extension-connection), an
  [editor](/features/editor-connection) or an [MCP client](/features/mcp) to connect, which creates a key or a
  connection for the account;
- changing the account's password or its own email address, and disconnecting its OAuth provider.

A key therefore cannot create keys or change its own account's credentials, nor move the account's password reset to
another address. An administrator's key still manages the other users, their email addresses included, and creates
accounts with a password, so it is as powerful as the administrator's password: keep it with the same care.

## Creating an API key

Every signed-in user manages their own keys under **Settings → Account → API keys**. An administrator can also manage
any user's keys from **Settings → Users**, with the key icon next to the user; that is how you create a key for a
dedicated CI account.

1. Click **Create API key**, enter a descriptive name (e.g. "GitHub Actions"), and set an optional expiry.
2. Click **Generate key**, and copy the key **immediately**: it will never be shown again.
3. Store it as a CI secret (e.g. `PIWI_API_KEY`).

Connecting the [browser extension](/features/extension-connection), an editor or the desktop app creates a key too,
once you click **Allow** on the page it opens: it is named after the app ("Piwi Picker in Chrome on Windows") and
listed under **Settings → Account → [Connected apps](/features/run-on-my-machine#connected-apps)**, not with these
keys.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/user-api-keys.png" alt="A user's API keys dialog: one key named GitHub Actions CI with its prefix, creation date and Never used, a revoke button, and Create API key">
  <figcaption>A user's API keys: each shown by its prefix, with its last use.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Revoking an API key

Click the trash icon next to the key, in the same place you created it. The key stops working immediately.

## Using the API key in the reporter

The reporter needs a credential only once authentication is on, and sends its key as an `Authorization: Bearer`
header. **Settings → Connect a suite** creates a key in place. The reporter reads it from `PIWI_API_KEY`, in the
environment or in the `.env` beside the Playwright config (`init --api-key` writes it there, unless git tracks that
file or cannot say whether it does, or the file is a link), so the config needs no change: store the key as a CI
secret under that name, and locally in that `.env`. To read it from another variable, pass it as the `apiKey` option,
in the [`wrapConfig`](/guide/reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig) options or the reporter entry:

```typescript
// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from '@playwright/test'
import { wrapConfig } from '@piwitests/reporter'

export default wrapConfig(defineConfig({ testDir: './tests' }), {
  serverUrl: 'https://your-dashboard.example.com',
  projectName: 'my-project',
  apiKey: process.env.MY_DASHBOARD_KEY,
})
```

## Using the API key in raw HTTP calls

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
# Authorization: Bearer header (recommended)
curl -X POST https://your-dashboard.example.com/api/test-runs/submit -H "Authorization: Bearer pd_<your-key>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ ... }'

# X-API-Key header (alternative)
curl -X POST https://your-dashboard.example.com/api/test-runs/submit -H "X-API-Key: pd_<your-key>" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{ ... }'
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
# Authorization: Bearer header (recommended)
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri https://your-dashboard.example.com/api/test-runs/submit `
  -Headers @{ Authorization = 'Bearer pd_<your-key>' } `
  -ContentType 'application/json' -Body '{ ... }'

# X-API-Key header (alternative)
Invoke-RestMethod -Method Post -Uri https://your-dashboard.example.com/api/test-runs/submit `
  -Headers @{ 'X-API-Key' = 'pd_<your-key>' } `
  -ContentType 'application/json' -Body '{ ... }'
```

:::

## Using the reporter with a username and password

As an alternative to API keys, give the reporter the credentials of a dedicated [CI account](./project-access#ci-accounts),
created in **Settings → Users**: set `PIWI_USERNAME` (its username or email address) and `PIWI_PASSWORD` as secrets in
your CI provider (or the `username` and `password` options). An API key wins when both are set.

The reporter signs in once per run, when it opens the run's stream (at the end of the run with `streaming: false`), and
uses the session for every request of the run; the global setup step signs in once more, in its own process, when it
registers the run. A sign-in that fails while the dashboard is down is tried again with the stream. API keys are still
preferred for CI: they need no sign-in round-trip, and each one can be revoked on its own.

- [Metrics and rollup export](./metrics): scraping with an API key

# Credentials

A credential is a secret Piwi sends to another service, saved once under **Settings → Credentials** and named wherever
it is needed: a CI server action, [source control](/guide/source-control), an AI role, a Jira or Zephyr Scale
connection or a Slack channel. A rotation is one change, and every use is logged.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/credentials-settings.png" alt="Settings → Credentials: four Jenkins, two GitHub and a Zephyr Scale credential, a Jenkins one open in a panel with its user, destination, projects, the three CI actions that name it and its log of dispatches and checks">
  <figcaption>Settings → Credentials: a credential's panel, with the CI actions that name it and its log.</figcaption>
</figure>

## What a credential holds

| Field | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Service** | **CI server**, **Source control** for a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket token, **AI provider**, **Jira Cloud**, **Zephyr Scale** or **Slack**. |
| **Name** | Unique on the instance, ignoring case; the name the pickers and the log show. |
| **Destination** | The base URL the secret may be sent under (`https://jenkins.example.com/`). A request to any other address, or outside its path, is refused. |
| **User** | The user name sent with the secret as HTTP Basic authentication, when a CI server takes one; for Jira, the account's e-mail. |
| **Secret** | The API token, saved encrypted with `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`, together with the destination, or read from a server variable (below). Never returned by any page, API answer or log. |
| **Projects** | The projects that may name it: a list, or all projects, present and future. |
| **Inputs** | For a CI server, the CI action inputs a request carrying it may send beside the arguments and the dispatch id: every input, or the names listed. |
| **Custom requests** | For a CI server, whether a Custom request may carry it. Off by default: a Custom request can reach any path under the destination, a CI server's script console included. |

Saving a secret needs `PIWI_SECRET_KEY` (see the [production checklist](./production-checklist)); without it, the
form says so and nothing is saved. Changing the destination asks for the secret again, since the secret is sealed with
the one destination it may be sent under.

## A secret from a server variable

An administrator can have a credential read its secret from a variable of the server's environment instead of saving
it: **Secret source** → **Read from a server variable**, then the variable's name. Only a variable named
`PIWI_CREDENTIAL_…` (capitals, digits and `_`) can be named, so no other variable of the server, such as
`PIWI_SECRET_KEY` or a database URL, can be sent anywhere. Set it as the server's other variables are set, from a
secrets store or the container's environment:

```bash [.env]
PIWI_CREDENTIAL_JENKINS=11a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6
```

The variable is read at each use, so changing it and restarting the server is the rotation. Its name is sealed with
the destination like a saved secret, so a new destination is saved with the name again (the form sends it). The
panel says when the variable is not set on the server, and a dispatch is then refused and logged. Only an
administrator may change a credential that reads a variable.

## Who manages them

An administrator (the `credentials:manage` permission) creates, changes, disables and deletes any credential, and is the
only one who may share one with all projects. A Project admin opens **Settings → Credentials** too, and sees there the
credentials they manage: the ones they created, shared only with projects they manage and reading no variable. They
create them there or from a project's **CI** or **Source control** settings. A credential an administrator saved or
changed is the administrator's: a Project admin picks it, and never loosens its rules or undoes a **Disable**. Anyone
who manages a project picks any credential shared with it, for its CI actions or its source control, without ever
reading its secret. See
[Access, roles and groups](./project-access).

**Disable** refuses every use of a credential at once, for an incident, without touching the actions that name it.
**Delete** is refused while something names the credential (a CI action, source control, an AI role, a connection, a
Slack channel): the answer lists them.

## Using one in a CI action

In **Project → Settings → CI**, a CI server action's editor has a **Credential** picker and a **New credential**
button. The action's base URL may stay empty: it is then the credential's destination. The request preview shows which
credential the request carries, the inputs it does not allow, and when it would refuse the request.

Each dispatch and each **Check** checks the credential again before anything is sent: still active, shared with the
project, and holding the request's URL under its destination, and allowing a Custom request when the action sends one.

## What names a credential

- **A CI action**: a CI server action's requests, or the dispatch, **Check** and listings of a GitHub, GitLab or
  Bitbucket action ([CI actions](/features/ci-actions)).
- **Source control**: a project's repository calls, else the instance's, with a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket token sent
  to the host's API ([Source control](/guide/source-control#set-the-credential)).
- **An AI role**: the key of a role of **Settings → AI**, sent to its provider ([AI provider](/guide/ai-provider#api-keys)).
- **A Jira or Zephyr Scale connection, or a global Slack channel**: its token
  ([below](#connections-and-slack-channels)).

Whatever names it, a credential is checked and logged as this page says; each page says what its feature sends and
how the secrets saved before credentials existed were moved.

## The CI server credential of the environment

The operator can set one CI server credential through the environment: `PIWI_CI_SERVER_URL`, `PIWI_CI_SERVER_USER` and
`PIWI_CI_SERVER_TOKEN`. It shows on the page as a read-only credential, shared with all projects, and is sent by a CI
server action that names no credential, only with a preset's request under `PIWI_CI_SERVER_URL`, and with only the
inputs `PIWI_CI_SERVER_ALLOWED_INPUTS` lists. Its uses are logged like any other. See the
[configuration reference](/reference/configuration).

A CI server token stored on a project (`projects.ci_server_token`) is moved to a credential at startup: bound to the
URL it was saved with, shared with its project, allowed with a Custom request and every input, and named by the CI
server actions it served. Two projects holding the same token for the same URL and user share one credential. An
administrator manages it, since the database does not say who saved the token. A token that cannot be opened (a
changed `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`) stays where it is, with a warning in the log at each start.

## Connections and Slack channels

The token typed for a Jira or Zephyr Scale connection (**Settings → Integrations**) or a global Slack channel's bot
(**Settings → Notifications**) becomes its credential, named after it, shared with all projects
and sent only under the Jira site (a scoped token's Atlassian gateway counts as the site), the Zephyr Scale region's
API or Slack's Web API. **Saved credential** picks another. A token typed later rotates the connection's credential, or saves a new one while
something else names it. Opening a
connection is a counted read; each write (an issue, a comment, a transition, an attachment, a results upload, a link)
and each Slack message is a row. A personal channel keeps its own token. Deleting one asks whether to delete its
credential too.

`PIWI_JIRA_*` and `PIWI_ZEPHYR_*` make a read-only credential that reads the token from the variable. At startup, each
connection's token moves to a credential of its own, and equal tokens of global channels to one.

## The log

A credential's panel lists its uses, newest first, and the page's **Log**, for an administrator, those of every
credential, a deleted one and the environment's included:

- **What**: a CI dispatch, Check or job listing, with the CI action it was for; a repository read, a commit status, a
  pull-request comment or an auto-heal write, with its commit, pull request or branch; an AI model call; a read or a
  write of a Jira or Zephyr Scale connection; a Slack message, with its channel.
- **Where**: the project, and the request's origin and path (never its query).
- **Who**: the user who started it, and the API key when it came through one (an MCP tool, a script); for counted
  Checks and listings, the last of the hour.
- **How it ended**: `sent` until the service answers, then `ok` or `failed` with the reason; `refused` when the
  credential's rules stopped it before anything was sent, with the reason.

A dispatch or another write is one row. A Check or a repository read only reads, so the reads of a project are counted
in one row per result and hour. The secret is masked in any reason a service's answer holds. The log is kept 365 days, or
`PIWI_RETENTION_CREDENTIAL_LOG_DAYS` (0 keeps it forever), by the nightly sweep; a deleted credential's rows stay in the
page's **Log**, under its name, until then.

## Related

- [Per-user credentials](./per-user-credentials): each person's own token
- [Source control](/guide/source-control): what reads and writes a repository with an SCM credential
- [Jira Cloud](./integrations) and [Zephyr Scale](./zephyr-scale): the connections that name a credential
- [Access, roles and groups](./project-access): who holds `credentials:manage` and `project:manage`
- [Production checklist](./production-checklist): `PIWI_SECRET_KEY`, which encrypts every secret

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/operate/per-user-credentials -->

# Per-user credentials

A per-user credential runs a CI action in the name of whoever starts it. A shared [credential](./credentials) sends
one secret, so Jenkins shows its account (a `piwi-bot`) as the user who started every build and applies that account's
rights. A per-user credential holds no user and no secret: an administrator sets it up once, each person gives their
own Jenkins user name and API token for it, and a build started from Piwi shows "Started by user alice" and runs with
Alice's rights.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/credentials-per-user.png" alt="A per-user Jenkins credential's panel: it acts as whoever starts an action, each person's own token, the three people who gave theirs with their Jenkins account and its state, one refused by Jenkins, and its log with Quinn's dispatch and Jordan's, which Jenkins refused">
  <figcaption>A per-user credential's panel: who gave their token, as which Jenkins account, and its log.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Set one up

In **Settings → Credentials**, **New credential**, service **CI server**, then **Who it acts as** → **Per user**. Only
an administrator (the `credentials:manage` permission) creates or changes one, and creates it only while sign-in is
on: it collects other people's tokens, so its destination is one an administrator chose. The destination is https, or
a host `PIWI_CI_SERVER_HOSTS` lists, since a token is never sent in the clear. Its fields are a shared credential's
without the user and the secret, plus an optional link to the page where a person creates their token (Jenkins: their
user's **Security** page).

A Project admin then picks it in a CI server action's **Credential**, as any credential shared with the project. It
never goes with a Custom request. To bound what a token can build, give the credential a folder as its destination
(`https://jenkins.example.com/job/qa/`): an action outside it is refused.

## Give your token

Each person gives their token once, under **Account → Credentials**, or in the run dialog the first time they start an
action on it. The form says where the token goes and who set the credential up. Piwi tests the token before saving it,
by reading Jenkins' `whoAmI` at the root of the destination, and keeps the account Jenkins names.

- **An API token only**: 32 or 34 hexadecimal characters, as Jenkins makes them. An account password, which Jenkins
  also takes, is refused and never stored.
- **One account per person**: a token for a Jenkins account another person already gave is refused, so a shared
  service account cannot be saved as someone's own.
- **10 tests per person and credential in 10 minutes**, and a failed test says only that Jenkins refused the token,
  did not recognize it as a signed-in user, or could not be reached, never Jenkins' own answer.

**Test** sends the saved token again; **Remove** takes it out of Piwi. A removed token stays valid on Jenkins: revoke
it there too.

## GitLab and Bitbucket

A per-user **Source control** credential runs a GitLab pipeline or a Bitbucket custom pipeline in the name of whoever
starts it. Each person authorizes it once at the host, in a popup, instead of typing a token: the host shows the
pipeline as theirs, and its rights apply. A GitHub destination cannot be per user: the form offers it for GitLab and
Bitbucket only.

- **Set it up**: register an OAuth application, on GitLab (scope `api`, on gitlab.com or a host
  `PIWI_SCM_GITLAB_HOSTS` lists) or on Bitbucket (an OAuth consumer with the Account read, Repositories read and
  Pipelines write permissions), with the callback URL the credential form shows. Then create the credential with
  service **Source control**, the host's API as destination, **Per user**, and the application's client id and
  secret. The secret is sealed with the host's token endpoint and sent only to its OAuth endpoints (token and
  revocation).
- **Authorize**: **Authorize with GitLab** (or Bitbucket) under **Account → Credentials**, or in the run dialog. The
  authorization is bound to you and the credential, used once, and expires after 10 minutes; Piwi then reads the
  account the token belongs to and keeps it.
- **Refresh and revocation**: an access token is refreshed when it is used within 5 minutes of its expiry, and marked
  refused when the host refuses the refresh. **Remove**, an administrator's removal and the deletion of an account
  revoke a GitLab token at GitLab; Bitbucket offers no revocation, so revoke it in Bitbucket's settings.

A per-user source control credential serves CI actions only, never a project's or the instance's source control.

## What runs in your name

- **Only from a signed-in page.** An API key, an MCP agent included, never starts an action in someone's name: the
  request is refused before anything is sent.
- **Only your own token.** A person without one is asked for it before the dispatch is sent or stored; a token is
  never sent for anyone else.
- **Only the action you saw.** The run dialog shows the job, the fixed inputs and your Jenkins account, and a dispatch
  refuses an action changed since the dialog showed it.
- **A token Jenkins refuses** (401) is marked refused and no longer sent, until you give it again or a test passes.

The action editor's credential picker says which credential runs in the starter's name; its **Check** and job
listings read with the editor's own token.

## What an administrator sees

The credential's panel lists who gave a token, with their Jenkins account, its state and its last use, never the
token, and removes one or all. **Disable** stops every token at once. A new destination removes every token, each
sealed with the one it leaves. The log names each use's person, and their Jenkins account for a use of their saved
token, and counts each person's reads in rows of their own.

- [CI actions](/features/ci-actions): the CI server action that names the credential
- [CI re-run](/features/ci-rerun): the run dialog that asks for your token
- [Access, roles and groups](./project-access): who holds `credentials:manage`

# Localization

Piwi formats every date and time in the browser with the `Intl` API, so how they read follows a
locale (day/month order, 12-hour vs 24-hour time) and which moment they show follows a time zone.
Out of the box dates read in US English (`9/22/2026, 2:30:05 PM`) in the viewer's own time zone.

You can change both, at three levels, and each person can keep their own format.

## Who sets what

- **Each viewer** picks their own format under **Settings → Localization**. It is saved in that
  browser and overrides everything below, for that person only.
- **An administrator** sets the instance default on the same page. Everyone who has not chosen their
  own format gets it.
- **The environment** can pin the instance default with `PIWI_LOCALE` and `PIWI_TIME_ZONE`. Those
  fields then show read-only in the UI, but a viewer can still override the format for their own
  browser.

Precedence, highest first: the per-viewer override, then the env var, then the stored instance
default, then the built-in default (`en-US`, in the viewer's own browser time zone).

## Date and time format

The format follows a [BCP-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IETF_language_tag) locale. A few examples
of the same instant:

| Locale  | Formatted                 |
| ------- | ------------------------- |
| `en-US` | `9/22/2026, 2:30:05 PM`   |
| `en-GB` | `22/09/2026, 14:30:05`    |
| `fr-FR` | `22/09/2026 14:30:05`     |
| `de-DE` | `22.9.2026, 14:30:05`     |
| `ja-JP` | `2026/9/22 14:30:05`      |

The settings dropdown lists common locales; `Intl` accepts any valid tag, so an environment value is
not limited to that list. The keyword `auto` follows each viewer's browser.

```bash
PIWI_LOCALE=fr-FR
```

## Time zone

Absolute times are shown in an [IANA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_tz_database_time_zones)
time zone. The default, `auto`, uses each viewer's own browser time zone, so a distributed team each
reads times in their local clock. Set a fixed zone when everyone should read the same wall-clock
time (a shared CI region, for example).

```bash
PIWI_TIME_ZONE=Europe/Paris
```

## Related

- [Configuration reference](/reference/configuration): `PIWI_LOCALE`, `PIWI_TIME_ZONE` and every other setting
- [Configuration generator](/reference/configuration/generator): writes the block for you

<!-- https://piwitests.dev/operate/capabilities -->

# Choose what you use

**Settings → Capabilities** (`/settings/capabilities`, administrators only) is where an instance says what else it does once results arrive. It opens on one coarse question, *What do you want Piwi for?*, with **See why tests fail** always on and three opt-out groups: **Triage as a team** (notifications, [quarantine](/features/flaky-tests#quarantine-with-a-way-out), pull-request feedback, issue tracking), **Fix faster** (locator healing, auto-heal), and **Let agents in** (AI diagnosis, the assistant). Below it, a ladder lists every optional capability grouped by state: **Active** (evidence has arrived), **Available** (configured but not used yet), **Not set up**, and a folded **Declined** group. The page ends with **Off until turned on**: [Run on my machine](/features/run-on-my-machine) and [Pass reuse](/features/reuse-forecast) stay off until an administrator turns them on.

## Declining a capability

Not every team uses every capability. Any optional one can be **declined** so the dashboard stops showing it everywhere: the evidence tabs, empty panels, settings page, sidebar entry, project actions and MCP tools it owns all go, rather than lingering half-visible. Decline instance-wide from the ladder (*Not for this instance*) or the presets, or per project from the **Capabilities** section of the project's **Settings** tab and the places the capability appears (for example the execution page's evidence footer, *Not for this project*). A project override can also **enable** a capability the instance declined.

Declining instance-wide is for administrators, and per project for the project's [Project admin](./project-access#project-roles) role. It is never final: each declined capability keeps a *Reconsider* link on the ladder that clears the decision, and because data always wins, a declined capability that starts receiving data reads as active again with the stored decision shown next to it. [Why a card is empty](#why-a-card-is-empty) says how this reads on the execution page.

<figure>
  <img src="/screenshots/setup-ladder-declined-wide.png" alt="The Capabilities settings page's list of what is switched on, Notifications among the active capabilities, marked declined with a Reconsider link beside its docs link">
  <figcaption>A declined capability that still receives data reads as active, its decision and Reconsider link beside it.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Why a card is empty

On the [execution page](/features/evidence), a tab that needs the capture fixtures appears only when it holds data or
the fixtures ran and found nothing; otherwise one footer line names the missing tabs. An empty card says which case
applies: **captured, nothing happened**, **not applicable** (backend logs need a
[backend integration](/guide/backend-logs)), or **declined** for this project
([Declining a capability](#declining-a-capability)). The AI diagnosis's **Data coverage** block uses the same words.

- [Getting started](/guide/getting-started): connect a first suite
- [All features](/reference/features): every capability and what it needs
- [Jira Cloud](./integrations) and [Zephyr Scale Cloud](./zephyr-scale): connect the issue tracker and the test management tool some capabilities use
