# Glossary

Every word the documentation and the dashboard use, each defined in a few lines with a link to the page that holds its
rule. A word that names two things elsewhere keeps one meaning here, and [Words kept to one meaning](#words-kept-to-one-meaning)
names the others. New to Piwi? [Core concepts](./core-concepts) reads the dozen words a first run meets, with the object
model.

## The object model

How projects, test runs, test cases, executions and failure clusters hold each other:
[Core concepts](./core-concepts#the-object-model).

## Results

### Project

A named container for one suite's results, usually one repository or one suite within it. A project is created the
first time results arrive under a new `projectName`, and carries its own tags, [role grants](#role-and-group), source
control connection, default branch, capability decisions and AI-diagnosis instructions; retention is set for the
whole instance ([Storage & retention](/operate/storage)). Its **status** is the outcome of its latest run, or of its
[status filter](/features/branches#the-project-status)'s.

### Test run

Everything one `npx playwright test` invocation produced: counts, duration, the HTML report, CI and git metadata, and
its [executions](#execution). One CI pipeline's shards make one run ([Sharding](./ci#sharding)), and
a run fills in while it goes ([Live streaming](./reporter#live-streaming)). A run **ran to its end** when it passed,
failed or hit the global timeout; only such runs count in [a project's health](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts).
A **requested run** is one a person asked for from the dashboard and ran on their own machine
([Run on my machine](/features/run-on-my-machine#a-requested-run-is-yours-alone)).

### Test case

The **identity of a test across time**: its project, file, `describe` path and title. It is created and reused as
results arrive, never submitted, so renaming a test or moving its file makes a new one
([External test IDs](/reference/test-metadata#external-test-ids)). It is browser-independent: `login.spec.ts › signs
in` is one test case on every browser of your matrix. "This test is flaky" is a statement about a test case. What a
**run** of a test is on its pages: [How a result counts](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts).

### Execution

**One attempt of one test case, in one run, on one browser**: the error, steps, trace, screenshots and the diagnosis
of one failure. A retry is an execution of its own, and so is each `--repeat-each` repetition. The docs also call it a
*test-run case*. "Here is the stack trace" is a statement about an execution. When a test counts as flaky, failed or
**interrupted** in a run, and how every view reads it: [How a result counts](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts).

### Pass rate

**The share of a test's, a run's or a project's results that passed**, counted over the results that passed or
failed, so skipped tests do not lower it. Every view computes it by one rule, and shows a dash rather than a number
when nothing passed or failed: [How a result counts](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts).

### Flaky rate

**The share of a test's runs that passed only on a retry**, over the same runs the [pass rate](#pass-rate) counts. A
file's or a directory's flaky rate reads its tests' runs the same way. The [flakiness score](#flakiness-score) and
Flake Lab's rate are other numbers: [How a result counts](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts).

### Baseline (last green run)

**The earlier run a run is compared with** to answer "what changed?": by default the same project's most recent
passing run, chosen by environment first, then branch. The Changes tab, the regression signals, the CI gate,
pull-request feedback and the AI diagnosis all read it, and so do the environment, visual and page diffs of one
failing execution. Which run it is, and what happens when none passed: [The baseline](/features/run-changes#the-baseline).
The default and base branches it falls back to: [Branches](/features/branches).

### Closest CI pass

**The passing CI execution of the same test a run of the desktop app is compared with**, read on the team instance:
in the run's environment and on its commit first, then in its environment, then on its commit, then any, each on the
same branch first. [Compare with team instance](/features/compare-with-team) lists what differs between their
environments.

### New regression, newly flaky

**What a test did differently from the [baseline](#baseline-last-green-run)**: a **new regression** fails here and
passed there; a **newly flaky** test passed here only on a retry and passed at its first attempt there. Both name a
change between two runs, not its cause: a newly flaky test can be your change or an old flake. How to tell:
[What newly flaky says about your change](/features/run-changes#what-newly-flaky-says-about-your-change).

### Environment

A deployment of the application a project's tests run against (Local, Staging, Production), kept as a record of the
project. A run reports a **label**, the reporter's `environment` option or `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`, which resolves to an
environment by its key or an alias, ignoring case; a label nothing takes adds a **discovered** one. Filters and
analytics narrow to one, and a run Piwi starts for one gets its run variables: [Environments](/features/environments).

### Default environment

The [environment](#environment) a project's views read when none is picked, as they read its default branch: the
project page and its tabs, Analytics, quarantine candidates and pull-request feedback. A run with no environment counts
only under **All environments**. Unset, every environment counts:
[Default environment](/features/environments#default-environment).

### Deployed environment

An [environment](#environment) a project admin marks as not built from the run's checkout, such as Staging (every
environment is built from the checkout until then): it runs whatever was last deployed there. A run of one tested a **deployed commit**, which its server under test reports or
the environment's latest deploy marker carries. Suspect lines, the Changes tab and the AI diagnosis read the
application's changes between deployed commits: [Deployed environments](/features/deployed-environments).

### Protected environment

An [environment](#environment), Production as a rule, that Piwi starts a run against only for a project admin, after
a confirmation, and only for the tests carrying one of its **required tags** (`@smoke`). It is never picked by default
and never an agent's. A command typed in a terminal stays the person's own:
[Protected environments](/features/environments#protected-environments).

### Run variable

One `NAME=value` environment variable of a **project**, such as the tenant one app serves it as (`TENANT=acme`),
that every run Piwi starts for the project gets and every command it gives to copy starts with. An
[environment](#environment) has run variables of its own, set over the project's on the runs Piwi starts for it. The
names it may set and where it applies: [Run variables](/features/run-variables).

### Environment incident

A **test run** whose failures come from the environment under test being down or broken (staging refusing
connections, a host that does not resolve), not from the tests or the code. Piwi flags it when the run finishes, or a
person marks it, and leaves it out of the analysis that would blame the tests: see
[What a flagged run changes](/features/environment-incidents#what-a-flagged-run-changes).

### Tags & ownership

Two ways to say what a test *is*, both declared in the spec file. **Tags** come from Playwright (`@smoke`); they slice
the test catalog and the flaky leaderboard, and a [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate) rule can require one.
**Ownership metadata** comes from `piwi:` annotations such as `piwi:owner`: who answers for the test, shown as badges
and carried into pull-request feedback. A test with no owner annotation takes its owner from `CODEOWNERS`. Accepted
values and the fallback: [Test metadata](/reference/test-metadata#test-tags).

## Live runs

The words every tool uses for a run while it goes ([Follow a run](/features/watch-a-run)).

### Run number

**A run's id on the instance it reports to, `#78`, and its page there.** The reporter learns it as the run starts and
tells it to the editor or the desktop app that follows the run, so every tool links the same page
([The run's number and page](/features/watch-a-run#the-run-s-number-and-page)).

### Run name

**The name a run carries before it has a number** (`piwiRunRef` in its metadata): the one its launcher gave it, an
editor's ref or a run request's id, else one Piwi makes up for a run outside CI. A CI run has none: its number names
it. See [Test metadata](/reference/test-metadata#run-origin).

### Worker

**One of the run's Playwright processes, named by its lane, `Worker 2`.** A worker Playwright starts again after a
failure takes the same lane ([Worker lanes](/reference/test-metadata#worker-lanes)).

### Stop

**A test standing at a call, waiting to be answered:** at a breakpoint, after a step, at a Pause, at `page.pause()`,
or at a failure held for a look. Each tool names it by why it stopped, in the same words
([Where a test stopped](/features/watch-a-run#where-a-test-stopped)). A test ended there is skipped
([End the test](/features/end-the-test)). How the test timeout and the dashboard's durations treat the time paused:
[Time paused at a stop](/features/slow-tests#time-paused-at-a-stop).

### CI position

**The call a running test of a CI run is at, in your code:** a plain, read-only mark at the end of its line in the
editors. Never a stop: nothing waits there, and no tool answers it. Which CI runs the editor and Piwi Picker follow:
[A CI run of your branch](/features/editor-ci-runs).

### Hold failures

**Whether a failed test waits at its line for an answer, in one run.** Off, a failure goes on at once, as without
Piwi. Some runs start with it on, any tool that follows a run can turn it on or off, and a run nobody attends never
holds a failure. Which runs, and what a held test keeps: [Hold failures](/features/watch-a-run#hold-failures).

### Presence, driving a stop

**Who else is on a run, and who acts at its stop.** Each tool says which others have the run open, who watches each
worker's page, and who drives a stop. One tool drives a stop at a time, a person or an agent, and a person can take
the stop from an agent. How a stop is taken and given back:
[Who drives a stop](/features/runs-window#who-drives-a-stop).

### Watch, Share live

**Watch** shows a worker's page live, in your editor, Piwi Picker or the desktop app
([Watch a local test](/features/watch-running-test)). **Share live** lets a teammate watch a run on your machine
from its page on the team instance ([Share a local run live](/features/share-live)), where a CI run is watched in the
[live view](/features/live-view), every worker at once with [Watch all](/features/watch-all), and a running page read
as a document with [Inspect](/features/live-inspect). What each sends and keeps is on those pages.

### Trace so far

**A running test's trace up to now, opened in Playwright's trace viewer** on the machine the run runs on, with **Open
the trace so far**. The attempt must be traced. Where the button shows and what it needs:
[Open the trace so far](/features/watch-running-test#open-the-trace-so-far); the desktop app's **Inspect**, which reads
the same trace: [Desktop app runs](/features/desktop-runs#watch).

### Verification

**A test run several times without retries and without the breakpoints, to see how often it passes** (**Verify ×3**
in the editors). It says how many of its repetitions passed (`Passed 3 of 3`, `Failed 1 of 3`) and never holds a failure.
How it counts and what it says: [When your run ends](/features/editor-runs#when-your-run-ends).

## Failures

### Error fingerprint & failure cluster

The **error fingerprint** is a hash of a failed execution's error with what changes from one occurrence to the next
masked out: numbers, ids, URLs, timestamps, an assertion's values. Every failed execution sharing a fingerprint joins
one **failure cluster**, so fifty red tests from one broken endpoint become one cluster you triage once, with a status
(open / resolved / ignored) and a note. What is masked, and when clusters merge:
[How failures are grouped](/features/failure-clusters#how-failures-are-grouped).

### Story

The **one explanation** a failure page leads with when several [clues](/features/evidence#clues) (deterministic,
rule-based findings) form a known combination: *"the Pay button stayed disabled because POST /api/checkout/quote was
still in flight"*, at the strongest member's strength, with every clue folded under it. The combinations, and what
leads instead: [Clue rules](/reference/clues#stories).

### Situation

The **context** of a failing execution, on its page: since when it has been failing and whether a newer execution
failed again or passed, then the cluster it joins, its status and its issue. It also reads, condensed, in
[alerts](/features/notifications). Each line: [Your first failure, explained](./first-failure).

### Next step

The **one recommended action** a failure page leads with, chosen by a policy rather than offered as a menu: apply a
diagnosed patch, replace a broken locator, reproduce locally, re-run in CI, mark a cluster resolved. Every other action
lives in the toolbox. The policy and its order: [Fix plans](/features/fix-plans#the-next-step).

### Cluster state

Where a **failure cluster** stands, in one sentence with one verb next to a colored dot (*still failing*, *stopped
failing*, *regressed*, …). It reconciles the human triage status with what the runs show, and offers the action that
closes a gap between them. Every state and which runs count: [The state line](/features/failure-clusters#the-state-line).

### Flakiness score

A test case's **score** from how often it passed only on a retry and how often its status flips across runs, with a
**root-cause class** and an **impact ranking** by the CI time it wastes. It is a property of the test case, computed
over its history, so a test needs a few runs before it can be called flaky. The weights and the classes:
[Flaky tests](/features/flaky-tests#flaky-test-detection).

### Flake experiment

A `piwi flake` session on one flaky test: a **control arm** with no condition, then one **arm** per suspect, each
applying the suspect's condition (a delayed route, another test alongside) with retries off. An arm **reproduced** the
flake when it fails, with the test's own error, significantly more often than the control; a **verify** experiment reruns
that arm after a fix. The verdicts: [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab#reading-the-verdict).

### Fix attempt

A change a person or an agent reports having made to fix a failure cluster (a patch, a locator edit, a fix plan
carried out), on a commit or a branch. It is recorded **applied**, then **verified** when the cluster's tests pass on a
run that carries it, or **regressed** when the cluster fails again. See
[Agent skills](/features/agent-skills#what-agents-report-back).

### Locator snapshot

What an element looked like when a locator call on it succeeded (role, accessible name, test id, structural anchors),
recorded by the [capture fixtures](./capture-fixtures) and keyed by the **call site** (`file:line`) rather than the
selector text. When that locator later fails, its snapshots are what Piwi ranks replacement locators from. See
[Locator healing](/features/locator-healing#what-it-does).

## Analytics

### Metric, dashboard and quality report

A **metric** is a named number with one definition every surface reads ([Analytics](/features/analytics)). An
**analytics dashboard** is a named arrangement of widgets with a default scope ([Dashboards](/features/dashboards)); *the dashboard* alone means the Piwi web app. A **quality report**
is an analytics dashboard rendered as a document, not the run's Playwright **run report**; a **report schedule** sends
it on a cadence, and each one sent is kept as a **report snapshot** ([Quality reports](/features/quality-reports)).

## Test Map

The **Test Map** is one graph per project of what the application exposes (pages, controls, links, routes, the
handlers and dependencies behind them) and which tests reach each of them. See
[Scenario gaps & the Test Map](/features/scenario-gaps).

### Reach

A test **reaches** a route, a page, a control or a link when a run observes it doing so: a request to the route, a
locator call on the page, a locator that names the control. Triage can record reach too. The route and page gaps are
read from observed reach; the code detectors read coverage. Only a trusted test's reach counts in full. The rules:
[Gap detectors & exposure](/reference/gap-detectors#detectors).

### Feature and hub

A **feature** is a product area named by the [`piwi:feature` tag](/reference/test-metadata) on tests. It groups what
those tests reach, and what they miss nearby. A **hub** is a node most tests reach, such as a session route: it belongs
to no one feature. See [how features group](/reference/gap-detectors#features).

### Code reach

The application source files a test executed, in the page from Chromium's JavaScript coverage with
[code reach](/features/code-reach) on, in the backend with [server coverage](/features/server-coverage) on: observed
reach at file level, never line coverage. It feeds [impact-from-diff](/features/change-impact) and
[Uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes).

### Coverage

Which source code a test ran, per file and **runtime** (`browser` or `server`), at a **granularity**: the files only,
the functions that ran, or the executed lines too. [Code reach](#code-reach) is its file-level view. A test's coverage
is **incomplete** when part of it could not be collected. The granularities and their cost:
[Coverage cost](/reference/coverage-cost).

### Coverage report and suite

A **coverage report** is one tool's coverage of one suite's whole run at one commit, attributed to no test. A
**suite** is the tests a report comes from, named when uploading (`unit-back`), of kind `unit` or `e2e`; not
Playwright's `describe` block. The **coverage scope** decides which files a project's coverage counts. See
[Combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage).

### Coverage and the Test Map

Two answers to "what do the tests miss". **Coverage** measures the code: which lines and functions ran, as a ratio;
the lines no test or suite ran are **lines not run**. The **Test Map** measures the application: which routes, pages
and controls the tests reach; what they miss becomes a [scenario gap](#scenario-gap), never a percentage. They meet on
the project's [Coverage tab](/features/scenario-gaps#the-coverage-tab) and on a
[file's coverage page](/features/code-reach#which-tests-run-a-file).

### Uncovered change

A changed file of a pull request that no test reached and no suite ran a changed line of. One rule decides it for the
pull-request comment, the gate, MCP and the *changed, unreached* gap. **Patch coverage** is the same question by line:
the share of the changed lines that ran. See
[Uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes#one-rule-for-every-changed-file).

### Reusable result

A test result whose code had already passed unchanged: an earlier pass of the same test ran the same file versions, so
the run could have kept that pass instead. A reusable result that failed came from the test, its data or its
environment. See [Reuse forecast](/features/reuse-forecast#what-counts-as-reusable).

### Suspect lines

The lines changed since a failing test's last passing run that the failing tests executed, read from their
[coverage](#coverage), ranked by how few passing tests executed them too. The failure pages, the cluster's diff, the
AI diagnosis and the fix plan name them. How they are ranked:
[Suspect lines](/features/server-coverage#suspect-lines).

### Locator index

The locator chains each test used in its steps, recorded per branch and per Playwright project. It answers which tests
use a locator, and it feeds [Who uses a locator](/features/locator-usage) and
[Tested elements](/features/tested-elements).

### Locator break

A locator of the index that a change stops matching: the diff removes or renames a string one of its calls finds the
element by. [Locator preflight](/features/preflight) lists them, *likely* or *possible*.

### Page key

A page's URL reduced to its path pattern, ids replaced by placeholders: `/orders/123?tab=items` and `/orders/456` are
both `/orders/:id`, on staging and in production alike. The Test Map's page nodes, the page each locator was used on
and Piwi Picker's **This page** all use it. The rules: [What the graph includes](/reference/gap-detectors#what-the-graph-includes);
Piwi Picker's path prefixes: [URL patterns](/features/extension-connection#url-patterns).

### Brittle locator

A locator a test uses that breaks on a change unrelated to what the test checks: a position, a styling class, the
document structure, a generated id. Piwi judges each locator of the index *brittle*, *watch* or *stable*; see
[Locator stability rules](/reference/locator-stability). Not to be confused with the *fragile*
[gap class](#gap-class), which is about the tests reaching a node, not a locator.

### Scenario gap

A test the suite does not have yet, proposed from the Test Map with its evidence and a next step: a route no test
reaches, a control nobody exercises, a changed file no test reaches. A gap is triaged like a failure cluster: accept
it, snooze it, dismiss it with a reason, or mark it covered by an existing test ([Triage](/features/scenario-gaps#triage)).

### Gap class

How serious a gap is: **blind-spot** (nothing exercises it), **false-comfort** (the tests pass without checking it)
or **fragile** (what reaches it could stop at any time). Server probes report **findings** instead, **unhandled** or
**degraded**. What each class covers: [Detectors](/reference/gap-detectors#detectors).

### Detector

A rule that reads the Test Map and the run history and reports one kind of gap, such as *declared, never hit* or
*single covering test*. Each gap names the detector that raised it; [Gap detectors & exposure](/reference/gap-detectors)
lists them all.

### Exposure

How much a gap's node matters, from how often its files change and for how long, whether they were part of an earlier escaped
failure, and the priority of the tests that reach it. A gap's score, which ranks it, is its exposure times the
detector's confidence. The factors: [Exposure](/reference/gap-detectors#exposure).

### Probe

A re-run of a passing test with one injected fault (a 500, an empty body, a dropped field, a slow response),
recording whether the test noticed. A client probe injects the fault at the Playwright boundary; a server probe asks
the [backend instrumentation](./backend-logs#server-probes) to inject it inside the server. A **probe run** is marked
as one ([What a probe run never counts](/features/probes#what-a-probe-run-never-counts)).

### Declared surface

The routes and pages the application says it has, from the instrumentation's route manifest, a committed
`piwi.manifest.json` or an OpenAPI document, as opposed to the ones tests reached. A declared route nothing reaches
is a *declared, never hit* gap ([Declared surface](/features/scenario-gaps#declared-surface)).

### Page inventory

The controls (role and accessible name) and links the reporter records on the pages a passing run visits, so the Test
Map knows what a page offers beyond what the tests clicked. Off by default: turn it on with `capturePageInventory`.
What it reads and keeps: [What the graph includes](/reference/gap-detectors#what-the-graph-includes).

### Map health

How complete a project's Test Map is, per input (the page inventory, route handlers, probes, the declared surface,
change history…), with the detectors each input wakes. A quiet Gaps view can mean a map that cannot see; the panel
names the step behind each input that is short ([Map health](/features/scenario-gaps#map-health)).

### URL pattern

A glob over a page's whole address that ties the pages of a site to a project, with an optional environment and
branch. Each project keeps its own list, and the browser extension reads them to know which project the page it is
on belongs to. See [Extension connection](/features/extension-connection#url-patterns).

## Access

### Role and group

With [authentication](/operate/authentication) on, every account holds an **instance role**, **Administrator** or
**Member**. A Member's rights in a project come from the **project roles** they hold there, granted on one project or
on all of them. A **group** is a named set of users that receives project roles the way a user does. See
[Access, roles and groups](/operate/project-access).

### Credential

**A secret Piwi sends to another service, saved once and named by id wherever it is needed**: a user, the secret, the
destination (the base URL it may be sent under) and the projects that may use it. A CI server action, source control,
an AI role, a Jira or Zephyr Scale connection and a Slack channel of the instance name one; every use is checked against
it and logged. See [Credentials](/operate/credentials).

## Words kept to one meaning

Some words name two things across the docs, the dashboard and the tools. Each keeps the meaning in the middle column
on these pages; the others take the name on the right, or are told apart by the place they are in.

| Word | Means | The other senses |
|---|---|---|
| stop | A test standing at a call ([Stop](#stop)) | **Stop**, in bold, is a button's label: it ends a run, a recording or an answer |
| share | **Share live**: a teammate watches a run on your machine | **Share with Playwright tools** binds a stopped test's browser for Playwright's tools; a [share link](/features/share-links) is a signed read-only link |
| On your machine | A run on a developer's machine: the run page's card for a desktop run and the mark of a [requested run](#test-run) | none |
| run | A [test run](#test-run) | A test's result in a run is a *run of a test* ([How a result counts](/reference/test-metadata#how-a-result-counts)); one of the times Flake Lab or a verification runs a test is a *repetition* |
| environment | A deployment a project's tests run against, a record of the project, which a run's *label* names ([Environment](#environment)) | The variables of a process are its *environment variables*, and the ones Piwi sets are [run variables](#run-variable); an *environment incident* is a run whose environment under test was down ([incident](#environment-incident)); the machine a run executed on is its [run environment](/features/run-environment); the flaky class `environment` means one browser, or one runner time zone or locale, fails |
| wasted | [Wasted time](/features/slow-tests#wasted-time): waits plus failed attempts, as Analytics counts it | The flaky list's *wasted CI minutes* of one test are its retry passes times its average failed attempt |
| coverage, reach | [Coverage](#coverage): the code a test ran; [reach](#reach): what a run observed a test touch | [Code reach](#code-reach) is coverage at file level; *Uncovered changes* and the **Coverage** tab keep their names |
| diverged | The dashboard's verdict for a replay that could not play a step | Piwi Picker says *Could not reach the bug*, or *Stopped at step N: the page went another way* for a recording that marks nothing wrong ([Replay a recording](/features/replay-a-bug-report)) |
| picker | **Piwi Picker**, always with its name, is the browser extension | A tool that turns a click into locators is named by where it works: the dashboard's *snapshot picker* (**Pick from snapshot**, **Open in picker**), the trace viewer's *Pick locator*, the *failure-time picker* in a local run's browser |
| dashboard | The web app a Piwi instance serves | A saved set of Analytics widgets is an [analytics dashboard](/features/dashboards); a hosting provider's web console is its *console* |
| report | Always with its kind | *quality report*, *HTML report* of a run, *offline export*, *bug report*, Playwright's *blob report* |
| test case | A test's identity across time ([Test case](#test-case)) | One attempt of it is an [execution](#execution) |
| project | A Piwi [project](#project), named by the reporter's `projectName` | A *Playwright project* (a `projects` entry of the config, whose name the `browser` field records) is always called so; the reader's code is their *repository* |
| integration | A *backend integration*: an instrumentation package in the app under test ([Backend instrumentation](./backend-logs)) | **Settings → Integrations** holds the *connections* to [Jira Cloud](/operate/integrations) and [Zephyr Scale Cloud](/operate/zephyr-scale); **Integrations** is also the group of a project's Settings that binds those connections and CI |
| baseline | The run a run is compared with ([Baseline](#baseline-last-green-run)) | A visual snapshot, a pinned commit or a starting value is named by what it is |
| exposure | How much a gap's node matters ([Exposure](#exposure)) | none |
| finding | Always with its kind: a *resilience finding* (the app did not cope with a server probe), a *leak finding* | A [clue](/features/evidence#clues) is a rule-based finding about one failure |
| verified | Always with its noun: *diagnosis verified*, *verified fixed*, a *verified* fix attempt, a [verification](#verification) | none |
| class | Always with its kind: the flaky *root-cause class*, the [gap class](#gap-class) | none |
| Performance, Timeline | A tab or a page, named by its place: **Project → Performance**, **Settings → Performance**, a run's **Timeline** tab | [Timeline markers](/features/timeline-markers) are the events drawn on the trend charts |

# Coverage cost

Coverage has two sides, each opt-in: the browser's, [code reach](/features/code-reach), and the backend's,
[server coverage](/features/server-coverage), with the style sheets' [CSS coverage](/features/css-coverage) a choice
of its own in the browser. This page owns what each mode records and costs; each feature page says how to turn its
mode on. Each mode below records more than the one above it on its side.

## The modes

| Mode | Turn it on | Records per test | Leaves the machine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Browser files | `coverage.browser: 'files'`, or `captureCodeReach: true` | the application files whose functions ran | paths |
| Browser functions | `coverage.browser: 'functions'` | also the start and end line of each function that ran | paths, line numbers, git blob ids |
| Browser lines | `coverage.browser: 'lines'` | also the lines that ran, and the run's executable lines | paths, line numbers, git blob ids |
| Server files | `coverage.server: 'files'`, with a coverage build | the backend files that ran | paths |
| Server functions | `coverage.server: 'functions'` | also the start and end line of each function that ran | paths, line numbers, git blob ids |
| Server lines | `coverage.server: 'lines'` | also the executed lines, and the run's executable lines | paths, line numbers, git blob ids |
| CSS rules | `coverage.css: 'rules'`, on its own | the start and end line of each style rule a page matched, and every rule of each sheet | paths, line numbers, git blob ids |

Never source code, never hit counts. Each variable form (`PIWI_COVERAGE_BROWSER`, `PIWI_COVERAGE_SERVER`,
`PIWI_COVERAGE_CSS`) fills the option the Playwright config leaves unset. Code reach and CSS coverage need the
[capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) and Chromium; server coverage needs a backend built for coverage.

## On a large ASP.NET Core and Vue application

Against the same suite, on the same coverage build, with every coverage option off:

| Mode | UI tests | API tests | Chromium CPU | Backend CPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Server lines | +2% (−7 to +6%) | 0% | −3% | −6% |
| Browser files | +40% (+38 to +58%) | −4% | +51% | +3% |
| Browser functions | +47% (+40 to +69%) | 0% | +55% | +5% |
| Server lines and browser functions | +51% (+40 to +64%) | +4% | +63% | +11% |

- **UI tests:** in each round, each UI test's time against its time in that round's pass with coverage off, and the
  median of those ratios; then the median over the rounds, their range in brackets. The UI tests that ran took 10 to 51
  seconds with coverage off; with browser coverage, the 51-second one took about 72.
- **CPU:** the run's total for Chromium's renderer processes, and for the four backend processes, against the same
  round's pass with coverage off.
- **Noise:** the passes with coverage off alone varied by more than 10% from one round to the next, which is why each
  mode is compared within its round: read a difference under 10% as none.
- **The coverage build itself,** every option off, ran within 1% of a normal build of the same backend.
- **Server files and server functions** were not measured apart: the build records the same way at every granularity,
  which only decides what each test's report names.

**The application:** an ASP.NET Core backend serving four web front-ends, each a Vue 3 application its own Vite dev
server serves, about 500 ES modules on a page, full page loads between screens, PostgreSQL. **The suite:** 18 tests,
6 driving the front-ends and 12 calling the backend through Playwright's `request` fixture, 3 workers, headless
Chromium, on a 20-core machine. After a warm-up pass, rounds ran one pass of each mode in turn, so each mode ran three
to five times.

**What the browser side spends.** For each document a test loads, the debugger reports every script, the reporter
reads the source of each application script its worker has not seen yet, and V8's precise coverage keeps a record of
every function the page runs; as the test leaves the document, the reporter stops the page to read that record and
resolves it to files. Each of these works on every module of every document, so the cost grows with the modules a page
loads and with the full page loads a test makes, beside a CDP session on each page the test has: an application that loads its modules once, then navigates on the
client, pays far less, as the synthetic pages below show. Files and functions cost about the same: both read the same
record, functions only keep more of it. Lines cost more: V8 counts every block a function runs, not only the call.

## On synthetic pages

Browser files, medians on a 4-core sandbox, headless Chromium, one page per test:

- **A script-heavy page** (Vue's development build rendering a 1,000-row table 30 times, 400 ES modules): 1,128 ms to
  1,220 ms per test, 8% more, and 16% for a worker's first test, where Playwright's `page.coverage` adds 50%.
- **A light page** (the reporter's capture benchmark, `npm run reporter:bench`): 61 to 103 ms more per test, where
  `page.coverage` adds 176 to 209 ms.

V8's coverage alone, on a script that spends its time in JavaScript (a recursive function, a loop with branches and a
sort, over 20,000 items, 20 times), medians of 5 runs: 285 ms with no coverage, 287 ms with the function coverage of
`files` and `functions`, 468 ms with the block coverage of `lines`, 64% more. A page whose time goes to the network,
the DOM or rendering pays a smaller share.

Server coverage, on a prototype of the coverage package: under 2% of test duration on Microsoft's eShopOnWeb, whose
CPU goes to the framework; up to 26% more backend CPU on an application written to spend its CPU in business logic, and
6% in its run-level mode. Functions cost about what lines cost: the cost is the recorder's call on every method call.

Server coverage on a Nitro backend, on the sample application's suite against production builds: no measurable
change in test duration (72.8 s of tests without coverage, 72.2 s with, medians of 5 runs), 5.6% more server CPU, and
a server bundle 7.8% larger. On the same suite, the ASP.NET Core coverage build costs 12.5% more server CPU, and no
measurable test time either. Per call, the Nitro recorder costs 5 to 13 ns, about what the .NET one costs.

## CSS rules

The cost of CSS coverage is Chromium's style recalculation, not the reads: about 10% more per test on the sample
application, close to what function coverage costs there, and up to 57% on a page with 2,000 rules and frequent
re-renders, where function coverage costs 4%.

## Choosing

- **Server coverage** can stay on in every run: against a backend that is not a coverage build, it collects nothing
  and costs nothing, so the build decides. On a coverage build, every granularity costs what lines cost, under 10% of
  the UI tests' time: record lines, unless the reports' size matters more than their detail.
- **Browser coverage** belongs in a scheduled run on a large application served by a dev server, where it adds 40 to
  50% to the UI tests. Files and functions cost about the same, so a scheduled run may as well record functions. On an
  application that loads its modules once, it costs little enough to stay on. Record lines where the front end's
  line ratio in the [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage) is worth the slower scripts.
- **CSS coverage** belongs where style changes are frequent, or in a scheduled run.

## Related

- [Code reach](/features/code-reach): the browser coverage these numbers measure
- [Server coverage](/features/server-coverage): the backend lines each test runs
- [CSS coverage](/features/css-coverage): the style rules a run uses

# Piwi CLI

The `@piwitests/reporter` package ships a command-line tool, `piwi`, for the things that happen *around* a test run: wiring a project up, gating a CI job on the dashboard's analysis, running a saved test selection, turning a recording into a spec, and managing AI-step artifacts and agent skills. This page is the reference for every command and flag; each command's own `--help` prints the same list.

## Invoking it

Run it through the package name so `npx` resolves this package:

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter <command> [options]
```

> The package is `@piwitests/reporter`; its command is `piwi`. A plain `npx piwi …` would fetch an unrelated `piwi` from npm — invoke it through the package name. Once the reporter is a project dependency, `npx piwi <command>` resolves the local binary and works too.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| [`init`](#init) | Wire a Playwright project up to a Piwi Dashboard |
| [`skills`](#skills) | Install the Piwi agent skills into this project |
| [`gate`](#gate) | Fail a CI job on the dashboard's analysis of a run |
| [`report`](#report) | Print a [quality report](/features/quality-reports) as Markdown, PDF, HTML, CSV or JSON |
| [`coverage`](#coverage) | Upload another tool's coverage report of a commit, for [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage) |
| [`select`](#select-run) | Print the Playwright args for a saved test selection |
| [`run`](#select-run) | Run a saved test selection with `playwright test` |
| [`plan`](#plan) | Plan a run that reuses the passes whose code has not changed (experimental) |
| [`rerun`](#rerun) | Run the tests a [CI re-run](/features/ci-rerun) from the dashboard asked for |
| [`probe`](#probe) | Run the dashboard's probe plan and record what the suite noticed |
| [`flake`](#flake) | Make a flaky test fail on demand under its suspects' conditions, then verify the fix |
| [`ai`](#ai) | Manage committed natural-language AI-step artifacts |
| [`codegen`](#codegen) | Turn a steps file (a Piwi Picker recording) into a Playwright spec |
| [`preflight`](#preflight) | List the test locators your change breaks, and fix them |
| [`bug`](#bug) | Write a bug report's failing test into the project and run it once |
| [`mcp`](#mcp) | Serve the run tools of this machine's editors and desktop app to a coding agent, over stdio |

The commands that talk to a dashboard, all but `ai resolve`, find it in their flags first, then in the environment: `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` (dashboard URL), `PIWI_API_KEY` (API key) and `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME` (project), then in the project's `.env` (the one `init` writes), then in the running [desktop app](/features/desktop). `bug`, `codegen` and `preflight` read the `.env` of the Playwright config's folder (the nearest one within the repository), the working directory and the repository root, in that order: the URL comes from the first of them that names one, with that file's API key or none, and the project from the first that sets one. A key in a `.env` that names no URL is never sent to another file's URL. The other commands read the working directory's `.env`. An empty variable counts as unset. `PIWI_DESKTOP_APP` places the desktop app with the reporter's three modes: `off` never uses it, `prefer` uses it before the environment and the `.env` outside CI (a `--server-url` flag still wins), and `fallback`, the default, uses it only when no flag, variable or `.env` names a URL or an API key. The command line reads the mode from `PIWI_DESKTOP_APP` only, not from the `desktopApp` option of the Playwright config that `init --desktop-app` writes: set `PIWI_DESKTOP_APP=prefer` in the environment to get the same behavior from the commands. `ai resolve` reads `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` and `PIWI_API_KEY` from the environment only.

The desktop app's token is held to a proof: the first request that carries it waits for the server at the address to prove it holds the token, and a command whose server does not stops with one line instead of sending it. A command the app starts marks the key it exports with `PIWI_DESKTOP_KEY=1`; a key you set yourself is sent as before.

An API key goes only to the URL it came with: a key exported in the environment is never sent to a URL the `.env` names, and an `--api-key` flag is never sent to a URL that comes from a `.env` or the desktop app. The command then says so in one line on stderr; pass `--server-url` with the key to name the instance it is for.

## `init`

Wire a Playwright project up to a dashboard. It installs the reporter as a dev dependency, wraps `export default defineConfig(...)` with [`wrapConfig(...)`](/guide/reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig), creates the [capture-fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) file, records `PIWI_*` connection settings in `.env` / `.env.example` (and `.gitignore`), and installs the [agent skills](/features/agent-skills). **Every step is idempotent** — safe to re-run — and a config shape it will not rewrite is reported as `manual` with the exact change to make. See the [one-command setup](/guide/getting-started#fast-path-one-command) in Getting started.

The `.env` it writes sits next to the Playwright config, where `npx playwright test` reads it: the reporter takes `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `PIWI_API_KEY` and `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME` from it for whatever the config and the environment leave unset, so the config needs no dotenv loading ([Values from `.env`](/reference/reporter-options#values-from-env)). The file stays out of git; in CI, set the same variables as secrets.

When git already tracks that `.env`, adding it to `.gitignore` would not untrack it, so `init` writes no API key into it: the `env` step is reported as `manual`, and the rest of the setup goes on. Set `PIWI_API_KEY` in the environment (in CI, as a secret), or untrack the file with `git rm --cached .env` and run `init` again. The same goes for a `.env` in a repository git gives no answer about (git missing, or refusing a repository another user owns): make `git ls-files .env` work there, or set the key in the environment. Nor does `init` write the key through a `.env` that is a link (symbolic or hard) to another file: put a file of its own in its place. With `PIWI_API_KEY` set in the environment and no `--api-key`, such a `.env` needs no key, and `init` reports the step as done.

In a monorepo, run `init` in the package that holds the Playwright config, or point `--cwd` at it: every step then applies to that package, with the package manager its workspace's root names (the `packageManager` field or the lockfile). Run at the root of a workspace (`workspaces` in `package.json`, as npm, Yarn and Bun declare one, or a `pnpm-workspace.yaml`) that holds no Playwright config of its own, `init` looks for the workspace packages that hold one:

- **One**: it wires that package, and says which.
- **Several**: in a terminal, it lists them and asks which one to wire. In CI, without a terminal or with `--json`, it wires none, names them, and asks you to run it again with `--cwd <package>`; the JSON plan lists them under `workspace.packages`.
- **None**: it reports the missing config, as in any other folder.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter init --server-url http://localhost:3000 --project my-project
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL to write into the config (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, default `http://localhost:3000`) |
| `--no-server-url` | Write no URL into the config: the reporter finds the [desktop app](/features/desktop) running on the machine, or reads `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` |
| `--project <name>` | Project name to report under (default: your package/folder name) |
| `--desktop-app <mode>` | Write [`desktopApp`](/guide/reporter#local-runs-to-the-desktop-app-ci-to-a-team-server) into the config: `prefer` sends local runs to the desktop app while it runs, and CI runs to `--server-url`; `fallback` or `off` |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key to write into `.env` (env `PIWI_API_KEY`), where the reporter reads it; never into a `.env` git tracks or cannot say it does not, nor through a link. Omit to leave a `.env.example` placeholder you fill in yourself |
| `--cwd <path>` | Project root to operate on (default: current directory) |
| `--skills <list>` | Comma-separated skills to install, or `all` / `none` (default: the six workflow skills) |
| `--skills-dir <path>` | Directory to install skills into (default: `.claude/skills`) |
| `--skills-only` | Only install skills; do not touch the config or env |
| `--no-skills` | Configure the project but install no skills |
| `--no-install` | Do not run the package manager; record the dependency only |
| `--force` | Overwrite skill files that already exist |
| `--dry-run` | Report every change without writing anything |
| `--json` | Print the plan/result as JSON (for agents) |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

## `skills`

Install the Piwi [agent skills](/features/agent-skills) into a project — agent-agnostic Markdown that lets a coding agent investigate failures, heal locators, and stabilize flaky tests. `init` installs these for you; use `skills` to add them to a project that already has the reporter, or to a different skills directory.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter skills list
npx @piwitests/reporter skills add [names...] [options]
```

The seven skills are `setup-piwi`, `investigate-failure`, `apply-locator-healing`, `stabilize-flaky-tests`, `run-the-right-tests`, `write-the-missing-test` and `fix-a-reported-bug`. `add` with no names installs all of them. Each installed file is stamped with the reporter's version (`piwi-version`) and a hash (`piwi-hash`); `add` reports a skill as `outdated` when an older release installed it and it was never edited, and replaces it, and as `edited` when it changed since it was installed, and keeps it.

| Flag (for `add`) | Description |
|---|---|
| `--dir <path>` | Directory to install into (default: `.claude/skills`) |
| `--cwd <path>` | Project root to operate on (default: current directory) |
| `--force` | Replace a skill that was edited since it was installed (an untouched skill from an older release is always updated) |
| `--dry-run` | Report what would be written without writing |
| `--json` | Print the results as JSON |

## `gate`

Fail a CI job on the dashboard's analysis of a run: the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate), which says what each rule counts, what it leaves out and how its verdict reaches the pull request. Point it at a run, give it at least one policy rule, and it exits non-zero when the rule is violated. The run defaults to `./piwi-run.json` (the reporter's [output file](/guide/ci#getting-the-run-url-back-out-of-ci)) when present.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter gate --max-new-regressions 0 --fail-on-flaky
```

**Exit codes:** `0` satisfied · `1` violated · `2` could not evaluate: bad arguments, an unreachable dashboard, or a run still running or in its global setup, or one the key cannot see · `3` inconclusive: the run is an [environment incident](/features/environment-incidents), so it cannot say whether the change is good.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--run-id <id>` | Run id to evaluate |
| `--from-file <path>` | Read `runId` from the reporter's output JSON |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--require-tag <tags>` | Comma-separated; every test carrying the tag must pass |
| `--max-failed <n>` | Fail when more than *n* tests failed |
| `--max-new-regressions <n>` | Fail when more than *n* tests newly started failing |
| `--max-new-flaky <n>` | Fail when more than *n* tests newly became flaky |
| `--max-quarantined <n>` | Fail when more than *n* tests are quarantined |
| `--fail-on-new-cluster` | Fail when this run introduced a new failure cluster |
| `--fail-on-flaky` | Fail when this run contains any flaky test |
| `--require-selection <key>` | Fail when a test the named selection matches did not run or failed |
| `--max-leaks <n>` | Fail when the run left more than *n* browsers, contexts or pages open, counted per opening line |
| `--max-new-leaks <n>` | Fail when more than *n* of those were never seen on the base branch |
| `--max-reused <n\|p%>` | Fail when the run reused more than *n* tests, or *p*% of its tests, from earlier passes ([pass reuse](/features/reuse-forecast#skipping-reusable-tests)) |
| `--require-executed <tags>` | Comma-separated; fail when a test carrying the tag was reused instead of executed. A reused test otherwise counts as passed for `--require-tag` and `--require-selection` |
| `--max-uncovered-changes <n>` | Warn when more than *n* changed files are [uncovered changes](/features/uncovered-changes): no test reached them (warn-only — never fails the gate) |
| `--min-patch-coverage <percent>` | Warn when fewer of the change's added and modified lines ran, in the head commit's [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage) (warn-only — never fails the gate) |
| `--json` | Print the raw result as JSON instead of a summary |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

The run source is resolved first-match-wins: `--run-id`, then `--from-file`, then `PIWI_OUTPUT_FILE`, then `./piwi-run.json`. At least one policy rule or warn-only flag is required. How each rule counts (retries, quarantined tests, a tag no test carries, a run with no resource report) is on the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-fails-it) page, and so is the [JSON result](/features/merge-gate#the-verdict). The CI key's evaluations are stored, so [merges overriding a failed gate](/features/merge-gate#on-the-pull-request) are counted; a read-only key gets the verdict only.

## `report`

Print a [quality report](/features/quality-reports) from the dashboard, so a CI scheduler can post it every
week. It calls the report endpoint with the API key; the scope and the dashboard are the ones the
*Quality report* dialog offers.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter report --project checkout --period 7d --format md
```

**Exit codes:** `0` written · `1` written, and the verdict is at or below `--fail-on` · `2` no report.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <names>` | Comma-separated project names or ids (default: every project the key can see) |
| `--period <period>` | `7d`, `30d` (default), `last-month`, `this-quarter`, `2026-08-01..2026-08-31`, … |
| `--compare <mode>` | `previous` (default), `year` or `none` |
| `--dashboard <name>` | `executive` (default), `engineering` or `overview` |
| `--branch <names>` / `--environment <names>` | Narrow the runs (default: each project's default branch) |
| `--selection <key>` | Only the tests of this [selection](/features/test-selection) |
| `--lang <en\|fr>` | Report language |
| `--format <fmt>` | `md` (default), `json`, `html`, `pdf`, `csv` |
| `--output <file>` | Write to a file instead of stdout (required for `pdf`) |
| `--fail-on <tone>` | `bad`: exit 1 on a bad verdict; `mixed`: on a mixed or bad one |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

## `coverage`

Upload another tool's coverage report of a commit to the dashboard, for [combined coverage](/features/combined-coverage):
the unit tests of a front end or a back end, from Cobertura or LCOV. The command reads each report as a stream,
resolves its paths against the checkout, keeps the files in the project's coverage scope and sends paths, line numbers
and git blob ids, with the commit's tracked files in scope. Uploads of one commit and suite merge, so shards upload
separately. When a newer commit has superseded this one on its branch (a CI job run again), the upload
still exits `0`, the summary says so in one line, and the dashboard keeps the commit's totals as they were.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter coverage upload "**/coverage.cobertura.xml" --suite unit-back
```

**Exit codes:** `0` uploaded · `1` nothing to upload (no report, or no file of the reports in the checkout) · `2` the upload could not be made.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--suite <name>` | The suite the report covers, e.g. `unit-back` |
| `--kind <kind>` | `unit` (default) or `e2e`, for a backend's own run-level report |
| `--format <format>` | `cobertura`, `lcov` or `piwi` (a .NET test host's report, written at exit with `PIWI_COVERAGE_OUTPUT`); detected from the content when absent |
| `--root <dir>` | The directory the reports' relative paths start from |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--branch <name>` | The branch (env `PIWI_BRANCH`, the CI's, else git's) |
| `--dry-run` | Read and resolve the reports, print the summary, send nothing |
| `--json` | Print the summary as JSON |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

Patterns are expanded by the command, so a quoted `**` works the same in every shell. Without `--root`, a relative path
is tried against the report's `<source>`, the current directory, the report's directory and its parent (Vitest writes
`coverage/` under its root), and the repository root; the first that names a file of the checkout wins, and the
summary counts the paths none did. An absolute path is taken under the repository root, and the `/_/` of a .NET build
with `ContinuousIntegrationBuild` is read as the repository root, in a path or in the `<source>` it is joined to.

Each file is named by the git blob of its content in the checkout. When `git hash-object` fails on a file, the command
says so on stderr and goes on: a changed tracked file is left out of the commit's inventory, a file git does not track
is sent without its blob.

## `select` / `run` {#select-run}

Resolve a saved [test selection](/features/test-selection) to the tests it matches. `select` prints the Playwright args (so you can compose them yourself); `run` executes `playwright test` with them. `run impact --base <ref>` runs the tests your working-tree diff impacts, down to the tests that ran the changed lines when tests record coverage ([line level](/features/change-impact#line-level)).

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter select smoke
npx @piwitests/reporter run smoke -- --workers=4
npx @piwitests/reporter run impact --base origin/main
```

**Exit codes:** `0` ok · `1` the test run failed (`run` only) · `128` plus the signal's number when the runner stops
Playwright (`run` only; `143` for `SIGTERM`) · `2` could not resolve, or Playwright could not start.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `--format <fmt>` | `args` (`file:line`, default) · `grep` · `files`. For the full resolution use `--json`; `run` rejects `--format json` |
| `--budget <duration>` | Cap total time, e.g. `5m`, `90s`, `300000` (ms) |
| `--shard <i/n>` | Keep only shard *i* of *n* (up to 1,000 shards), balanced by summed test duration and lock-aware: every holder of a [lock](/reference/test-metadata#test-locks) stays in one shard, which Playwright's own `--shard` would split, so a resolution whose tests share a lock carries a `split-lock` warning. `run` reports the shard to the dashboard (`PIWI_SHARD`), so the shards merge into one run |
| `--fail-fast` | Order the least-reliable tests first. It reorders and never drops, so a `--require-selection` gate still sees the whole set |
| `--base <ref>` | For `impact`: the ref to diff the working tree against |
| `--strict` | Fail (exit 2) instead of falling back when unreachable |
| `--pkg-runner <cmd>` | Package runner for the printed command (default `npx`) |
| `--json` | Print the full resolution as JSON (`select` only) |
| `--reuse` | Experimental, `run` only: [plan](#plan) the selection with pass reuse, then run only the tests the plan keeps. `full` plans the whole suite. Not with `--shard` |
| `--plan <id>` | Experimental, `run` only: run the tests of a stored [plan](#plan), or with `--shard` one shard of them |
| `--environment <key>` | Experimental, with `--reuse` or `--plan`: the [environment](/features/environments) the run reports (env `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`, which `run` sets for Playwright): only passes of that environment are reused. With `--plan`, the plan's environment when none is named; a run naming another runs every test. The reporter's `environment` option, when the config sets it, wins over the variable: name the same one |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

Pass extra Playwright arguments after `--`: `piwi run smoke -- --headed --workers=1`.

When the dashboard is unreachable, `run` reuses the last good resolution from `.piwi/selection-cache.json`. An entry is
keyed by the `--project` value as written, the selection key and the flags that shape the resolution, so a project given
by name is found offline, and a name and an id for the same project are separate entries. With nothing cached, `run`
runs the full suite, or exits `2` under `--strict`.

`run --shard` sets `PIWI_SHARD=<i/n>` for the Playwright process, which the reporter reports as the run's shard, so the
shard jobs of one pipeline merge into one [run](/guide/ci#sharding) and do not cancel each other's runs. Playwright gets
no `--shard` of its own, since the resolved tests are already the shard's. A `select` job that passes the printed
arguments to `playwright test` sets `PIWI_SHARD` itself, to the same `i/n` it gave `--shard`.

When `run` spawns Playwright and the target config has **no Piwi reporter**, it appends `--add-reporter @piwitests/reporter` so the run still reaches the dashboard — provided the installed Playwright is **1.63 or later** (the version that added the flag; it appends to the configured reporters rather than replacing them). It logs one line naming what it added. On older Playwright it logs that the reporter is not configured and runs as before. This trial append gives you results, traces and screenshots but not the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) or [`wrapConfig`](/guide/reporter#installing-via-wrapconfig) defaults — wire the reporter into the config (via [`init`](#init)) for the full set. A config that already lists the reporter is left untouched.

## `plan`

**Experimental.** Plan a run that skips each test whose code has not changed since it last passed, and print the
plan's id. Needs the pass reuse capability, which an administrator turns on in Settings. `<key>` is a saved or built-in
selection, or `full` for the whole suite. The dashboard names the commits of each test's newest reusable pass, `plan`
diffs the working tree against each one, and the dashboard keeps a test only when the change reaches its code. How a
test is decided, how long a plan lasts and which jobs may use it:
[Reuse forecast](/features/reuse-forecast#skipping-reusable-tests).

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter plan full
npx @piwitests/reporter run --plan 42 --shard 2/4
```

In a CI matrix, one job runs `plan` and hands the id to the shard jobs. `run --plan` runs the plan's selection less
the reused tests, and the plan names only those, so a test the dashboard has not seen yet runs. With
Playwright 1.62 or later in the project, it sets `PIWI_PLAN` and `PIWI_PLAN_SKIP=true` for the reporter, which reads the
plan and skips each reused test itself, naming the run whose pass stands in for it; below 1.62, it passes Playwright's
`--test-list-invert` naming them. Each shard passes Playwright's own `--shard`. A run whose own arguments after `--`
choose no tests also passes `--pass-with-no-tests`, so a plan whose tests were all renamed or deleted runs none and
passes; one that chooses its own (a file filter, `--grep`, `--grep-invert`, `--last-failed`, `--only-changed`,
`--test-list`, `--test-list-invert`) fails as Playwright does when they match nothing. A shard that cannot use the plan
runs the whole suite, or exits `2` under `--strict`; a shard whose reporter cannot read it runs the whole suite too.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `--environment <key>` | The [environment](/features/environments) the planned run reports (env `PIWI_ENVIRONMENT`): only passes of that environment are reused |
| `--json` | Print the plan as JSON instead of its id |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

**Exit codes:** `0` planned · `2` could not plan.

## `rerun`

Run the tests a [CI re-run](/features/ci-rerun) dispatched from the dashboard asked for,
in a GitLab, Bitbucket or Jenkins job. The dashboard hands the job its Playwright arguments in the `PIWI_RERUN_ARGS` variable,
each one double-quoted (`"tests/login.spec.ts:10" --project="chromium"`). `rerun` splits them as they were quoted,
without reading them through a shell, and starts `playwright test` with them, followed by any arguments given on its
own command line, after an optional `--`. The same command works on Linux, macOS and Windows runners.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter rerun --workers=2
```

`PIWI_RERUN_ARGS` set and empty runs the whole suite. Unset, the command fails instead: the job did not receive the
variable, and running everything would hide it.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help (as the first argument only; any other argument goes to `playwright test`) |

**Exit codes:** Playwright's own · `128` plus the signal's number when the runner stops Playwright (`143` for
`SIGTERM`) · `2` `PIWI_RERUN_ARGS` is unset or holds a quote left open, or Playwright could not start.

## `probe`

Run the dashboard's [probe plan](/features/probes) and record what the suite noticed. `probe` fetches the (test, route, fault) pairs the dashboard wants checked, runs `playwright test` with the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in probe mode — each fault injected at the network boundary, one per test — and posts the outcomes back. The run is stamped as a probe run, which the dashboard [never counts as a real run](/features/probes#what-a-probe-run-never-counts), and retries are forced off.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter probe --project my-app
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project name or id (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `--budget <n>` | Max pairs to probe this run (default the server's) |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

Everything after `--` is passed to `playwright test`. A probed test fails by design when it notices the injected fault, so a non-zero Playwright exit is expected and is not a command error.

## `flake`

Run a [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab) experiment on one flaky test, in the checkout you are in. `flake` fetches the
test's plan from the dashboard: a control arm with no condition, then one arm per suspect of its
[flake profile](/features/flaky-tests#suspects), most likely first. It runs the control, then each arm, one test at a
time with retries off and the [capture fixtures](/guide/capture-fixtures) in flake mode, and counts only the failures
whose error matches the test's failures in history. It prints each arm against the control with its verdict, and saves
the experiment on the test's Flakiness tab.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter flake 1842
npx @piwitests/reporter flake tests/checkout.spec.ts:42 --suspect 1
npx @piwitests/reporter flake verify 1842
git bisect run npx @piwitests/reporter flake verify 1842 --bisect
```

`<test>` is a test case id (the number in its dashboard URL) or a spec file and line, looked up in the project.
`flake verify` reruns the arm that last reproduced the test, and its control, until a matching failure appears or
enough runs pass to say the fix holds. `flake verify --bisect` runs that arm alone at the commit checked out, saves
nothing, and answers in the exit codes `git bisect run` reads, so a bisect can find the commit where the flake started.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--suspect <n>` | Run only the arm of suspect `n`, its rank on the Flakiness tab |
| `--all` | Also run every condition at once when none reproduces alone |
| `--runs <n>` | Runs of the control and of each arm (default 10; `verify`: the number that proves the fix at the rate the arm reproduced) |
| `--budget <duration>` | Start no new arm after this long: `15m` (default), `90s`, `1h` |
| `--no-upload` | Keep the results off the dashboard. The plan still comes from the dashboard, or from `--plan` when it cannot be reached |
| `--plan <file>` | Read the plan from a file (a saved plan response, or the `plan` of the `plan_flake_experiment` MCP tool) and run it without the dashboard; implies `--no-upload` |
| `--bisect` | `verify` only: one bisect step, the reproducing arm alone with nothing saved; implies `--no-upload` |
| `--source <where>` | Where the lab ran, recorded on the experiment: `cli`, `ci` or `desktop` (default `ci` when `CI` is set, else `cli`) |
| `--json` | Print the arms, their counts, verdicts and p-values as JSON |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | The Piwi project, for a `file:line` test (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

An arm stops at 3 failures with the same error as in CI. It runs in batches of up to five repeats and its attempts are
counted in start order, cut after the third matching failure, since Playwright's `--max-failures` counts every failure.
An `alongside` arm runs both tests on two workers and keeps only the rounds where they overlapped; an `after` arm runs
both on one worker and keeps only the rounds where the other test ran just before.

**Exit codes:** `0` an arm reproduced the failure (`verify`: the fix held) · `1` nothing reproduced (`verify`: it still
fails, or there were too few runs to say) · `2` error: the plan could not be read, or an arm recorded no attempt of the
test. With `--bisect`: `0` good (no matching failure in the runs that prove it) · `1` bad (a matching failure) · `125`
skip (too few clean runs, or this commit could not run the arm) · `2` error: the plan could not be read.

## `ai`

Manage committed natural-language [AI-step](/features/ai-steps) artifacts (`page.piwiLocator(...)` / `page.piwiRun(...)`). The LLM authors each entry once; CI replays the committed JSON deterministically with no model calls, so these commands are how you keep the committed set healthy.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter ai check
npx @piwitests/reporter ai resolve --grep "checkout"
```

| Subcommand | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check` | Scan committed entries for orphans, non-canonical files and duplicate templates. Read-only; exits `1` on errors (orphans, non-canonical or invalid files) — duplicate templates are reported as warnings and do not fail it |
| `resolve` | Author missing entries by running the suite in resolve mode against the configured authoring server (forces `--workers=1`). Needs `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL` (plus `PIWI_API_KEY` when auth is on) and exits `2` without it |
| `prune` | Reserved for cleaning up orphaned/dormant entries — not available in this build; it prints a notice and exits `2` |

| Flag | Applies to | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--dir <name>` | `check` | Entry directory name per spec (env `PIWI_AI_DIR`, default `__piwi__`) |
| `--cwd <path>` | `check` | Root to scan (default: current directory) |
| `--json` | `check` | Emit findings as JSON |
| `--grep <re>` | `resolve` | Only author entries for matching tests |
| `--project <name>` | `resolve` | Author under one Playwright project (a resolve profile) |
| `--env K=V` | `resolve` | Extra env for the run (repeatable — flags/viewport profiles) |
| `--update-ai` | `resolve` | Re-author entries that already exist |

**Exit codes:** `0` clean (or `--help`) · `1` hygiene errors found · `2` bad arguments / command unavailable. `resolve` passes through the test run's exit code.

## `codegen`

Turn a [steps file](/reference/steps-format) into a Playwright spec. Piwi Picker's **Download .piwibug** saves one as
the `steps.json` of the [bug report file](/reference/bug-report-file) of a [recording](/features/record-actions): rename
the file to `.zip` to take it out. The spec is written for a test project: URLs on the recorded
site become paths, so your config's `baseURL` applies; each element uses the first of its recorded locators that the
[stability rules](/reference/locator-stability) call stable; and after each step that leads to another page, the spec
waits for that page's URL. Nothing is sent anywhere unless a project is configured.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter codegen steps.json --out tests/checkout.spec.ts --test-import ./fixtures
```

`codegen bug:<id>` reads the steps of a [bug report](/features/bug-reports) from the dashboard (`--server-url`) instead
of a file.

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--out <file>` | Write the spec to this file instead of printing it; an existing file is kept unless `--force` |
| `--force` | Replace the file `--out` names |
| `--body` | Print only the test's lines, to paste into an existing test, with the imports they need as comments |
| `--title <text>` | Test title (default: the steps file's own title) |
| `--test-import <mod>` | Module `test` and `expect` are imported from, such as your fixtures file (default `@playwright/test`) |
| `--absolute-urls` | Keep the recorded URLs instead of paths |
| `--no-url-checks` | Do not wait for each new page's URL |
| `--env-values` | Read every typed value from an environment variable named after its field (`E2E_EMAIL` for a field labeled Email) instead of writing it into the spec |
| `--fail` | Mark the test as expected to fail (`test.fail()`) |
| `--fail-reason <text>` | The reason written beside `test.fail()`, such as a ticket key |
| `--tag <tag>` | Add a tag; repeat for more (`@` is added when missing) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`): its [function catalog](/features/test-functions) turns matching steps into calls to your own functions, and a locator your tests already use is preferred when it is not brittle |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--offline` | Do not contact the dashboard, even when one is configured |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

Warnings go to stderr, one per step worth a look: a password read from the environment, an element with no locator,
or one whose best locator is brittle. A dashboard that cannot be reached only costs the catalog and the preferred
locators; the spec is still written.

**Exit codes:** `0` written or printed · `2` the steps file could not be read or checked, or the spec could not be
written.

## `preflight`

List the test locators a change breaks, before it runs: [Locator preflight](/features/preflight) explains what it
reads and how it matches. It diffs the working tree against a ref, compares the strings the diff removes or renames
with the project's locator index, and prints each broken chain with its tests, its call sites and its rewrite.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter preflight
npx @piwitests/reporter preflight --base @{upstream} --strict
npx @piwitests/reporter preflight --fix --run -- --workers=2
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--base <ref>` | Diff the working tree against this ref (default `HEAD`: uncommitted changes) |
| `--branch <name>` | Compare with this branch's locator index (default: the project's default branch) |
| `--test-root <dir>` | Where call sites resolve (default: the directory of the nearest `playwright.config`) |
| `--locale <code>` | Translation files of this locale resolve keys first (default `en`) |
| `--fix` | Write the rewrites into the call sites whose line holds the string |
| `--run` | Run the tests that reach the changed files and the specs of the broken locators; Playwright arguments go after `--` |
| `--strict` | Exit 1 when a likely break is left unfixed |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `--project <name\|id>` | Project (env `PIWI_PROJECT_NAME`, `.env`) |
| `--json` | Print the breaks, their call sites, the edits and the impact as JSON |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

The index is cached in `.piwi/locator-index.json` per dashboard, project and branch, and used when the dashboard
cannot be reached.

**Exit codes:** `0` ok, breaks or not · `1` a likely break left unfixed with `--strict`, or `--run`'s tests failed ·
`2` the index could not be fetched and there is no cached copy, or the diff could not be read.

## `bug`

Get a [bug report](/features/bug-reports)'s failing test from the dashboard, written with the project's
[generated specs settings](/features/bug-reports#the-failing-test): `test.fail()` while the bug exists, `@bug`, and
`piwi:bug <id>` so the report follows its runs. Printed by default; `--write` puts it in the project's bugs folder
(`tests/bugs` unless the project names another) and runs it once with `playwright test`, so you see the bug reproduce
before you fix it.

```bash
npx @piwitests/reporter bug 37 --write
```

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `--write` | Write the spec to the project's bugs folder (from the repository root), then run it once |
| `--out <file>` | Write it to this file instead, then run it once; its test import is written for that file's folder |
| `--no-run` | With `--write` or `--out`: write it without running it |
| `--force` | Replace an existing file |
| `--run-mode` | The spec without `test.fail()`, as a reproduction runs it |
| `--server-url <url>` | Dashboard URL (env `PIWI_DASHBOARD_URL`, `.env`, the desktop app) |
| `--api-key <key>` | API key (env `PIWI_API_KEY`, `.env`) |
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |

**Exit codes:** `0` printed or written, and when run, the test failed on the bug as `test.fail()` expects · `1` the run
did not: the bug may be fixed, or a step no longer matches the page · `2` the report could not be read, the file
could not be written, or Playwright could not start or was stopped by a signal.

## `mcp`

Serve the run tools of this machine to a coding agent, as one MCP server over stdio: the runs of every editor with
Piwi (whose runs are served to agents) and of the [desktop app](/features/desktop), under one entry for every
repository. It finds each editor's server in the editors' discovery files, and the desktop app's in its own, once the
app's server proved it holds the token there. It holds no run logic: `run_list` asks every host and names each run's
host, `run_start` goes to the editor whose workspace holds the spec, else to the desktop app, which runs a spec of a
folder it links to a project, and every other tool goes to the host of its `run`; a host that does not answer is named
in the answer. See [Run control for agents](/features/agent-run-control).

A relative `file` of `run_start` is read against the agent's working directory, else against each editor's workspace
folders and the desktop app's linked folders, and a spec reached through a link goes to the editor under its own folder. Each host is named with its first
folder (`Visual Studio Code (shop)`), and an agent's cancel of a call reaches its host. `@latest` runs the newest
reporter, whichever version a repository installs.

::: code-group

```bash [Linux / macOS]
claude mcp add --scope user piwi-runs -- npx -y @piwitests/reporter@latest mcp
```

```powershell [Windows (PowerShell)]
claude mcp add --scope user piwi-runs -- cmd /c npx -y @piwitests/reporter@latest mcp
```

:::

| Flag | Description |
|---|---|
| `-h`, `--help` | Show help |
