# Test metadata

The [reporter](/guide/reporter) records more than pass or fail. This page lists what it collects on its own, what each
field drives in the dashboard, and how to add your own metadata or turn collection off.

## Automatic metadata collection

Without any configuration, the reporter records the following with every run. [Disabling automatic collection](#disabling-automatic-collection) turns the collectors off.

### SCM information (Git)

When `collectScmInfo` is enabled (default), the reporter collects:

- Commit hash and message
- Branch name
- Author name
- Remote URL, without the user name or token a URL can carry (`https://gitlab-ci-token:…@host/…`), which
  [Source control](/guide/source-control#which-repository) uses to find the repository
- The pull-request number and the pull request's target branch, on a pull-request build

The branch is resolved through a fallback chain so a CI pull-request build never records the literal
`HEAD` git reports on a detached checkout: an explicit `PIWI_BRANCH` override, then the CI provider's
branch variables (`GITHUB_HEAD_REF`/`GITHUB_REF_NAME`, `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_SOURCE_BRANCH_NAME`/
`CI_COMMIT_REF_NAME`, `CIRCLE_BRANCH`, and the equivalents for Travis, Azure, Jenkins and Bitbucket),
then the local git checkout. On a pull-request build the target branch (`GITHUB_BASE_REF`,
`CI_MERGE_REQUEST_TARGET_BRANCH_NAME`, `TRAVIS_BRANCH` on a Travis pull-request build, `SYSTEM_PULLREQUEST_TARGETBRANCH`,
`BITBUCKET_PR_DESTINATION_BRANCH`, `CHANGE_TARGET`, or `PIWI_BASE_BRANCH` to name it yourself) is
recorded as the run's **base branch**, which [baselines](/guide/concepts#baseline-last-green-run) fall
back to when the branch has no history of its own.

### CI information

When `collectCiInfo` is enabled (default), the reporter auto-detects:

| Platform        | Collected fields                                          |
|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| GitHub Actions  | Run ID, run number, workflow, actor, repository, ref, SHA |
| Jenkins         | Build number, build URL, job name                         |
| GitLab CI       | Pipeline ID, pipeline URL, job ID, job URL, job name      |
| CircleCI        | Build number, build URL, job name, workflow               |
| Travis CI       | Build number, build URL, job number                       |
| Azure Pipelines | Build number, build ID, build URL, job name               |
| Bitbucket Pipelines | Build number, build URL, pipeline UUID, step UUID, repository |

These seven platforms get rich per-provider fields. The **run label** that ties [sharded](/guide/ci#sharding) runs together comes from the provider's build id: `GITHUB_RUN_ID`, `CI_PIPELINE_ID`, `CIRCLE_WORKFLOW_ID`, `TRAVIS_BUILD_ID`, `BUILD_BUILDID`, `BUILD_ID`, `BUILDKITE_BUILD_ID`, `TEAMCITY_BUILD_ID`, `BITBUCKET_BUILD_NUMBER`, `SEMAPHORE_WORKFLOW_ID`, `APPVEYOR_BUILD_ID` or `DRONE_BUILD_NUMBER`; set `runLabel` when your CI is not among them.

### Run origin

Whatever the collectors, every run records what launched it as `piwiOrigin`, so analyses that compare runs can leave
out the ones that say nothing about the branch's current state. The reporter records `ci` when it detects a CI provider
and `local` otherwise. A launcher names itself through these environment variables on the Playwright process:

| Variable | Value |
|---|---|
| `PIWI_ORIGIN` | `ci`, `ci-rerun`, `local`, `desktop`, `editor`, `preflight`, `bug`, `flake-lab`, `probe`, `bisect` or `reproduce` |
| `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF` | Optional: what the run was launched for, such as a dispatch, a cluster or a bug report id (letters, digits and `._:/#@-`, up to 200 characters) |
| `PIWI_RUN_REF` | Optional, with `PIWI_ORIGIN`: the launcher's name for the run itself, recorded as `piwiRunRef` (same characters as `PIWI_ORIGIN_REF`) |

Piwi's own launchers set them: the desktop app (`desktop`, and `reproduce` or `bisect` with the cluster id), the
editors (`editor`, with a ref of their own on each test run, which they find the run by), `piwi preflight --run`
(`preflight`), `piwi bug --write` (`bug` with the report id), Flake Lab and probes. The desktop app also names each
run it starts with `PIWI_RUN_REF`, so two runs started for the same cluster each find their own Piwi run. Every run
outside CI records a `piwiRunRef`, with `@piwitests/reporter` 0.68.0 or later: the one given, else an editor's
`PIWI_ORIGIN_REF`, else one of its own, `local-<pid>-<time>`. A
[re-run dispatched from the dashboard](/features/ci-rerun) is recorded as `ci-rerun` once
Piwi recognizes it, an imported report as `import`, and a run a person asked for from the dashboard as `request`,
by the server from the request token that started it: a `request` the reporter sends is dropped. You rarely set them
yourself.

A run whose workers connect to an editor or the desktop app, which steer it at their breakpoints (a run either of them
started, or one [started in a terminal](/features/terminal-runs) that follows an editor), also records
`piwiInteractive`: the editor's name (else the `PIWI_ORIGIN` its launcher set) as `client`, and the run's name there
as `ref`.

What each origin feeds:

- **Flake Lab and probe runs** feed nothing: they replay tests under conditions Piwi injected.
- **Bisect steps and reproductions** run at a commit chosen to investigate a failure. They stay out of baselines, fix
  verification, flaky scores, selections, change coverage, the stored locators and test metadata, the bug-report
  lifecycle and a failure cluster's occurrences (its count, its last seen run, the wake of a snooze), and have no
  outbound effect: no [notification](/features/notifications#events), no
  [pull-request comment or commit status](/features/pr-feedback), no automatic AI diagnosis or auto-heal, and no
  [automatic write to an issue tracker](/features/issue-automation#the-runs-that-write).
- **`piwi bug` runs** do not move the bug report they were written for.
- **Local runs** (`local`, `desktop`, `editor`, `preflight`) count like CI runs, with four exceptions. An editor's CI
  failures come from the newest complete CI run on the branch, and a local run stands in only while the branch has
  none. An `editor` run's failures join their clusters without counting as occurrences. An `editor` run, or a `local`
  or `desktop` run of part of the suite, fires no run, new-cluster, fixed, regressed, flakiness or
  performance [notification](/features/notifications#events), posts no
  [pull-request comment or commit status](/features/pr-feedback), starts no automatic AI diagnosis or auto-heal, and
  writes nothing to an [issue tracker](/features/issue-automation#the-runs-that-write) on its own. No local run, and
  no `piwi bug` run, sends [`test.stuck`](/features/stuck-tests#the-notification), complete or not.
- **Partial runs** (a `--grep`, a file filter, a selection, `--last-failed`, `--only-changed` or `--test-list`) never count for change
  coverage, which asks whether a file was reached in the recent runs, nor as a commit's end-to-end coverage.

A finished run posts no [pull-request comment or commit status](/features/pr-feedback), starts no automatic AI
diagnosis or auto-heal, makes no [automatic write to an issue tracker](/features/issue-automation#the-runs-that-write)
and fires no [notification](/features/notifications#events), an environment incident's own event aside, when it is:

- a Flake Lab or [probe](/features/probes#what-a-probe-run-never-counts) run, a bisect step or a reproduction;
- a run a person requested from the dashboard (`request`), which only its requester sees;
- a run from an editor (`editor`), complete or not;
- a `local` or `desktop` run of part of the suite;
- a run flagged as an [environment incident](/features/environment-incidents), which sends one
  [`environment.incident`](/reference/notification-events) event in place of its failure, flakiness, performance and
  new-cluster events (`run.finished` still fires) and gets the verdict *inconclusive* from the
  [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-it-leaves-out);
- an imported report, which runs none of a finished run's side effects.

A complete `local` or `desktop` run, a `preflight` run and a `piwi bug` run send them like a CI run, except
[`test.stuck`](/features/stuck-tests#the-notification), which no run started on a developer's machine sends.
[Results in Zephyr Scale](/features/test-management#when-a-run-is-sent) take a narrower set: complete CI runs only.

### Playwright configuration

The reporter also records browser project configs, worker count, the global timeout, and parallel settings. A sharded
run keeps the configuration of the shard that began it, and each shard's own worker count under `shards`.

### Browser configuration per execution {#browser-configuration-per-test-case}

The reporter automatically captures each execution's Playwright project configuration — `projectName` (the Playwright project's name, not the reporter's `projectName` option, which names the Piwi project), `browserName` (a `devices` preset's `defaultBrowserType` when the project sets none), `channel`, `viewport`, and the rendering options `colorScheme`, `reducedMotion`, `forcedColors` and `contrast` (Playwright 1.63's standalone contrast option) — via `test.parent.project()`. This is stored in the `browser` field of every execution and feeds the [environment diff](/features/evidence#one-execution-diagnosis-first) that compares a failing execution against its last passing one.

In the dashboard UI, every row of a run's Tests tab shows the browser icon (from the channel, else the engine, else the project name), and `browser:<project name>` in its [search](/reference/test-search) narrows the list to one project.

### Suite hierarchy (describe blocks)

The reporter traverses the test's parent chain (`test.parent`) to build a `suitePath` array — the list of describe-block names from the root to the test's immediate parent. Each level's `suiteConfig` (mode: `parallel` | `serial` | `default`, plus any suite-level `annotations`) is captured alongside the path. This data is sent in both streaming and batch submission payloads and stored in the `test_suites` and `test_cases` tables.

In the dashboard UI, **Group by: File + Describe** on a run's Tests tab groups the tests under their file and describe blocks, each of which collapses.

### Test annotations (Playwright marks)

The reporter captures Playwright test marks set via `test.info().annotations` (e.g. `@fixme`, `@slow`, `@skip`) and sends them as `testAnnotations` with every execution. These are stored per run on the `test_runs_cases` table and rendered as badges on the execution's row in the run and on the execution page. A `@slow` mark combined with a test's duration history powers the **stale `test.slow()`** detection in [Timeout opportunities](/features/slow-tests#timeout-opportunities).

### Test tags

The reporter reads each test's tags (`TestCase.tags`) and sends them as `tags`. Playwright already folds together both
ways of declaring one, so either works:

```typescript
test('checkout applies the discount @smoke', async ({ page }) => { /* … */ })

test('checkout applies the discount', { tag: ['@smoke', '@critical'] }, async ({ page }) => { /* … */ })
```

Tags are stored twice: on the execution (`test_runs_cases.tags`, what that run saw) and on the test case
(`test_cases.tags`, the latest declaration). The leading `@` is stripped on the way in, so a tag reads the same however
it was written — filter for `smoke` or `@smoke` and you get the same rows. Removing a tag from a spec clears it on the
next run that reports the test.

Tags drive the `tag:` qualifier of the Tests tabs' [search](/reference/test-search), the tag filter on the flaky
leaderboard, and the `--require-tag` rule of the [CI merge gate](/features/merge-gate#what-fails-it).

#### Tag limit

Piwi keeps at most 20 tags per test, each cut to 60 characters, in the order Playwright lists them; duplicates count
once. A test that declares more keeps its first 20 and loses the rest. The reporter warns about it once as the run
begins, naming the tests (20 at most), and records them on the run: the run page shows "Tags cut at 20 on N tests",
with the tests in its Details. When more than 20 tests lost tags, the page shows "at least 20 tests", the number it
lists, since merging a run's reports (shards, or a payload sent in batches) can count a test twice. The dashboard does
the same for a run sent without the reporter, or imported from a blob report.

Which tags are cut depends on Playwright's order. Playwright 1.64.1 builds `TestCase.tags` from the config's `tag`
first, then each `describe` from the outermost in (the @-words of its title, then its `tag` option), then the @-words
of the test title, and the test's own `tag` option last. So a tag in the test's `tag` option is the first to go. To
keep the tags that matter:

- keep config and `describe` tags few;
- put the tags that matter in the test title (`test('checkout @SHOP-T123', …)`), which comes before the `tag` option;
- for the one identifier that matters most, use an [external test ID](#external-test-ids) instead of a tag.

#### Keys in test tags

A tag can name the issue a test is tracked in (`SHOP-1234`) or the test case it covers (`SHOP-T123`). Two patterns, under
**Project → Settings → Keys in test tags**, tell Piwi which tags are which:

- **Issue key**: a tag naming an issue, such as `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9]+-[0-9]+$`. Piwi
  [links the issue](#issues-the-tests-declare) to the failure cluster of a test that carries the tag.
- **Test case key**: a tag naming a test case, such as `^SHOP-T[0-9]+$`.

A pattern is a regular expression without flags, tested against the tag without its `@`, at most 200 characters. Anchor
it with `^` and `$` and use letters, digits, character classes and quantifiers only, with no groups or `|`:
`^SHOP-T[0-9]+$` matches `SHOP-T123` and not `SHOP-1234`. An issue key pattern must match the whole tag as an issue key
of the tracker binding's project, such as `SHOP-1234`, so `^bug-SHOP-[0-9]+$` or a lower-case pattern links nothing.
A pattern that breaks that rule, does not compile, or matches an empty tag (and so every tag) is refused. Leave a
field empty to turn it off; both are off by default, and neither needs a tracker connection. Saving needs the same
role as the rest of the project's settings.

When both patterns are on, the section lists the tags of the project's last complete run (the whole suite, finished;
partial, lab and private runs are skipped) that both patterns match, each with a test that carries it. Piwi would read
such a tag as an issue and as a test case, so anchor the patterns until the list is empty. It lists 20 tags at most.

### Test locks

Playwright 1.63 lets a test or a `describe` declare a **lock** — a named shared resource the runner never lets two
holders run at once:

```typescript
test('writes an order', { lock: 'database' }, async ({ page }) => { /* … */ })

test.describe('payments', { lock: ['database', 'external-api'] }, () => { /* every test inside inherits both */ })
```

Playwright 1.65 adds one built-in lock, `-exclusive-`: a test that holds it runs only while no other test runs, whatever
locks the others declare.

```typescript
test('rebuilds the search index', { lock: '-exclusive-' }, async ({ page }) => { /* … */ })
```

Piwi shows it as **Runs alone** wherever it shows a lock. Within a sharded run, Playwright holds it in each shard's own
run: a test that holds it runs alone in its shard, while the other shards run their tests on other machines. Piwi's
[lock-aware sharding](/features/test-selection#print-shard-and-reorder) places its holders as it places tests without a
lock, and never warns about it.

The reporter reads the lock names and sends them as `locks`, stored on the execution (`test_runs_cases.locks`) and
denormalized onto the test case (`test_cases.locks`, the latest declaration) — the same treatment as tags. They power
the [Timeline tab's lock lanes and *Locks* table](/features/slow-tests#the-run-s-timeline), the `lock:` search qualifier on
the Tests tabs and *Group by lock* on a run's, lock badges on every test row, and two [clues](/features/evidence#clues) (a lock's previous holder failed;
a lock was held on two shards at once).

Capture is **best effort**. Playwright exposes locks only to an in-process reporter — there is no public API property,
and the tele protocol that backs blob reports and `merge-reports` carries none — so a run recorded live has its locks
and a run [rebuilt from a blob import](/guide/importing-runs) has none. Locks also serialize only within one
`npx playwright test` process: two `--shard` runs are separate processes and can hold the same lock at the same time,
which the cross-shard clue points out.

### Ownership metadata (`piwi:` annotations)

Six `piwi:`-prefixed annotations attach ownership to a test, and a seventh, `piwi:id`, its [external ID](#external-test-ids). They are ordinary Playwright annotations, so no new API is
involved:

```typescript
test(
  'checkout applies the discount',
  {
    tag: '@critical',
    annotation: [
      { type: 'piwi:owner', description: '@checkout-team' },
      { type: 'piwi:priority', description: 'critical' },
      { type: 'piwi:feature', description: 'Checkout' },
      { type: 'piwi:link', description: 'https://issues.example.com/PROJ-412' },
    ],
  },
  async ({ page }) => {
    /* … */
  },
)
```

| Field | Accepts |
|---|---|
| `piwi:owner` | Any text — a team handle, a squad name, an email |
| `piwi:priority` | `critical`, `high`, `medium` or `low` (anything else is ignored) |
| `piwi:feature` | Any text — the product area, for grouping across spec files |
| `piwi:link` | An absolute `http(s)` URL; other schemes are dropped rather than stored |
| `piwi:bug` | The id of the Piwi bug report the test reproduces (`37` or `#37`); written by the spec a [bug report](/features/report-a-bug) generates |
| `piwi:issue` | The issue the test's failures are tracked in: its absolute `http(s)` URL or its key (`SHOP-412`). Repeat the annotation to name several, up to 10; a failure cluster is [linked to it](#issues-the-tests-declare) |
| `piwi:id` | The test's ID in your test management tool, see [External test IDs](#external-test-ids) |

Metadata shows as badges next to the test wherever it is listed, is searchable with `owner:`, `priority:` and `feature:`
on the Tests tabs ([test search](/reference/test-search)), and is carried into [pull-request feedback](/features/pr-feedback) so a failure comment names the team
that owns it. Unknown `piwi:` fields and unparseable values are ignored — a typo costs you the field, not the run.

The values are also re-validated server-side, because a payload can reach the ingest API without passing through the
reporter.

**A test that declares no `piwi:owner` takes its owner from the repository's `CODEOWNERS`**, matched against its spec
file, so ownership works with no test edits; a `piwi:owner` annotation wins wherever a team wants to be explicit. That
derived owner is used in pull-request comments, on the flaky leaderboard, and by the `owners`
[notification filter](/features/notifications#subscriptions), which routes a run only to the team whose tests broke. A
public repository's `CODEOWNERS` is read without a token; a private one needs an [SCM credential](/guide/source-control),
and without it ownership comes from the annotations alone.

### Issues the tests declare

A `piwi:issue` annotation names the issue a test's failures are tracked in, by its URL or its key:

```typescript
test(
  'pays with a saved card',
  {
    annotation: [
      { type: 'piwi:issue', description: 'https://acme.atlassian.net/browse/SHOP-412' },
      { type: 'piwi:issue', description: 'SHOP-415' },
    ],
  },
  async ({ page }) => {
    /* … */
  },
)
```

It stays apart from `piwi:link` and from Playwright's own `{ type: 'issue' }`, which suites use for any related page.
When a [run that writes to the ticket](/features/issue-automation#the-runs-that-write) finishes, on a project
[bound](/features/issue-tracking#the-project-binding) to a Jira connection and a Jira project, Piwi links each failure
cluster to the issues its failing tests name ([Issue tracking](/features/issue-tracking#links-the-tests-declare)). A
test counts by its last attempt, so one whose retry passed names nothing:

- **Only issues of the bound Jira project.** A key needs the shape `SHOP-412` with the binding's project as its
  prefix, a URL must point at the connection's site, and Jira must return the issue under that key and project, so an
  issue moved to another project is dropped. Anything else is dropped, not stored as a plain link. A binding without a
  Jira project links nothing.
- **One lookup per run**, of at most 50 keys, the ones the most tests name first and, last, the ones Jira did not
  return and the ones only tags name that the project's issue types dropped, within 10 seconds for the whole step.
  That memory lasts a day and is kept per server process, so a restart clears it. With Jira down or slow, nothing is
  linked, and the next failing run that names the issue tries again.
- **At most 10 per cluster**, the first linked staying; links pinned by hand or filed by Piwi do not count. The other
  keys of the bound project its tests named in that run, neither linked nor removed, show as *and N more named by its
  tests* at the end of its links. A cluster already linking a key, by any route, gets no second link to it.
- The link's chip says *From the test's annotation*.
- **A tag can name the issue too**, when the project has an [issue key pattern](#keys-in-test-tags) and the binding has
  an issue type to link. A key in a tag is linked only when Jira says its issue is of one of the types in the
  binding's *Issue types linked from test tags* (by default the binding's issue type; a number matches a type id or a
  type named with that number, any other text a type name), since a tag can also name a story. A key the filter drops
  is left out of *and N more*. An annotation has no type filter and wins when both name the key.
  The chip says *From the tag @SHOP-123*.
- **Removing one keeps it off.** A link from the tests removed on the dashboard or through the MCP tools is not linked
  to that cluster again, even once the issue moves; a merge keeps the removal on the surviving cluster and a split
  copies it to the new one. Pinning the issue on that cluster by hand lifts it.
- **Read-only.** No [policy](/features/issue-tracking#keep-the-ticket-honest) or [rule](/features/issue-automation)
  comments on it, moves it or updates its description, its status never resolves or reopens the cluster on its own
  (a person can still mark the cluster resolved once it is Done), and the issue body Piwi writes does not list it. The sync refreshes its status and removes it once the issue leaves the bound
  project.
- **It counts as tracked.** The cluster's known issue is its latest ticket filed or pinned while that is not Done,
  else the oldest link from its tests that is not Done, else that Done ticket, else the oldest link from its tests. So
  a Done pinned issue gives way to an open one its tests name, though the write-backs still act on the pinned one. While that issue is not Done, automatic creation files no issue and
  the cluster leaves *Needs ticket*; the inbox, the pull-request comment and the `cluster.*` notifications name it.
- Pinning it with *Link an issue*, by its URL on the connection's site, turns it into a pinned link, which the
  write-backs then act on. The same key on another site stays a plain link beside it.

### External test IDs

Piwi recognizes a test by its file (its path relative to the folder holding your Playwright config, whatever directory
Playwright runs from), its describe blocks and its title. Renaming a test, or moving it to another file or
describe block, would otherwise start a new test with no history: no flakiness stats, failure clusters, quarantine or
trends. When your tests already have an ID in a test management tool, give it to Piwi: a test with an **external ID**
is matched on that ID first, and a renamed or moved test keeps its history, under its new title and place.

Declare it with a `piwi:id` annotation:

```typescript
test('Log in with Email', { annotation: { type: 'piwi:id', description: '12526' } }, async ({ page }) => {
  /* … */
})
```

Or, when the ID is already in every title, read it from there with the reporter's `externalId.pattern`:

```typescript
reporter: [
  ['@piwitests/reporter', { externalId: { pattern: /^(\d+),\s*/, stripFromTitle: true } }],
],
```

| Option | Default | Does |
|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | none | A regular expression (or its source as a string) applied to the test's own title. The ID is its first capture group, or the whole match without a group. Also `PIWI_EXTERNAL_ID_PATTERN`. |
| `stripFromTitle` | `false` | Show the title without the ID in the dashboard, next to the ID. The title stored and matched on stays whole, so commands that select tests by title keep working. |
| `onDuplicate` | `'report'` | Two tests declaring the same ID are listed in the console before the first test runs, and on the run page. `'fail'` also fails the run. Also `PIWI_EXTERNAL_ID_ON_DUPLICATE`. |

- A `piwi:id` annotation wins over the pattern. Put it on the test, not on a `describe` block, where every test inside
  would declare the same ID.
- The ID is read from the annotations declared on the test, never from one added at run time with
  `testInfo.annotations.push()`.
- An ID is up to 120 characters, case-sensitive.
- The first run that declares an ID gives it to the existing test it matches by file, describe blocks and title, so
  turning the option on keeps every history. A test that already has an ID never takes another one: a test whose ID
  changed in your test management tool starts a new history, which you can join to the old one by merging them.
- Imports of older runs and Flake Lab runs match tests by their ID but never rename, move or give an ID to a test.
- **Duplicates:** an ID names one test. Tests declaring the same ID are matched by file, describe blocks and title, as
  if they had none, until each has its own. The same test in several Playwright projects is one test, not a duplicate.
  With `--shard`, each shard only sees its own tests: the dashboard also checks across shards and lists what it finds
  on the run page.
- The ID shows before the title in the test lists, on the test's page and on the execution page; click it to copy
  it. Search for it with `id:` ([test search](/reference/test-search)).
- **Test ID link:** in the project's settings (General), give the address of a test in your test management tool,
  with `{id}` where the ID goes (`https://tcm.example.com/case/{id}`). The ID chip then opens the test there.
- Pull-request comments, notifications and exports name a test by its ID and title: `12526 · Log in with Email`.
- **Merging two tests:** a rename or a move that was not matched (before the test had an ID, for example) leaves the
  history in two halves. On the test's page, project managers can use **Merge…** to pick the other half: its
  executions, quarantine, failure clusters, locators, coverage, bug reports and links move to this test, and the
  other test is deleted. Two tests that ran in the same run are two tests, and are never merged. This cannot be
  undone.

### Expected failures (`test.fail()`)

The reporter sends each test's `expectedStatus` as Playwright reports it (`failed` for a `test.fail()` test), stored on
`test_runs_cases.expected_status`; for a reporter or an import that does not send it, the server derives it from the
`fail`, `skip` and `fixme` annotations. The status follows Playwright: an expected failure that failed counts as passed,
and one that passed counts as failed, with "Expected to fail, but passed.". That second row is shown as **Looks fixed**
rather than as a failure: it joins no failure cluster, the pull-request comment tells you to remove `test.fail()`, and
the `bug.looks_fixed` [notification event](/reference/notification-events) fires once, on the first run of a branch
where it passes. A test that runs in several browser projects looks fixed only when it passed in all of them.

### Per-test timeout

The reporter records each test's effective per-test timeout (`TestCase.timeout`) and sends it as `timeout` (milliseconds) with every execution, stored on `test_runs_cases.timeout`. `0` means the test has no timeout (unbounded); runs reported by an older reporter that predates this field store `null`.

Together with the test's duration history this drives the **Timeout opportunities** analysis (see [Slow tests & wasted time](/features/slow-tests#timeout-opportunities)), which flags tests whose timeout far exceeds their real p95 duration so failures and hangs stop wasting time waiting.

### Skipped vs "didn't run"

The reporter distinguishes two outcomes that Playwright both reports as `skipped`:

- **`skipped`** — an intentional skip via `test.skip()` / `test.fixme()` (static, conditional, or runtime). These always carry a `skip`/`fixme` annotation, so the skip reason (when provided) is preserved in `testAnnotations` and shown on the execution. The annotation also decides the grey the status bars draw: a `fixme` skip is counted apart from a plain `skip` (it stays part of `skippedTests`), so a test switched off as known broken does not blend into the deliberate skips.
- **`didnotrun`** — a test that never actually executed. This covers three cases:
  - a test skipped as a side effect of an **earlier failure in a `describe.serial` group** (Playwright reports it as `skipped` with no annotation; the reporter reclassifies it);
  - a test of a project whose **[project dependency](https://playwright.dev/docs/test-projects#dependencies) failed**, such as the tests that need a `setup` project's login (Playwright runs none of them);
  - a test that Playwright **never started because the run was cut short** (no `onTestEnd` fires for these or the previous case — the reporter materializes them from the planned test list so they still appear, with zero duration and no error).

  A test declared skipped (`test.skip()`, `test.fixme()`, a skipped `describe`) is `skipped` even when the run stopped before reaching it.

Each `didnotrun` case also carries **`didNotRunReason`**, so the dashboard can say _why_ a test never ran rather than just that it didn't:

- `previous-failure` — skipped because an earlier test (or hook) in its serial group failed, or because a `beforeAll` hook failed, which skips the rest of its group in any mode. The reporter also records **`blockedBy`**, the location of the failing test that blocked it — so the did-not-run case links to its cause, names the hook when the failure happened in one, and the failing test lists the downstream tests it stopped from running.
- `dependency-failure` — not run because a test failed in a project its project depends on (`dependencies`), directly or through another project. `blockedBy` holds the location of that failing test, as for `previous-failure`.
- `global-timeout` — the run's `globalTimeout` elapsed before the test could start.
- `max-failures` — the run reached its configured `maxFailures` budget.
- `interrupted` — the run was otherwise cut short (a worker crash or a cancellation).

The run-level counter `didNotRunTests` aggregates these, and the dashboard renders them as a distinct "Didn't run" segment/badge separate from skipped.

### How a result counts

The reporter sends every attempt, and the dashboard reads them by one set of rules:

- **An execution is one attempt** of one test, in one run, on one Playwright project. A retry is an execution of its
  own, and so is each `--repeat-each` repetition, which Playwright runs as a test of its own, with its own retries:
  `--repeat-each=3` contributes three executions of the test, more with retries. The run counts each repetition once,
  as Playwright's summary does, and a test failed in a run when one of its repetitions failed, whatever the others did.
- **The last attempt decides.** A test is **flaky** in a run when its last attempt passed after an earlier attempt
  failed or timed out; a retry alone does not make it flaky. When one test of a `describe.serial` group fails,
  Playwright retries the whole group: the tests that passed before and a `test.fail()` test that failed as expected
  pass again, and a test that did not run behind the failure passes, none of them flaky. A test that passed, then
  failed on the group's retry, counts as failed, where Playwright's summary calls it flaky.
- **One reading everywhere.** The run page and the run list, a test's history, status and Trend tab, the catalog, the
  analytics, the notifications, the exports and the MCP tools read a result the same way. The dashboard stores the
  verdict with each result's last attempt as it ingests it, and gives the results and the flaky counts of runs stored
  by an earlier version theirs when it upgrades.
- **A run of a test**, on a test's own pages (its page and Trend tab, the project's Tests tab, selections and spec
  health), is one result per run, Playwright project and `--repeat-each` repetition: its final attempt. A retry is
  never a run of its own, and a test that failed, then passed on its retry, is one flaky run.
- **Interrupted**: a test the run's interruption (Ctrl+C, a crashed worker) cut short counts in no outcome: neither
  passed, failed, skipped nor did not run, and in no pass rate. The dashboard, the exports and the notifications draw
  it in a neutral slate labelled *Interrupted*, and a count bar names the gap it leaves.
- **Pass rate**: the passed results over the results that passed or failed. A timed-out result counts as failed, a
  flaky one as passed; a skipped, did-not-run or interrupted result is in neither term, so a suite that skips tests by
  design, or a run stopped halfway, is rated on the tests that ran to an outcome. With no passed or failed result
  there is no pass rate: the dashboard shows a dash, never 0% or 100%. Every pass rate follows this rule: a run's, a
  project's, Home's, a test's, the [test pass rate metric](/reference/metrics) of Analytics and the
  quality reports, and a share link's README badge.
- **Flaky rate**: a test's flaky runs over its runs that passed or failed, the results the pass rate divides by. With
  no passed or failed run there is no flaky rate, and the dashboard shows a dash. A file's or a spec directory's flaky
  rate divides its tests' runs the same way: the Trend tab of a test, the file headers of the project's Tests tab and
  the Spec health widget follow this rule. Other numbers about flakiness divide differently and are not a flaky rate:
  the [flakiness score](/features/flaky-tests#flaky-test-detection), a run's share of flaky tests (the
  `flakiness.spike` [notification](/reference/notification-events)), and Flake Lab's **flaky N%**, the share of the
  test's recent runs that passed or failed (those the flaky ranking reads) in which it failed or passed on a retry.
- **A run that ran to its end** passed, failed or hit Playwright's global timeout. A project's health (Home's
  Project health table and stat strip, the project header) reads only such runs: a run still in progress,
  interrupted or cancelled shows in every list and in the trend bars with its status, and in none of those figures.

### Test errors

The reporter sends a failed test's errors as one text, with the call log Playwright writes. What may be a secret in it
is written `<hidden>`:

- the text a fill or a typing typed, and the value of a credential header a request's log writes;
- the values an assertion quotes of a password field, or of a field whose locator names a secret (`Mot de passe`);
- a credential's shape wherever it stands, colored or not: a JWT, a bearer token, a service's key such as `sk_live_…`,
  `ghp_…` or `AKIA…`, a key or a token Piwi issues such as `pd_…`.

Each step's error, and the error line of a hook or a fixture that failed, are hidden the same way. A step's subtitle
and its `url` param, where Playwright writes the address of a navigation or an API request (in its title up to
Playwright 1.62), and the params of a `test.step` have a credential in a URL, a cookie or a JSON field hidden too, and a credential's shape, on the live
timeline as in the stored steps. The dashboard hides them again as it stores a result, whatever sent it. An error that holds no secret is kept as it is, so it joins the
[failure cluster](/features/failure-clusters) it did. An error stored before the dashboard hid a credential's shape
has it hidden at the first start of the version that does, its failure cluster kept.

### Errors outside the tests

The reporter keeps the errors Playwright reports beside the tests (its `onError`), each with its message, the frames of
its stack and the place it was thrown, named relative to the Playwright config's folder:

- a global setup or global teardown that threw;
- a spec file that did not load: a syntax error, an import that failed, a `test()` call where none is allowed. `No
  tests found` and a web server that did not start come the same way, before any test runs, and the run then has none;
- a worker fixture whose teardown threw, with the tests the worker ran;
- the failure budget (`maxFailures`) that stopped the run.

An error a worker reported, as a worker fixture's teardown, also names that worker, as Playwright 1.60 and later give
it: its [lane](#worker-lanes), with its shard in a sharded run, and its Playwright project. The run page shows it under
the error (**Worker 2 · Shard 3 · Playwright project webkit**).

The first 20 go with the run's end, as its `runErrors`, each message and stack cut to 4,000 characters, with what may
be a secret hidden as in a [test's error](#test-errors), and also a credential in a URL, a cookie or a JSON field, and a
value shaped like a token. A sharded run adds each shard's to the others'. The run page shows them under its header,
and the MCP `get_run` tool returns them as `runErrors`, an error's worker as `worker`, `shardIndex` and
`playwrightProject`. **Collapse** folds them there to one line, the first error's
first line, so a long stack leaves its height to the tab below, the Video tab's video among them; **Expand** shows them
again, and the browser remembers which you chose. A [blob report you import](/guide/importing-runs) keeps them
the same way.

### Test output

The reporter keeps what each attempt wrote to stdout and stderr (`TestResult.stdout` and `stderr`): the test's
`console.log` lines and what the code it ran printed, text or bytes read as UTF-8. Each stream has what may be a
secret hidden, as above, colored or not, and the value it gives a name like a credential's (`password: '…'`,
`API_KEY=…`), and past about 64 KB keeps its first and last lines, cut at a line break, with a line saying how many
lines and characters were cut between them. The dashboard stores each stream once per project however many
executions wrote it, and shows it on the execution's **Output** tab ([Failure evidence](/features/evidence)), in its
[offline export](/features/offline-export) and through the MCP `get_test_run_case` tool. An
[imported blob report](/guide/importing-runs) keeps each attempt's output the same way.

### Worker lanes

The reporter sends each attempt's worker twice: Playwright's `workerIndex`, the worker process, which is new every time
Playwright starts one (after a failed test, or for a test that needs another project or other worker options), and
its `parallelIndex`, the lane the process runs in, which the process started in its place keeps. The dashboard names a
worker by its lane, from 1 in each shard: **Worker 2** on the run's Timeline, in the Tests list's **Worker** sort, on
the execution page, in its [offline export](/features/offline-export) and in a `test.stuck`
[notification](/reference/notification-events), and `worker: 2` in the MCP `get_run` and `get_test_run_case` tools.
A [blob report you import](/guide/importing-runs) keeps both. A run from a reporter that sends no lane names a worker
by its process, and its Timeline works the lanes out from when each process ran; the MCP tools then give its
`workerIndex` in place of `worker`.

### Hooks

Playwright 1.59 and later give every hook step to a test: a `beforeAll` or `afterAll` hook and the setup of a worker
fixture are steps of the test they ran for. The run's timeline draws them inside that test's bar, as its setup and
teardown sections, never on a lane of their own. A worker fixture that throws as its worker shuts down, after its last
test, is one of the [errors outside the tests](#errors-outside-the-tests).

## With custom metadata

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['@piwitests/reporter', {
      serverUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
      projectName: 'my-project',
      projectDescription: 'End-to-end tests for the main application',
      environment: 'staging',
      relatedIssue: 'PROJ-123',
      tags: ['regression', 'critical'],
      customData: {
        version: '1.2.3',
      },
    }],
  ],
})
```

## Disabling automatic collection

```typescript
export default defineConfig({
  reporter: [
    ['@piwitests/reporter', {
      serverUrl: 'http://localhost:3000',
      projectName: 'my-project',
      collectScmInfo: false,
      collectCiInfo: false,
      collectPerformanceMetrics: false,
    }],
  ],
})
```

# Steps file format

A **steps file** is a recording as data rather than code. A [Piwi Picker recording](/features/record-actions) keeps
one as the `steps.json` of the [`.piwibug`](/reference/bug-report-file) it saves and sends one to a paired editor, and
[`piwi codegen`](/reference/cli#codegen) turns one into a Playwright spec. Because it
holds steps and not code, the same file can be rendered for different projects (their `test` import, their
`baseURL`) and read again by newer tools.

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "title": "Coupon not applied",
  "origin": "https://staging.acme.test",
  "recordedAt": 1790467200000,
  "note": null,
  "steps": [
    { "action": "goto", "target": null, "value": "/cart", "redacted": false, "pageUrl": "/cart", "timestamp": 0 },
    {
      "action": "click",
      "target": {
        "tagName": "button",
        "role": "button",
        "accessibleName": "Apply",
        "testId": null,
        "text": "Apply",
        "alternatives": [{ "locator": "getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' })", "method": "getByRole", "score": 90 }]
      },
      "value": null,
      "redacted": false,
      "pageUrl": "/cart",
      "timestamp": 1
    }
  ]
}
```

## The document

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `v` | `1` or `2` | The format version: `2` when the file uses a `manual` step or the `toContainText`, `toHaveCount` or `toBeChecked` matcher, `1` otherwise. |
| `title` | string or null | The test's title when rendered. |
| `origin` | string or null | The origin the steps were recorded on, such as `https://staging.acme.test`. |
| `recordedAt` | number | When the recording started, in milliseconds since 1970. |
| `note` | string or null | Free text from whoever recorded it. |
| `steps` | list | The steps, in order. |
| `viewports` | list | Optional: the viewport sizes the steps were recorded at; see below. |

URLs on `origin` are stored as paths (`/cart?from=mail`), so a spec rendered from the file can use the project's
`baseURL` instead of the site the steps were recorded on.

## A step

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | string | `goto`, `click`, `dblclick`, `hover`, `fill`, `check`, `uncheck`, `selectOption`, `press`, `setInputFiles`, `dragTo`, `assert` or `manual`. |
| `target` | object or null | The element the step acted on; null for `goto`, a key press on the page, or an `assert` on the URL. |
| `value` | string or null | The URL for `goto`, the typed text for `fill`, the option for `selectOption`, the key for `press`, the chosen files' names for `setInputFiles`, one per line. |
| `redacted` | boolean | The value was typed in a password field, or in one whose `autocomplete` names a password, a card number, its security code or a one-time code, and was not kept; the spec reads it from an environment variable named after the field, such as `E2E_PASSWORD`. |
| `pageUrl` | string | The page the step happened on; empty when it is not known, as in steps made from a test run after an action that may have left the page. Replay then waits for no particular page. |
| `timestamp` | number | When it happened. |
| `assertion` | object | On `assert` steps only; see below. |
| `dropTarget` | object | On `dragTo` steps only: the element the target is dropped on, a target like the other. |
| `manual` | object | On `manual` steps only; see [Manual steps](#manual-steps). |

A `hover` step moves the pointer over its target and is written as `await <locator>.hover();`. Piwi Picker records
one before a click on an element that shows only while another is hovered (a row's actions, a menu that opens on
hover); the hover is on the element that shows it.

A `setInputFiles` step keeps the names of the files chosen, never their content. The spec writes
`await <locator>.setInputFiles('invoice.pdf');`, which reads the file from the directory Playwright runs in, and the
converter warns that the file is needed. A `dragTo` step is written as `await <locator>.dragTo(<drop locator>);`.

A target holds what identifies the element: `tagName`, `role`, `accessibleName`, `testId`, `text`, and
`alternatives`, its locators ranked best first. Each alternative has a `locator` (a Playwright locator chain such as
`getByRole('button', { name: 'Apply' })`), the `method` it ends with, and a `score`.

An assertion states what the page should show:

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `matcher` | string | `toHaveText`, `toContainText`, `toHaveValue`, `toHaveAccessibleName`, `toHaveCount`, `toHaveURL`, `toBeVisible`, `toBeHidden`, `toBeEnabled`, `toBeDisabled` or `toBeChecked`. |
| `expected` | string or null | The expected value, required for the first six. A `toHaveURL` value is a path or a URL; a `toHaveCount` value is a whole number, such as `"3"`, written as a number in the spec. |
| `actual` | string or null | What the page showed when it was recorded, kept when it differs; the spec writes it in a comment. |
| `negated` | boolean | Written as `expect(…).not.…`. |
| `note` | string or null | Written as a comment above the assertion. |

`toContainText` finds its value inside the element's text, `toHaveCount` counts every element the target's first
locator finds, and `toBeChecked` checks a checkbox, a radio or an element with `aria-checked`.

## Manual steps

A `manual` step is one nothing can play: a person does it by hand. Piwi writes one when it makes steps from a test run,
as a failed execution's [Export](/reference/bug-report-file#a-report-made-from-a-test-run) does. Those steps hold the
test's steps up to the failure, setup hooks included, and its failing assertion with what it expected and what the
run received; a call the run did not keep enough of to play becomes a manual step naming the line of the test it
stands for: a click at a point of the page, a value the run kept only in part, a file choice, an option chosen by its
index or several options chosen at once, a check with a regular expression. API requests, scripts run in the page,
route mocks and checks on values are not steps at all: the report's Markdown lists them under **Not replayed**, with
why.

```json
{
  "action": "manual",
  "target": null,
  "value": null,
  "redacted": false,
  "pageUrl": "",
  "timestamp": 1790467201000,
  "manual": {
    "description": "Choose in `getByLabel('Invoice')` the file the test chose; the run does not keep its name",
    "location": "tests/billing.spec.ts:31",
    "call": "Set input files getByLabel('Invoice')",
    "instruction": { "kind": "setInputFiles", "locator": "getByLabel('Invoice')" }
  }
}
```

`description` says what to do and is required; `location` (the test's `file:line`) and `call` (the Playwright call it
stands for) are optional. The spec writes a manual step as a comment, `// Manual step: …`, never as code, and the
converter warns about it. [Replay](/features/replay-a-bug-report#when-a-step-cannot-be-played) hands it to you.

`instruction` is optional: the same step without its words, which Piwi writes beside the English `description` when it
makes steps from a test run. Its `kind` says what to do, and its other fields hold the values the sentence names:
`locator`, `call`, a check's `matcher` and the `expected` and `received` values of its error, `what` the test checked,
a select's `options` (a value or a label as a string, an index as a number), a point's `x` and `y`, and a `count` and a
`limit` of steps. Piwi Picker and the report write it in their own language. A reader that does not know its `kind`,
or finds a value that does not check, leaves it out and shows `description`; a step a person wrote has none.

The kinds are `goBack`, `goForward`, `reload`, `gotoUnknown`, `setContent`, `keyboardType`, `mouseAt`,
`mouseOrKeyboard`, `failedCall`, `locatorCall`, `fillUnknown`, `fillPartial`, `pressUnknown`, `selectOptionUnknown`,
`selectOptions`, `setInputFiles`, `dragTo`, `drop`, `focus`, `blur`, `dispatchEvent`, `scrollIntoViewIfNeeded`,
`expectPoll`, `expectValue`, `expectLocator`, `expectURL` and `leadingSteps`.

## Viewports

A [recording](/features/record-actions) keeps the size of the page's viewport, in CSS pixels: the size the recording
started at, then each size the window settled at after a resize. Each entry names the step it applies from:

```json
"viewports": [
  { "step": 0, "width": 1280, "height": 720 },
  { "step": 3, "width": 390, "height": 664, "zoom": 1.5 }
]
```

The browser's zoom is already in the size: at 200%, a 1,280-pixel window is 640 CSS pixels wide, and the page lays out
for 640. `zoom` keeps the factor itself when it was not 100%, for whoever reads the report; the spec sets the size as
it is.

The spec sets each one with `await page.setViewportSize({ width, height });`, the first before the first page opens
and the others before the step they apply from. A function call from the project's catalog never stands for steps a
resize falls between. Replay sets the tab's viewport the same way in Chrome and Edge. A file without `viewports` is
played at whatever size the browser or the project has.

## Checks

A file is checked in full before anything uses it, and every problem found is reported with its path
(`steps[2].target.alternatives[0].locator: is not a Playwright locator chain`).

- Each locator must parse as a Playwright locator chain: the `getBy…`, `locator`, `filter`, `nth` family of calls, with
  string, number, regex and object arguments. It is written into the spec from its parsed form, so a file can choose
  locators but can never add code. A regex must be a valid pattern on one line.
- `origin` must be an `http` or `https` origin.
- A redacted step never keeps a value.
- A `hover` or `dblclick` step needs a target and never keeps a value; a `setInputFiles` step needs a target; a
  `dragTo` step needs a target and a `dropTarget`, and never keeps a value; a `manual` step needs a `manual` object
  with a description that is not empty, and never keeps a value.
- A `toHaveCount` assertion's `expected` is a whole number.
- A viewport names a step the file has, after the one before it, with a whole width and height from 1 to 10,000, and
  a `zoom` from 0.25 to 5 when it has one.
- Limits: 200 steps, 50 viewports, 10 alternatives per target, 50 options in a manual step's instruction, 2,000
  characters for values, expected values, URLs and notes, 500 for titles, names, texts and locators, and 5 MB for the
  file.

A recording saved before the format existed (`{ "steps", "startedAt", "startUrl" }`) is read too, and the old
`assertVisible` action is read as an `assert` step with `toBeVisible`. A file is written with the oldest version that
holds its steps, so a reader that only knows version 1 refuses a file using the `manual` action or the
`toContainText`, `toHaveCount` and `toBeChecked` matchers with a message naming the version, and reads every other
file as it did.

## Related

- [Record a test](/features/record-actions): the recorder that writes these files
- [Record a bug report](/features/report-a-bug): a report's steps, in the same format
- [Replay a recording](/features/replay-a-bug-report): how the steps play back
- [Piwi CLI](/reference/cli#codegen): `piwi codegen`, from steps to a spec

# Bug report file format

A [recording](/features/record-actions) of Piwi Picker, a [bug report](/features/report-a-bug) or not, is saved as one
`.piwibug` file with **Download .piwibug**, named after the time it was finished: `piwi-bug-2026-11-17-15-25.piwibug`
once a step is marked wrong, `piwi-recording-…` otherwise. A failed execution's
[Export](/features/offline-export#replay-the-failure-in-a-browser) writes one from the test run. Piwi Picker's
[Replay](/features/replay-a-bug-report) plays it, and the [desktop app](/features/desktop#importing-local-files)
imports it into a project as a [bug report](/features/bug-reports).

## The archive

A `.piwibug` file is a zip archive, its entries stored without compression:

| Entry | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `mimetype` | `application/vnd.piwi.bug-report+zip`, always the first entry |
| `steps.json` | The steps, as a [steps file](/reference/steps-format), with the viewport sizes they were recorded at |
| `<title>.spec.ts` | The test, named after the title, such as `coupon-not-applied.spec.ts`: the failing test once a step is marked wrong, else a test that passes |
| `bug-report.md` | The report as Markdown, in the language Piwi Picker shows |
| `evidence.json` | The evidence and the context; see below |
| `screenshots/<n>-<moment>.png` | Up to three screenshots: `marked` (a step marked as wrong), `finish` (a report made from a test run holds its failure screenshot as `screenshots/1-finish.png`) or `manual` |
| `steps/<nnn>.jpg` | The page as step `<nnn>` began (`steps/001.jpg` for the first), as wide as the viewport in CSS pixels, 1,280 at most; up to 100 |

The `mimetype` entry is stored first and uncompressed, as EPUB and OpenDocument files do, so its text sits at a fixed
place at the start of the file. Piwi reads a file by that content, never by its name: renamed to `.zip`, to look
inside or to attach it where only known file types are accepted (a GitHub issue), it opens the same way. A zip
holding `steps.json` and `evidence.json` without the `mimetype` entry is read too.

## evidence.json

```json
{
  "v": 1,
  "context": {
    "origin": "https://staging.acme.test",
    "pageKey": "/checkout",
    "path": "/checkout",
    "browser": "Chrome 141",
    "userAgent": "Mozilla/5.0 …",
    "viewport": { "width": 1280, "height": 720 },
    "time": 1790467200000,
    "extensionVersion": "0.43.0"
  },
  "evidence": {
    "console": [{ "level": "error", "source": "console", "message": "Coupon failed: 500", "page": "/cart", "time": 1790467201000 }],
    "consoleDropped": 0,
    "requests": [{ "method": "POST", "url": "/api/cart/coupon?code=<redacted>", "status": 500, "page": "/cart", "time": 1790467201000 }],
    "requestsDropped": 0,
    "screenshots": [{ "file": "screenshots/1-marked.png", "step": 3, "moment": "marked", "takenAt": 1790467202000 }],
    "screenshotNote": null,
    "outline": "- heading \"Your cart\" [level=1]\n- textbox \"Coupon\": SPRING10"
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `context` | The page the report was finished on, the browser, the window's viewport then, the time and the extension's version |
| `console` | Console errors and warnings, uncaught errors and unhandled rejections, at most 100; `consoleDropped` counts the rest |
| `requests` | Requests that failed or answered 400 or more: method, path with query values removed, status; at most 100 |
| `screenshots` | Each screenshot's file, the step it was taken after (0-based) and when |
| `stepShots` | Optional: for each step with a screenshot, its `step` (0-based), its `file`, the `box` of the step's element on it (`x`, `y`, `width`, `height` in CSS pixels from the top left corner, or null) and the `viewport` it shows |
| `screenshotNote` | Why there is no screenshot, when there is none |
| `outline` | An outline of the page in the YAML form of an ARIA snapshot, built by Piwi Picker, at most 400 lines |

## A report made from a test run

A report exported from a failed execution adds an `export` block beside `context` and `evidence`:

```json
"export": {
  "source": "execution",
  "executionId": 4512,
  "testTitle": "coupon applies to the total",
  "failedStep": 6,
  "notes": [
    { "title": "POST /api/seed", "location": "tests/cart.spec.ts:8", "reason": "An API request the test sends itself; Replay sends none." }
  ],
  "notesDropped": 0
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `executionId` | The execution on the instance the report was made from |
| `testTitle` | The test's title |
| `failedStep` | The step the test failed at, 0-based, or null when it failed outside the steps (a teardown hook) |
| `notes` | The calls of the test the steps leave out, with where they are and why; at most 100, `notesDropped` counts the rest |

The steps hold what Replay can play: the test's actions and its checks of a state, its failing assertion with the
`expected` and `actual` values of its error, and [manual steps](/reference/steps-format#manual-steps) for the rest.
A step's `pageUrl` is empty once an action may have left the page, since the run does not record where it went.

Everything in `evidence.json` is checked when a file is read: a list past its limit is cut, an entry that does not fit
its shape is dropped (an `export` block whose `source` is not `execution` is dropped whole, and a `failedStep` that
names no step is read as null), and a screenshot is kept only when its name is one the table above allows; a step screenshot,
only when it is named after its step. The steps are checked
as a [steps file](/reference/steps-format#checks) is, and a file whose steps fail that check is refused.

- [Record a bug report](/features/report-a-bug): recording a report and what it collects

- [Steps file format](/reference/steps-format): the format of `steps.json`

# Clue rules

A **clue** is a one-line finding a deterministic rule draws from the evidence Piwi already stores for a failing
execution; no model is involved. This page lists every rule, the stories that chain them, and how the
[**Most likely**](#most-likely) line picks what it shows. The same clues are handed to the
[AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis) as evidence to confirm or refute. Where clues appear on the page:
[Failure evidence](/features/evidence#clues).

## Rules

Each rule emits at most one clue (two for a failed request), with a strength and a citation to the evidence section it
came from. The **failure window** is the timeline's default view: from 10 seconds before the failed step to 2 seconds
after it.

| Rule | Strength | Fires when |
|---|---|---|
| Failed request before the failure<br>`failed-request-before-failure` | strong | A request returned 5xx, or failed without a response (the clue names the browser's error, such as `net::ERR_CONNECTION_RESET`), in the 10 seconds before the moment of failure. |
| Slow request overlapping the failure<br>`slow-request-overlapping-failure` | medium | A request slower than `PIWI_AI_SLOW_REQUEST_MS` (default 1,500 ms) was still in flight during the failed step. |
| Console mentions the target<br>`console-mentions-target` | strong for an error or an uncaught page error, medium for a warning | A console entry in the failure window names the failing locator or route. |
| Dialog open at the failure<br>`dialog-open-on-failure` | strong | A browser dialog (`alert`, `confirm`, `prompt`, `beforeunload`) closed in the failure window, so it was open when the action ran. Needs Playwright 1.63 or later. |
| Backend error attached<br>`backend-error-attached` | strong | A request in the failure window carries an error-level [backend log](/guide/backend-logs). |
| Element renamed<br>`element-renamed` | strong | [Locator healing](/features/locator-healing) found the element under a new identity, or flagged the stored name as stale while still recommending a fix. |
| Page structure changed near the failing locator<br>`page-structure-changed` | strong when the locator never resolved, else medium | The [page diff](/features/evidence#page-diff) against the last green sample shows the element the locator names was removed or renamed. |
| Element present but blocked<br>`element-present-but-blocked` | strong | The call log says the element resolved but was disabled, hidden, not visible, inert or covered by another element, and the ARIA snapshot still shows it. |
| Locator matched nothing<br>`locator-matched-nothing` | strong when [locator healing](/features/locator-healing) names, from the failure-time ARIA snapshot, the element the page had instead, else medium | The call log says the locator never found an element, and no clue says the element was renamed or removed, the page was the wrong one, a lock holder failed or a request around the failure was slow, failed or erred on the backend: a locator written wrong, as in a test being written, or an element that never showed. A crash or a failed navigation is not one. A flaky test's clue names no replacement. |
| Wrong page<br>`wrong-page` | strong | The page ended on a login, sign-in, auth, error, 404 or not-found route, or somewhere other than the last navigation the test asked for. The end URL comes from the captured app state, else from the last navigation step. |
| Worker pollution<br>`worker-pollution` | medium | The previous test on the same worker failed, timed out or was interrupted. |
| Previous lock holder failed<br>`lock-holder-failed` | strong | The execution that held the same [lock](/reference/test-metadata#test-locks) just before this test, in this run, failed or timed out. |
| Lock held on two shards<br>`lock-cross-shard` | medium | A lock this test held overlapped in time with a holder on another shard. Locks serialize only within one `playwright test` process. |
| Timeout budget<br>`timeout-budget` | medium; weak when the failed step itself spent the time waiting for a locator that matched nothing | The failed step used at least 80 % of the test timeout, or the execution used at least 95 %. |
| Environment changed<br>`environment-changed` | medium when the browser, channel, viewport, locale, timezone, base URL or environment label changed, else weak | The environment differs from the same test's last green run in the same environment. Tool versions and color scheme alone stay weak. |
| Browser-specific<br>`browser-specific` | medium | The same test passed on at least one other browser in this run. |
| Known flake suspect<br>`known-flake-suspect` | strong when a [Flake Lab](/features/flake-lab) experiment reproduced the suspect, else weak | This failure shows one of its test's [suspects](/features/flaky-tests#suspects), when it shows several, the one an experiment reproduced, else the highest ranked: a slow or failed route, a runner time zone or locale, a test alongside or just before, load or a browser. The detail gives this failure's value and the suspect's counts, and, once reproduced, the arm against its control ("3 of 4 under delay GET /api/cart 1.8 s, against 0 of 10 without"). |

Clues are ranked by strength, then by membership of the story, then by how close they sit to the moment of failure, and
the list is capped at eight. An earlier fix that regressed is not a clue: the execution's **Cluster** line carries it.

## Stories

When several clues form a known combination, they are chained into one **story** sentence at the strongest member's
strength. The first combination that matches, in this order, wins:

| Story | Clues it chains | Example sentence |
|---|---|---|
| Blocked by a pending request | element present but blocked, with a slow or failed request, and the console clue when present | *The button "Pay" stayed disabled because POST /api/checkout/quote was still in flight (28 s).* |
| Renamed | element renamed and page structure changed | *The button the locator names was renamed from "Pay" to "Pay now" since the last pass.* |
| Removed | page structure changed, without element renamed | *The button "Pay" is no longer on the page since the last pass.* |
| Wrong page | wrong page, with a failed request or an open dialog | *The test ended on /login instead of /checkout after the request.* |
| Polluted worker | worker pollution, and the lock holder clue when present | *The previous test on this worker failed and left state behind.* |
| Backend error | backend error attached, with a failed or slow request | *POST /api/orders failed on the server.* |
| Timing | timeout budget and slow request | *The step used 92 % of the timeout waiting on /api/search.* |

When no combination matches, there is no story, and the strongest clue stands alone.

## Most likely

The **Most likely** line of the [situation block](/guide/first-failure#_2-most-likely-why) shows one explanation,
chosen by one rule on the execution page and the cluster page alike:

1. a story graded strong or medium;
2. else the cluster's completed [AI diagnosis](/features/ai-diagnosis), whoever wrote it;
3. else a weak story;
4. else the top clue, in its own words.

With none of them, the line is absent. It carries the story's or the clue's strength (*Strong*, *Medium*, *Weak*), or
the diagnosis's confidence (*Diagnosed, high confidence*), and how many clues agree: the story's members (*3 clues
agree*), all the clues when the top clue leads and others exist, or, under a diagnosis, the clues supporting it
(*supported by 2 clues*).
A story or a clue marks the evidence its clues cite; a diagnosis cites sections, not rows. When the
[Next](/features/fix-plans#the-next-step) step's change comes from a diagnosis that Most likely does not show, its line
names that diagnosis and its summary.

## Related

- [Failure evidence](/features/evidence#clues): where the clues appear, with the evidence they cite
- [Your first failure, explained](/guide/first-failure): the situation block the **Most likely** line belongs to
- [Glossary](/guide/concepts#story): the story

# Locator stability rules

A **brittle locator** breaks on a change unrelated to what its test checks: a restyle, a wrapper added around an
element, an item added to a list, a copy edit, other data. `locator('.btn-primary').nth(1)` breaks when the button is
restyled or another button appears before it. This page holds the rules Piwi judges a locator by, the levels they
give, and how a replacement for a brittle one is chosen; the pages that show a level link here.

## Levels

Piwi judges every locator of the [locator index](/features/locator-usage), and every locator
[Piwi Picker](/features/pick-an-element) offers, with the rules below, from the locator's text alone, and gives it one
of three levels:

- **Brittle**: at least one rule gives it that level. The [Tested elements](/features/tested-elements#brittle-locators)
  overlay lists it under **At risk**, and offers a replacement; the Locators page says why.
- **Watch**: a rule has something to say, but the locator does not break on its own. Shown on the Locators page, and
  in Piwi Picker's pick results, DevTools sidebar and Tested elements cards; never listed under **At risk**.
- **Stable**: no rule has anything to say.

A locator takes the level of its worst part: a stable container cannot save a brittle target, and a brittle container
breaks every locator searching inside it. Locators nested in `filter({ has })`, `and()` and `or()` count as parts.

## Rules

| Rule | Level | Catches | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Position<br>`position` | brittle for `nth(1)` and beyond; watch for `first()`, `last()` and `nth(0)` | An element picked by its order. An element added above it, or a list sorted another way, moves it. | `getByRole('listitem').nth(2)` |
| CSS class<br>`css-class` | brittle for a utility, hashed or CSS-in-JS class; watch for a named class | An element found by a class. Classes change with the styling. | `locator('.bg-blue-500')`, `locator('.css-1q2w3e')` |
| CSS structure<br>`css-structure` | brittle | A child or sibling combinator, `:nth-child()` and its kind, three or more selectors deep, or a descendant chain of tags only. A wrapper added or moved breaks it. | `locator('form > div:nth-child(2) input')` |
| XPath<br>`xpath` | brittle when absolute or indexed; watch otherwise | XPath follows the document structure. | `locator('//main/div[2]//button')` |
| Generated id<br>`generated-id` | brittle | An id a framework or a build generates, which changes from one render or build to the next. | `locator('#radix-:r4:')`, `locator('#input-1748291')` |
| Style attribute<br>`style-attribute` | brittle | The `style` or `class` attribute matched as a string, which any styling edit changes. | `locator('[style*="display: block"]')` |
| Long text<br>`long-text` | watch | An exact string over 40 characters in `getByText`, a `name` or `hasText`: copy changes long before behavior does. | Marketing copy |
| Number in text<br>`data-text` | watch | A count, price, date, time or percentage inside an exact string, which changes with the data. | `getByRole('button', { name: 'Cart (3)' })` |
| Long chain<br>`deep-chain` | watch | More than three locating calls: each container is one more thing a change can break. | Four chained `getBy…` calls |

Not flagged: `getByTestId`, `getByRole` with a name, `getByLabel`, `getByPlaceholder`, `getByAltText`, `getByTitle`, an
id that is not generated, `[name=…]` and `[data-testid=…]`, a single tag inside a container, a regular expression, and
a short text. A locator matching several elements is not a stability problem: the overlay shows it as ambiguous.

## Replacements

On a live page, the [Tested elements](/features/tested-elements#brittle-locators) overlay offers a replacement for a
brittle locator that finds exactly one element of the top-level document. It ranks the locators for that element the
way [Pick an element](/features/pick-an-element) does, a candidate that finds the element among others
[narrowed](/features/pick-an-element#narrowing-a-locator-that-finds-several) first (an element of a list, a grid or a
table gets `getByTestId('product-card').filter({ hasText: 'Blue mug' }).getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' })`
rather than `getByRole('button', { name: 'Add to cart' }).nth(1)`). It keeps those these rules call stable and that
find only that element on the page, and picks one as
[locator healing picks its recommended fix](/features/locator-healing#the-recommended-fix): the brittle locator's own
method, then its family, when one of those is stable enough; otherwise the most stable one, which the row then also
shows as **Most stable** when it differs. When no stable locator finds only that element, the overlay says to give it
a test id.

A replacement is checked against the page as it is now. A test that uses the locator in another state of the page
may need a different one.

## Related

- [Tested elements](/features/tested-elements)
- [Who uses a locator](/features/locator-usage)
- [Locator healing](/features/locator-healing)
